units.la: DOcet nos observatio quotidiana, magnificum illud Dei opus quod Aristoteles τὸ ἀνόνατον
units.tr: Daily observation teaches us that magnificent work of God which Aristotle calls the highest [τὸ ἀνώτατον

units.la: τατον Θεῦ οἰκητήριον, Philosophi autē coelum stelliferum appellant, & quod merito Gentiles in stuporem, christianos in admirationem dedit, multis varijsquè stellis, veluti elegantissimis picturis variegatum esse : ejusquè lucidissima lumina diu, noctuquè insignem utilitatem præstare hominibus, ex Creatoris ordinatione. Docet quinetiam eadem invariabilis observatio, idem maximum opus, super quod Deus decorem suum posuit, in suo nitore, claritate & ἀεικινήσει hactenus perstitisse, & perstiturum esse usquè ad terminum illum, quem ὁ τῶν ὅλων ποιητὴς, ut cum Iustino Martyre loquar, ipsi destinavit.
units.tr: dwelling place of God [τατον Θεοῦ οἰκητήριον], while the philosophers call it the starry heaven, a work that has deservedly filled the Gentiles with wonder and Christians with admiration, being adorned with many and various stars, like most elegant paintings; and that its brightest lights, by day and by night, afford remarkable usefulness to human beings by the ordinance of the Creator. The same unchanging observation also teaches that this greatest work, upon which God has set his beauty, has so far persisted in its splendour, brightness and perpetual motion [ἀεικινησία], and will persist until that end which the Maker of all things, to use the words of Justin Martyr, has appointed for it.

units.la: Quanquam autem nec motus ejus impediri, nec claritas obscurari unquam possit, fit tamen ut à nubibus nebulisque, ex maris & terræ visceribus in infimam regionem aëris elevatis, ibique condensatis, aspectus ejus, luxque hominibus intercipiatur. Quod potissimum eo tempore fit, quando sol in Zodiaco signa meridionalia transiens, longius à nobis recedit.
units.tr: Yet although its motion can never be hindered nor its brightness dimmed, it nonetheless happens that its aspect and light are cut off from men by clouds and mists, raised from the bowels of sea and land into the lowest region of the air and there condensed. This happens especially at the time when the sun, passing through the southern signs of the zodiac, withdraws farther from us.

units.la: Simile quid de vera & orthodoxa religione dici potest. Est illa è cœlo orta, & plurimis pulcherrimisque documentis veluti lucidissimis stellis ornata. Quæ hominibus insignem præstant utilitatem, illuminando obtenebratas eorum mentes, lucemque præstando in via ad æternam salutem.
units.tr: Something similar can be said of the true and orthodox religion. It has arisen from heaven and is adorned with very many and most beautiful teachings, like the brightest stars. These afford remarkable usefulness to men, illuminating their darkened minds and giving light on the way to eternal salvation.

units.la: Et quanquam veræ hujus Religionis (quæ jam in paradiso incepit & per varias ætates Patriarcharum, Prophetarum & Apostolorum ad hunc usque diem, quoad autorem salutis, invariata mansit, & manebit usque ad finem mundi) nec cursus nec splendor in sese impediri potest, fit tamen ut illa à nubibus, nebulis & fumo hæresium & mendaciorum e tartaro excitatis, non parum apud homines obscuretur. Hoc testabitur triplex Gentilium Theologia, fabulosa politica & naturalis. Testabuntur veterum Arianorum, Euthychianorum, Nestorianorum aliorumque hæreticorum impiæ conclusiones. Testatur etiam hodierna praxis papistica, Qui non
units.tr: And although neither the course nor the splendour of this true religion (which began already in paradise, and through the various ages of the Patriarchs, Prophets and Apostles has remained unchanged to this day, as far as its author of salvation is concerned, and will remain until the end of the world) can be hindered in itself, it nonetheless happens that it is not a little obscured among men by the clouds, mists and smoke of heresies and lies, raised up from Tartarus. The threefold theology of the Gentiles, the fabulous, the political and the natural, bears witness to this. The impious conclusions of the ancient Arians, Eutychians, Nestorians and other heretics bear witness to it. The present practice of the Papists also bears witness to it, who,

units.la: non contenti novitates multas à multis annis, ad obscurandam religionem orthodoxam in Ecclesiam introduxisse, nunc novo artificio eunt per libros Theologorum nostrorum, eorumque verba, phrases, sententias falsando, corrumpendo, mutando, traducunt. Quô ut multum proficiunt apud suos, qui libros nostros non legerunt, ita apud veritatis amantes tam turpiter audiunt, ut nunc circulatoribus qui theatra conscendunt, & quid pro quo vendunt similes habeantur. Quàm verò turpe hoc, quàm indecorū in Theologis in sociis Christi, in spiritualibus!
units.tr: not content to have introduced many novelties for many years into the Church to obscure the orthodox religion, now proceed by a new artifice, through the books of our theologians, falsifying, corrupting and changing their words, phrases and sentences, and passing them off. As they gain much among their own people, who have not read our books, so among lovers of truth they are heard with such disgrace that they are now regarded as similar to the mountebanks who mount the stages and sell one thing for another. How truly base this is, how unbecoming in theologians, in companions of Christ, in spiritual matters!

units.la: Non longius abibo, inspiciantur parallela Harscheriana in quibus vix legitur testimoniū ex Calvino productum, quod ille non quo ad sensum perverterit. Quæ, cum in parvis quibusdam libellis hinc inde in patria nostra disseminarentur, consilio quorundam castigare cepi, & notorias falsitates palàm demonstrare, propter causas,quas in præfatione ad primam disputationem commemoravi. Nunc castigationem disputationis secundæ in lucem edo, eodem fine, easdemque ob causas.
units.tr: I will not go further. Let the Harscherian parallels be examined, in which hardly a single testimony quoted from Calvin can be read that he has not perverted in sense. When these were disseminated here and there in our country in certain small pamphlets, I began, at the counsel of some men, to correct them and openly to demonstrate the notorious falsehoods, for the reasons I mentioned in the preface to my first disputation. Now I publish the correction of the second disputation, with the same aim and for the same reasons.

units.la: Cur verò V. V. D. D. illam inscripserim plurimæ causæ mihi sunt, quas consultò in præliminari hoc ad vos alloquio, omitto. Scio veram religionem vobis curæ esse, scio vos veritatem diligere,mendacia detestari, pacem patriæ sartam tecta optare, ad quos fines cum hæc mea scriptio tendat, audacius eam vobis offerre, mihiq; promittere audeo, illam vobis ingratam futuram non esse. Sub hac spe finio, Deumque precor, ut dulcissimam patriam nostram perpetua pace & orthodoxa fide beare, & vos magna fidei & pacis fulcra, in ea diutissimè conservare velit.
units.tr: There are very many reasons why I have inscribed it to your Most Worthy Lordships, which I deliberately omit in this preliminary address to you. I know that true religion is a concern to you, I know that you love the truth, detest lies, and desire the peace of the fatherland to remain whole and intact. Since this writing of mine tends toward these ends, I dare to offer it to you more boldly, and I venture to promise that it will not be unwelcome to you. Under this hope I conclude, and I pray God that he may bless our most sweet fatherland with lasting peace and orthodox faith, and may be pleased to preserve you, the great supports of faith and peace, in it for a very long time.

units.la: Dabam ipsis Cal. Decemb. M. DC. XLVII. V. V. D. D. addictissimus Christophorus Lüthardus.
units.tr: Given at the Kalends of December 1647. Your Most Worthy Lordships' most devoted, Christoph Lüthard.

units.la: SECVLVM IV. A NATO CHRISTO.
units.tr: SECVLVM IV. A NATO CHRISTO.

units.la: ARIANI.
units.tr: ARIANI.

units.la: Quarto seculo vixerunt Ariani ab Ario Alexandrino Presbytero. Negant filium Dei esse Patri consubstantialem & coæqualem sive ὁμοούσιον, sed docent esse patre minorem, & tantùm ὁμοιούσιον sive similis substantiæ. De hac hæresi Ecclesiæ Catholicæ pernitiosissima scribit Chronicon Carionis l. 3. Monarchia 4. ætate 3. in hunc modum. Ex hac hæresi aliæ plures suppullularunt sensim, & post: Erant una in urbe variæ opiniones & sectæ diversæ, persequebantur se mutuò adeò ut alii in aliorum templa irruentes tumultuarentur & cladem committerent.
units.tr: In the fourth century lived the Arians, named after Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria. They deny that the Son of God is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] and coequal with the Father, and teach instead that he is less than the Father and only of like substance [ὁμοιούσιον]. Carion's Chronicle, book 3, Monarchy 4, age 3, writes about this heresy, most pernicious to the Catholic Church, in the following way: "From this heresy many others sprang up gradually and afterwards. In one city there were various opinions and different sects, which harassed one another so much that some rushed into the churches of others, stirred up tumults and caused slaughter."

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATIO.

units.la: Non correxit Harscherus vitium A impuimpudentiæ, sed quo cœpit pede pergit calumniari, & falsis opinionibus onerare Ecclesias nostras. Juxta illud tritum, calumniare audacter semper aliquid hæret. Nos autem Christum non ita didicimus, ut qui novimus ex Apostolo Jacobo, non ex eodem ore benedictionem Dei & maledictionem hominis procedere debere. Non oportet fratres mei hæc ita fieri, inquit cap. 3: 10.
units.tr: Harscher has not corrected his vice of impudence, but, as he began, he goes on slandering and burdening our churches with false opinions. This fits the well-worn saying, slander boldly, something always sticks. We, however, have not learned Christ in such a way, since we know from the Apostle James that blessing from God and cursing from men ought not to proceed from the same mouth. My brethren, these things ought not so to be, he says in chapter 3, verse 10.

units.la: Quocirca modeste calumnias & maledictiones Harscherianas abstergam præsenti libello, quas magno numero in parallelis secularibus, seculi quarti & quinti, disputatione secunda nobis affricat.
units.tr: Accordingly, in this little book I will modestly wipe away the slanders and curses of Harscher, which he heaps upon us in great number in his second disputation in the Parallels of the fourth and fifth centuries.

units.la: Primò producit Arii blasphemiam, qui Christi cum Deo Patre ὁμοούσιαν negavit. Cuius tragædiam scribit, magnum insecutum esse sententiarum divortium testante Chronico Carionis. Et concludit, Calvinum, Bezam (imò totam Ecclesiam reformatam) huiuss quoque damnosissimæ hæresewς reos esse. Et semel orta reformatione plures sectas inter nos exstitisse.
units.tr: First, he brings forward the blasphemy of Arius, who denied that Christ is ὁμοούσιος with God the Father [ὁμοούσιον]. He writes about the tragedy of this man, and says that, as the Chronicle of Carion attests, a great division of opinions followed. And he concludes that Calvin and Beza, indeed the whole Reformed Church, are guilty of this most harmful heresy too, and that once the Reformation had begun, many sects arose among us.

units.la: Refert Arii & Arianorum hæresin ad seculum quartum. Minus recte. Vixit enim Arius circa annum Christi CCC. Et quæcunque gesta sunt inter Arium & Alexandrum Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ Episcopum; item in diversis synodis sub Constantino Magno, & post huius mortem sub filiis eius, Constantino, Constante & Constantio, omnia inquam, intra seculum tertium evenerunt.
units.tr: He refers the heresy of Arius and the Arians to the fourth century, but not correctly. For Arius lived around the year 300 of Christ. And everything that happened between Arius and Alexander, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and likewise in the various synods under Constantine the Great, and after his death under his sons Constantine, Constans and Constantius, all of it, I say, took place within the third century.

units.la: Dicam pauca de hæresewς Arianæ initio. Explicuit Alexander Episcopus in Ecclesia Alexandrina versiculum 22: cap. 8. Proverbiorum qui ita habet: κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ, εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐθεμελίωσέ με, ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸ τοῦ τὴν γῆν ποιῆσαι, Dominus condidit me, initium viarum suarum in opera sua, ante seculum fundavit me in principio antequam terram faceret.
units.tr: I will say a few things about the beginning of the Arian heresy. Alexander, bishop in the Alexandrian Church, explained verse 22 of chapter 8 of Proverbs, which reads thus: "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways, for his works; before the age he founded me; in the beginning, before he made the earth" [κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ, εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐθεμελίωσέ με, ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸ τοῦ τὴν γῆν ποιῆσαι]. The Lord possessed me, the beginning of his ways in his works; before the age he founded me, in the beginning, before he made the earth.

units.la: Hæc cùm paulò subtilius explicasset Alexander, quàm ut ab omnibus intelligi posset, ansam accepit Arius calumniandi Alexandrum, & Sabellianismi accusandi, ac si unam saltem in Deitate personam assereret. Quæ mera fuit calumnia, orta ex invidia ob reiectum Arium, post mortem Achillis, cui Alexander in Episcopatu successit. Ipse verò Arius ex prædicto loco statuit; Filium Dei esse patris ποίημα creaturam, creatam a Deo Patre antequam mundus esset creatus, ut idoneum foret rerum creandarum organum. Fuisse autem filium a Deo creatum ἐκ μὴ ὄντων ex non entibus. Et sic filium Dei, Dei nomine quidem ornavit, sed æterna divinitate spoliavit, clamans filium quidem Deo Patri esse ὅμοιον non vero ὁμοούσιον. Nam in confessione Arii, quæ apud Athanasium extat, ita loquitur: Credo in unum aeternum Deum & filium ipsius, quem ipse creavit ante secula, & filium suum fecit, ita ut quicquid habet filius aliquando non habuerit. Sed & spiritum sanctum a Filio creatum esse, asseruit. Contra hunc haereticum coacta fuit Synodus Nicena anno cccxxv, ubi ipsius haeresis fuit damnata a 300. Episcopis, & Symbolum, quod Nicenum dictum, conscriptum, in quo quid de Filio Dei orthodoxe credendum perspicue traditum fuit.
units.tr: When Alexander had explained these things somewhat too subtly for everyone to understand, Arius seized the chance to slander Alexander and accuse him of Sabellianism, as if he asserted only one person in the Deity. This was pure calumny, arising from envy because Arius had been passed over after the death of Achillas, whom Alexander succeeded in the episcopate. Arius himself, from that passage, laid down that the Son of God is a creature [ποίημα] of God the Father, created by God the Father before the world was made, so that he might be a fit instrument for creating things. He claimed that the Son was created by God out of non-beings [ἐκ μὴ ὄντων]. Thus he adorned the Son of God with the name of God, but stripped him of eternal divinity, crying out that the Son is indeed like [ὅμοιον] God the Father, but not of the same substance [ὁμοούσιον]. For in Arius's confession, which is extant in Athanasius, he speaks thus: I believe in one eternal God and his Son, whom he himself created before the ages and made his Son, so that whatever the Son has, he did not at some time have. He also asserted that the Holy Spirit was created by the Son. Against this heretic the Synod of Nicaea was convened in the year 325, where the heresy itself was condemned by 300 bishops, and the creed called Nicene was drawn up, in which what is to be believed orthodoxly about the Son of God was clearly set out.

units.la: De progressu huius haeresewos plura non dicam, quia apud Athanasium, Theodoretum, alios haec fuse leguntur. Unum hoc addam, verisimile esse Jesuitas novam suam artem mentiendi per reservationem mentalem ab hoc haeretico didicisse. Nam postquam Constantia Constantini Imperatoris soror, fratri obiiceret, quod cum Ario inique actum esset in synodo Nicena, & quod Arius nihil aliud crederet, quam quod ipsa synodus credit, permisit Imperator, ut Arius revocaretur, & exhiberet confessionem fidei suae, haereticus fecit, sed ita; Exhibuit una manu Imperatori confessionem terminis quidem ambiguis consignatam, quam tamen in bonam partem interpretatus est optimus Imperator, altera vero manu aliam confessionem iuxta sensum haereticum conscriptam, & sub pallio occultatam tenuit, & sic iuravit confessionem quam manu teneret, esse suam, intelligens illam, quam sub pallio tenebat. Quid aliud hodie docent Jesuitae, cum statuunt (ut scribit Toletus Lib. 4. Instruct. Sacerdotum cap. 21.) Si crimen est occultum, non debet quis jurare. Aut si cogatur, utatur aequivocatione, puta nescio, intelligendo intra se, ut dicam tibi; vel simile. Item 3. 9. Si Vir ab uxore petat, an sit adultera, ista potest dicere, non sum (quamvis verum fuerit) intelligendo, ut tibi revelem.
units.tr: I will not say more about the progress of this heresy, since it is read at length in Athanasius, Theodoret and others. I will add only this: it is likely that the Jesuits learned from this heretic their new art of lying by mental reservation. For after Constantia, sister of the Emperor Constantine, objected to her brother that Arius had been treated unjustly in the Synod of Nicaea, and that Arius believed nothing other than what the synod itself believed, the Emperor permitted Arius to be recalled and to present his confession of faith. The heretic did so, but in this way: with one hand he handed the Emperor a confession written in ambiguous terms, which the very good Emperor nevertheless interpreted in a good sense; but with the other hand he kept hidden under his cloak another confession, written according to the heretical sense, and so he swore that the confession he held in his hand was his own, meaning the one he kept hidden under his cloak. What else do the Jesuits teach today, when they lay down (as Toletus writes in book 4 of the Instruction of Priests, chapter 21): If the crime is secret, one ought not to swear. Or if one is compelled, let him use equivocation, for instance, "I do not know," understanding within himself, "as I shall tell you," or something similar. Likewise, in case 3, 9: If a husband asks his wife whether she is an adulteress, she may say, "I am not" (although it is true), understanding, "as I shall reveal to you".

units.la: Haec de Ario haeretico, cuius damnatam hæresin etiam nos amplecti, ex Genebrardo & Canisio docet Harscherus. Gregorius de Valentia Jesuita magis modeste & subdubitans : Si Calviniani, inquit, doctrinam præceptoris sui probant jure etiam eos in illorum haereticorum numero ponimus, qui filij divinitatem inficiati sunt. Disp. 2. q. 1. punct. 1. In primam Thom. Quamvis Valentiani consequentia recte negetur, ut postea ex ipso hoc Jesuita & Bellarmino probabo.
units.tr: Harscher teaches these things about the heretic Arius, whose condemned heresy we too embrace, drawing on Genebrardus and Canisius. Gregory of Valencia, a Jesuit, speaks more modestly and with some doubt: If the Calvinists, he says, approve the doctrine of their teacher, we rightly also place them in the number of those heretics who denied the divinity of the Son. Disputation 2, question 1, point 1, on the first part of Thomas. Yet the consequence drawn by Valencia may rightly be denied, as I will later show from this same Jesuit and from Bellarmine.

units.la: Dico itaque Genebrardum, Canisium, Bellarminum, Harscherum, & quotquot sunt qui scribunt nos Deitatem Christi negare, nihil potuisse dicere aut scribere magis a veritate alienum, adeoque per contumeliam & insignem iniuriam praeterquam omne aequum, Ecclesias nostras diffamare.
units.tr: I say, therefore, that Genebrardus, Canisius, Bellarmine, Harscher, and all who write that we deny the Deity of Christ, could say or write nothing more alien to the truth, and so, by insult and gross injury, and quite contrary to all fairness, they defame our churches.

units.la: Confitemur enim & publice in conspectu totius mundi testamur.
units.tr: For we confess, and bear witness publicly in the sight of the whole world, that:

units.la: 1. Cum sacra Scriptura, Filium Dei esse esse verum & aeternum Deum benedictum in secula, Rom. 9: 5. Magnum Deum, Tit. 2: 13. Aeternum qui fuit antequam Abraham esset, Joh. 8: 38. Idcirco α & ω. Apoc. 1: 8. Qui est, qui fuit & qui futurus est & propterea ipsum יהוה.
units.tr: 1. Holy Scripture teaches that the Son of God is the true and eternal God, blessed for ever (Rom. 9:5); great God (Tit. 2:13); eternal, who was before Abraham was (John 8:38); therefore the α and the ω (Rev. 1:8); who is, who was and who is to come, and therefore himself [יהוה].

units.la: 2. Cum patribus Nicenis; esse ἀληθινὸν θεὸν ἐκ θεοῦ ἀληθινοῦ, verum Deum de vero Deo, scilicet Patre: γεννηθέντα, και ποιηθέντα genitum, non factum, ut Arius voluit: ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ δι' οὗ πάντα ἐγένετο, coessentialem patri, per quem omnia facta sunt.
units.tr: 2. With the Nicene Fathers: he is true God of true God [ἀληθινὸν θεὸν ἐκ θεοῦ ἀληθινοῦ], that is, the true God of the true God, namely of the Father; begotten and made [γεννηθέντα καὶ ποιηθέντα], that is, begotten, not made, as Arius wished; consubstantial with the Father [ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ], through whom all things were made [δι' οὗ πάντα ἐγένετο], that is, co-essential with the Father, through whom all things were made.

units.la: 3. Cum S. Athanasio; τῷ πατρὸς καὶ τῷ υἱῷ καὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύματος μία ἐστὶν ἡ θεότης, ἴση ἡ δόξα συναΐδιος ἡ μεγαλειότης, patris & filij & spiritus sancti una est divinitas, aequalis gloria, coaeterna maiestas. Item οὕτω θεὸς ὁ πατήρ, θεὸς ὁ υἱὸς. Ita Deus Pater, Deus Filius.
units.tr: 3. With St Athanasius: of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit there is one divinity [τῷ πατρὸς καὶ τῷ υἱῷ καὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύματος μία ἐστὶν ἡ θεότης], equal glory, coeternal majesty [ἴση ἡ δόξα συναΐδιος ἡ μεγαλειότης], that is, of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit there is one divinity, equal glory, coeternal majesty. Likewise: thus God the Father, God the Son [οὕτω θεὸς ὁ πατήρ, θεὸς ὁ υἱὸς], that is, so God the Father, God the Son.

units.la: Unde confessio Helvetica art. III.
units.tr: Whence the Helvetic Confession, art. III.

units.la: Tres sunt personae consubstantiales, coaeternae & coaequales, distinctae quoad hypostases, & ordine alia aliam antecedens, nulla tamen inæqualitate. Nam quo ad naturam & essentiam ita sunt coniuncta, ut sint unus Deus, essentia, divina communis sit Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto. Quid magis perspicuum?
units.tr: There are three persons, consubstantial, coeternal and coequal, distinct as to their hypostases, and one preceding another in order, yet with no inequality. For as to nature and essence they are so joined that they are one God, one essence, the divine essence being common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. What could be plainer?

units.la: Atqui loca produxit Harscherus ex Calvino, Beza, psalterio Gallico, in quibus Deitas Christi aperte negatur. Falsum hoc. Nam quæcunque ab Harschero & aliis Jesuitis proferuntur nihil aliud sunt, quàm malitiosæ verborum contorsiones, falsæ allegationes & παρεφθαρμένα, quod nunc probabo, accedens ad
units.tr: But Harscher has produced passages from Calvin, Beza, and the French Psalter, in which the deity of Christ is plainly denied. This is false. For whatever Harscher and the other Jesuits put forward is nothing but malicious twisting of words, false citations and corrupted passages [παρεφθαρμένα], which I will now prove, proceeding to

units.la: PARALLELUM PRIMUM.
units.tr: First Parallel.

units.la: Primò scribit P. Harscher: Calvinum in admonitione ad Fratres Polonos vocare illud ex symbolo Niceno, Deum de Deo (quod de Christo dicitur) durum. Est revera magna impudentia, homini alii ni alicui hærefin attribuere in eo ipso loco, in quo ipse hærefin illam refutat. Quod hîc accidit Calvino. Nam in tota illa ad fratres Polonos admonitione, Arii, Blandratæ, Gentilis & Gribaldi blasphemias refutat, qui Deitatem Christi negabant. Ubi inter cætera scribit: Porrò quod in symbolo Niceno Deus ex Deo vocatur, tametsi dura est locutio, non tamen aliò tendit, nisi obstaculo non esse discrimen inter personas, quò minus una sit essentia. Ideo sic resolvi debet oratio, quamvis ex Deo sit, est tamen Deus, & quidem verus Deus. Imò verisimile est quum fraudem metuerent sancti patres, consultò illud additum curasse, Deum verum de Deo vero.
units.tr: First, Father Harscher writes that Calvin, in his admonition to the Polish brethren, calls that phrase from the Nicene creed, God of God (which is said of Christ), harsh. This is truly great impudence, to attribute a heresy to a man in the very place where he refutes that heresy. This is what happened to Calvin. In that whole admonition to the Polish brethren he refutes the blasphemies of Arius, Blandrata, Gentilis and Gribaldi, who denied the deity of Christ. There, among other things, he writes: Moreover, although the expression God of God in the Nicene creed is harsh, it aims at nothing else than to show that the distinction of persons is no obstacle to there being one essence. So the sentence must be resolved thus: although he is of God, he is nevertheless God, and indeed true God. Indeed, it is likely that when the holy fathers feared fraud, they deliberately added the phrase, true God of true God.

units.la: Non loquitur ergo de dogmate ipso generationis filii à patre ab æterno, sed de phrasi. Nam cùm vox Deus ὑποωδὼς & ὑποστατικῶς accipiatur, certè in priori sensu non potest dici Deum ex Deo esse, quia Deus ab omnibus orthodoxis Catholicis creditur unus, ἀνάρχος & omnimodè independens. Secus est si accipiatur ὑποστατικῶς. Hanc fuisse mentem Calvini ex eodem tractatu cognosci potest, quando scribit: Dura locutio fateor, sed ad cujus tollendam ambiguitatem nemo potest esse magis idoneus interpres, quàm Athanasius qui eam dictavit. Et certè non fuit aliud patrum consilium, nisi manere originem, quam ducit à patre filius respectu personæ, nec obstare quò minus eadem sit essentia & Deitas utriusque atque ita quoad essentiam sermonem esse Deum absque principio, in persona autem filij habere principium à patre.
units.tr: He is therefore not speaking about the doctrine itself, of the eternal generation of the Son from the Father, but about the phrasing. For when the word God is taken in the essential sense [ὑποουσιωδῶς] and in the hypostatic sense [ὑποστατικῶς], it certainly cannot be said in the former sense that God is of God, because God is believed by all orthodox Catholics to be one, without beginning [ἀνάρχος] and wholly independent. It is otherwise if it is taken hypostatically. That this was Calvin's meaning can be recognised from the same treatise, where he writes: I admit the expression is harsh, but no one can be a more suitable interpreter for removing its ambiguity than Athanasius, who dictated it. And certainly the intention of the fathers was nothing other than to affirm that the origin which the Son has from the Father, with respect to the person, does not prevent the essence and Godhead of both from being the same; and so, as to essence, the Word is God without beginning, but in the person of the Son he has a beginning from the Father.

units.la: Placeat autem Patri Harschero suum sympresbyterum audire, Gregorium de Valentia Jesuitam non indoctum, sic ille de Calvini hac locutione in primam Thom. disp. 2. q. 1. punct. 1. Tribuit etiam Genebrardus hunc errorem Calvino. Sed revera si attentè legatur Calvinus, tantùm videbitur voluisse, Filium, ut Deus quidem essentialiter est ex se esse, & solummodo ut persona est esse ex patre. Id quod verum est. Nam licet verissime patres & Concilia afferant, Deum esse ex Deo, accipiendo vocabulum Dei personaliter, ut scilicet significet quoq; personam ipsam patris & Filij; tamen Filius quatenus essentialiter Deus est, id est, ut est illud unum simplicissimum quod est Deus non est ab alio, quia ut sic est quid absolutum; Idem plane quod Calvinus.
units.tr: Let Father Harscher, then, be willing to hear his fellow presbyter, Gregory of Valencia, a Jesuit by no means unlearned, who speaks thus of Calvin's expression in his commentary on the first part of Thomas, disputation 2, question 1, point 1: Genebrardus also attributes this error to Calvin. But if Calvin is read carefully, he seems only to have meant that the Son, as God is essentially, has being from himself, and only as a person has being from the Father. This is true. For although the fathers and councils most truly affirm that God is of God, taking the word God personally, so that it signifies also the very person of the Father and the Son, yet the Son, insofar as he is essentially God, that is, insofar as he is that one most simple thing which is God, is not from another, because as such he is something absolute. This is exactly what Calvin means.

units.la: Secundò scribit Harscherus: Calvinum irridere Symbolum Nicenum. Et cur? Quia in synodo Lausannensi obstinatissime negavit Filium esse Deum de Deo, & Niceni symboli verba; Lumen De Lumine Deum Verum De Deo Vero, vocavit ineptum & stultum rythmum battologiae ut testatur Simon Vigor, & Petrus Caroli in refutatione blasphemiarum Farelliftarum contra SS. Trinitatem.
units.tr: Secondly, Harscher writes that Calvin mocks the Nicene creed. And why? Because at the Synod of Lausanne he most obstinately denied that the Son is God of God, and he called the words of the Nicene creed, Light of Light, true God of true God, a foolish and silly jingle of battology, as Simon Vigor testifies, and Peter Caroli in his refutation of the blasphemies of the Farellists against the Holy Trinity.

units.la: An Lausannae synodus sit habita ego non scio, nec eius acta apud nos exstant. Petrum Caroli vero hominem levem, mendacem & contentiosum varia habuisse certamina cum Calvino & Farello in diversis classibus, ut vocant, non ignoro.
units.tr: Whether a synod was held at Lausanne I do not know, and its records are not extant among us. But I am not unaware that Peter Caroli, a frivolous, lying and quarrelsome man, had various disputes with Calvin and Farel in the different classes, as they are called.

units.la: Non possum non hoc loco breviter attexere historiam de Petro Caroli, idque propter Bellarminum caeterosque Jesuitas, qui fere quidquid contra Calvinum circa Deitatem Christi obiiciunt, ex hoc homine habent. Fuit Petrus Caroli Sorbonista Parisiensis, homo a natura ad contentiones & convitia natus. Is fidem pontificiam anno 1534. publice abiuravit. Ab Amplissimo Magistratu nostro Pastor ecclesiae Lausannensis factus, superbire incepit, & Calvino ut & Farello invidere eruditionem & authoritatem. Quapropter incepit phrases ipsorum potissimum Calvini, quibus in disputatione cum Gentili usus erat, examinare, praedictos viros, Arianismi, Sabellianismi, & Nestorianismi accusare, publice
units.tr: I cannot refrain from briefly setting out here the history of Peter Caroli, and this on account of Bellarmine and the other Jesuits, who derive almost everything they object against Calvin concerning the deity of Christ from this man. Peter Caroli was a Sorbonnist of Paris, a man born by nature for contention and abuse. He publicly abjured the papal faith in the year 1534. Made pastor of the church of Lausanne by our most distinguished magistracy, he began to grow proud, and to envy Calvin and Farel their learning and authority. Therefore he began to examine their phrases, especially those of Calvin which he had used in his disputation with Gentilis, and to accuse the aforesaid men of Arianism, Sabellianism and Nestorianism, and publicly

units.la: publicè etiam clamare Calvinum, Farellum, Viretum negare Symbolum Athanasii, & Nicenum Concilium reiicere. Cùm verò anno 1537. Bernæ Synodus haberetur ad eandem vocati sunt Calvinus, Farellus, Petrus Caroli; ubi phrases Calvini ut & mores Petri Caroli examinati. Tandem totum negotium ad supremum Magistratum delatum, à quo Petrus Caroli officio pastorali privatus fuit. Hoc hominem adeò male habuit, ut relicta propria uxore, religione & ditione Bernensi, Romani abierit, & à Paulo III. (quem antea in omnibus ferè concionibus Antichristum nominabat) gratiam petiit. Quam ut eò citius impetraret, religionem semel suscep-tam iterum abiurat, Calvinum, Farellum, Viretum Arianismi accusat, illustrem verò Rempublicam Bernensem bene multis & gravibus convitiis petulanter lacessit.
units.tr: to cry out also that Calvin, Farel and Viret denied the Athanasian creed and rejected the Nicene Council. But when a synod was held at Bern in the year 1537, Calvin, Farel and Peter Caroli were summoned to it; there the phrases of Calvin and the conduct of Peter Caroli were examined. At last the whole affair was referred to the supreme magistracy, which deprived Peter Caroli of his pastoral office. This so distressed the man that, leaving his own wife, religion and the territory of Bern, he went off to Rome and sought favour from Paul III (whom he had previously called Antichrist in almost all his sermons). To obtain this the more quickly, he again abjured the religion he had once embraced, accused Calvin, Farel and Viret of Arianism, and petulantly assailed the illustrious Republic of Bern with many grave insults.

units.la: Romà reversus cum transiret propè lacum Nidovianum, ex petitione senatus Bernensis Neostadii captus, & à duobus Nobilibus Legatis Johanne Rudolpho à Diesbach & Johanne Ludovico Amman ob læsæ maiestatis crimen ad supplicium postulatus fuit. Ipse vero Caroli, omnia quæ ex impuro & venenato stomacho exhalaverat, tanquam falsa & calumniosè dicta publicè revocare, religionem pontificiam iterum abiurare, orthodoxam amplecti, dimissus ad vomitum redire & non saltem priora convitia repetere, sed etiam maiora contra Farellum publico scripto divulgare cæpit. Hic est egregius ille & idoneus testis à Jesuitis citatus homo quadruplicis periurii reus, petulans calumniator, & Calvini hostis acerrimus. Qui tandem etiam miserè, ab omnibus derelictus Romæ in hospitali mortuus fuit. Ego vero testimonia eorum qui Jesuitis sunt infesti, non produco (quamvis plura mihi suppetant) quia nihil quàm veritatem quæro.
units.tr: When he was returning to Rome and was passing near the lake of Neuchâtel, he was seized at Neustadt at the request of the senate of Bern, and at the instance of two noble envoys, Johann Rudolf von Diesbach and Johann Ludwig Amman, he was demanded for execution on the charge of treason. Caroli himself, however, was dismissed and, after publicly retracting everything that he had breathed out from his impure and venomous stomach as false and slanderously spoken, after again abjuring the papal religion and embracing the orthodox one, he returned to his vomit, and began not only to repeat his former insults, but also to publish, in a public writing, even greater ones against Farel. This is that eminent and suitable witness cited by the Jesuits, a man guilty of fourfold perjury, a shameless slanderer and the bitterest enemy of Calvin. He finally died wretchedly at Rome in a hospital, abandoned by everyone. As for me, I do not produce the testimonies of those who are hostile to the Jesuits (although many are at hand), because I seek nothing but the truth.

units.la: Quod vero rem ipsam concernit quis credat Calvinum symbolum Nicenum contempsisse, qui duobus annis antequam adversus Gentilem calamum stringeret, anno nimirum 1561. Confessioni Gallicæ subscripsit, in qua art. 6. ista habet: Deniq; in hoc mysterio (Trinitatis) approbamus quod vetera ista Concilia quatuor determinarunt, & omnes sectas à vetustis illis sanctis Doctoribus, veluti Athanasio, Hilario, Cyrillo, Ambrosio & cæteris ex verbo Dei damnatas, detestamur.
units.tr: As for the matter itself, who would believe that Calvin despised the Nicene creed, when two years before he took up his pen against the Gentile, that is, in the year 1561, he subscribed the French Confession, in which article 6 has these words: Finally, in this mystery (of the Trinity) we approve what those ancient councils of four decided, and we detest all the sects condemned by those ancient holy doctors, such as Athanasius, Hilary, Cyril, Ambrose and the others, on the authority of the Word of God.

units.la: Si quid ergo divinare possum puto Calvinum non de Symbolo Niceno locutum, sed ipsum Petrum Caroli verba Symboli sæpe obiicientem, nec recte percipientem, ineptum & stultum battologum appellasse.
units.tr: If I can guess at anything, I think that Calvin did not speak of the Nicene creed, but called Peter Caroli himself, who often objected the words of the creed and did not understand them correctly, a foolish and silly battologist.

units.la: Pergit Harscher: Calvinus Filium Dei esse proprie creatorem cœli & terræ negat. Fides Calvini de hoc dogmate legitur in coment. Joh. cap. 1. ad verba illa, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Ad quae verba ita Calvinus: Ubi sermonem esse Dei asseruit, & aeternam ejus essentiam praedicavit, nunc ab operibus ejus divinitatem probat. Apte autem praedicat de Filio Dei, quod in ejus personam proprie competit. Interdum quidem simpliciter dicit Paulus, omnia per Deum esse Rom. 11:36. Sed quoties comparatur Filius cum Patre, hac nota distingui solet. Quare hic mos loquendi usitatus est, Patrem omnia fecisse per Filium, & a Deo per eundem Filium omnia esse. Apparet ergo Calvinum creationem mundi Christo proprie tribuere, prout & ipsa scriptura ei creationem universi adscribit, Col. 1: 16. Nam per eum condita sunt omnia. Cui etiam Paulus illud psalmistae applicat: Tu initio, Domine, terram fundasti & opera manuum tuarum sunt coeli, Heb. 1: 10.
units.tr: Harscher goes on: Calvin denies that the Son of God is properly the creator of heaven and earth. Calvin's belief on this doctrine is found in his commentary on John, chapter 1, on the words, All things were made by him. On these words Calvin says: Where he asserted that the Word is God and proclaimed his eternal essence, he now proves his divinity from his works. He rightly predicates of the Son of God what properly belongs to his person. Indeed, Paul sometimes says simply that all things are of God (Rom. 11:36). But whenever the Son is compared with the Father, this distinction is usually marked. Hence the customary way of speaking is that the Father made all things through the Son, and that all things are from God through the same Son. It appears, therefore, that Calvin attributes the creation of the world properly to Christ, just as Scripture itself ascribes the creation of the universe to him: Col. 1:16, For by him all things were created. To him Paul also applies that verse of the psalmist: You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands (Heb. 1:10).

units.la: Quomodo ergo Calvinus asserit, se fateri Christum improprie vocari creatorem coeli & terrae? Respondeo; hoc ex scopo disputationis Calvinianae cum Gentili percipi posse. Volebat Gentilis, Deum Patrem possidere totam essentiam Deitatis, Filium vero aliam à Patre habere essentiam, eamque creatam non quidem ab æterno, sed tamen antequam mundus esset conditus. Item; Solum Patrem esse creatorem cœli & terræ, de quo solo Prophetarum dicta sint intelligenda cum de Deo Israëlis loquuntur. Inter cætera adduxit hæreticus locum Jeremiæ: Ego sum, cujus manus fundavit terram & expandit cælos, quæ verba de solo Patre Filii essentiatori (ut loquebatur) intellexit.
units.tr: How then does Calvin assert that he admits Christ is improperly called the creator of heaven and earth? I answer that this can be gathered from the purpose of Calvin's dispute with the Gentile. The Gentile wanted God the Father alone to possess the whole essence of the Godhead, while the Son had an essence other than the Father's, one created not from eternity but still before the world was made. He also held that only the Father is the creator of heaven and earth, and that the sayings of the Prophets must be understood of him alone when they speak of the God of Israel. Among other passages the heretic cited the words of Jeremiah: I am he whose hand founded the earth and stretched out the heavens, and he understood these words of the Father alone, who (as he put it) gives essence to the Son.

units.la: Has blasphemias refutat Calvinus in brevi scripto contra impietatem Gentilis, & primò scribit, maledictionem fore super Christo iuxta Prophetam Jeremiam, si Christus non sit creator, dicit enim Propheta cap. 10: 11. Dii qui non fecerunt cælos & terram pereant è mundo. Quia autem prius impium sit vel cogitare posterius omninò afferendum esse. Secundò, ad instantiam Gentilis respondet, quando nostris obiecit: Cur ergo Pater dicitur creator? & hoc titulo scorsim ornatur? Respondet Calvinus, ita dici ratione ordinis cùm respicitur ad personas, cum ratione essentiæ Filius non minùs sit creator quàm Pater. Unde subiicit; Si VERE creator esl Christus, neq; id persona respectu, sequitur necessariò referri hoc ad essentiam.
units.tr: Calvin refutes these blasphemies in a short writing against the impiety of the Gentile. First he writes that a curse would fall upon Christ, according to the Prophet Jeremiah, if Christ were not the creator, for the Prophet says in chapter 10, verse 11: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the world. He adds that, since it is impious even to think such a thing, it must be affirmed without qualification that the Son is creator. Second, in answer to the Gentile's objection, when he asked our side: "Why then is the Father called creator, and why is this title given to him alone?", Calvin replies that he is so called by reason of order, when the persons are considered, whereas by reason of essence the Son is no less creator than the Father. Hence he adds: If Christ is truly creator, and not merely in respect of person, it necessarily follows that this is to be referred to the essence.

units.la: Quæ verba Calvini ut melius percipiantur (sunt enim paulò obscuriora) notandum est, Calvinum omnia sua argumenta in disputatione allegata direxisse adversus Gentilis hæresin, adeoque adversarium docere voluisse. Primò, in Deitate tres esse personas suis proprietatibus personalibus differentes, unam quoque essentiam omnibus tribus personis communem. Secundò, essentiam hanc æternam immensam, infinitam non minùs Filio & Spiritui sancto tribui, quàm Patri, unde etiam ὁμοούσιοι dicuntur. Tertiò, propterhanc essentiæ ἰσότητα tres personas esse in actionibus essentialibus æquales, ita ut Filius non minus sit creator quàm Pater, quia operationes ad extra sunt indivisæ ut habet Augustini regula. Quartò, si verò personæ considerentur inter se non respectu essentiæ, tùm rectè dici Patrem à seipso esse, originem non habentem, Filium non à se esse sed à Patre, à quo originem habeat: Spiritum S. verò ab utroque procedere. Quintò; essentiam tribus personis communem esse sine principio, quia essentia Patris ἀνάρχος est etiam essentia Filii non alia.
units.tr: So that these words of Calvin may be better understood (for they are somewhat obscure), it must be noted that Calvin directed all his arguments in the dispute against the Gentile heresy, and so wished to teach his opponent. First, that in the Godhead there are three persons, differing by their personal properties, and also one essence common to all three persons. Second, that this essence, eternal, immense and infinite, is attributed to the Son and the Holy Spirit no less than to the Father, whence they are also called homoousioi [ὁμοούσιοι], of one essence. Third, that on account of this equality of essence the three persons are equal in the essential actions, so that the Son is no less creator than the Father, because the external operations are undivided, as the rule of Augustine has it. Fourth, that if the persons are considered among themselves and not in respect of essence, then it is rightly said that the Father is of himself, having no origin; that the Son is not of himself but of the Father, from whom he has his origin; and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Fifth, that the essence common to the three persons is without beginning [ἀνάρχος], because the essence of the Father is also the essence of the Son, and not another.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus hæc πρείσματα deducit Calvinus: Primum, si Filius Dei eandem habet essentiam quam Pater habet, sequitur. 1. Essentiam divinam non esse in solo Patre. 2. Essentiam Filii non esse factam aut creatam à Patre, ut ex Arii schola docuit Gentilis. Secundum; communis huius essentiæ respectu, Filium cum Patre & Spiritu sancto esse illum ipsum Jehovam, qui se in verbo suo & operibus creationis patefecit. Tertium; hac ratione Filium quoque cum Patre & Spiritu S. illum creatorem cœli & terræ esse, & quidem verè ut ipse Calvinus habet. Quartum; si autem Filius consideretur respectu personæ, improprie vocari creatorem, non quidem quatenus improprie idem est quod metaphoricum, ut est apud Arnoldum de bello visu tract. 3. cap. 7. quomodo venter dicitur Deus pseudo-doctorum improprie : nec per aliquam similitudinem tantùm, quomodo Angeli & Magistratus improprie dicuntur Dii. Sed 1. Quatenus de persona prædicatur, quod est totius essentiæ. Quo argumento maximè stringebat Gentilem. Si enim Christus non esset eiusdem essentiæ cum Patre, ne creator quidem esset. 2. Quatenus de una persona prædicatur, quod est omnium trium personarum in unitate essentiæ consideratarum. Docebo hoc exemplo. Dicit Athanasius in symbolo: Omnipotens Pater, omnipotens Filius, omnipotens Spiritus sanctus, verum non tres omnipotentes, sed unus omnipotens. Hic quæro an Filius possit dici ille unus omnipotens? Certè non potest. Sic creator Pater, creator Filius & creator Spiritus sanctus, verum non tres creatores, sed unus creator. Atqui Filius Dei non est ille unus creator, sed Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus in unitate essentiæ consideratí. Cùm itaque de una persona prædicatur quod est omnium trium, improprie id dici fatendum est. Et revera hoc Calvinus in scripto contra Gentilem præcipuè inculcat & urget, qui ubique volebat Patrem esse illum unum & solum creatorem cœli & terræ.
units.tr: From all these things Calvin deduces the following conclusions. First: if the Son of God has the same essence that the Father has, it follows (1) that the divine essence is not in the Father alone; (2) that the essence of the Son was not made or created by the Father, as the Gentile taught from the school of Arius. Second: with respect to this common essence, the Son together with the Father and the Holy Spirit is that very Jehovah who revealed himself in his word and in the works of creation. Third: on this ground the Son together with the Father and the Holy Spirit is also the creator of heaven and earth, and indeed truly, as Calvin himself holds. Fourth: but if the Son is considered in respect of person, he is improperly called creator. This is not in the sense that "improperly" means the same as "metaphorically", as Arnold has it in his De bello visu, tract. 3, chap. 7, where the belly is called the god of the false teachers improperly; nor merely by some likeness, as angels and magistrates are improperly called gods. Rather: (1) insofar as it is predicated of the person what belongs to the whole essence, and this was the argument with which he pressed the Gentile most strongly: for if Christ were not of the same essence as the Father, he would not even be creator; (2) insofar as it is predicated of one person what belongs to all three persons considered in the unity of essence. I shall illustrate this with an example. Athanasius says in the creed: The Father is almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty, and yet not three almighties, but one almighty. Here I ask whether the Son can be called that one almighty. Certainly he cannot. So too: the Father is creator, the Son is creator, and the Holy Spirit is creator, and yet not three creators but one creator. But the Son of God is not that one creator; rather the Father, Son and Holy Spirit considered in the unity of essence are. Therefore, when something belonging to all three is predicated of one person, it must be confessed that it is said improperly. And indeed Calvin in his writing against the Gentile especially insists on and presses this point, since the Gentile everywhere wanted the Father to be that one and only creator of heaven and earth.

units.la: Rogo autem lectorem ut animadvertat fraudem Jesuiticam. Nam ubi Calvinus dicit Christum Filium Dei vocari creatorem improprie, Harschaerus pro vocari substituit esse, longe alio sensu in prima assertione. Praeterea omittit quod nervum habet, quando Calvinus limitate loquitur, personae respectu. Imo maius crimen falsi committit, quando postea Calvini verba ita recitat: Confitemur uno consensu quod Christus improprie sit appellatus creator coeli & terrae ob distinctionem personarum. Ubi Calvinus respectu personarum scripsit. Atque hoc primum est, in quo declarando Calvinus plurimum fuit occupatus. Alterum deinde est, quod filium Dei etiam in relatione ad Patrem considerat, eiusque etiam respectu Filium improprie creatorem vocari affirmat. Sed improprie ipsi idem est quod non Κυρίως, vel non ἀδρόχως sive non appropriate, qua voce, licet minus latina, si Calvinus usus suisset, non tot crabrones ad nocendum etiam levi de causa paratos, contra se irritassent. Nam nemo potest negare, quod non Deo Patri per singularem appropriationem (ut in scholis loquimur) creatio, Filio redemptio, Spiritui sancto sanctificatio tribuatur, non quidem inchoative seu principii ratione, sic enim recte cum Oecumenio loquimur, ἐπ᾽ ἀπὸ μερισμένην... ἀρχῆς ἐνεργείας: sed terminative seu ratione termini. Hoc ex scriptura addisci potest: Matth. 11: 25. inquit filius Dei; Gloriam tibi tribuo Pater, Domine cæli & terræ. Act. 4: 24. & 27. Dixerunt Apoftoli δέσποτα; Domine tu es Deus ille, qui fecisti cælum ac terram, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt, coacti sunt in hac civitate verè adversus sanctum Filium tuum.
units.tr: But I ask the reader to notice the Jesuitical trickery here. For where Calvin says that Christ is improperly called creator, Harscher substitutes is for called, which in the first assertion has a quite different sense. Moreover he omits what is the crux of the matter, namely that Calvin speaks in a limited way, "in respect of person". Indeed he commits a greater crime of falsification when he afterwards quotes Calvin's words thus: "We confess with one accord that Christ is improperly called creator of heaven and earth on account of the distinction of persons." Whereas Calvin wrote in respect of persons. And this is the first point, in explaining which Calvin was chiefly occupied. The second follows, namely that he also considers the Son of God in relation to the Father, and affirms that in respect of the Father too the Son is improperly called creator. But "improperly" for him is the same as "not kyriōs" [Κυρίως], or "not adrochōs" [ἀδρόχως], that is, not appropriately. If Calvin had used this word, though it is less Latin, he would not have stirred up against himself so many hornets ready to do harm even for a slight cause. For no one can deny that creation is attributed to God the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Holy Spirit, by a special appropriation (as we speak in the schools). This is not in an inchoative sense, that is, by reason of principle, for so we may rightly speak with Oecumenius, who says "from a divided beginning of action" [ἐπ᾽ ἀπὸ μερισμένην... ἀρχῆς ἐνεργείας], but in a terminative sense, that is, by reason of the term. This can be learned from Scripture. In Matthew 11:25 the Son of God says: I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. In Acts 4:24 and 27 the Apostles said despota [δέσποτα]: Lord, you are the God who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; for truly in this city they have gathered together against your holy Son.

units.la: Et in Symbolo Apostolico, credo in Deum Patrem omnipotentem creatorem cæli & terræ.
units.tr: And in the Apostles' Creed: I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.

units.la: Rationes cur Patri creatio singulariter tribuatur sunt. 1. Quia Pater ut fons est Deitatis sic etiam omnium actionum. 2. Quia Pater à fe operatur, Filius autem à Patre. Alii tertiam addunt, quia Pater se in creationis opere primò manifestavit, dicendo, faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Gen. 1:26. Catechismus Romanus idem agnoscit quaest. 14. Praecipua quadam ratione Patrem hoc nomine (omnipotens) quia omnis originis fons est, vocamus. Gregorius de Valentia plane idem quod Calvinus Disp. II. quaest. I. S. 23. De Irenaeo loquens, dicit: potentiam & creationem singulariter tribuens Patri tanquam principio primo.
units.tr: The reasons why creation is attributed singularly to the Father are these. (1) Because the Father, as the fountain of the Godhead, is also the fountain of all its actions. (2) Because the Father acts of himself, but the Son acts from the Father. Others add a third: because the Father first revealed himself in the work of creation, when he said: Let us make man in our image (Gen. 1:26). The Roman Catechism acknowledges the same in question 14: We call the Father by this name (almighty) for a certain special reason, because he is the fount of all origin. Gregory of Valencia says plainly the same as Calvin, Disp. II, quaest. I, §23, speaking of Irenaeus: ascribing power and creation singularly to the Father as the first principle.

units.la: Quarta accusatio sequitur his verbis: Tenet praeterea Calvinus cum Valentino Gentili: Filium Dei genitum a Patre, quia voluit Pater, sive, quod idem est, libere Patrem genuisse. Quod constat ex verbis Gentilis & Calvini quae habentur in libro contra Gentilem pag. 1930. Ubi prothesin decimam Gentilis recitat Calvinus in hunc modum: Deus habuit vim generandi & producendi, quia id voluit, quare genuit verbum ante secula & Spiritum sanctum produxit. Quam prothesin deinceps probat hoc modo Calvinus; per hanc sententiam nostra fides nullatenus corrumpitur, quia liberè diximus, quòd κατ' ἐκεῖνον per prerogativam nomen Dei proprie Patri attributum sit. Lib. 2. Instit cap. 13. §. 23. Nomen Dei Patri tribuit κατ' ἐκεῖνον per eminentiam. Est ergo Calvino Deus Pater Ens necessarium, Filius verò liberè genitus, ita ut esse non posset. Est Calvino Pater Deus proprie, Filius non est proprie Deus.
units.tr: The fourth accusation follows in these words: Calvin further holds, with Valentinus and the Gentile, that the Son of God was begotten by the Father because the Father willed it, or, which is the same thing, that the Father begat him freely. This is clear from the words of the Gentile and of Calvin found in the book against the Gentile, p. 1930, where Calvin recites the Gentile's tenth proposition in this manner: God had the power of begetting and producing because he willed it; wherefore he begat the Word before the ages and produced the Holy Spirit. Calvin then proves this proposition in the following way: through this statement our faith is in no way corrupted, because we have said freely that the name God is properly attributed to the Father by prerogative, kat' ekeinon [κατ' ἐκεῖνον]. Institutes, book 2, chap. 13, §23: he gives the name God to the Father kat' ekeinon, by eminence. Therefore for Calvin God the Father is a necessary being, but the Son is freely begotten, so that he could not not be. For Calvin the Father is God properly; the Son is not properly God.

units.la: Dicunt Medici, febricitantibus propter calorem adustum in lingua omnem cibum esse amarum. Idem accidit Jesuitis, qui quoniam invidiæ & maledicentiæ morbo veluti febri quotidiana laborant, etiam rectè dicta sinistrè accipiunt. Reprehendit in Calvino Harscherus duo. Primò; Quod statuat Filium liberè à Patre genitum. Secundò, quòd partim Lib. contra Gentilem, partim Instit. Lib. I. cap. 13. §. 29. Deo Patri nomen Deus κατ' ἐκεῖνον per eminentiam tribuat. Unde duo consectaria deducit; Ergò 1. Deus Pater Calvino est ens necessarium, Filius vero liberè genitus ut esse non possset. 2. Calvino Pater est Deus proprie, Filius impropriè. Utrumque consectarium longissimè abest à fide & religione Calvini, deducta ambo ex malè intellectis & malitiosè contortis verbis Calvini. Quod nunc contra Harscherum & reliquos Jesuitas (nam plerique haec de Calvino nobis obiiciunt) perspicuè docebo.
units.tr: Physicians say that for those with fever, a burnt tongue makes every food taste bitter. The same happens to the Jesuits: since they suffer from envy and slander, as if from a daily fever, they take even correct statements in a bad sense. Harscher criticises two things in Calvin. First, that he holds the Son to have been begotten freely by the Father. Second, that in part of the book against the Gentile and in part of the Institutes (Book 1, chapter 13, §29) he gives the name God to the Father κατ' ἐκεῖνον, by eminence. From this he draws two corollaries: therefore (1) for Calvin God the Father is a necessary being, but the Son, begotten freely, is such that he could not exist. (2) For Calvin the Father is God properly, the Son improperly. Both corollaries are far removed from Calvin's faith and religion, since both are drawn from words of Calvin that have been misunderstood and maliciously twisted. I will show this clearly, against Harscher and the other Jesuits (most of them raise these charges against us about Calvin).

units.la: Primò notanda fraus Jesuitæ, quem non pudet verba Calvini permutare, & ei adscribere, quod nunquam ne per somnium quidem cogitavit. Nam Patrem liberè genuisse Filium nullibi scripsit Calvinus, sed est mera glossa Jesuitica. Deinde quod Calvinus dicit, ingenuè tradimus, Harscher pervertit scribendo, liberè diximus. Ubi est fides horum Theologorum?
units.tr: First, the Jesuit's fraud deserves notice: he is not ashamed to alter Calvin's words and to attribute to him what Calvin never thought, not even in a dream. For Calvin nowhere wrote that the Father begot the Son freely; this is a mere Jesuit gloss. Next, where Calvin says we have frankly stated, Harscher distorts it by writing we have freely stated. Where is the honesty of these theologians?

units.la: Deinde, si Calvinus illud quia voluit Pater, aliquo modo approbavit, nec hac ratione à fide catholica defecit. Cuius rei ut authenticum sibi habeat autorem Harscher, ascribam verba Jesuitæ de Valentia, quæ huiusmodi sunt: Augustinus refert, Arianum quendam opposuisse cuidam catholico; aut Pater genuit Filium volens aut nolens. Si volens, ergo libere, si nolens, ergo est miser. Hoc argumentum catholicus, teste eodem Augustino, acute refutavit, quærendo vicissim ab Ariano; Utrum Pater esset Deus volens aut nolens? Ut si volens responderet, inferret, Patrem non naturâ, sed liberè esse Deum, si nolens, concluderet esse miserum. Dicendum est igitur, inquit Valentia, Patrem & voluntariè & nihilominus naturaliter Filium genuisse, sicuti & voluntariè & naturaliter est Deus, voluntate scilicet concomitante. Tomo 1. Disputat. 2. quæst. 15. punct. 4. Sic etiam Athanasius. Theologi quoquè nostri in hunc sensum perspicuè: Patrem genuisse Filium suum naturâ quemadmodum etiam bonus, iustus & sapiens est natura suâ, voluntate scilicet generationem hanc semper comitante & probante, non eam antecedente nec producente, unde Filius ὑιοθεσίας & ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ appellatur, Matth. 17: 15. Col. 1: 3. Apud Walæum.
units.tr: Next, even if Calvin approved, in some sense, the phrase because the Father willed it, he did not on that account depart from the Catholic faith. To give Harscher an authoritative witness for this, I will cite the words of the Jesuit Valentia, which run as follows: Augustine reports that a certain Arian put this to a Catholic: either the Father begot the Son willing or unwilling. If willing, then freely; if unwilling, then he is wretched. This argument, as the same Augustine testifies, a Catholic cleverly refuted by asking the Arian in turn: whether the Father was God willing or unwilling? For if he replied "willing," he would infer that the Father is God not by nature but freely; if "unwilling," he would conclude that he is wretched. It must therefore be said, says Valentia, that the Father begot the Son both willingly and at the same time naturally, just as he is God both willingly and naturally, the will namely accompanying. Vol. 1, Disputation 2, question 15, point 4. Athanasius also speaks thus. Our own theologians clearly speak in the same sense: the Father begot his Son by nature, just as he is good, just and wise by his own nature; by will, namely, this generation always accompanying and approving, not preceding it nor producing it. Hence the Son is called of adoption and of his love, Matt. 17:15, Col. 1:3. From Walaeus.

units.la: Quod ergo consectarium primum attinet quod ita sonat: Est ergo Calvino Pater ens necessarium, Filius vero liberè genitus, ita ut esse non posset, dico omnia esse inepta. 1. Quia Harscher hæc non ex Calvini verbis deduxit (qui talia nunquam scripsit) sed ex sua salsa & ficta hypothesi. Nam ex quibus verbis Calvini sequitur, ergo Calvino Deus Pater est ens necessarium? 2. Et quomodo Filius Calvino posset esse ens contingens, qui plus quam centies scripsit, Filium cum Patre esse eiusdem simplicis, infinitæ & æternæ essentiæ?
units.tr: As to the first corollary, which runs: Therefore for Calvin God the Father is a necessary being, but the Son, begotten freely, is such that he could not exist, I say that all of it is absurd. (1) Because Harscher did not deduce this from Calvin's words (for Calvin never wrote such things), but from his own salty and fictitious hypothesis. For from what words of Calvin does it follow that therefore for Calvin God the Father is a necessary being? (2) And how could the Son be, for Calvin, a contingent being, when he wrote more than a hundred times that the Son is of the same simple, infinite and eternal essence as the Father?

units.la: Accedo ad alterum: Calvinus nomen Dei, Patri κατ' ἐξοχὴν tribuit & proprie. Ergo Calvino Deus Pater est proprie Deus, Filius non est proprie Deus.
units.tr: I turn to the second: Calvin attributes the name God to the Father κατ' ἐξοχήν and properly. Therefore for Calvin God the Father is God properly, the Son is not God properly.

units.la: Primò de excellentia Patris. Quemadmodum veteres Patres, Filium Dei respectu essentiæ consideratum Patri æqualem fecerunt in omnibus proprietatibus essentialibus, gloriâ & honore: ita Deo Patri respectu originis & modi subsistendi præ Filio quandam excellentiam tribuerunt, dum Christum considerabant in persona. Quomodo Ignat. aut quisquis autor in epistola ad Philip. Filiû Dei loquentem introduxit ὁμολογῶ τ᾽ ἰσσπο γὴν. Bellarminus annuit Lib. I. de Christo cap. 10. cùm inquit: Porrò excellentiam Patris, Filius confitetur ratione principij tantum, unde statim subjungit novi generationis mea autorem Patrem. Hos imitatus est Calvinus ut ipsius verba clarissimè docent, & ubique cum Nazianzeno τὸ μεῖζον τῆς αἰτίας, τὸ δὲ ἴσον τῆς φύσεως esse dixit. Id carpunt nunc Jesuitæ in Calvino, cùm tamen veteres Patres plerique ita locuti fuerint, teste Maldonato Jesuita Comm. in Joh. cap. 14. Quando ita scribit: Tertia verò erat (explicatio catholicorum authorum verf. 28. Pater maior me est) Patrem majorem dici Filio, etiam quatenus Filius Deus erat, non quidem reipsa, sed hoc ipso quod ille Pater, hic Filius erat: Patris enim nomen honorificentius naturâ suâ esse, quàm Filij: quia principium & ut Graeci vocant, caussam Filij significat. Sic exponunt Athanasius, Hilarius, Epiphanius, Gregorius Nazianzenus & Caesarius in iis locis quos supra citavimus, & Cyrillus & Damascenus, Chrysostomus & Leontius, Theophylactus & Euthymius. Ecce undecim Patres, qui cum Calvino locuti, & idem quod ipse. Addit tamen Maldonatus; sed haud scio an plus adversariis concesserint, quàm aequum erat. Utinam ita modeste iudicarent Jesuitae de Calvino, qui suam sententiam ex praedictis Patribus hausit.
units.tr: First, concerning the excellence of the Father. Just as the ancient Fathers made the Son of God, considered with respect to essence, equal to the Father in all essential properties, in glory and in honour, so with respect to origin and mode of subsistence they attributed a certain excellence to God the Father above the Son, when they considered Christ in his person. So Ignatius or whatever author, in the Epistle to the Philippians, introduced the Son of God speaking [ὁμολογῶ τ᾽ ἰσσπο γὴν]. Bellarmine agrees in Book 1 on Christ, chapter 10, when he says: Moreover, the Son confesses the excellence of the Father only by reason of the principle, whence he immediately adds, "the Father, the author of my new generation." Calvin imitated these writers, as his own words very clearly show, and everywhere with Nazianzen he said that the Father has the greater by reason of cause, but the equal by reason of nature. The Jesuits now carp at this in Calvin, although most of the ancient Fathers spoke in this way, as the Jesuit Maldonatus testifies in his Commentary on John, chapter 14, where he writes: The third explanation, given by the Catholic authors (on verse 28, "the Father is greater than I"), is that the Father is called greater than the Son even in so far as the Son was God; not indeed in reality, but by this very fact, that the one was Father and the other Son: for the name of Father signifies in its own nature something more honourable than that of Son, because it signifies the principle and, as the Greeks call it, the cause of the Son. So expound Athanasius, Hilary, Epiphanius, Gregory Nazianzen and Caesarius in the passages we cited above, and Cyril and Damascene, Chrysostom and Leontius, Theophylact and Euthymius. Behold eleven Fathers who speak with Calvin, and hold the same as he does. Maldonatus adds, however: but I do not know whether they conceded more to the adversaries than was fair. Would that the Jesuits judged Calvin with such moderation, since he drew his opinion from the Fathers just mentioned.

units.la: Quod deinde scribit, Filium Calvino esse improprie Deum merae sunt nugae & gerrae. Nam ne unus locus adduci potest ex omnibus Calvini scriptis, ubi dicat, Filium Dei esse Deum improprie. Contrarium ex supra allegatis testimoniis satis perspicuè intelligi poterit. Præcipuè ex Lib. I. Inst. cap. 13. §. 23.
units.tr: What they write next, that for Calvin the Son is God improperly, is mere trifling and nonsense. For not a single passage can be cited from all of Calvin's writings in which he says that the Son of God is God improperly. The contrary can be understood quite clearly from the testimonies cited above, especially from Book 1 of the Institutes, chapter 13, §23.

units.la: Si non alium censemus Deum quàm Patrem non obscurè deÿcitur Filius ab hoc gradu. Ergo quoties Deitatis sit mentio, minimè admitti debet antithesis inter Filium & Patrem, quasi huic tantùm conveniat nomen veri Dei. Nam sanè Deus, qui Iesaja apparuit, verus & unicus fuit Deus, quem tamen Iohannes affirmat fuisse Christum. Phrasis, quam Harscherus citat, in qua dicit Calvinus, nomen Deus Patri proprie tribui, habet homonymiam, pro appropriatè & quidem saltem respectu missionis Filii, ubi vox Deus plerunquè Patri per appropriationem præ Filio tribuitur. Exempli gratiâ: Psal. 2: 7. Iehova dixit mihi Filius meus es. Gal. 4:4. Postquam venit plenum tempus, emisit Deus Filium suum. Eph. 3: 9. Deus omnia condidit per Iesum Christum. Joh. 3: 16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit. Nam cùm hoc Gentilis pro sua sententia adduxisset, quod olim etiam fecerunt Ariani, placuit Calvino ad meliorem scripturæ intelligentiam ita loqui.
units.tr: If we judge that there is no other God than the Father, the Son is not obscurely removed from this rank. Therefore, whenever mention is made of the Deity, the antithesis between Son and Father ought by no means to be admitted, as though the name of the true God belonged to the Father alone. For certainly the God who appeared to Isaiah was true and the only God, and yet John affirms that this was Christ. The phrase which Harscher cites, in which Calvin says that the name God is properly given to the Father, has an ambiguity: it means appropriately, and that especially with respect to the mission of the Son, where the word God is for the most part attributed to the Father by appropriation before the Son. For example: Ps. 2:7, Jehovah said to me, You are my Son. Gal. 4:4, When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son. Eph. 3:9, God created all things through Jesus Christ. John 3:16, God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son. For when the Gentile had brought this forward for his own opinion, as the Arians once also did, Calvin chose to speak thus for a better understanding of Scripture.

units.la: Expendat Harscher conclusionem Thomæ Aquinatis ad art. 8. quæst. 39. primæ part. summ. In qua ista leguntur: In consideratione Dei, qua Deus absolutè secundùm esse suum consideratur, Patri æternitas appropriatur: in consideratione verò Dei secundùm rationem causalitatis, Patri potentia appropriatur.
units.tr: Let Harscher weigh the conclusion of Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa, first part, question 39, article 8: In the consideration of God by which God is considered absolutely according to his being, eternity is appropriated to the Father; but in the consideration of God according to the reason of causality, power is appropriated to the Father.

units.la: Ultimò obiicit; Calvinum negare, Filium Dei habere essentiam suam à Patre, sed Filium esse per se, lib. contra Gentilem pag. 1948. Quod sit Filium Dei negare, qui aliter Filius naturalis esse non posset nisi accipiendo naturam à Patre. Video Harscherum nimiùm somnolenter legisse Calvinum. Quid enim hoc, Calvinus dixit Filium esse per se? Accuratiùs C multò hanc controversiam tractarunt Jesuitæ alii. Eam nunc videamus.
units.tr: Lastly he objects: that Calvin denies that the Son of God has his essence from the Father, but holds that the Son is of himself, in the book against the Gentile, page 1948. This is to deny the Son of God, who otherwise could not be a natural Son unless he received his nature from the Father. I see that Harscher read Calvin far too drowsily. For what does this mean? Did Calvin say that the Son is of himself? Other Jesuits have treated this controversy far more accurately than C. Let us now look at it.

units.la: Docuit Gentilis, 1. Solum Patrem esse verum atque æternum Deum & creatorem mundi, qui se per Prophetas in V. Testamento revelaverit.
units.tr: Gentilis taught: (1) that only the Father is the true and eternal God and the creator of the world, who revealed himself through the prophets in the Old Testament.

units.la: 2. Patrem esse divinam & æternam essentiam, & vice versa, essentiam æternam nihil esse aliud, quàm Patrem, 3. Filium habere essentiam à Patre efsectam sive creatam, adeoque non esse verum & æternum Deum, sed à Patre essentiatum. Quam hæreticam sententiam ut posset probare sic argumentabatur: Quicunque suæ essentiæ habet principium & est ab alio, is non est verus & æternus Deus. Atqui Filius suæ essentiæ habet principium & est ab alio effectus. Ergo Filius non est verus & æternus Deus.
units.tr: (2) That the Father is the divine and eternal essence, and conversely, that the eternal essence is nothing other than the Father; (3) that the Son has an essence produced or created by the Father, and so is not the true and eternal God but essentiated by the Father. To prove this heretical opinion he argued thus: Whoever has a beginning of his essence and is made by another is not the true and eternal God. But the Son has a beginning of his essence and is made by another. Therefore the Son is not the true and eternal God.

units.la: Calvinus propositionem maiorem concessit, & ad minorem respondit distinguendo. Filium posse considerari vel ratione essentiae vel ratione personae. Essentiae respectu, quam cum Patre & Spiritu S. communem habet, non esse ab alio, idcirco eius essentiam nec principium habere, nec effectam esse ab alio, ratio, quia est essentia Patris, quae principio caret. Et hac ratione esse αὐτοθεόν, quemadmodum etiam a Patribus Graecis, praesertim Epiphanio & Basilio, Filius Dei respectu essentiae consideratus, appellatur modo αὐτου-σία, modo αὐτοζωή, modo αὐτοφῶς modo τὸ ὄντως ὤν, modo αὐτοτέλεσος. Personae vero respectu esse a Patre non efsectum sed genitum ab aeterno per communicationem essentiae.
units.tr: Calvin granted the major premise and answered the minor by distinguishing. The Son can be considered either with respect to his essence or with respect to his person. With respect to essence, which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is not from another, and so his essence has neither a beginning nor is it made by another, because it is the essence of the Father, which lacks a beginning. On this ground he is autotheon [αὐτοθεόν], just as the Son of God, considered with respect to his essence, is called by the Greek Fathers, especially Epiphanius and Basil, now autousia [αὐτουσία], now autozoe [αὐτοζωή], now autophos [αὐτοφῶς], now to ontos on [τὸ ὄντως ὤν], now autoteleso [αὐτοτέλεσος]. With respect to his person, however, he is not made by the Father but begotten from eternity by communication of essence.

units.la: Calvini sententiam catholicam & orthodoxam esse aliquot argumentis probat Bellarminus, lib. 2. de Christo cap. 19. Eius verba hic adscribam. Primo dicit: Dum rem excutio & Calvini sententias diligenter considero, non facile audeo pronunciare, illum in hoc errore fuisse, nempe quem ipsi Genebrardus, Lindanus, Canisius & hoc loco Harscherus tribuunt. Deinde rationes addit Bellarminus;
units.tr: Bellarmine proves by several arguments that Calvin's opinion is Catholic and orthodox (Book 2 on Christ, ch. 19). I will set down his words here. First he says: While I examine the matter and carefully weigh Calvin's statements, I do not readily dare to pronounce that he fell into this error, namely the error which Genebrardus, Lindanus, Canisius, and here Harscher, attribute to him. Then Bellarmine adds his arguments:

units.la: I. Quia Calvinus fatetur lib. 1. Instit. cap. 13. §. 13. Unam numero naturam esse in tribus distinctis personis, & ibi dicit Filium à Patre genitum. At certè non est intelligibile quomodo Filius sit à Patre & habeat eandem naturam cum Patre, & non habeat illam à Patre, nec enim Filius dici potest sola relatio, sed aliquid subsistens in natura;
units.tr: I. Because Calvin admits (Institutes, book 1, ch. 13, §13) that there is one nature, numerically one, in three distinct persons, and there he says that the Son is begotten of the Father. But it certainly cannot be understood how the Son is from the Father and has the same nature as the Father, and yet does not have that nature from the Father; for the Son cannot be called merely a relation, but is something subsisting in nature.

units.la: II. Quia ibid. §. 23. Calvinus apertè dicit essentiam à Patre Filio esse communicatam, his verbis; si in essentia est discretio, respondeant annon cum Filio eam communicaverit? Hoc verò non potuit esse ex parte, quia dimidium fabricare Deum nefas esset.
units.tr: II. Because in the same place (§23) Calvin plainly says that the essence was communicated to the Son by the Father, in these words: "If there is a distinction in essence, do they not reply that he communicated it to the Son? But this could not be on the Father's part, because it would be impious to make God half-made."

units.la: III. Quia, qui afferunt Filium à seipso habere essentiam ideò errant, quia coguntur vel facere Filium ingenitum & eandem personam cum Patre, vel multiplicare essentias, vel certè distinguere essentiam à persona realiter & sic introducere quaternitatem. At Calvinus lib. 1. Institit. cap. 13. §. 19. Filium asserit genitum à Patre & unam numero ponit essentiam in tribus personis: item §. 23. docet essentiam Patris Filio communicatam esse. Deniq; §. 25. Non distinguit essentiam à personis realiter, sed solùm ratione.
units.tr: III. Because those who maintain that the Son has his essence from himself are led into error, since they are forced either to make the Son unbegotten and the same person as the Father, or to multiply essences, or else to distinguish the essence from the person really and so introduce a quaternity. But Calvin, in Institutes 1.13.19, asserts that the Son is begotten of the Father and posits one essence in number in the three persons; likewise at 1.13.23 he teaches that the Father's essence is communicated to the Son. Finally, at 1.13.25, he does not distinguish the essence from the persons really, but only in thought.

units.la: IV. Idem probat Bellarminus ex caussa quæ impulit Calvinum ad hanc sententiam.
units.tr: IV. Bellarmine proves the same point from the cause that moved Calvin to this opinion.

units.la: Caussa fuit, inquit Bellarminus, quia Valentinus Gentilis perpetuò jactabat solum Patrem esse αὐτόθεον & per hoc nomen intelligebat solum Patrem habere essentiam verè divinam & increatam: Filium autem & Spiritum sanctum habere aliam essentiam productam à Patre, & ideo quo ad essentiam eos non esse autotheos. Calvinus igitur occurrere volens Valentino contrarium asseruit, nempe Filium esse autotheon quoad essentiam, id est, in eo sensu, quo id à Valentino negabatur.
units.tr: The cause was, says Bellarmine, that Valentinus Gentilis constantly boasted that the Father alone is autotheos [αὐτόθεος], and by this name he understood that the Father alone has a truly divine and uncreated essence, while the Son and the Holy Spirit have another essence produced by the Father, and therefore are not autotheoi as to essence. Calvin, therefore, wishing to oppose Valentinus, asserted the contrary, namely that the Son is autotheos [αὐτόθεος] as to essence, that is, in that sense in which Valentinus denied it. Further, in the Greek of Epiphanius, God is sometimes called agennētos [ἀγέννητος], sometimes autogennētos [αὐτογέννητος], that is, either unbegotten or begotten of himself.

units.la: V. Ex discipulorum Calvini do- ctrina, Bezæ & Josiæ Simleri.
units.tr: V. From the teaching of Calvin's disciples, Beza and Josias Simler.

units.la: Nam Beza, in axiomatibus de Trinitate axiomate 14. dicit Filium esse à Patre per ineffabilem totius essentiæ communicationem, ab æterno, & tamen ipse etiam cum suo magistro facit Christum autotheon. Item Josias Simlerus Calvini sectator in epistola ad Polonos defendit autusian Filij & sic explicat suam & Calvini sententiam: Non negamus Filium habere essentiam à Deo Patre, sed essentiam genitam negamus. Quæ Josiæ sententia (iudicium Bellarmini de tota hac controversia) non video, cur catholica dicenda non sit. Sic ergo Jesuita Jesuitam nervosè refutat. Obiiciet Harscher: Bellarminum, modum loquendi Calvini simpliciter reycere. Verum hoc est. Sed merus est lusus apud Bellarminum homonymias in phrasi à se esse, quæ accipi potest vel positivè, ut idem sit ac à se effectum esse, in quo sensu nec Filius est à seipso, nec Pater quoquè: vel negativè, ut idem sit, quod à nulâ nullo esse productum, seu suæ essentiæ nullam habere caussam, quomodo phrasi ista usus est Calvinus adversùs Gentilem. Qua in significatione apud Epiphanium, Deus modò ἀγέννητος, modò αὐτογέννητος, id est, vel ingenitus, vel à se genitus dicitur.
units.tr: For Beza, in his axioms on the Trinity, axiom 14, says that the Son is from the Father by an ineffable communication of the whole essence, from eternity, and yet he himself, together with his master, calls Christ autotheos [αὐτόθεος].
