Likewise Josias Simler, a follower of Calvin, in his letter to the Poles defends the autousia [αὐτουσία] of the Son, and so explains his own and Calvin's opinion: We do not deny that the Son has his essence from God the Father, but we deny that the essence is begotten. I do not see why Josias' opinion (Bellarmine's judgement on this whole controversy) should not be called catholic. So the Jesuit vigorously refutes the Jesuit. Harscher will object that Bellarmine simply rejects Calvin's manner of speaking. That is true. But Bellarmine's play on the ambiguity of the phrase "from himself" is mere trifling, which phrase may be taken either positively, so that it means the same as "made by himself", in which sense neither the Son nor the Father is from himself, or negatively, so that it means the same as "produced by no one", or "having no cause of its essence", in which sense Calvin used the phrase against the Gentile.

units.la: Ex hisce omnibus, sic secundùm veritatem enarratis manifestum esse potest, Calvinum de Deitate Filii Dei planè iuxta catholicam fidem sensisse, & scripsisse, ipsius quoquè phrases ex Patribus desumtas ab ipsis Jesuitis, Bellarmino, Valentia, Maldonato, approbari: Jesuitas verò Calvini scripta contra omnem æquitatem & pietatem flectere, torquere, mutilare, & mutare, ut ipsum hæresewss quocunquè modo accusare possint. In propriis verò suis, ita cæci sunt & iniusti, ut etiam ea, quæ verissimâ historiâ ab authoribus etiam pontificiis conscribuntur, dissimulare & fuco palliare audeant. Pro exemplo sit Liberius Papa, qui teste Athanasio, Hieronymo, Platina aperte Arianus factus est, subscribendo in damnationem Athanasii, cum Arianis palam communicando, eorumque haeresi subscribendo & sententias Arianorum amplectendo, quam ob caussam a pontificatu depositus fuit. Et tamen iuxta Bellarminum & Gretserum salte actu externo peccavit, non in mente consensit. Itane? Certe, quia Jesuitae sic dicunt & volunt.
units.tr: From all these things, set forth here according to the truth, it is manifest that Calvin thought and wrote altogether in accordance with the Catholic faith, and that the phrases he took from the Fathers are approved by the Jesuits themselves, Bellarmine, Valentia and Maldonatus. But the Jesuits bend, twist, mutilate and alter Calvin's writings against all fairness and piety, so that they can accuse him of heresy in any way at all. In their own affairs they are so blind and unjust that they dare to disguise and gloss over even those things which are recorded in the truest history by the Papist authors themselves. Let Pope Liberius serve as an example: according to the testimony of Athanasius, Jerome and Platina, he openly became an Arian, subscribing to the condemnation of Athanasius, communicating openly with the Arians, subscribing to their heresy and embracing their opinions, for which reason he was deposed from the papacy. And yet, according to Bellarmine and Gretser, he sinned only in external act, and did not consent in mind. Really? Certainly, because the Jesuits say so and wish it so.

units.la: Quae hactenus ab Harschero ex Calvino proposita sunt & a nobis explicata pertinent ad personam Christi ἀσυγχύτως, seu, ut Patres Graeci loquebantur, κατὰ θεολογίαν consideratam. Reliqua, quae sequuntur personam Christi attinent quatenus consideratur, κατ' οἰκονομίαν seu gratiosam dispensationem in officio mediatorio. Nam huius respectu scriptura aliter de Christo loquitur. Augustinus duabus regulis proposuit: Quaedam ita ponuntur in scripturis de Deo Patre & Filio, ut indicent unitatem, æqualitatem, substantia, sicuti est: ego & Pater unum sumus. Quædam vero ita, ut minorem ostendant Filium propter formam servi, id est, propter assumtam creaturam mutabilis humanæ substantiæ, sicuti est: Quoniam Pater major me est. Et huiusmodi dicta plurima sunt in veteri & novo Testamento. Esaias ipsum vocat servum Iehovæ, cap. 53: 11. in eodem capite v. 3. abiectissimum virorum. Apostolus Heb. 2: 9. Facit ipsum Angelis inferiorem. Est humilis ancillæ Filius Luc. 1: 48. hominibus subjectus Luc. 2: 51. Hæc & similia nomina plura ipsi tribuuntur, sed iuxta Athanasii regulam dial. 1. contra Maced. οὐ φύσει τῆς Θεότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆ οἰκονομία τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος. Idcirco Deitati eius nihil derogant.
units.tr: What Harscher has so far set out from Calvin, and what we have explained, pertains to the person of Christ considered asygchytos [ἀσυγχύτως], or, as the Greek Fathers spoke, kata theologian [κατὰ θεολογίαν]. The remaining points that follow concern the person of Christ as he is considered kat' oikonomian [κατ' οἰκονομίαν], that is, in the gracious dispensation of his mediatorial office. For Scripture speaks differently of Christ with respect to this. Augustine laid down two rules: Some things are said in Scripture of God the Father and the Son so as to indicate unity, equality and substance, as in: "I and the Father are one." Others are said so as to show the Son to be inferior, on account of the form of a servant, that is, on account of the creature he assumed, of mutable human substance, as in: "The Father is greater than I." There are very many sayings of this kind in the Old and New Testaments. Isaiah calls him the servant of Jehovah (ch. 53:11), and in the same chapter (v. 3) the most abject of men. The Apostle (Heb. 2:9) makes him lower than the angels. He is the son of a humble handmaid (Luke 1:48), subject to men (Luke 2:51). Many such names are attributed to him, but according to the rule of Athanasius (Dial. 1 against the Macedonians), they belong not to the nature of the Godhead but to the economy of the humanity [οὐ φύσει τῆς Θεότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆ οἰκονομία τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος]. Therefore they take nothing away from his Deity.

units.la: Si igitur Calvinus Christum secundum officium mediatorium consideratum vocavit vicarium Dei nihil contra scripturam dixit. Quia non est sermo de Christo tanquam Deo simpliciter, sed quatenus Deus per ipsum ultimis diebus locutus Heb. 1: 1. quatenus Deus ipsum misit ad Evangelizandum mansuetis, ad obligandum fractos animo, ad proclamandum captivis libertatem & vinctis aperturam ergastuli: ad proclamandum annum acceptum Iehova &c. Esa. 61: 1, 2. Unde toties Christus in Evangelio de ista missione: esca mea est exequi voluntatem ejus qui misit me, & perficere ipsius opus Ioh. 4. 34. adhuc paulisper ero vobiscum, deinde abibo ad eum qui misit me. Et quemadmodum Apostoli erant vicarij Christi, cujus nomine legatione fungebantur 2. Cor. 5: Ita Christus erat vicarius Dei Patris in hoc mundo.
units.tr: If therefore Calvin, considering Christ according to his mediatorial office, called him the vicar of God, he said nothing contrary to Scripture. For the discussion is not about Christ simply as God, but insofar as God has spoken to us through him in the last days, Heb. 1:1; insofar as God sent him to preach good tidings to the meek, to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; to proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD, etc. Isa. 61:1, 2. Hence Christ so often speaks in the Gospel of this mission: My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work John 4:34; Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go unto him that sent me. And just as the Apostles were vicars of Christ, in whose name they discharged their embassy, 2 Cor. 5, so Christ was the vicar of God the Father in this world.

units.la: Observandum autem, officii mediatorii Christi duas esse partes; unam quâ τὰ πρὸς ἡμᾶς exequitur propter Deum, id est, quâ Dei Patris partes agit apud homines, ipsis annuntiando voluntatem Dei de qua supra: altera, quâ τὰ πρὸς τ θεὸν exequitur nostro loco, dum pro nobis apud Deum intercedit, pro nobis Deo satisfecit, & in omnibus personam nostram sustinuit. Priori respectu est vicarius Dei, posteriori vero vicarius noster. Priori respectu dicitur Pater, neminem judicare, sed dedisse Filio omne judicium Joh. 5: 22. Item Christo datam esse omnem potestatem in Cælo & in terra, nempe tanquam vicario, Matth. 28: 18. Usque dum Patri traditurus est regnum illud œconomicum I. Cor. 15: 24.
units.tr: It must be observed, however, that the mediatorial office of Christ has two parts. In one he performs the things that pertain to us on account of God, that is, he acts the part of God the Father among men, announcing to them the will of God, of which we have spoken above. In the other he performs the things that pertain to God in our place, while he intercedes for us with God, has made satisfaction to God for us, and in all things has borne our person. In the former respect he is the vicar of God; in the latter, our vicar. In the former respect the Father is said to judge no one, but to have committed all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. Likewise all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, namely as vicar, Matt. 28:18, until he hands over that economic kingdom to the Father, 1 Cor. 15:24.

units.la: Perspicuè hac de re Tertullianus lib. adversf. Praxean: Nemo ad Patrem venit nisi per me: & nemo ad me venit nisi Pater eum adduxerit: & omnia mihi Pater tradidit, & sicut Pater vivificat ita & Filius, & si me cognovistis, & Patrem cognovistis. Secundum hac enim vicarium Patris se ostenderat, per quem Pater & videretur in factis, & audiretur in verbis, & cognosceretur in Filio, facta & verba Patris administrante.
units.tr: Tertullian sets this out clearly in his book against Praxeas: No one comes to the Father except through me; and no one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him; and the Father has delivered all things to me; and as the Father quickens, so also does the Son; and if you have known me, you have known the Father also. For in this way he showed himself to be the vicar of the Father, through whom the Father was both seen in deeds and heard in words, and was known in the Son, the Son administering the deeds and words of the Father.

units.la: Quod deinde Harfcherus fcribit Calvinum vocare Chriftum Dei fecretarium intimum & miniftrum. Illud in cap. Joh. primo, hoc in cap. 17. pro more fuo ipfi affingit. Nam in commentario capitis primi ita loquitur: Quum dicit Filium in finu Patris fuiffe, fumta eft ab hominibus tranflatio, qui in finum fuum admittere dicuntur, quibus cum arcana omnia communicant. Sedes confilij, pectus eft. Ergo Filium ab intimis fecretis Patri fuiffe docet, ut fciamus in evangelio nos habere quafi apertum Dei pectus. Maldonatus Jefuita idem quod Calvinus & iifdem verbis: Chriftum quafi ex Dei pectore thefauros fapientiæ & fcientiæ depromere, omnia Dei nofle confilia. Hoc enim eft effe in finu Patris; effe illi conjunctiffimum, effe in ejus fecreto confilio.
units.tr: Next, Harscher writes that Calvin calls Christ God's most intimate secretary and minister. He attributes this to him, as is his custom, the first in the chapter on John 1 and the second in chapter 17. For in his commentary on the first chapter Calvin speaks thus: When he says that the Son was in the bosom of the Father, the figure is taken from men, who are said to admit into their bosom those with whom they share all secrets. The seat of counsel is the breast. Therefore he teaches that the Son was from the innermost secrets of the Father, so that we may know that in the Gospel we have, as it were, the open breast of God. The Jesuit Maldonatus says the same thing as Calvin, and in the same words: that Christ, as it were from the breast of God, draws forth the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and knows all the counsels of God. For this is to be in the bosom of the Father: to be most closely joined to him, to be in his secret counsel.

units.la: In caput vero 17. ita fcribit Calv. Rurfum eodem argumento utitur minime decere, ut Pater unquam abyciat quos Filius ejus mandato usq; in finem ministerÿ sui servavit. Apostolus Paulus Rom. 15: 8. omnia complectitur quæ Calvinus de Christo in officio mediatorio considerato, dixit: Illud autem dico, inquit, Jesum Christum ministrum fuisse circumcisionis pro Dei veritate, ut confirmaret promissiones Patrum.
units.tr: On chapter 17, however, Calvin writes thus: Again he uses the same argument, that it is by no means fitting that the Father should ever cast off those whom the Son has kept by his command to the very end of his ministry. The Apostle Paul, Rom. 15:8, embraces everything that Calvin said about Christ considered in his mediatorial office: I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

units.la: DEFENSIO
units.tr: DEFENCE

units.la: Pro Calvino Arianismi accusato.
units.tr: In defence of Calvin, accused of Arianism.

units.la: Respondebunt forsan Calvinistæ nimis iniquè censeri verba Calvini, neque recte illum inde Arianum probari quod optime defendi hæc possint catholica distinctione, quâ Christum confitemur Deum & hominem, secundùm quam distinctionem, si dicatur Calvinus locutus fuisse, de Christo tantùm ut homine, apparebunt textus locaq; præcedentia calumniosè adducta.
units.tr: Perhaps the Calvinists will reply that the words of Calvin are judged far too unfairly, and that he is not rightly proved an Arian by these, since they can be well defended by the Catholic distinction by which we confess Christ to be God and man. If, according to that distinction, Calvin is said to have spoken only of Christ as man, the texts and the preceding passages, which have been slanderously cited, will appear otherwise.

units.la: Nimium est officiosa DominatioPatris
units.tr: Too officious is the lordship of Father Harscher,

units.la: Harfcheri, quod etiam non vocata patrocinium suscipit Calvinistarū, uti per contemptum vocat nos,qui verbum Dei absque fermento traditionum humanarum sequimur. Maiorem forte laudem sibi acquisivisset, si Liberium Papam ab Arianismo, Honorium Papam a Monothelitmo, Anastasium II. Papam a Nestorianismo vindicasset. Quāvis frustra in eo fuisset, quia Alphonsus a Castro ipse Pontificius scribit: qui historias legit, de his non dubitat, & paulò post: res est omnium manifestissima. Sed videamus egregium nostrum disputatorem.
units.tr: which takes up the defence of the Calvinists even though it was not called upon to do so, as he contemptuously calls us, who follow the Word of God without the leaven of human traditions. He would perhaps have won greater praise for himself if he had vindicated Pope Liberius from Arianism, Pope Honorius from Monothelitism, and Pope Anastasius II from Nestorianism. Yet he would have laboured in vain in this, because Alphonsus a Castro, himself a Papist, writes: whoever reads the histories does not doubt these things; and a little later: the matter is most evident to all. But let us look at our excellent disputant.

units.la: I. Scribit nos forsan responsuros, nimis iniquè censeri verba Calvini, neq; rectè illum Arianismi accusari: Item textus & loca præcedentia, calumniosè adducta. In hoc non errat Iesuita. Verissimum namque est verba & loca calumniosissimè adduci & tractari, non quidem ob distinctionem illam, quam producit Harscher, sed alias ob caussas graviores. Nempe quòd illa nefariè contorta, mutilata, à sensu & scopo Calvini aliena à Jesuitis citantur: quòd dicitur symbolum & concilium Nicenum negare, cui ille subscripsit: quòd dicitur negare Deitatem Filii, quam ille calidissimè contra Gentilem & Arianos teste Bellarmino defendit: quòd dicitur Filium, quâ Deum, Patri inferiorem & inæqualem facere, cùm is plus quàm centies ὁμοούσιον Patris & Filii confessus fuerit: quòd dicitur Filium facere tantùm secretarium & ministrum Patris, cùm hæc in ipsius scriptis non reperiantur. Hæc & similia calumniosè & mendaciter de Calvino & Orthodoxis recitata, sunt nobis caussa, cur coram tota Ecclesia conqueramur de iniqua illa & diabolica disputandi ratione.
units.tr: I. He writes that we will perhaps reply that the words of Calvin are judged too unfairly and that he is not rightly accused of Arianism; likewise that the texts and the preceding passages are cited slanderously. In this the Jesuit is not wrong. For it is most true that the words and passages are cited and treated most slanderously, not indeed on account of that distinction which Harscher brings forward, but for other, weightier reasons. Namely, because the Jesuits cite those passages wickedly twisted and mutilated, alien to the sense and purpose of Calvin; because it is said that he denies the Nicene creed and council, to which he subscribed; because it is said that he denies the Deity of the Son, which, according to Bellarmine, he defended most ardently against the Gentiles and the Arians; because it is said that he makes the Son, as God, inferior and unequal to the Father, although he confessed the Son to be consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father more than a hundred times; because it is said that he makes the Son merely a secretary and minister of the Father, although these things are not found in his writings. These and similar things, recited slanderously and falsely about Calvin and the orthodox, are our reason for complaining before the whole Church about that unjust and diabolical manner of disputing.

units.la: Magis adhuc calumniosè quod totam Ecclesiam nostram Arianismi accusat, cuius confessionem non ausus fuit producere, in qua confitemur: in Deitate tres personas consubstantiales & coæquales, distinctas quoad hypostases, quoad naturam vel essentiam ita coniunctas, ut sint unus Deus, essentiaque divina communis sit Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto. Quæ an ex Arii schola desumta sint, quivis amans veritatis christianus iudicare potest.
units.tr: Even more slanderous is that he accuses our whole Church of Arianism, whose confession he did not dare to produce, in which we confess: in the Deity three persons, consubstantial and co-equal, distinct as to their hypostases, yet so joined as to nature or essence that they are one God, and the divine essence is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Whether these things have been taken from the school of Arius, any Christian who loves the truth can judge.

units.la: II. Subiunctam distinctionem quod attinet, ita inepti non sumus, ut existimemus multis esse probandum, Christum, quâ hominem, Deo Patri inseriorem esse, aut inæqualem : aut non proprie Deum, aut improprie creatorem. Non ego vel in meis discipulis istas nugas ferrem. Quomodo respondeamus ad obiectiones Jesuiticas ex antecedentibus manifestum est, nec opus repetitione. Videantur duæ regulæ Augustini de quibus supra.
units.tr: As for the distinction added, we are not so foolish as to think that it must be proved to many that Christ, as man, is inferior and unequal to God the Father, or not properly God, or improperly the Creator. I would not tolerate these trifles even among my own disciples. How we reply to the Jesuitical objections is clear from what has gone before, and there is no need for repetition. Let the two rules of Augustine, mentioned above, be consulted.

units.la: III. In responsione ad fictam suam distinctionem valde occupatus est Harscher. Primo vocat sententiam Calvini blasphemum errorem, Bellarminus & Valentia catholicam assertionem. Secundò dicit phrases Calvini de humana Christi natura omnes nō posse intelligi. Et quis affirmavit? annon hoc est, ἀσεβαστεῖν? Tertiò testimonium, ex comment. in cap. 14. Johannis, Harscherus falsissimè citat. Vult Calvinus, inquit, hæc verba, Pater major me est, de natura divina sola, vel simul cum humana intelligenda esse, cùm alteri rei nec per somnium applicari possint. Nihil tale dixit Calvinus. Ita enim ille: Hic neque de humana Christi natura, neque de æterna ejus divinitate sermo habetur. Et postea; non confert hic Patris divinitatem cum sua, nec humanam suam naturam divina Patris essentia comparat, sed potius statum præsentem cælesti gloriæ, ad quam mox recipiendus erat. De reliquis verbis Harscheri, nempe, cùm alteri rei nec per somnium applicari possint, ne gry quidem habetur. An autem licet Jesuitis etiam cum facultate superiorum, tàm impunè mentiri?
units.tr: III. Harscher is very busy in replying to his feigned distinction. First, he calls Calvin's opinion a blasphemous error, and Bellarmine and Valentia call it a Catholic assertion. Secondly, he says that Calvin's phrases about the human nature of Christ cannot all be understood. And who has affirmed this? Is this not to act impiously [ἀσεβαστεῖν]? Thirdly, Harscher falsely cites a testimony from the commentary on chapter 14 of John. Calvin, he says, wishes the words the Father is greater than I to be understood of the divine nature alone, or of both together with the human, since they cannot be applied to anything else even in a dream. Calvin said nothing of the sort. For he says: Here there is discussion neither of the human nature of Christ nor of his eternal divinity. And afterwards: Here he does not compare the Father's divinity with his own, nor does he set his human nature against the divine essence of the Father, but rather the present state with the heavenly glory to which he was soon to be received. As for the remaining words of Harscher, namely, since they cannot be applied to anything else even in a dream, not even a grain of them is found. But is it permitted to Jesuits, even with the permission of their superiors, to lie so freely?

units.la: IV. Doctrinam Calvini lib. 2. Institt. cap. 14. propositam, Harscherus aut non intelligit, aut calumniatur. Eam hic dilucide explicabo. Non instituit Calvinus loco citato sermonem de Christo, quâ Deus unus est cum Patre & Spiritu sancto: sed, ut titulus capitis habet, de persona Mediatoris unica, & duabus eius naturis. Et §. 3. dicit, regnum sive dominium Christi duplex esse; Unum, cuius nullum est initium, & quod nullum habiturum est finem, hoc cum Patre & Spiritu sancto ab æterno in æternum obtinet. Nos vocamus regnum sive dominium essentiale & naturale.
units.tr: IV. Harscher either does not understand or slanders the doctrine of Calvin set out in book 2 of the Institutes, chapter 14. I will explain it clearly here. In the cited place Calvin does not institute a discussion of Christ as he is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but, as the title of the chapter says, of the unique person of the Mediator and his two natures. And in §3 he says that the kingdom or dominion of Christ is twofold: one, which has no beginning and will have no end, which he holds with the Father and the Holy Spirit from eternity to eternity. We call this an essential and natural kingdom or dominion.

units.la: Alterum quòd à Patre accepit, quod est ecclesia, ad quam illud dominium relationem habet particularem, quia totum comparatum ad ecclesiæ illius salutem promovendam & redemptionem peragendam Nos vocamus regnum œconomicu, personale, vicariu & donativu. Quia Christus illud obtinet partim donatione partim acquisitione per λύτρον quod solvit pro ecclesia redimeda. Unde dicitur Dominus ecclesiae, quia eam proprio sanguine sibi acquisivit, Act. 20: 28. De hoc dominio loquuntur sequentia loca, Psal. 2: 8. pete a me & dabo Gentes in haereditatem tuam & fines terrae in jus possessionis tuae Psal. 110:
units.tr: The other is that which he has received from the Father, which is the Church, to which that dominion bears a particular relation, since the whole is directed to promoting the salvation of that Church and accomplishing its redemption. We call this an economic, personal, vicarious and bestowed kingdom, because Christ holds it partly by gift and partly by acquisition, through the ransom [λύτρον] which he paid to redeem the Church. Hence he is called the Lord of the Church, because he acquired it for himself with his own blood, Acts 20:28. Of this dominion the following passages speak: Psalm 2:8, Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession. Psalm 110:

units.la: 1. Dixit Dominus Domino meo sede ad dextram meam, donec posuero inimicos tuos in scabellum pedum tuorum. Heb. 2: 2. quem (Filium) constituit haeredem omnium.
units.tr: 1. The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. Heb. 1:2, whom (the Son) he appointed heir of all things.

units.la: Haec, inquam, de dominio Christi oeconomico sunt intelligenda, quia aeternum illud & essentiale nec θέσει est, nec haereditas dici potest, nisi velis simul asserere, Filium a Deo Patre constitutum esse Deum, & Deitatem haereditario iure obtinere, quo nihil possit dici magis absurdum.
units.tr: These things, I say, are to be understood of the economic dominion of Christ, because that eternal and essential dominion is neither by adoption nor can it be called an inheritance, unless you wish at the same time to assert that the Son, appointed by God the Father, is God, and holds the Deity by hereditary right, than which nothing could be said to be more absurd.

units.la: Competit autem dominium hoc Christo, qua Mediator est, id est, secundum utramque naturam, & qua Deus & qua homo, estque Christi proprium, quod Patri traditurus est in fine mundi 1. Cor. 15: 24. Hanc ob causafam Calvinus dicit, Christum medium gradum constituere inter Deum & nos, quia non consideratur ut purus Deus, ficuti Pater, nec ut purus homo, sed ut θε ἀνθρώπως Deus & homo in una persona, secundùm illud vetus:
units.tr: Moreover, this dominion belongs to Christ as he is Mediator, that is, according to both natures, both as God and as man; and it is Christ's own, which he will deliver to the Father at the end of the world, 1 Cor. 15:24. For this reason Calvin says that Christ constitutes a middle rank between God and us, because he is not considered as pure God, as the Father is, nor as pure man, but as God-man [θεάνθρωπος], God and man in one person, according to that old saying:

units.la: Sum quod eram, nec eram quod sum, nunc dicor utrumq;.
units.tr: I am what I was, and I was not what I am; now I am called both.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim Christus ecclesiam redemit, ita eius factus est Dominus. Atqui eam redemit & quà Deus & quà homo. Ergo eiusdé Dominus est quâ Deus & quâ homo. Nam nisi Deus fuisset noster Mediator, se apud Deum interponere non ausus fuisset, nec potuisset infinitam Dei iram, Satanæ potestatem & mortem æterna tollere, aut imaginem Dei, Spiritus sancti dona & vitam æternam nobis impetrare. Unde in symbolo Apostolico, Filium Dei unigenitum ex Maria virgine natum confitemur Dominum nostrum. Hanc fidem Calvini etiam veteres Patres confessi sunt. Athanasius n. ad confessionem haeretici dicentis, εἰ μόνον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ Χριστὸς, ἢ εἰ μόνον Θεὸς, ἢ ἂν ὡς μέσος θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, si Christus esset tantum homo, vel tantum Deus, non esset medius inter Deum & homines) exclamat, Benedictus sit Deus in omnibus quod hæc confiteris Dialog. 5. de Trinit. Et Epiphanius docet Christum κατὰ τὰ ἐνάντια, secundum utraque, id est, secundum Deitatem & humanitatem, πρὸς τὰ ἀμφότερα μεσιτεύοντα, apud utrosque Deum & homines medium agere.
units.tr: For just as Christ redeemed the Church, so he became its Lord. But he redeemed it both as God and as man. Therefore he is the Lord of it both as God and as man. For unless he had been God, he would not have dared to interpose himself as our Mediator before God, nor could he have removed the infinite wrath of God, the power of Satan and eternal death, or obtained for us the image of God, the gifts of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. Hence in the Apostles' Creed we confess the only-begotten Son of God, born of the virgin Mary, to be our Lord. The ancient Fathers also confessed this faith of Calvin. For Athanasius, in reply to a heretic who said if Christ is only as man [εἰ μόνον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ Χριστός], or only God [εἰ μόνον Θεός], or as mediator between God and men [ἢ ὡς μέσος θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων], that is, if Christ were only man, or only God, he would not be a mediator between God and men, exclaims: Blessed be God, in all things, that you confess these, Dialogue 5 on the Trinity. And Epiphanius teaches that Christ, according to the contrary [κατὰ τὰ ἐναντία], that is, according to both, namely the Deity and the humanity, mediating [μεσιτεύοντα] between both, acts as mediator with both God and men.

units.la: Summa ergo huc redit, Filium Dei considerari vel secundum naturam divinam ἁπλῶς, eatenus si quis dicat Filium esse minorem Patre, aut in statu quodam intermedio inter Deum & hominem esse, verè is Arianus dici potest: aut οἰκονομικῶς, quatenus sese exinanivit, formam servi accepit, & homo factus est, eatenus si quis dicat in statu medio esse non Arianus sed Orthodoxus est. Neque hæc sunt contradictoria, quia unum re, substantiave fieri potest duplex, statu, modo & qualitate, ut regula habet. Calvinus autem cum in posteriori sensu de Christo locutus fuerit, inepte ipsum Arianismi accusat Harscherus, cum dicit, Calvinus ergo vere Arij sectator est.
units.tr: The sum of the matter comes to this. If someone says that the Son of God, considered simply [ἁπλῶς] according to the divine nature, is less than the Father, or that he stands in some intermediate state between God and man, then he may truly be called an Arian. But if someone says that he is in an intermediate state when considered economically [οἰκονομικῶς], in that he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was made man, then he is not an Arian but an Orthodox teacher. These positions do not contradict each other, because, as the rule has it, one thing in substance can be twofold in state, mode and quality. Calvin, when he spoke in the latter sense about Christ, is foolishly accused of Arianism by Harscher, who says: "Calvin, therefore, is truly a follower of Arius."

units.la: Haec de Calvino. Bezam nunc sub censuram vocat & clamat quòd Filii consubstantialitatem impugnet. Qui sic? Quia in confess. puncto primo art. 2. confiteatur, essentiam divinam esse realiter & vere & ab aeterno distinctam in tribus personis. Ergo, inquit, Filius est alia essentia quàm Pater & non consubstantialis. Non vidi, Deum testor, ullum librum in quo tot apertae falsationes testimoniorum reperiantur, ut in his parallelis Jesuiticis. Videtur Harscherus ex proposito voluisse mentiri. Dicit, Bezam Filii consubstantialitatem cum Patre loco citato impugnare, quam tamen ibidem rotunde fatetur his verbis: Sunt̄ hae personae consubstantiales & coaeternae æterna absq; ulla proprietatum aut relationum confusione, itemq; absq; ulla inter se imparitate sive inæqualitate. Quid magis perspicuum?
units.tr: So much for Calvin. Now he calls Beza before the censure and cries out that Beza assails the consubstantiality of the Son. On what grounds? "Because in the confession, point one, article 2, he professes that the divine essence is really and truly distinct from eternity in three persons." Therefore, he says, the Son is another essence than the Father and not consubstantial. I have not seen, God is my witness, any book in which so many open falsifications of testimonies are found as in these Jesuit parallels. Harscher seems to have deliberately wished to lie. He says that Beza, in the place cited, assails the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, yet Beza there plainly admits it in these words: "These persons are consubstantial and coeternal, eternal without any confusion of properties or relations, and likewise without any inequality or disparity among themselves." What could be clearer?

units.la: Observanda autem hic venit duplex falsitas, quâ decipit Harscherus lectorem, dum scribit, Bezam confiteri, essentiam divinam realiter distinctam esse in tribus personis. Primò illud realiter non est in confessione Bezæ, deinde non dixit in tribus personis, sed in tres personas, casu accusativo. Richeomi Jesuitæ hoc primum fuit λέξεως σφάλμα, quod Harscherus imitari maluit, quàm veritatem dicere.
units.tr: Here a twofold falsehood must be noted, by which Harscher deceives the reader when he writes that Beza confesses the divine essence to be "really distinct in three persons." First, the word "really" is not in Beza's confession; second, he did not write "in three persons" but "in three persons" in the accusative case, "in tres personas." This was the first verbal slip of the Jesuit Richeomus, which Harscher preferred to imitate rather than to tell the truth.

units.la: Tandem Psalterium nostrum producit, quod vocat musicam Arianam. Impudens os. Arguit nos quòd clarâ voce testemur in templis publicis, Christo nihil restare, nisi ut sit Deus. Unde sequatur ipsum non esse Deum, si ipsi restet, aut si est, non restare. Addit esse mendacium luculentum quocunq; modo nos torqueamus. Si verum effet quod de nobis scribit Harscher, non saltem mendacium, sed blasphemia effet insignis. At contrarium testabuntur quotquot sunt capita omnium Ecclesiarum reformatarum in Gallia, Belgio, Germania, & Helvetia. Latina nostra versio sic habet: Quid est mortalis. (אנוש emphaticè, denotans mortiferam & miseram hominis post lapsum conditionem) quòd memor sis ejus, aut Filius hominis, ut visites eum. Minorem quidem eum fecisti paulisper Angelis, sed gloriâ & majestate coronasti eum. Versio Gallica rhytmica sic habet: Adonc je di à part moy (ainsi comme Tout esbahi) & qu'est ce que de l'homme? D'auoir daigné de luy te souuenir Et de vouloir en ton soin le tenir? Tu las fait tel que plus il ne luy reste Fors d'estre un Ange en l'ayant (quant au reste Abondamment de gloire environné Rempli des biens & d'honneur couronné.
units.tr: At last he brings forward our Psalter, which he calls Arian music. Shameless mouth! He accuses us because we testify with a clear voice in public churches that "nothing remains for Christ except that he be God. Hence it would follow that he is not God, if anything remains for him, or if he is God, that nothing remains." He adds that this is "a manifest lie, however we twist it." If what Harscher writes about us were true, it would be not merely a lie but a notorious blasphemy. But the contrary will be attested by all the heads of the reformed churches in France, Belgium, Germany and Switzerland. Our Latin version reads thus: "What is man [mortalis] (enosh [אנוש], emphatically denoting man's deadly and wretched condition after the fall), that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You have made him a little less than the angels, but you have crowned him with glory and majesty." The French metrical version reads thus: "Then I say to myself, quite astonished, 'What is man, that you have deigned to remember him, and to hold him in your care? You have made him such that nothing more remains to him, except to be an angel in having (as to the rest) abundantly surrounded him with glory, filled with goods and crowned with honour.'"

units.la: In Germanico ita canimus.
units.tr: In German we sing it thus:

units.la: Dann muß ich mich verwundren vnd so sagen Was ist der mensch für den du sorg thust tragen Was ist deß menschen kind zu achten doch Daß du dich seinen anmimpst also hoch. Nur daß du ihn den Englen mit gar gleiche Geschaffen hast/ gemacht hastu ihn reiche Mit lob vnd ehr du ihne hast gezieret Mit heil herrlich geschmucket vnd coroniert.
units.tr: "Then I must marvel and so say: What is the man for whom you take such care? What is the child of man, that you should regard him so highly as to visit him? Only that you have made him with the angels nearly equal, you have made him rich with praise and honour, you have adorned him, crowned and glorified him with salvation."

units.la: Non diffiteor Maronem in prima sua compositione, ista verba posuisse fors estre Dieu, quod exemplar forte Richeomus vidit, qui primus hoc nostris obiecit. Sed primo Maro nihil de Christo cecinit, sed de homine communiter, quemadmodum etiam alii Interpretes hunc locum de homine mortali, ægro, misero, ut hebræus textus habet, intelligunt, & iudicant Apostolum hæc verba per sensum accommodativum Christo applicasse. Mariana in notis: ego hujus versus priorem partem de homine intelligo, in quo etiam Dei gloria apparet. Deinde, an solus Maro Arianus? annon etiam Chrysostomus & Hieronymus, aut Mariana Jesuita? Chrysostomus enim vertit, ὀλίγον ᾠδὴ θεῶ paululum à Deo. Hieronymus iuxta hebraicam veritatem, paulò minus à Deo. Sic etiam Theodotio & sexta editio, Mariana, h. à Deo, אלוהים enim Dei nomen est. Non potest charitas Jesuitica ferre in homine politico, quod fert in viris doctissimis & in scriptura versatissimis. Quanquam per אלוהים rectius Angeli intelliguntur.
units.tr: I do not deny that Maro, in his first composition, put in these words "perhaps being God" [fors estre Dieu], a reading which perhaps Richeomus saw, and who first objected it to our people. But first, Maro sang nothing about Christ, but about man in general; and other interpreters also understand this passage of mortal, sick, wretched man, as the Hebrew text has it, and judge that the Apostle applied these words to Christ by an accommodated sense [sensum accommodativum]. Mariana in his notes: "I understand the first part of this verse of man, in whom also the glory of God appears." Next, is Maro alone an Arian? Are not Chrysostom and Jerome also, or Mariana the Jesuit? For Chrysostom translates it "a little from God [ὀλίγον ᾠδὴ θεῶ]." Jerome, following the Hebrew truth, "a little less than God." So also Theodotion and the sixth edition, and Mariana, "from God": for elohim [אלוהים] is a name of God. Jesuit charity cannot endure in a political man what it tolerates in the most learned men and those most versed in Scripture. Although, by elohim, the angels are more rightly understood.

units.la: Testimonia ex scripturis citata nihil contra Calvinum, nihil contra Bezam aut fidem nostram. Sunt enim illa quibus ad Deitatem Christi probandam contra haereticos utimur, quibusque Calvinus contra Arianos & Gentilem fortiter pugnavit. Symbola verò tùm Apostolicum, tùm Athanasianum, tanquam verbo Dei consentanea, cum veteri ecclesia amplectimur.
units.tr: The testimonies cited from Scripture are nothing against Calvin, nothing against Beza or our faith. For they are the very passages which we use to prove the deity of Christ against the heretics, and with which Calvin fought vigorously against the Arians and the Gentile. The creeds, however, both the Apostles' and the Athanasian, as agreeing with the Word of God, we embrace together with the ancient Church.

units.la: PARALLELUM II.
units.tr: Parallel II.

units.la: In Parallelo fecundo scribit Harfcher in quàm varias sectas Reformati sint distincti, & numerat ultrà centum. In tertio verò parallelo tractat, quâ ratione iidem reformati vel fe mutuò insectentur, vel inter fe consentiant.
units.tr: In the second parallel Harscher writes of how many different sects the Reformed have been divided into, and he counts more than a hundred. In the third parallel, he treats of how the same Reformed either attack one another or agree among themselves.

units.la: Revera Jesuitæ meras fabulas fcribunt, quod eò maiori cum audacia faciunt, quia laici in papatu puri sunt pythagorici, quorum summa lex est: digito compesce labellum: coguntur enim vel inviti credere quidquid hi Magistri præits predicant. Nam si fides divina (definiente Canisio) est quâ creditur, quod ecclesia Romana proponit, sive id in scriptura sacra expresse extet, sive non. Cur, non fides humana Pontificia, definiretur quòd sit, quâ creditur quod proponunt ac scribunt Jesuitæ sive verum sit, sive falsum?
units.tr: Indeed, the Jesuits write sheer fables, and they do so all the more boldly because the laity under the papacy are pure Pythagoreans, whose supreme law is: press your little lip with your finger. For they are forced, even against their will, to believe whatever these masters put forward. For if divine faith (to use Canisius's definition) is that by which one believes what the Roman church proposes, whether or not it is expressly contained in holy Scripture, why should Papist human faith not be defined as that by which one believes what the Jesuits propose and write, whether it is true or false?

units.la: Quòd ergo Harfcherus ex suis autoribus nobis infestis & adversis calumniosis titulis nos onerat vocans Sacramentarios, Zwvinglianos, Calvinistas, Servetianos, Anabaptistas, Libertinos, Trinitarios, Adessenarios, Metamorphistas, Iscariotistas, Energicos, Arrhabonarios, Epicureos, Atheos, Significativos, Tropistas, Neutrales, Iconoclastas &c, quòd, inquam, ita nos appellat, totque sectas in ecclesia nostra fingit. dico primò ipsum cœlum terræ miscere, dùm omnis generis sectarios absque omni iudicio, vel saltem malo proposito, partes facit nostræ ecclesiæ. Quid enim ad nos Libertini, Servetiani, Anabaptistæ, Trinitarii, Athei? Hi enim omnes à nobis sunt reiecti, communionem nobiscum nullam habentes. Contra Serveti blasphemias scripsit Calvinus, ut notum est. Cuius quidem hæretici sententiæ tam horrendæ fuerunt, ut Genevæ iusto supplicio assectus sit. Libertinos vocat Calvinus vertiginosos, qui Spiritus Magisterium fastuosissimè sissime obtendentes, lectionem scripturæ respuunt. Vocat item nebulones, qui extrema vesania vexentur Instit. lib. i. cap. 9. §. 1.
units.tr: As for Harscher burdening us with calumnious titles taken from his authors, who are hostile and adverse to us, calling us Sacramentarians, Zwinglians, Calvinists, Servetians, Anabaptists, Libertines, Trinitarians, Adessenarians, Metamorphists, Iscariotists, Energists, Arrhabonarians, Epicureans, Atheists, Significativists, Tropists, Neutrals, Iconoclasts, and so on, and so inventing so many sects in our church, I say first that he mixes heaven and earth, when he makes all sorts of sectaries parts of our church without any judgment, or at least with a malicious purpose. For what have we to do with Libertines, Servetians, Anabaptists, Trinitarians and Atheists? All of these have been rejected by us, and we have no communion with them. Calvin wrote against the blasphemies of Servetus, as is well known, and the opinions of that heretic were so horrible that he was put to a just death at Geneva. Calvin calls the Libertines giddy men, who most proudly claim the magisterium of the Spirit and reject the reading of Scripture. He also calls them scoundrels, who are tormented by extreme madness (Institutes, book 1, chapter 9, section 1).

units.la: Quod si igitur Libertini vocamur à Becano, Servetiani ab aliis, mera est calumnia, ex malitia nobis imposita. Sed bene habet, non est discipulus supra Doctorem, nec servus supra Dominum, si ipsum Patremfamilias Beelzebulem vocarunt, quanto magis domesticos ejus, inquit Christus Matth. 10: 24, 25.
units.tr: So if we are called Libertines by Becanus and Servetians by others, it is pure calumny, imposed on us out of malice. But it is well: The disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household, says Christ (Matthew 10:24, 25).

units.la: Sed hæc nugamenta vel ex eo pervideri possunt, quod nemo Jesuitarum ferret, si quis diceret, Papatum esse in multas sectas divisum. Esse Legendarios, Missaticos, Transsubstantiarios, Papistas, Romanistas, Traditionarios, Thomistas, Scotistas, Infallibiliarios, Nominales, Reales. Et quia Pontificii cum Samaritis scripturas imperfectionis accusant, cum Offenis per creaturas iurant, cum Carpocratianis imagines, cum Cajanis Angelos, cum Armenianis crucem, cum Collyridianis B. Virginem adorant, cum Manichaeis coniugium Clericorum prohibent, cum Montanistae ieiunia imperant, cum Marcionitae fæminis baptismum permittunt, cum Heracleonitae morientes oleo cum certis precibus ungunt, cum Catharis de meritis suis gloriantur, esse Pontificios Samaritanos, Offenios, Carpocratianos, Cajanos, Armenianos, Collyridianos, Manichaeos, Heracleonitas, Catharas?
units.tr: But these trifles can be seen from this alone: no Jesuit would tolerate it if someone said that the papacy is divided into many sects, namely Legendarians, Missaticians, Transubstantiarians, Papists, Romanists, Traditionarians, Thomists, Scotists, Infallibilists, Nominalists, Realists. And since the Papists charge Scripture with imperfection together with the Samaritans, swear by creatures together with the Ophites, venerate images together with the Carpocratians, angels together with the Cainites, the cross together with the Armenians, and the Blessed Virgin together with the Collyridians, forbid the marriage of clergy together with the Manichaeans, impose fasts together with the Montanists, permit women to baptize together with the Marcionites, anoint the dying with oil and certain prayers together with the Heracleonites, and boast of their own merits together with the Cathari, why should they not be called Samaritans, Ophites, Carpocratians, Cainites, Armenians, Collyridians, Manichaeans, Heracleonites and Cathari?

units.la: De reliquis nominibus, quod ex nostris alii sint Significativi, alii Tropistae (quia quidam in verbis Institutionis Coenae, voculam est per significat, quidam per tropum explicant) alii Energetici, Arrhabonarij, Neutrales, Iconoclastae, quàm ridiculè omnia?
units.tr: As for the other names, that some of ours are Significativists, others Tropists (because some explain the little word est in the words of the Institution of the Supper as signifies, and some as a trope), others Energists, Arrhabonarians, Neutrals and Iconoclasts, how ridiculous all of this is!

units.la: An illico nova secta facienda ex unius loci varia explicatione, sensu eodem manente? Quod si placeret nobis cum ipsis ineptire, quid non possemus? Ecce specimen. In verbis institutionis Eucharistiæ, particula Hoc Innocentio II. nihil demonstrat, sed profertur recitative: Thomæ idem est quod significatum per hoc. Rich. de S. Victore, demonstrans panem transsubstantiandum: Bellarmino, accidentia panis: Thomæ de Argent. Corpus Christi. Verbum EST, Thomæ idem valet, quod continetur. Argentinæ, idem quod erit. Bonaventurae, idem quod transmutatur. CORPUS, Durando significat corpus non quantum: Becano quantum sed inextensum: Bellarmino utrumque sed non commensuratum. Dicamus ergò ut nugemur, diversas esse sectas in pontificia religione, nam alios esse Recitativos, alios Significativos, alios Transsubstantiandos, alios Transsubstantiatos, alios Accidentarios, alios Corporistas, alios Contentarios, alios Eristas, alios Transmutarios, alios Extensivos, alios Commensurarios.
units.tr: Is a new sect to be made at once out of the various explanations of one passage, while the sense remains the same? And if it pleased us to play the fool with them as they do with us, what could we not do? Here is a specimen. In the words of the institution of the Eucharist, the particle Hoc demonstrates nothing for Innocent II, but is uttered recitatively. For Thomas it means the same as signified by this; for Richard of St Victor, demonstrating the bread to be transubstantiated; for Bellarmine, the accidents of the bread; for Thomas of Argentina, the body of Christ. The word EST, for Thomas, has the same force as is contained; for the Argentine, the same as will be; for Bonaventure, the same as is transmuted. As for CORPUS, for Durandus it signifies a body not quantitative; for Becanus, quantitative but unextended; for Bellarmine, both, but not commensurate. Let us say then, in jest, that there are diverse sects in the Papist religion: for some are Recitativists, others Significativists, others Transubstantiandists, others Transubstantiatists, others Accidentarians, others Corporists, others Contentarians, others Eristics, others Transmutarians, others Extensivists, others Commensurarians.

units.la: Atque hæ sunt res illa sacræ scilicet, quas in societate Jesu, & in diatribis
units.tr: And these are the sacred matters which the Jesuits treat in the Society of Jesus and in their

units.la: suis theologicis tractant Jesuitæ, magno nostrorum politicorum cum admiratione & scandalo, addo etiam confirmatione in religione nostra. Expertus loquor, idque ex ore multorum qui super istis parallelis mecum contulerunt. Adeo verum est quod Augustinus dicit: lib. cont. mend. cap. 4. Dum per mendacium tenditur ut doceatur fides, id agitur ut nulli habenda fit fides.
units.tr: theological disputations, to the great admiration and scandal of our politicians, and, I may add, to the confirmation of our own religion. I speak from experience, and from the mouths of many who have compared these parallels with me. So true is what Augustine says (On Lying, against Mendacium, chapter 4): When one tries by lying to teach the faith, the result is that no one can be trusted.

units.la: Obiiciet Jesuita; id tamen negari non posse; post exortam illam novam reformationem, per Lutherum, Zwinglium & Calvinum, ianuam fuisse apertam ad hæreses omne genus Gentili, Blandratæ, Serveto, Anabaptistis, Samosatenianis &c. quod in papatu ante non factum. Respondeo, Reformationi hoc per se & fidei orthodoxæ tribui non potest, sed malitiæ hominum & invidiæ Diaboli. Id enim plerumque agit Satan & vetus est ipsius artificium, orienti soli salvificæ doctrinæ nubes & nebulas obiicere, ut eius splendor obscuretur. Quod etiam initio temporis Novi Testamenti factitavit. Nam seculo primo vivente adhuc Johanne Evangelista, orta fuit haeresis Nicolaitarum, Ebionitarum, & Cerinthianorum, contra quos Evangelium suum conscripsit, ut docent Epiphanius & Hieronymus. Et hi haeresiarchae omnes erant ex Christianis. Consideret Harscher parallela a se conscripta.
units.tr: The Jesuit will object that this cannot be denied: after that new reformation arose through Luther, Zwingli and Calvin, the door was opened to heresies of every kind, to Gentile, Blandrata, Servetus, the Anabaptists, the Samosatenians and so on, which had not happened before under the papacy. I reply that this cannot be attributed to the Reformation itself, nor to orthodox faith, but to the malice of men and the envy of the Devil. For this is what Satan usually does, and it is his old trick: to throw clouds and mists before the rising sun of saving doctrine, so that its splendour is darkened. He did this also at the beginning of the New Testament age. For in the first century, while the Evangelist John was still alive, the heresies of the Nicolaitans, the Ebionites and the Cerinthians arose, against which he wrote his Gospel, as Epiphanius and Jerome teach. And all these heresiarchs were from among Christians. Let Harscher consider the parallels he has written.

units.la: Verum dicet amplius: hi omnes ex vobis orti sunt, quia Hedio conqueritur de suis Evangelicis (quod & catholici passim per Germanias, Galliasque perdolenter in ipsis videmus ut scribit Lindanus) ex Catholicis fieri Lutheranos, ex Lutheranis Zwinglianos, ex Zwinglianis Swenckfeldianos tum mox Atheos sive Epicureos.
units.tr: But he will say further: all these came from you, because Hedio complains of his own Evangelicals (which Catholics also see everywhere in Germany and France, to their great distress, as Lindanus writes) that from Catholics Lutherans are made, from Lutherans Zwinglians, from Zwinglians Schwenckfeldians, and soon after Atheists or Epicureans.

units.la: Cur ex Pontificiis Lutherani, ex Lutheranis Zwingliani fiant, illi viderint, cur ex orthodoxis aliquando fiant haeretici, pro nobis respondeat Tertullianus, quando vetustam Romanae eccle-siae, fiæ,& simplicem veramq; fidem (quam etiam ecclesiæ nostræ cum omni pietate amplectuntur) describit, lib. de præscriptionibus adversus hæreticos, pag. 109. his verbis: Videamus quid didicerit (vetus Romana ecclesia) quid docuerit, cum Aphricanis quoque ecclesiis contesserarit. Vnum Deum novit creatorem universitatis, & Christum Iesum ex virgine Maria, filium Dei creatoris, & carnis resurrectionem: legem & Prophetas cum Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis miscet, & inde potat fidem eam: aqua (baptismo) signat, sancto spiritu vestit, Eucharistia pascit, martyrio exhortatur, & ita adversus hanc institutionem neminem recipit. Hæc est institutio, non dico jam quæ futuras hæreses prænuntiabat, sed de qua hæreses prodierunt. Sed non fuerunt ex illa, ex quo factæ sunt adversus illam. Etiam de Oliva nucleo & mitis & optimæ, & necessariæ, asper oleaster exoritur, etiam de papavere fici gratissimæ & suavissimæ, ventosa & vana caprificus exurgit. Ita & hæreses de nostra fructifructificarunt non nostrae: degeneres veritatis grano & mendacio sylvestres. Hactenus Tertullianus.
units.tr: Why Lutherans come from Papists and Zwinglians from Lutherans, let them look to it. Why orthodox men sometimes become heretics, let Tertullian answer for us, when he describes the ancient Roman church, its simple and true faith (which our churches too embrace with all piety), in his book On Prescription against Heretics, page 109, in these words: Let us see what the ancient Roman church learned and taught, what it has in common with the African churches. It knows one God, the creator of the universe, and Christ Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, the Son of God the Creator, and the resurrection of the flesh. It joins the Law and the Prophets with the Evangelical and Apostolic writings, and from them draws that faith. It seals it with water (baptism), clothes it with the Holy Spirit, feeds it with the Eucharist, and encourages it to martyrdom; and so it admits no one who opposes this teaching. This is the teaching, I am not now speaking of what foretold the heresies to come, but from which the heresies came forth. But they were not from it; they came out after they were made against it. Also, from the kernel of the olive, which is gentle, excellent and necessary, the harsh wild olive arises; and from the poppy of the fig, which is most pleasant and sweet, the windy and empty wild fig springs up. So also heresies have sprung from our fruit, they have borne fruit not ours: degenerate, wild, from the grain of truth and of lies. Thus far Tertullian.

units.la: PARALLELUM III.
units.tr: PARALLELUM III.

units.la: Exempla insectantium sese sectariorum.
units.tr: Examples of sectarians attacking one another.

units.la: In parallelo tertio duo facit Jesuita, primo Reformatorum dissensiones & varias easque aculeatas contra se invicem scriptiones commemorat. Deinde in quibus partibus consentiant, ostendit.
units.tr: In the third parallel the Jesuit does two things. First he recounts the dissensions among the Reformed and their various and biting writings against one another. Then he shows in which points they agree.

units.la: Circa primum non multum contradico Harschero, nam proh dolor & proh pudor ingens fuisse & etiamnum esse certamen Theologorum Reformatorum de quibusdam fidei articulis, verissimum est. In quo plus quàm vel pietas vel christiana charitas permittit, affectibus indulgent. Sed non pariter inter partes litigantes. Nam quod nostras ecclesias attinet & potissimùm Helveticas, suspirarunt illæ aliquoties, quando tot coccysmos, & tot amarulenta & virulenta Theologorum scripta viderunt & legerunt. Neque tamen harum pastores obtrectationis & invidentiæ funem cum adversariis reciprocarunt, aut convitium pro convitio reddiderunt, sæpius obiicientes Apostolicum illud: si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos ejusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesiæ Dei 1. Cor.11.16. Videantur nostrorum Irenica & adhortationes ad unanimem consensum in negotio religionis Evangelicæ.
units.tr: On the first point I do not greatly contradict Harscherus. It is very true that, to our shame and sorrow, the contest among the Reformed theologians over certain articles of faith has been, and still is, enormous. In it they give free rein to their passions more than piety or Christian charity allows. But this does not apply equally to all the parties in dispute. As for our churches, especially the Helvetic, they have often groaned when they saw and read so many squabbles and so many bitter and venomous writings of theologians. Yet their ministers have not returned the rope of envy and detraction to their adversaries, nor have they paid insult for insult, but have often quoted that apostolic saying: if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither does the Church of God (1 Cor. 11:16). Let our Irenica and exhortations to unanimous agreement in the matter of the Evangelical religion be consulted.

units.la: Tria illa exempla quæ Harscherus in præsenti parallelo adducit huiusmodi sunt, ut nemo illa iustè reprehendere possit. Non primum, quod est Zwinglij, qui in libello de vera & falsa religione, non nominatis adversariis (quod modestiæ est) vocat homines obstinatos & invidentes aliis dona Dei, qui more furiosorum hominum, criminentur alios, cùm vident eos veritatem Dei in lucem proferre, quod mallent fieri à se. Credibile omninò est, Zvvinglium hæc de Luthero dixisse, sed tamen verissima sunt, utpote quæ ex illius temporis historia facilè demonstrari possent. Idem fecit olim Gregorius septimus Episcopus Romanus, qui Johannem Episcopum Hierofolymitanũ, universalis Episcopi titulum quærentem, præcursorem Antichristi appellavit.
units.tr: The three examples that Harscherus adduces in the present parallel are of such a kind that no one could justly find fault with them. Not the first, which is that of Zwingli, who in his little book on the true and false religion, without naming his adversaries (which is a mark of modesty), calls men obstinate and envious of others' gifts from God, who, like madmen, accuse others when they see them bringing the truth of God to light, which they would rather have done by themselves. It is quite credible that Zwingli said this of Luther, but it is nonetheless most true, since it could easily be shown from the history of that time. Gregory the Seventh, Bishop of Rome, did the same long ago, when he called John, Bishop of Jerusalem, who sought the title of universal bishop, a forerunner of Antichrist.

units.la: Nec secundum,quod est Calvini, qui discipulos Lutheri, Magistro thrasonicos aliquos titulos tribuentes, præcipuè quòd ipsum ultimum Eliam appellarent, reprehendit, dicens, ipsos Johannem Baptistam titulo suo, quo Christus ipsum ornavit, spoliare, & Deo iniuriam facere, ac si manus eius ita esset præcisa ut nullum præstantiorem aut parem mittere posset. In quo Calvinus procul dubio Harscherum non habebit adversarium.
units.tr: Nor the second, which is that of Calvin, who rebuked the disciples of Luther for bestowing boastful titles on their master, and especially for calling him the last Elijah. He says that they despoil John the Baptist of the title with which Christ himself honoured him, and do wrong to God, as if his hand were so cut off that he could send no greater or equal. In this Harscherus will certainly not find Calvin an adversary.

units.la: Nec tertium quod est Pastorum Tigurinorum qui pluribus lacesiti à Luthero (imprimis post receptum Carolstadiu ab Helvetiis) eundem exemplo Prophetarum & Apostolorum ad modestiam & fraternam charitatem adhortantur, in sua apologia, & dicunt ipsum pertinaciorem in opinionibus efferri insolentiâ nimiâ, & Satanæ tradere illos, qui sententiæ suæ subscribere nolint. In quo nihil dixerunt, quod charitati christianæ sit contrarium.
units.tr: Nor the third, which is that of the Pastors of Zurich, who, provoked by many attacks from Luther (especially after Carlstadt was received by the Swiss), exhort him, by the example of the Prophets and Apostles, to modesty and brotherly charity in their apology. They say that he is too proud in his opinions, carried away by excessive arrogance, and hands over to Satan those who refuse to subscribe to his opinion. In this they said nothing contrary to Christian charity.

units.la: Cæterùm ratiocinatio Harscheriana ab istis contentionibus ad hærefin Arianorum concludendam omni fundamento caret. Nam ecclesiæ nunquam defuerunt contentiones & rixæ. Jam olim in ecclesia Corinthiaca dissidia exstiterunt, quod noverat Paulus 1.Cor. 11: 18. imò prædixerat oportere esse hæreses, ut probati manifesti fiant, ibid. v. 19. Nihilominus tamen ipsos in praefatione epistolae vocat ecclesiam Dei, & sanctificatos Jesu Christi. Augustinus epist. 118. ad Januarium dicit, Se cum dolore & gemitu vidisse multas infirmorum perturbationes fieri per quorundam fratrum contentiosam obstinationem. Ecce contentiosos & obstinatos vocat fratres.
units.tr: Moreover, Harscher's reasoning, which from these contentions concludes to the heresy of the Arians, has no foundation at all. The Church has never lacked contentions and quarrels. Already long ago there were divisions in the church of Corinth, which Paul knew of (1 Cor. 11:18), and indeed he had foretold that there must be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest (ibid., v. 19). Nevertheless, in the preface of the letter he calls these same people the church of God and those sanctified in Jesus Christ. Augustine, in letter 118 to Januarius, says that he had seen with grief and groaning many disturbances of the weak caused by the contentious obstinacy of certain brothers. Behold, he calls the brothers contentious and obstinate.

units.la: De toto autem hoc argumento recte Chrysostomus: Gentilis mihi dicit vellem fieri Christianus, sed tot sunt inter vos pugnae, ut cui adhaeream nesciam: quilibet dicit, ego verum dico, cui credam nescio: hoc multum pro nobis, nam omnes scripturas recepimus, quae cum sint simplices & apertae facile tibi erit judicare, si quis illis consentiat verus est Christianus, si contra pugnat procul est ab hoc canone, Hom. 33. in Act. Apost.
units.tr: On this whole subject Chrysostom rightly says: A Gentile says to me, I would like to become a Christian, but there are so many battles among you that I do not know whom to cling to. Each says, I speak the truth; I do not know whom to believe. This is much in our favour, for we have received all the Scriptures, which, since they are simple and plain, will be easy for you to judge. If someone agrees with them, he is a true Christian; if he fights against them, he is far from this rule (Hom. 33 on Acts).

units.la: Haec non eo fine a me dicuntur quasi laudare aut approbare velim, odia mutua, & ex his ortas illas amarulentas invectivas, & Theologis indignissima scommata, sed ut ne iudicemus ante tempus, aut festucam videamus in oculis fratris, trabem autem in oculo nostro non animadvertamus.
units.tr: I do not say these things as though I wished to praise or approve the mutual hatreds, the bitter invectives arising from them, and the most unworthy mockeries of theologians, but so that we may not judge before the time, or see the speck in our brother's eye while not noticing the beam in our own.

units.la: An enim nullæ contentiones, discordiæ nullæ inter Pontificios? quod tam audacter hæc, quamvis non magni momenti nobis obiicit Jesuita? De clandestinis non dicam, de publicis loquatur libellus a Monacho quodam S. Benedicti ordinis editus, cum titulo Astrum inexstinctum item alius ab Alphonso de Vargas Toletano conscriptus, autore pontificio, continens relationem ad Reges & Principes Christianos, in qua, ut ipse ait, Jesuitarum erga Reges ac populos, optime de ipsis meritos, infidelitas, ergaq; ipsum Pontificem perfidia, contumelia & in fidei rebus novandi libido illustribus documentis comprobatur.
units.tr: Or are there no contentions and no discords among the Papists? Why does the Jesuit so boldly throw these things at us, though they are of little importance? I will say nothing of the secret quarrels; let him consider the public ones, in the little book published by a certain monk of the Order of St Benedict under the title Astrum inextinctum, and another written by Alphonso de Vargas of Toledo, a papist author, containing a report addressed to Christian kings and princes, in which, as he himself says, the faithlessness of the Jesuits towards kings and peoples, who have deserved so well of them, and their treachery and insolence towards the Pope himself, and their lust for innovation in matters of faith, are proved by clear documents.

units.la: Ego pauca huc reponam, ut videat Lector exemplum insectantium sese Monachorum.
units.tr: I will set down a few things here, so that the reader may see an example of monks attacking one another.

units.la: De Monachis ita Iacobus Kellerus Iesuita in cavea Turturis cap. 17. Haeretici maximè in opinione confirmantur, quod intra suarum regionum fines nihil generosum & excellens (in Monasteriis) sed meri pepones, allia & nasturtia nascantur. Cap. 14. In Monasteriis multitudo fuit malorum, raritas bonorum. Pharisaei domum orationis verterunt in speluncam latronum. Vetus ibi regula laudatur, novis moribus vivitur. Pronae in casum animae pendent. Sunt ibi ulcera, vulnera, putredines.
units.tr: Concerning the monks, Jacob Keller, Jesuit, in the Cage of the Turtle-dove, chapter 17, says thus: Heretics are especially confirmed in their opinion because within the borders of their own regions nothing noble or excellent grows (in the monasteries), but only mere melons, garlic and cress. Chapter 14. In the monasteries there is a multitude of evils and a scarcity of good men. The Pharisees have turned the house of prayer into a den of thieves. The old rule is praised, but they live by new customs. Souls hang close to ruin. There are ulcers, wounds and putrefactions there.

units.la: Ex Astro inexstincto: Dicunt Iesuitae, quod Ordines, id est Monachi, exceptis Iesuitis omnes, vineam sibi commissam ipsi exterminaverint, quòd domos orationis in latronum speluncas converterint, quòd multò maius quàm ullum genus hominum Ecclesiæ damnū intulerint, quòd hodie quoque in Monasteriis Germaniæ sint ulcera, vulnera, putredines, homines otiosi, ignavi, inutilia
units.tr: From Astrum inextinctum: The Jesuits say that the Orders, that is the monks, all except the Jesuits, have destroyed the vineyard entrusted to them; that they have turned the houses of prayer into dens of thieves; that they have done far more harm to the Church than any other class of men; and that today too in the monasteries of Germany there are ulcers, wounds and putrefactions, men idle, lazy, useless

units.la: Ex astro inextincto: ... utilia terræ pondera, ventres pigri, stupidæ pecudes.
units.tr: From Astrum inextinctum: ... heavy burdens on the earth, lazy bellies, stupid cattle.

units.la: Quid ad hæc Monachi? studiose ferram reciprocant, ac Jesuitarum vitam, mores & doctrinam nigro theta notant.
units.tr: What do the monks reply to this? They eagerly strike back with the iron, and mark the life, morals and teaching of the Jesuits with a black theta.

units.la: 1. Qui legerit hist. Societ. par. 2. (inquit Alphonsus de Vargas) obstupescet, scio, ad tantam Jesuitarum in mentiendo audaciam, cum ipsis etiam Societatis primoribus, qui summam virtutis ac fidei opinionem apud magnos Principes obtinent, adeo verecundia non sit de rebus in propatulo positis palam mentiri. p. 21.
units.tr: 1. He who has read the second part of the history of the Society (says Alphonso de Vargas), will be astonished, I know, at such boldness in lying among the Jesuits, even among the leaders of the Society, who hold the highest reputation for virtue and faith with great princes; so little shame do they have in openly lying about matters that are plainly before everyone. p. 21.

units.la: 2. Jesuitæ à Rege Catholico petierunt, ut novam Madriti Academiam conderet, eique dena aureorum millia annui vectigalis constitueret. Huic Societatis postulationi Universitates sive Academiæ Hispaniarum libello ad Regem missō, typisque descripto intercessere: in quo Jesuitas describunt, ut homines palam avaros, insatiabiles, æruscatores, regiorum vectigalium sures, arrogantes, ambitiosos, Principum assentatores, aulicos, & negotiis secularibus ubique se implicantes, fraudulentos, mendaces, veritatis interversores, infamatores virtutis, vitæ religiosæ hostes, deliciarum amatores, impostores pietatis velo opertos, lupos in vestimentis ovium, novitatum amicos. Sanctorum Doctorum contemptores, Lutheri ac Calvini partiarios, ac de hæresi suspectos, pacis publicæ perturbatores, Diabolicæ industriæ homines, serpentesipsosque Cacodæmones, ac omnibus cavendos ac fugiendos, pag. 37, 38.
units.tr: 2. The Jesuits asked the Catholic King to found a new Academy at Madrid, and to assign to it ten thousand gold pieces of annual revenue. The Universities or Academies of Spain intervened against this request of the Society by a little book sent to the King and printed, in which they describe the Jesuits as men openly avaricious, insatiable, extortioners, thieves of royal revenues, arrogant, ambitious, flatterers of princes, courtiers, and everywhere entangled in secular business; fraudulent, liars, subverters of truth, defamers of virtue, enemies of the religious life, lovers of pleasures, impostors covered with a veil of piety, wolves in sheep's clothing, friends of novelties, despisers of the holy Doctors, partisans of Luther and Calvin, suspected of heresy, disturbers of public peace, men of diabolical industry, serpents, indeed Cacodaemons, and to be avoided and fled by all. p. 37, 38.

units.la: Bone Deus quot tituli! Potuisset ne quis credere, hæc dicta scriptave esse ab ipsis Pontificiis, quod nemo aulus fuisset facere ex nobis? Non audeo plura addere ex Astro inexstincto, nam hæc summam continent reliquorum.
units.tr: Good God, what a list of titles! Could anyone have believed that these things were said or written by the Papists themselves, which no one of us would have dared to say? I will not venture to add more from the Astrum inextinctum, for these contain the sum of the rest.

units.la: 3. Doctrinam verò Jesuitarū, quam Anthonius Sanctarellus in peculiari tractatu de hæresi & potestate summi Pontificis conscripsit, Theologi Parisienses condemnarunt veluti exitialem & pestilentem meritoq; damnandam, aversandam, detegstandam & abhorrendam, cum sit nova, falsa erronea, verbo Dei contraria, pacis publicæ perturbativa, Regnorum, Statuum, rerumq; publicarum eversiva, subditos ab obedientia & subiectione avocans, & ad factiones, rebelliones, seditiones & Principum parricidia excitans.
units.tr: 3. The doctrine of the Jesuits, which Anthony Sanctarelli wrote in a special treatise on heresy and the power of the supreme Pontiff, the Parisian theologians condemned as deadly and pestilential, and rightly to be damned, avoided, uncovered and abhorred, since it is new, false, erroneous, contrary to the Word of God, disturbing public peace, subversive of kingdoms, states and commonwealths, calling subjects away from obedience and submission, and stirring up factions, rebellions, seditions and the murder of princes.

units.la: Animadvertis ne Lector, quomodo Harscherus festucam videritin oculis nostris, trabem autem non viderit in oculo suo? Sed hoc Hypocritarum est ut Christus docet, Matt. 7: 3. Pergit Harscherus.
units.tr: Do you notice, reader, how Harscherus has seen the speck in our eyes, but has not seen the beam in his own? But this is the mark of hypocrites, as Christ teaches (Matt. 7:3). Harscherus goes on.

units.la: CONCORDANTIA.
units.tr: CONCORDANCE.

units.la: Discordantium sectariorum.
units.tr: Of the discordant sectarians.

units.la: FRidericus Staphylus in sua apologia (ut refert Prateolus in elencho alphabetico lib. 17. titulo Sectarij) scribit: omnes sectarios unanimi consensu quatuor articulos, praeter illos jam pridem perpetua dissensione intellectuq; contrario penitus convulserunt, retinere.
units.tr: Friedrich Staphylus, in his apology (as Prateolus reports in the alphabetical index, book 17, under the title Sectarii), writes that all the sectarians, by unanimous consent, retain four articles, apart from those which have long since been utterly shaken by their perpetual disagreement and contrary interpretations.

units.la: Planè angelicam nobis reliquit Tertullianus patientiæ ideam. Ideam dico, quia vix cadunt in hominem quamdiu hoc corporis ergastulum circumfert, quæ de patientia scripsit lib. de patient. pag. 16. Dicit eam habere vultum tranquillum & placidum, frontem puram, nulla mæroris aut iræ rugositate contractam. Divinus planè sit homo qui Jesuitarum libros & imprimis quoque que hæc parallela legat, nec frontem contrahat mœroris aut iræ rugositate. Adeo multa de ecclesiis nostris, & à veritate & fide nostra aliena, adeo multa scommata, multaque mendacia absque fine in iis commemorantur: Vocat nos subinde Sectarios, Hæreticos, Arianos, impuros bufones & quid non? Ex schola pharisaica hæc sunt deprompta, apud quos Christus nullam aliam gratiam meruit, quàm, dæmonium habes, Joh. 7: 20. Est homo edax, vinipotor, amicus peccatorum Matt. 11: 19. & per contemptum, Fabri filius, Matt. 13: 55. Omnia item ipsius dicta falsò exposita. Id quod etiam nobis evenit, ut ex iam dictis & adhuc dicendis manifestum est.
units.tr: Tertullian has indeed left us an angelic idea of patience. I say an idea, because scarcely does a human being fall into it while he carries this prison of the body. In his book on patience (p. 16) he writes that it has a calm and gentle countenance, a clear brow, not drawn together by any wrinkle of sorrow or anger. A man would have to be divine indeed who could read the books of the Jesuits, and especially these parallels, without his brow being drawn together by the wrinkles of sorrow or anger. So many things about our churches, so many things alien both to the truth and to our faith, so many jests and endless lies are recited in them. From time to time they call us Sectarians, Heretics, Arians, foul buffoons, and what not? These insults are drawn from the Pharisaical school, among whom Christ earned no other favour than you have a demon (John 7:20), a man who is a glutton, a winebibber, a friend of sinners (Matt. 11:19), and, as a term of contempt, the son of the carpenter (Matt. 13:55). Likewise all his sayings are falsely interpreted. This has happened to us too, as is plain from what has been said and what is yet to be said.

units.la: In articulo primo in quo dicit omnes sectarios consentire quatuor membra ponit, inter quæ primum est;
units.tr: In the first article, in which he says that all sectarians agree, he sets out four points, of which the first is this:

units.la: I. Secta omnes nunc volunt vocari Evangelici.
units.tr: I. All sects now want to be called Evangelical.

units.la: Quando & â quo illi qui secessionem à Papatu fecerunt, dicti fuerint Evangelici non constat. Credibile autem est illius nomenclaturæ autores refpexiffe partim ad verba Apostoli, Gal. 1: 8. Si nos aut Angelus è cælo evangelizet vobis, præter id quod evangelizavimus, anathema esto: partim ad traditiones & legendarū fabulas,loco Evangelii in ecclesia,proponi solitas,eoq; indicare voluisse, fe præter Evangelium in fcripturis sacris revelatum, nihil admittere velle in salutis negotio. Idcirco reiicere fe omne humanum figmentum & per aliquot secula à Pontificibus Romanis adiectas traditiones. Becanus ita de hoc titulo garrit: Atqui non solo evangelio contenti, sed recipiunt etiam Acta Apostolorum, Epistolas Pauli & Apocalypsin Iohannis, cur igitur non se vocant Apostolicos, Epistolares, Apocalypticos. Ridiculum caput. Quasi vero illi vocem Evangelii acceperint strictè pro historia Evangelica à quatuor Evangelistis conscripta, aut Apostoli non etiam scripserint Evangelium. Paulus dicit Deum iudicaturum in die illo ex evangelio suo Rom. 2: 16. Se separatum esse a Deo ad praedicandum evangelium, Rom. 1: 1. Imo se evangelizasse Gal. 1: 8. De prophetis idem dicitur, quod Deus in iis evangelium promisserit Rom. 1: 2. Et certe totius sacrae scripturae veteris & novi Testamenti nucleus est evangelium de Christo a Deo in Paradiso revelatum, per Patriarchas propagatum, typis adumbratum, in prophetis promissum, in novo Testamento impletum, ab Apostolis praedicatum. Et ita illi vocem Evangelii sumserunt.
units.tr: When, and by whom, those who seceded from the Papacy were first called Evangelicals is not established. It is believable, however, that the authors of this name looked partly to the words of the Apostle (Gal. 1:8), If we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you any gospel other than what we have preached, let him be accursed, and partly to the traditions and legendary fables that were usually put forward in the Church in place of the Gospel. By this they wished to show that, beyond the Gospel revealed in the holy Scriptures, they would admit nothing in the business of salvation. Hence they reject every human invention and the traditions added by the Roman Pontiffs over several centuries. Becanus chatters thus about this title: But they are not content with the Gospel alone; they also accept the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Paul and the Apocalypse of John. Why then do they not call themselves Apostolics, Epistolaries, Apocalyptics? A ridiculous objection! As if they had taken the word Gospel strictly for the Gospel history written by the four Evangelists, or as if the Apostles had not also written a gospel. Paul says that God will judge in that day by his gospel (Rom. 2:16); that he was set apart by God to preach the gospel (Rom. 1:1); indeed that he had preached the gospel (Gal. 1:8). The same is said of the prophets, that God promised the gospel through them (Rom. 1:2). And certainly the kernel of the whole of holy Scripture, of the Old and New Testaments alike, is the gospel of Christ revealed by God in Paradise, propagated through the patriarchs, foreshadowed by types, promised in the prophets, fulfilled in the New Testament, and preached by the Apostles. In this sense they took up the word Gospel.

units.la: Quod vero Harscherus dicit, in eo omnes sectarios convenire quod appellari velint Evangelici, ego non icio. Verum sit ita, quid hoc ad rem? Quod sic appellari volunt, in causa est, quod quicquid est pulchrum sequitur Momus, inquit Clemens Alexandrinus strom. lib. 7.
units.tr: As for Harscher's claim that all sectarians agree in wanting to be called Evangelicals, I do not admit it. Granted that it is so, what has this to do with the matter? That they wish to be called thus has this cause: whatever is beautiful, Momus pursues, as Clement of Alexandria says in the Stromata.

units.la: lib. 7. Sed iuxta communem regulam; à dici ad esse non valet consequentia. Nam evangelici esse non possunt, qui vel vetus Testamentum reiiciunt, ut Anabaptistæ, vel Deitatem Christi negant, aut Pelagiani aut semipelagiani, & similes, qui communionem nobiscum nullam habent.
units.tr: But by the common rule, an inference from what is to what is cannot hold. For those cannot be evangelical who either reject the Old Testament, like the Anabaptists, or deny the deity of Christ, like the Pelagians and Semipelagians and their like, who have no fellowship with us at all.

units.la: II. Omnes gloriantur, se purum ample- cti verbum Dei, & evangelium & sym- bolum Apostolicum & Athanasianum.
units.tr: II. All boast that they embrace the pure Word of God, and the Gospel, and the Apostles' Creed and the Athanasian Creed.

units.la: Assertione ista parum evincit Jesuita. Nam primò, non omne quod habent aut confitentur sectarii, statim etiam falsum est. Dæmonia credunt Deum unum esse, Jac. 2: 11. Et Pontificii idem credunt, an propterea Pontificii sunt Dæmones? Ita, si sectarii gloriantur se purum Dei verbum habere, traditionibus humanis non adulteratum, & si Reformati idem credunt, non idcirco sectarii sunt Reformati, præcipuè, quia in conclusionibus cum illis non consentiunt. Nec fecundò, propter falsum scripturarum intellectum sectariorum, qui scripturas detorquent suo ipsorum exitio 2. Pet. 3: 16. Verbum Dei ipsum deserendum, non minus quàm via erat relinquenda quinque virginibus prudentibus, licet in eadem ambulaverint fatuæ quinque aliæ ad interitum procedentes.
units.tr: The Jesuit proves little by this assertion. For first, not everything that the sectarians hold or confess is at once false. The demons believe that God is one (James 2:19), and the Papists believe the same. Are the Papists therefore demons?
