So too, if the sectarians boast that they have the pure Word of God, not corrupted by human traditions, and if the Reformed believe the same, the sectarians are not on that account Reformed, especially since they do not agree with them in conclusions. Nor, secondly, is the Word of God itself to be abandoned on account of the false interpretation of Scripture by the sectarians, who twist the Scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet. 3:16). It is no less necessary to leave the Word of God itself than it was for the five wise virgins to leave the way, although the five foolish ones walked in the same way and went on to perdition.

units.la: III. Omnes secta volunt, quod verbum Dei per se satis clarum atq; apertum, nec ulla egat interpretatione.
units.tr: III. All sects maintain that the Word of God is clear and plain in itself and needs no interpretation.

units.la: Quid alii faciant, nunc non disputo, de nobis hæc est mendax Jesuitæ oblatratio, dum nobis sententiam affingit, quæ nostra non est, nosque omnis ecclesiasticæ interpretationis hostes facit. Falsitatem huius assertionis manifestabit commemoratio sententiæ orthodoxorum circa sacræ scripturæ perspicuitatem, quam breviter hic proponam, quamvis de ea iam dixerimus ad hæresin Gnosticorum in seculo secundo.
units.tr: What others do I am not discussing now. This is the Jesuit's lying clamour against us, since he attributes to us an opinion that is not ours and makes us enemies of all ecclesiastical interpretation. The falsity of this charge will be shown by recalling the view of the orthodox on the perspicuity of Holy Scripture, which I shall set out briefly here, although we have already discussed it in dealing with the heresy of the Gnostics in the second century.

units.la: 1. Consideramus res in sacra scriptura contentas, & personas, quæ circa lectionem scripturæ versantur.
units.tr: 1. We consider the matters contained in Holy Scripture, and the persons who are engaged in reading it.

units.la: 2. Res in scriptura contentæ, aliæ sunt dogmaticæ, aliæ prophetiæ, vaticinia, visiones, historiæ.
units.tr: 2. The matters contained in Scripture are partly doctrinal and partly prophecies, prophetic utterances, visions and histories.

units.la: 3. Dogmaticæ sunt, quæ ad salutem & fidem hominis faciunt, quales in symbolo Apostolico continentur, in scriptura autem sacra αὐτολεξεὶ leguntur.
units.tr: 3. Doctrinal matters are those which bear on human salvation and faith, such as are contained in the Apostles' Creed, and are read in Holy Scripture word for word [αὐτολεξεὶ].

units.la: 4. Hæ perspicuè traditæ sunt à Deo, quia debebant hominem ad salutem perducere, Joh. 20: 21. Quod fieri non posset, si non intelligerentur. Idcirco rectè veteres. Primò Lactantius lib 6: cap. 21. Num Deus & mentis & vocis & linguæ artifex diserte loqui non posset? Imò summa providentia carere ea fuco voluit, quæ divina sunt, ut omnes intelligerent, quæ ipse omnibus loquebatur. Deinde Bernhardus Serm. de verb.Lib. sapient. Via Domini via recta, via pulchra, via plena, via plana. Recta sine errore, quia ducunt ad vitam, pulchra sine sorde, quia docent munditiem, plena multitudine, quia totus jam mundus est intra Christi sagena, plana sine difficultate, quia donant suavitatem.
units.tr: 4. These have been plainly delivered by God, because they were to bring man to salvation (John 20:21). This could not happen if they were not understood. Hence the ancients rightly said so. First, Lactantius, book 6, chapter 21: "Could not God, the artificer of mind, voice and tongue, speak clearly? Nay, in his highest providence he willed that the things that are divine should be free of disguise, so that all might understand what he spoke to all." Then Bernard, Sermon on the book of Wisdom: "The way of the Lord is a straight way, a beautiful way, a full way, a plain way. Straight without error, because they lead to life; beautiful without filth, because they teach purity; full, with a multitude, because the whole world is now within Christ's net; plain without difficulty, because they give sweetness."

units.la: 5. Circa has iterum consideranda veniunt, tum cognitio hominis, tum easdem tradendi modus Autoris sacrarum scripturarum.
units.tr: 5. Here two things must again be considered: the knowledge of the man, and the manner in which the Author of the sacred Scriptures delivers them.

units.la: 6. Quoad primum; multa sciuntur & pie creduntur ad salutem, quantum ad cognitionem τῆ ὅτι, quae nesciuntur sine dispendio salutis, quantum ad cognitionem τῆ ὅτι. Verbi gratia; credimus Deum unum esse, & trinum, & hoc ad cognitionem salutis perspicuè revelatum est in scriptura 1. Joh. 5: 7. ipsum vero mysterium Trinitatis in se homini est abscônditum.
units.tr: 6. As to the first: many things are known and piously believed as necessary to salvation as regards the knowledge of the that [τῆ ὅτι], while others are not known without loss of salvation as regards the knowledge of the why [τῆ διότι]. For example, we believe that God is one and three, and this has been clearly revealed in Scripture for the knowledge of salvation (1 John 5:7); but the mystery of the Trinity itself is hidden from man in its own nature.

units.la: 7. Modus tradendi huiusmodi est, ut primò Deus rationem habeat eorum, quibus loquitur. Nam cum infantibus balbutit præbens ipsis elementa eloquiorum Dei, adultis verò solidum cibum, Heb. 5: 12. Hinc Ambrosius l. 7. Epist. 44. ad Constant. Habes quod primum bibas, habes quod secundum, habes quod postremum.
units.tr: 7. The manner of delivery is such that God first takes account of those to whom he speaks. For when he lisps with infants, giving them the elements of God's utterances, but gives solid food to adults (Heb. 5:12). Hence Ambrose, book 7, letter 44 to Constantius: "You have what you should drink first, you have what comes second, you have what comes last."

units.la: 8. Secundò, sic stylum moderatur Spiritus sanctus, ut dogmata ad salutem alibi obscurius proponat, alibi clarius explicet, ut Augustinus loquitur lib. 2. de Doctr. Christiana, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus fastidia detergeret.
units.tr: 8. Secondly, the Holy Spirit so regulates his style that he sets forth doctrines necessary to salvation more obscurely in one place and explains them more clearly in another, as Augustine says in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine: "so that in the plainer passages he might meet hunger, and in the obscurer ones remove disgust."

units.la: 9. Tertiò, non sine gravi causa Deo placuit apertis obscura, facilibus difficilia immiscere. Nam apertis pascimur, inquit Augustinus, obscuris exercemur. Unde Gregorius; Magna utilitatis est obscuritas eloquiorum Dei, quia exercet sensum ut fatigatione dilatetur, & exercitatus capiat, quod capere non potest otiosus. Hom. 6. in Ezech.
units.tr: 9. Thirdly, it has not pleased God, without grave cause, to mingle obscure things with plain, and difficult things with easy. "For we are fed by the plain," says Augustine, "we are exercised by the obscure." Whence Gregory: "The obscurity of God's utterances is of great usefulness, because it exercises the mind so that it is widened by the effort, and the one who is exercised grasps what the idle man cannot grasp." Homily 6 on Ezekiel.

units.la: 10. Vaticinia, prophetiæ, visiones in scriptura contentæ difficillimę sunt & multis modis, obscurę, quarum pars aliqua ex eventu, pars ex interpretatione divinitus concessa in hac vita, pars denique in altera demum vita cognoscitur. Huc facit Ambrosij dictum: Mare est scriptura divina, habens in se sensus profundos, altitudinem propheticorum ænigmatum. Loco supra citato.
units.tr: 10. The prophecies, prophetic utterances and visions contained in Scripture are most difficult and in many ways obscure. Part of them is known from the event, part from the interpretation granted by God in this life, and part only in the life to come. To this belongs the saying of Ambrose: "Divine Scripture is a sea, having in itself deep senses, the height of prophetic enigmas." In the place cited above.

units.la: 11. Historiæ plerumque apertæ sunt, ut Bellarminus confitetur.
units.tr: 11. Histories are for the most part plain, as Bellarmine confesses.

units.la: 12. Distinguimus personas quoque.
units.tr: 12. We distinguish the persons as well.

units.la: 13. 1. Infideles, porci, canes, uti scriptura loquitur, non perveniunt ad sensum scripturarum, quia ipsorum mens obtenebrata est, & omni luce Spiritus sancti carens, unde fit, ut Christus crucifixus Judæis sit offendiculum, Græcis autem stultitia. 2. Cor. 4: 4.
units.tr: 13. First, unbelievers, swine and dogs, as Scripture calls them, do not attain to the sense of the Scriptures, because their mind is darkened and lacks all the light of the Holy Spirit. Hence it comes about that Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks (2 Cor. 4:4).

units.la: 14. 2. Fideles & à Spiritu sancto, deducente ipsos in omnem veritatem, illuminati, intelligunt & vident mirabilia in lege Dei, alii magis, alii minùs, omnes tamen sufficienter ad salutem. Qui etiam adhibitis precibus, diligenti meditatione & lectione verbi Dei, & institutione tandem crescunt, ut eveniant in virum adultum ad mensuram staturæ adulti Christi, Eph. 4. 13.
units.tr: 14. Second, believers, who are illuminated by the Holy Spirit leading them into all truth, understand and see wonderful things in the law of God, some more and some less, yet all sufficiently for salvation. These too, by prayers, diligent meditation and reading of God's Word, and finally by instruction, grow until they become a mature man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4:13).

units.la: Ex hisce nunc iudicare licet de iniuria, nobis ab Harschero & suis complicibus illata. Nam confitemur
units.tr: From these things we may now judge the injury done to us by Harscher and his accomplices. For we confess

units.la: 1. Cum Ambrosio; scripturam divinam esse mare, habens in se sensus profundos.
units.tr: 1. With Ambrose, that divine Scripture is a sea, having in itself deep senses.

units.la: 2. Cum Gregorio Magno, scripturæ sacræ (etsi multipliciter sit exposita) non deesse secreta, quibus servat occulta, quia ferè nunquam sic exponitur, ut ei non plura remaneant, quæ quotidie exponantur.
units.tr: 2. With Gregory the Great, that in holy Scripture (however variously it has been expounded) there is no lack of secrets, by which it keeps hidden things, since it is almost never so expounded that there do not remain more things which are expounded day by day.

units.la: 3. In historiis quoque plurimas esse
units.tr: 3. That in histories too there are very many

units.la: difficultates de tempore, & nominibus urbium, ut & fluviorum &c, unde ingens certamen Chronologorum & Criticorum tùm Hebræorum tùm Græcorum.
units.tr: difficulties concerning time, and the names of cities, rivers and so on, whence arises a huge contest among chronologists and critics, both Hebrew and Greek.

units.la: 4. Idcircò summopere opus esse oratione, meditatione, interpretatione tum privata, tum publica, in schola & ecclesia. Habetne hîc quod contradicat? Pergit.
units.tr: 4. Hence it is greatly necessary to have prayer, meditation and interpretation, both private and public, in school and in church. Does he have anything here to contradict? He goes on.

units.la: IV. Quòd licitum sit mulieribus æque ac viris, laicis non minùs, quàm sacerdotibus, tractare verbum Dei, & quicunq; scripturæ sensus cuiq; placuerit eum pro ipso Dei verbo habere atq; defendere.
units.tr: IV. That it is lawful for women as well as men, and for laymen no less than priests, to handle the Word of God, and that whoever has a sense of Scripture that pleases him should hold it and defend it as the very Word of God.

units.la: Calumniosè hæc ut & alia pleraque. Videamus. In primo lemmate huius assertionis ambiguitate ludit, ut lectorem decipiat. Nam si tractare verbum Dei ipsi significat occupatum esse circa sacram scripturam, ut sensus eius ex scopi consideratione, caussarum, circumstantiarum, antecedentium & consequentium notatione & analysi logica eruatur & postea ad usum Auditorum in doctrina, redargutione, correctione & institutione applicetur, ut docet Apostolus 2. Tim. 3: 16. Quòd alibi vocat ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, recte secare sermonem veritatis 2. Tim. 2: 15. tum nobiscum iniquè agit, si scribat istum morem in ecclesia nostra obtinere. Quemadmodum enim Apostolus mulieri docere non permittit, sed vult ut in silentio discat 1. Tim. 2: 11. 12. Viros etiam hortatur, ut quovis in loco puras manus attollant, id est, orent: Episcopos autem vult esse innutritos in sermonibus fidei & praeclarae doctrinae 1. Tim. 4: 6. id est, tenere mysterium fidei in pura conscientia 1. Tim. 3: 9. ut sint probati Dei operarii, apti ad docendum 2. Tim. 2: 15, 24. Ita nos nulli publicam verbi Dei tractationem permittimus, qui non legitimè ad sacrosanctum ministerium obeundum sit vocatus.
units.tr: These claims are slanderous, as are most of the others. Let us see. In the first part of this assertion he plays on an ambiguity to deceive the reader. For if to handle the Word of God means to be occupied with Holy Scripture, so that its sense is drawn out from consideration of the aim, the causes and circumstances, the noting of what goes before and after, and logical analysis, and is afterwards applied for the use of the hearers in teaching, refutation, correction and instruction, as the Apostle teaches (2 Tim. 3:16), and which elsewhere he calls rightly dividing the word of truth [ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας] (2 Tim. 2:15), then he deals unjustly with us if he writes that this practice prevails in our Church. For just as the Apostle does not permit a woman to teach, but wills that she learn in silence (1 Tim. 2:11, 12), so he also exhorts men to lift up pure hands in every place, that is, to pray; and he wills bishops to be nourished in the words of faith and sound doctrine (1 Tim. 4:6), that is, to hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience (1 Tim. 3:9), so that they may be approved workmen of God, apt to teach (2 Tim. 2:15, 24). So too we do not permit anyone to undertake the public handling of the Word of God who has not been lawfully called to discharge the holy ministry.

units.la: Si vero verbum Dei tractare ipsi sit verbum Dei legere, confitemur omninò nos tùm mulieribus, tùm laicis id permittere, multas ob causas, quarum aliquas hic commemorabo. Primò, quia (ut Damascenus scribit Inst. orthod. lib. 4. c. 18.) Scrutari scripturas est καλλισον τη ψυχωφελεστατον. Ideo comparat eas rivulis aquarum quibus irrigata anima pinguescat & tempestivu fructu ferat, nempe τῆσιν οδοδοξον, & actionibus θαρρησεως tanquam perpetuo virentib^o foliis decoretur. Et Basilius in Psal. 1. Sacram scripturam esse communem animarum ossicinam, unde omnes homines pharmacum pro ratione sui morbi deligerent. Deinde, quia psalmista beatum praedicat virum, id est, hominem illum, qui in lege Dei meditatur interdiu & noctu, Psal. 1: 2. Christus Judaeorum studium in scrutandis scripturis probat, Joh. 5: 39. Et Beroënses celebrantur generosiores illis, qui erant Thessalonicae, quia quotidie scrutabantur scripturas Act. 17: 11.
units.tr: But if to handle the Word of God simply means to read the Word of God, we confess that we altogether permit this to women as well as to laymen, for many reasons, some of which I shall mention here. First, because, as Damascene writes (Inst. orthod. book 4, chapter 18), "to search the Scriptures is most beautiful and most profitable to the soul" [καλλιστον τῇ ψυχωφελεστατον]. Therefore he compares them to streams of water, by which the soul is watered, grows fat and bears fruit in season, namely by right faith [τῆσιν ὀρθοδοξίαν], and is adorned by actions of confidence [θαρρήσεως] as with ever-green leaves. And Basil on Psalm 1: "Holy Scripture is the common workshop of souls, from which all men may choose a remedy according to the nature of their sickness." Then, because the psalmist pronounces blessed the man, that is, the man who meditates in the law of God day and night (Ps. 1:2). Christ approves the zeal of the Jews in searching the Scriptures (John 5:39). And the Bereans are praised as more noble than those at Thessalonica, because they searched the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11).

units.la: Tertiò quia Apostoli suas epistolas integris ecclesiis legendas miserunt, quod ex inscriptionibus patet. Paulus epistolam ad Romanos, misit omnibus qui Romæ erant, Rom. 1:7. Epistolam priorem ad Corinthios omnibus, qui invocant nomen Christi in omni loco 1.Cor. 1: 2. Johannes, scripsit patribus & adolescentibus 1. Joh. 2:12. Perversè igitur agunt omnes illi, qui necessarium hoc & plane divinū organum acquirendæ fidei & salutis æternæ, fidelibus è manu eripiunt. Imò, scriptura est animæ cibus, inquit Athanasius, qui igitur scripturam subtrahit, ille dirâ fame necat interiorem hominem, Tom. II. p. 295.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Apostles sent their letters to be read by whole churches, as the inscriptions show. Paul sent his letter to the Romans to all who were at Rome (Rom. 1:7). His first letter to the Corinthians went to all who call upon the name of Christ in every place (1 Cor. 1:2). John wrote to the fathers and the young men (1 John 2:12). Those who take away from the faithful this necessary and wholly divine instrument for gaining faith and eternal salvation therefore act perversely. Indeed, Scripture is the food of the soul, says Athanasius, so whoever withholds Scripture starves the inner man with a dreadful hunger (vol. II, p. 295).

units.la: Posterius assertionis membrum est putidum scomma. Quis ex nobis scripsit? quis dixit, sensum cujusq; hominis legentis scripturam pro ipso verbo Dei habendum esse? Indicium malæ caussæ, adversæ partis sententiam fraudulenter pervertere. Sic sentimus. In lectione scripturæ sacræ Deum fidelibus gratiam
units.tr: The second part of the assertion is a foul jest. Which of us has written, or said, that the sense of each person who reads Scripture is to be held as the very Word of God? That is a sign of a bad cause, when the opposing side twists the other's view dishonestly. This is what we hold: in the reading of Holy Scripture God grants the faithful the grace

units.la: illam largiri, ut audire & cognoscere possint vocem pastoris sui, eumque sequi, alienum autem nequaquam, quia non norunt vocem alienorum, ita ut magis magisque sensus exercitatos acquirentes, ad discretionem boni & mali ipsi iudicare possint, quæ dicuntur in scripturis, & probare Spiritus an ex Deo sint, sibiq; cavere à falsis prophetis. Quæ omnia exserte in scriptura habentur Joh.10:3,5. Heb. 5:14. 1. Cor. 10: 5.
units.tr: of being able to hear and know the voice of their shepherd, and to follow him, but never a stranger, because they do not know the voice of strangers. So, by gaining ever more trained senses, they are able to judge for themselves, to discern good from evil, to decide what is said in the Scriptures, to test the spirits whether they are from God, and to guard themselves against false prophets. All of this is plainly found in Scripture: John 10:3, 5; Heb. 5:14; 1 Cor. 10:5.

units.la: 1. Joh. 4: 1. Matth. 7: 15. Idcirco Deo hanc gloriam, & fidelibus hanc gratiam ascribimus, ut per lectionem scripturæ in eiusdem sensum penetrare possint. Intelligimus, inquit Hilarius in Psal. 121, quia non mendax est qui dicit: petite & dabitur vobis, quærite & invenietis pulsate & aperietur vobis.
units.tr: 1 John 4:1; Matt. 7:15. For this reason we ascribe the glory to God and this grace to the faithful, that through reading Scripture they may penetrate into its meaning. We understand, says Hilary on Psalm 121, that he who says: ask and it will be given you, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you, is not a liar.

units.la: Si quis ergo homo fidelis per assistentiam Spiritus sancti scripturam sacram intelligit ex mente Dei & iuxta analogiam fidei Rom. 12: 6. Cur eius interpretatio non approbaretur potius quam quàm indocti alicuius Episcopi? Sic Johannes Gerson: Si aliquis simplex non authorisatus esset excellenter in sacris literis eruditus, plus ei esset credendum in casu doctrinali, quàm Papæ declarationi. Et quidem recte hæc: quia Berllarminus nos docet lib. II. de Conc. cap. 2. Sine dubio singulos Episcopos errare posse, & aliquando errare, & ita interdum dissentire, ut nesciamus quis eorum sequendus sit.
units.tr: If, then, a faithful man, by the help of the Holy Spirit, understands Holy Scripture according to the mind of God and in line with the analogy of faith (Rom. 12:6), why should his interpretation be less approved than that of some unlearned bishop? So John Gerson: If some simple layman, not authorised, were excellently learned in sacred letters, more should be believed to him in a doctrinal matter than to the Pope's declaration. And rightly so, because Bellarmine teaches us (On the Councils, book II, ch. 2): Without doubt individual bishops can err, and sometimes do err, and so disagree at times that we do not know which of them is to be followed.

units.la: Pergit Jesuita; Secundus articulus est in quo omnes concordes sunt; Quòd I. Universi pari studio ac odio oppugnant ecclesiam catholicam.
units.tr: The Jesuit goes on: The second article is one in which they all agree: first, that all of them with equal zeal and hatred attack the Catholic Church.

units.la: Veram & catholicam ecclesiam oppugnat Diabolus & membra eius, qui sunt hostes ecclesiæ. Prælium hoc inter Michaëlem & Draconem, eorumque angelos iam olim prævidit Johannes Apoc. 12: 17. Membra Draconis sunt Ethnici, Mahumetani, PseudoChristi, Antichristi & imprimis Antichristus ille magnus.
units.tr: The devil and his members, who are enemies of the Church, attack the true and Catholic Church. John foresaw long ago this battle between Michael and the Dragon and their angels (Rev. 12:17). The members of the Dragon are the heathen, the Mahometans, the pseudo-Christs, the Antichrists, and above all that great Antichrist.

units.la: Vox Catholica ἀ̓ξεαρος est. Legitur autem in titulis Jacobi, prioris & posterioris Petri, primæ & secundæ Johannis, & epistolæ Judæ. Posita procul dubio ab Amanuensibus, quod ad ecclesias universas, non ad certas ecclesias aut personas, ut reliquæ epistolæ, scriptæ essent. Quo tempore nulla adhuc ecclesia appellata fuit catholica, sed christiana tantum. Quod me movet, ut credam articulos symboli Apostolici, longè post Apostolos fuisse adornatos.
units.tr: The word catholic [ἀ̓ξεαρος] is found in the titles of James, of the first and second letters of Peter, of the first and second of John, and of the letter of Jude. It was undoubtedly placed there by the copyists, because these letters were written to the churches generally, not to particular churches or persons, as the other letters were. At that time no church was yet called catholic, only Christian. This moves me to believe that the articles of the Apostles' Creed were drawn up long after the Apostles.

units.la: Catholica autem dicta fuit ecclesia christiana propter articulos fidei, à Deo veracissimo ecclesiæ traditos,qui ita καθ' ὅλης sunt, ut sint πάσης ὑποδοχῆς ἄξιοι, & magis quàm axiomata catholica Aristotelis & Philosophorum ἀξιώματοι. Unde Apostolus 1. Tim. 3: 16. pietatis mysterium, dicit, esse sine controversia magnum. Rectè Augustinus de vera religione cap. 7. præcepta divina esse de spiritualibus percipiendis, quæ nec præterita junt. sunt, nec futura, sed eodem modo semper manentia, mutabilitati nulli obnoxia.
units.tr: The Christian Church, however, was called catholic because of the articles of faith handed down to the Church by the most truthful God, which are universal [καθ' ὅλης] and so worthy of every reception [πάσης ὑποδοχῆς ἄξιοι], and more than the catholic axioms of Aristotle and the philosophers [ἀξιώματοι]. Hence the Apostle says, 1 Tim. 3:16, the mystery of godliness is, he says, without controversy great. Augustine rightly says in On True Religion, ch. 7, that the divine precepts concerning spiritual things to be perceived are such that they are neither past nor future, but remain always in the same way, subject to no change.

units.la: Ab hisce præceptis divinis, quia vera sunt, fides christiana dicitur orthodoxa, & ecclesia, quæ illa recipit, orthodoxa, ut etiam quivis fidelis orthodoxus: quatenus illa perpetuò vera sunt, fides appellatur catholica ab Athanasio, & quivis christianus catholicus.
units.tr: From these divine precepts, because they are true, the Christian faith is called orthodox, and the Church which receives them is called orthodox, and so too any believer is orthodox. Insofar as these things are always true, the faith is called catholic by Athanasius, and any Christian is catholic.

units.la: Sic docet Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus in Catech. 18. quando dicit: Catholica vocatur, quia catholicè, hoc est, universaliter docet, & sine ullo defectu omnia dogmata, quæ debent venire in hominum cognitionem, de rebus visibilibus & invisibilibus, cœlestibus & terrestribus, & quia in universum curat omne genus peccatorum, & quæ per animam & quæ per corpus patrantur. Habeturq; in illa omne genus virtutis in factis & dictis & in omnigenis spiritualibus charismatibus.
units.tr: So Cyril of Jerusalem teaches in Catechesis 18, when he says: It is called catholic because it teaches catholically, that is, universally, and without any defect, all the doctrines that ought to come to men's knowledge, about visible and invisible things, heavenly and earthly; and because it deals generally with every kind of sin, both those committed by the soul and those committed by the body. And in it is found every kind of virtue, in deeds and words and in every sort of spiritual gift.

units.la: Et sicuti est una fides (quæ creditur) baptisma unum, una spes & Dominus unus omnium fidelium, ita etiam est unum corpus, hoc est, ecclesia una continens omnes credentes, sive iam in cœlo triumphent, sive in terra militent, quocunque tempore & loco, quæ idcirco peculiari modo dicitur catholica à Patribus. Atque hæc illa est, quam in symbolo apostolico credimus. Et definitur quod sit, cætus seu panegyris primogenitorum in cœlis conscriptorum (Heb. 12: 25.) in hac vita per prædicationem Evangelij & Spiritum sanctum efficaciter ex statu peccati ad statum gratiæ evocatorum, Christoq; capiti unitorum, ut in altera vita gloriosè triumphet in æternum.
units.tr: And just as there is one faith (which is believed), one baptism, one hope and one Lord of all the faithful, so there is also one body, that is, one Church containing all believers, whether they now triumph in heaven or wage war on earth, at whatever time and place; this is therefore called catholic in a special way by the Fathers. This is the Church which we believe in the Apostles' Creed. It is defined as the assembly or festal gathering of the firstborn written in heaven (Heb. 12:23), called in this life through the preaching of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit effectually out of the state of sin into the state of grace, and united to Christ their head, so that in the other life they may triumph gloriously for ever.

units.la: Si ergo Harscherus probare vult, nos ecclesiam catholicam oppugnare, necesse est, ut probet ante omnia, quòd fidem illam orthodoxam & catholicam ex puro Dei verbo desumptam: aut ecclesiam fidem illam rectè amplectentem oppugnemus. Id verò nec ipse, nec quisquam alius ex Pontificiis hactenus praestare potuit.
units.tr: If, then, Harscher wishes to prove that we attack the Catholic Church, he must first of all prove that we attack that orthodox and catholic faith, drawn from the pure Word of God, or the Church which rightly embraces that faith. But neither he nor anyone else among the Papists has so far been able to do this.

units.la: Nam quod ecclesiam hodiernam Romanam concernit, illa nec obiective nec collective catholica est, quia fidem illam orthodoxam & catholicam in verbo Dei perpetuo sibi consentiente, traditam, in multis abiecit, & articulos fidei praecipue circa officium Christi mediatorium, non quidem explicite sed implicite, tradit, Apostolis & primitivae ecclesiae incognitos, qui idcirco huius membra esse non potuerunt.
units.tr: For as far as the present Roman Church is concerned, it is neither objectively nor collectively catholic, because it has cast off in many points that orthodox and catholic faith, handed down in the Word of God which is always consistent with itself, and it hands down, especially concerning the mediatorial office of Christ, articles of faith not explicitly but implicitly, which were unknown to the Apostles and the primitive Church, and therefore could not be members of it.

units.la: Nec multum ad rem facit quod scribunt, ecclesiam Romanam hodiernam esse illam quoq; vetustam Romanam, cuius olim fides annuntiata fuit in toto mundo, ut habetur Rom. 1: 8. aut quod seipsos vocant catholicos.
units.tr: Nor does it much help their case that they write that the present Roman Church is also that ancient Roman Church whose faith was once proclaimed throughout the whole world, as is found in Rom. 1:8, or that they call themselves catholic.

units.la: Non primum; Nam si templum Hierosolymitanum, sanctuarium Jehovae, mons quem desideravit DEVS ad sedem suam, in quo habitaturus erat in aeternum Psal. 68: 17. Domus Patris caelestis, Matth. 21: 13. Regum populique Judaici impietate idolorum spurcitiis fuit profanatum, ut loquitur Adrichomius; cur non idem accidere potuisset ecclesiae Romanae?
units.tr: The first point does not help them. For if the temple at Jerusalem, the sanctuary of Jehovah, the mountain which God desired for his dwelling, in which he would dwell for ever (Ps. 68:17), the house of the heavenly Father (Matt. 21:13), was profaned by the impiety of kings and the Jewish people with the filth of idols, as Adrichomius puts it, why could not the same have happened to the Roman Church?

units.la: Non secundum; quia plurimi habent titulum sine re. Unde illud ortum philosophorum, a dici ad esse non valere consequentiam. De Donatistis scribit Augustinus quod se solos catholicos appellarint. In quo tamen acquiescere noluit vir sanctus, sed voluit ipsos in eo potius laborare, ut re ipsa ostendant se esse catholicos. Nam quid tibi prodest nomen, ubi res non invenitur, inquit idem Augustinus tract. 5. in Joh.
units.tr: Nor does the second point help them, because many have the title without the reality. Hence the saying of the philosophers, that the inference from being called to being is not valid. Augustine writes of the Donatists that they called themselves the only catholics. Yet the holy man would not rest content with this, but wanted them rather to labour at showing in fact that they were catholic. For what good is a name to you where the reality is not found? says the same Augustine in Tractate 5 on John.

units.la: Cum igitur ecclesia hodierna Romana (cuius fidei articulis in scriptura sacra non fundatis contradicimus) catholica non sit, iniquè nobiscum agit Harscherus, si dicat nos ecclesiam catholicam impugnare; quicquid sectarii, Mahumetani, Pseudochristi & Antichristi faciant.
units.tr: Since, then, the present Roman Church (whose articles of faith not founded in Holy Scripture we oppose) is not catholic, Harscher deals unjustly with us if he says that we attack the Catholic Church, whatever the sectaries, Mahometans, pseudo-Christs and Antichrists may do.

units.la: II. Quod nullum admittunt catholicum scripturæ sacræ intellectum.
units.tr: II. That they admit no catholic sense of Scripture.

units.la: Intellectum sacræ scripturæ catholicum voco, qui iuxta constantem & perpetuam scripturæ sententiam, ex eiusdem apertis & minimè obscuris locis traditur: catholicus igitur dicitur, tum propter fidem catholicam, cui est analogus, tum propter consensum totius scripturæ sacræ.
units.tr: I call the catholic sense of Scripture that which is drawn from the plain and least obscure passages of Scripture, in accordance with its constant and perpetual meaning. It is called catholic both because it corresponds to the catholic faith and because it agrees with the whole of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Huiusmodi intellectus sacræ scripturæ continetur in symbolis catholicis, Apostolico, Niceno, Constantinopolitano, Athanasiano, Ephesino, Chalcedonensi. Quæ sine controversia à nobis admittuntur & recipiuntur. Non quidem quatenus ab hominibus concinnata, sed quatenus scripturæ sacræ per omnia consentanea sunt.
units.tr: This catholic sense of Holy Scripture is contained in the catholic creeds: the Apostles', the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, the Athanasian, the Ephesine and the Chalcedonian. We admit and receive these without controversy, not indeed because they were composed by men, but because they are in every respect consistent with Holy Scripture.

units.la: Quem vero intellectum scripturæ sacræ catholicum nominet Harscherus, ex Concilio Tridentino colligi potest, seff. IV. Nempe quem tenuit & tenet sancta mater ecclesia (hodierna Romana) cujus sit judicare de vero sensu & interpretatione scripturarum sanctarum, aut etiam habetur ex unanimi consensu Patrum.
units.tr: What Harscher means by the catholic sense of Scripture may be gathered from the Council of Trent, session 4: namely, "that which holy mother Church (the present Roman Church) has held and holds, whose right it is to judge the true sense and interpretation of the holy Scriptures," or which is also found in the unanimous consent of the Fathers.

units.la: Sed hoc de ecclesia est ambiguum. Nam alii interpretationem & sensum scripturæ tribuunt pontifici, qui sit supra ecclesiam & omnes Patres. Unde Episcopus Bitontinus citante Domino Riveto: Ego ut ingenue fatear, inquit, plus uni summo pontifici crederem, in his, quæ fidei mysteria tangunt, quàm mille Augustinis, Hieronymis, Gregoriis, &c. Alii Papæ hoc derogant, ut Patres Concilii Basileensis, in responsione synodali his verbis: Reliquum totum corpus sæpe condemnavit & deposuit Papam, tam ratione fidei fidei, quàm morum. Potest enim, inquit Alphonsus à Castro homo Pontificius, omnis homo errare in fide, etiamsi Papa sit. Quod exemplo Liberii & Anastasii II. probat ex Platina.
units.tr: But this statement about the Church is ambiguous. For others ascribe the interpretation and sense of Scripture to the Pope, who is above the Church and all the Fathers. Hence the bishop of Bitonto, cited by Rivet: "To be frank, he says, I would trust one supreme pontiff more, in those matters which touch the mysteries of faith, than a thousand Augustines, Jeromes, Gregories, etc." Others detract this from the Pope, as the fathers of the Council of Basel did in their synodal reply, in these words: "The whole remaining body has often condemned and deposed the Pope, on grounds of faith as well as of morals." For, says Alphonsus a Castro, a Papist, "every man can err in faith, even if he is Pope." He proves this from the example of Liberius and Anastasius II, citing Platina.

units.la: De Patribus quidam affirmant ut Melchior Canus lib. 7. cap. 3. Locorum Communn: In expositione sacrarum literarum, communis omnium sanctorum veterum intelligentia certissima argumenta Theologo praestat, ad Theologicas assertiones corroborandas, quippe cum sanctorum omnium sensus, spiritus sancti sensus ipse sit. Consentit Salmero in primum caput Joh. Et tales omnes videri volunt Pontificii.
units.tr: Some affirm this concerning the Fathers, as Melchior Cano does in book 7, chapter 3 of the Loci Communes: "In the exposition of the sacred letters, the common understanding of all the holy ancients gives the theologian most certain arguments for strengthening theological assertions, since the sense of all the saints is the very sense of the Holy Spirit." Salmeron agrees on the first chapter of John. And all Papists wish to appear to be of this kind.

units.la: Attamen alibi negant, ut Baronius in Annal. ad Annum XXXIV. Sanctissimos Patres, inquit, quos Doctores ecclesiae ob illorum sublimem eruditionem merito nominamus, quantumvis Spiritus sancti gratiâ prae caeteris imbutos liqueat, in interpretatione non semper & in omnibus catholica tholica eccl sia sequitur. Baronio affurgit Bellarminus lib. III. de V. D. cap. 10. quando scribit; Patres interpretatos esse scripturas more & officio Doctorum, qui non proponunt sententiam suam, ut necessario sequendam, sed solum quatenus ratio suadet.
units.tr: Yet elsewhere they deny it, as Baronius does in his Annals at the year 34: "The most holy Fathers," he says, "whom we rightly call Doctors of the Church on account of their lofty learning, however much it is clear that they were steeped in the grace of the Holy Spirit above others, do not always, in interpretation, and not in all matters, follow the catholic Church." Bellarmine rises up against Baronius in book 3 of On the Word of God, chapter 10, when he writes: "The Fathers interpreted Scripture in the manner and office of teachers, who do not put forward their opinion as something to be necessarily followed, but only insofar as reason persuades."

units.la: Et Maldonatus magistraliter admodum iudicat de Patribus: Nulla mihi ex superioribus (Justini Martyris, Cyrilli, Chrysostomi, Ambrosii, Augustini, Hieronymi) placet interpretatio, itaque alia quærenda explicatio est. Comment. in Iob.
units.tr: And Maldonatus judges quite magisterially about the Fathers: "None of the above (Justin Martyr, Cyril, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome) pleases me as an interpretation, so another explanation must be sought." Commentary on Job.

units.la: Nostras ecclesias quod concernit, sicuti illæ catholicum scripturæ sensum, paulò ante descriptum, unicè admittunt: ita libenter fatentur,
units.tr: As for our churches, just as they admit only the catholic sense of Scripture described a little above, so they gladly confess

units.la: I. Se Pontificis Romani sensum in omnibus non approbare. Rationes nobis sunt firmissimæ. Primò, quia, ut Alphonsus à Castro supra citatus, recte asseruit, omnes homines etiam Papa in fide deficere potest. Et Salmero, communem esse opinionem Papam, ut Doctorem privatum, à fide posse deficere, seu ut Stapletonus, esse tam in fide defectibilem, quàm in moribus peccabilem. Quod verò de publica Papæ persona in cathedra sedente & fidei articulos præscribente Jesuitæ docent, ac fi tum errare non possit, omni fundamento caret.
units.tr: I. That they do not approve the sense of the Roman Pontiff in all things. Our reasons are most firm. First, because, as Alphonsus a Castro, cited above, rightly asserted, every man, even the Pope, can fall away in faith. And Salmeron holds the common opinion that the Pope, as a private teacher, can fall from the faith, or, as Stapleton says, is as liable to fail in faith as he is liable to sin in morals. But what the Jesuits teach about the public person of the Pope sitting in the chair and prescribing articles of faith, as if he could not err then, has no foundation at all.

units.la: Quia docere, leges præscribere, in Conciliis præsidere actiones sunt publicæ & hominis publici. Atqui Pontifices Romani fuerunt, qui hæreses publicè docuerunt, legesque posuerunt quâ Papæ, quæ omnibus bonis moribus & verbo Dei sunt contrariæ. De Liberio Papa gravissimi sunt Autores, qui testantur ipsum publicè Arianismo fubfcripfiffe, Athanafium virum fanctiffimum condemnaffe. Nicolaus primus docuit Baptismum fine expressione trium Trinitatis personarum esse ratum, Bellarminus vocat errorem in fide. Nihil dicam nunc de Honorio Monothelita, Anastasio Nestoriano & aliis, quos Concilia à pontificatu removerunt, quod indicium est publicæ doctrinæ. De moribus corruptis publicè à pontificibus approbatis, quà Pontifices in superioribus seculis diximus.
units.tr: Because teaching, prescribing laws and presiding over councils are public acts of a public man. But there have been Roman Pontiffs who publicly taught heresies and laid down laws contrary to all good morals and to the Word of God. Very weighty authors testify concerning Pope Liberius that he publicly subscribed to Arianism and condemned Athanasius, a most holy man. Nicholas I taught that baptism is valid without the expression of the three persons of the Trinity; Bellarmine calls this "an error in faith." I say nothing now of Honorius the Monothelite, Anastasius the Nestorian, and others whom councils removed from the papacy, which is a sign of public doctrine. Concerning corrupt morals publicly approved by pontiffs, we have spoken above regarding the Pontiffs of earlier centuries.

units.la: Responsiones Bellarminianæ,quibus Pontifices prædicti excusantur, vix dignæ sunt qui sub examen revocentur. Tu autem attende,quæso, quàm imperatorie omnia. Quando nostri ex Tertulliano obiiciunt Zepherinum Papam fuisse Montani hæresi imbutum, resp. Tertulliano fides non est habenda. Rhenanus mentitur, lib. 4. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 8: 2. Liberium esse Arianum ex clarissimis autoribus, respondet; Quamvis hæc ita se habeant, tamen non est hæreticus. Peccabat saltem externo actu. Non expresse expresse sed interpretative tantum in hæresin incidit. Patres sextæ Synodi damnarunt Honorium. Resp. falsa informatione decepti. Vide ut magni viri sese turpiter dent, si luci tenebras affundere conantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine's replies, by which the aforesaid Pontiffs are excused, are scarcely worth examining. But please consider how imperious everything is. When our people object from Tertullian that Pope Zephyrinus was imbued with the heresy of Montanus, the reply is: Tertullian's word is not to be trusted. Rhenanus lies, book 4 on the Roman Pontiffs, chapter 8. When they cite the most distinguished authors that Liberius was an Arian, the answer is: Although these things are so, nevertheless he was not a heretic. He sinned at least in outward act. He fell into heresy not expressly, but only by implication. When the Fathers of the sixth Synod condemned Honorius, the reply is: They were deceived by false information. See how shamefully great men expose themselves when they try to cast darkness over the light.

units.la: II. De Patribus iudicant ecclesiæ nostræ ex Patribus.
units.tr: II. How our churches judge the Fathers, from the Fathers.

units.la: Primò ex Augustino; Noli meis literis, quasi scripturis canonicis inservire. Proœm. lib. 3. de Trinit: Ibidem multa in hanc rem; non me amet (lector) amplius quàm catholicam veritatem; cum in omnibus literis meis non solum pium lectorem, sed etiam liberum correctorem desiderem. Postea iubet suas literas ex divina lectione vel inconcussa ratione corrigere. Secundò ex Cyrillo Catech. 4. Ne mihi ea tibi proferenti, simpliciter fidem adhibeas, nisi de divinis scripturis eorum quæ dicam demonstrationem accipias. Similia leguntur apud Athanasium, Cyrillum, Cyprianum, Hilarium.
units.tr: First, from Augustine: Do not serve my writings as if they were canonical Scripture. Preface to book 3 of On the Trinity. In the same place, on this matter: Let the reader not love me more than catholic truth, since in all my writings I desire not only a pious reader but also a free corrector. Afterwards he bids that his writings be corrected by divine reading or by unshaken reason. Second, from Cyril, Catechesis 4: Do not give simple faith to me while I say these things to you, unless you receive a demonstration of what I say from the divine Scriptures. Similar passages are read in Athanasius, Cyril, Cyprian and Hilary.

units.la: III. Con-
units.tr: III. Con-

units.la: III. Conciliis magnam autoritatem tribuunt, eadem tamen extra erroris aleam non ponunt. 1. Quia illa non semel errarunt, ita ut posteriora Concilia priora correxerint. 2. Quia intra tria prima secula nulla fuerunt Concilia, unde sequeretur ecclesiam per illa tempora sensu catholico caruisse. 3. Doctrina pontificia idem docet, quia Concilia rata non habet, nisi Papa decreta synodica approbarit. Argumentum certissimum pro nostra sententia. Ad quid enim opus esset Conciliorum decreta correctioni subiicere, si errare non possint?
units.tr: III. They grant great authority to councils, yet do not put them beyond the risk of error. (1) Because they have not erred only once, so that later councils have corrected earlier ones. (2) Because within the first three centuries there were no councils, from which it would follow that the Church in those times lacked catholic sense. (3) Papal doctrine teaches the same thing, since it does not hold councils valid unless the Pope has approved their synodal decrees. This is a most certain argument for our view. For why would it be necessary to subject the decrees of councils to correction, if they could not err?

units.la: IV. De ecclesia repraesentativa ex Car- dinalibus & Episcopis conflata ita iudi- cant.
units.tr: IV. On the representative church, made up of cardinals and bishops, they judge as follows.

units.la: Saepe coetum aliquem appellari ab hominibus ecclesiam, qui ecclesia non est in rei veritate. Et ecclesiam aliquam de iure esse debere ecclesiam, quae de facto ecclesia non est. Pro exemplo sit senatus sacerdotum tempore Christi. Debebant de iure esse ecclesia Dei, quia sedebant in cathedra Mosis, de facto non erant, quia consilium Dei aspernati sunt, adversus semetipsos, Luc. 7: 30. Unde ex invidia, odio, petulantia, Christum filium Dei & Messiam mundi reiecerunt. Nam si fuissent <bl>ἀναξιώντες τὰς γραφάς</bl> ut Beroenses, Act. 17: 11. facile de persona Christi iudicare potuissent. Illi vero neglectis iis, Christum captiosis quaestiunculis & sophisticationibus tentare, eundem contemptissime habere, apud populum tanquam publicanorum socium & seductorem traducere, & tandem veluti Dei blasphematorem morti adiudicare.
units.tr: Men often call an assembly a church which in truth is not a church, and some church ought by right to be a church which in fact is not one. Let the senate of priests at the time of Christ serve as an example. They ought by right to be the church of God, because they sat in the chair of Moses; in fact they were not, because they rejected the counsel of God against themselves, Luke 7:30. Hence, out of envy, hatred and petulance, they rejected Christ, the Son of God and Messiah of the world. For if they had been [ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφάς] examining the Scriptures, like the Bereans, Acts 17:11, they could easily have judged concerning the person of Christ. But they, neglecting these, tried to trap Christ with captious little questions and sophistries, held him in utter contempt, represented him to the people as a companion of publicans and a seducer, and at last condemned him to death as a blasphemer of God.

units.la: Ita certe ecclesiae representativae Romanae membra gloriantur, se sedere in cathedra sancti Petri & Pauli, quorum tamen scripta aspernantur. Dum non solum utriusque Apostoli libros pro canonicis non habent nisi ecclesiae accedat autoritas, id est, nisi ipsi velint; sed etiam integram scripturam, quam Apostolus Paulus Πετροτέρον, Petrus vero firmissimum sermonem vocat, ipsi vero appellant nasum cereū, atramentum sutorium, cuius non fit maior autoritas quàm fabularum AEsopi sine ecclesiæ autoritate.
units.tr: Thus indeed the members of the Roman representative church boast that they sit in the chair of Saints Peter and Paul, whose writings nevertheless they despise. For they not only do not hold the books of both Apostles as canonical unless the authority of the Church is added, that is, unless they themselves are willing; they also call the whole of Scripture, which the Apostle Paul calls [Πετροτέρον] and Peter calls the firmest word, a waxen nose and cobbler's ink, which has no more authority than the fables of Aesop without the authority of the Church.

units.la: Deinde doctrinam eorum, qui præter purum Dei verbum nihil admittunt in rebus ad salutem necessariis, ita perfidè tractant, ut infinitis propemodum falsitatibus & impertinentibus allegationibus eam populo suo proponant. Pro exemplo sint (ut alia omittam) hæc parallela seculiaria Harscheri, cum approbatione superiorum excusa. Ubi lector vel in tribus primis seculis nuper castigatis ultra quinquaginta mendacia reperiet.
units.tr: Then they handle the doctrine of those who admit nothing beyond the pure Word of God in matters necessary to salvation so perfidiously that they set it before their people with almost endless falsehoods and irrelevant allegations. For example (to omit others) let these secular parallels of Harscher serve, published with the approval of superiors. In them the reader will find, even in the first three centuries, recently corrected, more than fifty lies.

units.la: Præterea non attribuunt spiritum sensus catholici hominibus in scriptura potentibus & docentibus diligenter ea, quæ sunt Domini, quomodo his titulis ornatur quidam Apollos nomine, natione Alexandrinus, Act. 18:24,25. Sed episcopis in scriptura sacra hospitibus. Quomodo Stapletonus confitetur, illum consultius facere, qui in caussa fidei episcopum non perinde doctum consulat, quam doctorem theologum in scripturis versatissimum. Qualem ergo sensum catholicum ab his expectabimus?
units.tr: Moreover, they do not attribute the spirit of catholic sense to men who are powerful in Scripture and diligently teach the things of the Lord, such as the man Apollos, of Alexandrian nation, who is adorned with these titles, Acts 18:24,25. Rather, they attribute it to bishops who are strangers to Scripture. As Stapleton confesses, he acts more wisely who, in a matter of faith, consults not a bishop so much as a theologian most versed in Scripture as a teacher. What catholic sense, then, shall we expect from them?

units.la: Iniuste igitur accusamur, quasi intellectum catholicum nullum admittamus, etiamsi horum hominem sensum reiicimus.
units.tr: We are therefore accused unjustly, as if we admitted no catholic understanding, even though we reject the sense of these men.

units.la: Sed quid tandem? an ecclesiæ nihil hic tribuendum? Omninò multum, sed his cautionibus 1. Ut ante omnia dispiciatur, quæ nā sit vera Christi ecclesia. Ea autem est, quæ vocem sponsi Christi sequitur, nec vocem audit alieni 2. Ut illi, qui de sensu scripturæ iudicant sint in loco aliquo ecclesiæ & ius habeant iudicandi. 3. Sint quoque in scriptura potentes. 4. Habeant prae oculis regulam Pauli, Gal.1.8:9. Si quis fit, qui aliud evangelizet (hoc est aliud doctrinae genus proponat) quam quod Apostoli evangelizarunt, anathema sit. 5. Nullus sit episcopus episcoporum (sunt verba Augustini lib. II. contra Donat. cap. 2.) qui tyrannico terrore ad obsequendi necessitate collegas suas adigat. 6. Expectent universi judicium Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui solus habet potestatem de actu nostro judicandi. Idem Augustinus. 7. Judicent sine ulla inflata cervice arrogantia, cum sancta humilitate, cum pace catholica, cum charitate christiana, Augustinus. 8. Ut cum invocatione nominis divini, confessione propriae infirmitatis, & ad Dei omnipotentis gloriam omnia peragant.
units.tr: But what then? Should nothing be attributed to the Church here? Certainly a great deal, but with these cautions: (1) first of all, it must be examined what the true Church of Christ is; it is the one that follows the voice of Christ its Bridegroom and does not hear the voice of a stranger. (2) Those who judge the sense of Scripture must be in some place in the Church and have the right of judging. (3) They must also be powerful in Scripture. (4) They must keep before their eyes the rule of Paul, Gal. 1:8,9: If anyone comes preaching to you another gospel (that is, sets forth another kind of doctrine) than what the Apostles preached, let him be anathema. (5) Let there be no bishop of bishops (these are the words of Augustine, Against the Donatists book 2, chap. 2) who by tyrannical terror forces his colleagues into obedience by necessity. (6) Let all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has the power to judge our act. Augustine again. (7) Let them judge without any puffed-up, stiff-necked arrogance, with holy humility, with catholic peace, with Christian charity, Augustine. (8) That they do all things with invocation of the divine name, with confession of their own weakness, and for the glory of almighty God.

units.la: III. Quod omnes habent pontificem Romanum pro Antichristo, episcopos, praela- tos pro membris Satanae.
units.tr: III. That all hold the Roman pontiff to be Antichrist, and the bishops and prelates to be members of Satan.

units.la: Fateor plerosque ex nostris pontificem Romanum pro Antichristo agnoscere, idque propter summam analogiam prædictionum de Antichristo, & actionum Papæ Romani. Apostolus Paulus Thessalonicenses suos docet, Filium perditionis (notans Antichristū) 1. sese oppositurum adversùs quicquid dicitur Deus aut numen. 2. in templo Dei, tanquam Deum sessurum, id est, regnaturum. 3. præ se laturum se esse Deum 2. Thess. 2:4.
units.tr: I admit that many of our people acknowledge the Roman pontiff as Antichrist, and this on account of the close correspondence between the predictions about Antichrist and the actions of the Roman Pope. The Apostle Paul teaches his Thessalonians that the Son of perdition (meaning Antichrist) (1) will set himself against whatever is called God or divine; (2) will sit in the temple of God, as God, that is, will reign there; (3) will display himself as being God. 2 Thess. 2:4.

units.la: Johannes in Apocalypsi sua, de eodem loquens dicit: se vidisse bestiam aliam, id est, Antichristum 1. ascendentem e terra. 2. habentem duo cornua similia agno. 3. exercuisse omnem potestatem prioris bestiæ in conspectu eius. 4. fecisse ut ignis e cœlo descenderet in conspectu hominum. 5. dixisse incolis terræ, ut faciant imaginem bestiæ. 6. animasse imaginem bestiæ, ita ut imago illa loqueretur. 7. numerum eius esse 666. Nam locum hunc de Antichristo loqui Bellarminus asserit, & Irenæum testem provocat.
units.tr: John, speaking of the same figure in his Apocalypse, says that he saw another beast, that is, Antichrist: (1) coming up out of the earth; (2) having two horns like a lamb; (3) exercising all the power of the first beast in its sight; (4) causing fire to come down from heaven in the sight of men; (5) telling the inhabitants of the earth to make an image of the beast; (6) giving life to the image of the beast, so that the image could speak; (7) its number being 666. Bellarmine asserts that this passage speaks of Antichrist, and calls Irenaeus as a witness.

units.la: Complementum harum prædictionum in primatu Romano experientia ipsa evidenter demonstrat. De singulis breviter.
units.tr: The fulfilment of these predictions in the Roman primacy is clearly shown by experience itself. Briefly, point by point:

units.la: I. Sese effert pontifex Romanus supra quicquid dicitur Deus. Quia publicè in ecclesia dispensare audet contra expressum Dei mandatum, absolvendo certa summa pecuniæ maximos peccatores: quia canonisando sanctos gloriam invocationis aliis tribuit, quod Deus dixit se nunquam facturum, Esa. 42:8. quia in Glossa docetur, pontificem posse dispensare contra Evangelium, contra Apostolum, contra novum Testamentum, contra jus naturæ, id est, contra autorem naturæ & gratiæ.
units.tr: I. He exalts himself above whatever is called God. For he publicly dares to dispense in the church against the express command of God, absolving the greatest sinners for a sum of money; for by canonizing saints he gives to others the glory of invocation, which God said he would never do, Isa. 42:8; for it is taught in the Gloss that the pope can dispense against the Gospel, against the Apostle, against the New Testament, against the law of nature, that is, against the author of nature and of grace.

units.la: II. Sedet in templo Dei, hoc est, in ecclesia, quæ Dei est de iure, sed nunc de facto apostatica, quia admisit alienum, qui iam ipsam vocat Sponsam suam, Extrav. Tit. 5. cap.2. Ubi notandum singulari Dei providentia factū, quod in historiis Paparum, ubique ipsi dicuntur sedere.
units.tr: II. He sits in the temple of God, that is, in the church, which is God's by right but is now apostate in fact, because it has admitted a stranger, who now calls it his own Spouse, Extrav. Tit. 5, cap. 2. Here it should be noted that, by a singular providence of God, it has come about that in the histories of the Popes they are everywhere said to sit.

units.la: III. Tanquam Deus, quomodo appellari gaudet, & reipsa à iuis amasiis appellatur. Distinct. 96. argumentatur Papa Nicolaus; Pontificem à potestate seculari nec solvi, nec ligari posse, quòd Deus appelletur, cùm Deus ab hominibus non iudicari posse, manifestum sit. Sixto IV. Romam ingressuro in arcu triumphali scriptum:
units.tr: III. As God, as he delights to be called, and as he is indeed called by his followers. In Distinction 96, Pope Nicholas argues that the pontiff can be neither loosed nor bound by secular power, because he is called God, since it is plain that God cannot be judged by men. An inscription was written on the triumphal arch for Sixtus IV as he was about to enter Rome:

units.la: Et merito in terris crederis esse DEVS.
units.tr: And rightly you are believed to be God on earth.

units.la: IV. Effert se super omne, quod dicitur Numen, id est, super Imperatorem, Reges, Principes, qui in scriptura Dii appellantur. Hoc tam manifestum quàm quòd manifestissimum. Præter praxin ordinariam en duo exempla H verè extraordinaria. Quando Celestinus III. In coronatione Henrici VI. Imperatoris, coronam Imperatori imposuit, mox pede amovit (erat enim Imperator flexis genibus, Papâ infella sedente) ad significandum penes Pontificem Romanum esse coronam Imperatoribus imponere & auferre.
units.tr: IV. He exalts himself above every thing that is called divine, that is, above the Emperor, kings and princes, who in Scripture are called gods. This is as plain as anything could be. Besides the ordinary practice, here are two truly extraordinary examples. When Celestine III, at the coronation of the Emperor Henry VI, placed the crown on the Emperor's head and at once removed it with his foot (for the Emperor was kneeling while the Pope sat on his chair), to signify that it lies within the power of the Roman Pontiff to place the crown on emperors and to take it away.

units.la: Et Alexander III. pedibus cervici Imperatoris Friderici Barbarofsæ instituit, cum his verbi; super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis. Hæc reverâ hominibus horrorem incutiunt, & vix verisimilia viderentur, nisi Historici Pontificii ea in lucem dedissent. Vide Platinam in vita horum Pontificum.
units.tr: And Alexander III set his feet on the neck of the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, with these words: you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk. These things truly strike horror into men, and would hardly seem credible had not Papist historians brought them to light. See Platina in the lives of these Popes.

units.la: V. E terra ascendit, id est, ex obscuro statu ad maximam eminentiam, puta ex tuguriolo piscatorio ad lacum Tyberiadis, in Romanam Basilicam.
units.tr: V. He comes up out of the earth, that is, from an obscure condition to the greatest eminence: from a fisherman's hut to the Lake of Tiberias, and to the Roman basilica.

units.la: VI. Cornua duo, id est, duplicem potestatem prætendit, spiritualem & secularem. Unde Bonifacius in coronatione sua duos gladios præferre iussit. Imò duplicem potestatem ut agnus Dei Christus, nunc ad dextram Patris sedens, potestatem, inquam, in cœlo & in terra (nam illam secularem Christus in his terris non exercuit) Unde in Concil. Lateranensi Julio acclamatum: Tu es omnia & super omnia: Omnis potestas tibi data est in cœlo & in terra similiter ut Christus de seipso, Matth. 28: 18.
units.tr: VI. Two horns, that is, he claims a twofold power, spiritual and secular. Whence Boniface, at his coronation, ordered that two swords be carried before him. Indeed he claims a twofold power like Christ the Lamb of God, now sitting at the right hand of the Father: power, I say, in heaven and on earth (for Christ did not exercise that secular power in this world). Whence at the Lateran Council it was acclaimed to Julius: You are all things and above all things: all power is given to you in heaven and on earth, just as Christ said of himself, Matt. 28:18.

units.la: VII. Exercet potestatem prioris bestiæ, id est, veteris Imperii Romani.
units.tr: VII. He exercises the power of the first beast, that is, of the old Roman Empire.

units.la: Nam 1. sedet Romæ. 2. vult videri caput universi mundi in spiritualibus & secularibus, ut vetus Roma, quæ caput orbis erat. 3. est Pontifex maximus, ut olim Julius Cæsar seipsum appellavit, Christus verò non nisi Pontifex magnus, Heb. 4: 14. 4. bella gerit aperta in conspectu totius mundi. 5. ignem facit è cœlo descendere, dum fulmine excommunicationis ferit peccatores, & in excommunicationis signum ignem descendere facit ex capitolio.
units.tr: For (1) he sits at Rome; (2) he wishes to be seen as head of the whole world, in spiritual and secular matters, like old Rome, which was the head of the world; (3) he is Pontifex maximus, as Julius Caesar once called himself, whereas Christ is only a great high priest, Heb. 4:14; (4) he wages open war in the sight of the whole world; (5) he makes fire come down from heaven, when he strikes sinners with the thunderbolt of excommunication, and as a sign of excommunication he makes fire come down from the Capitol.

units.la: VIII. Facit per incolas terra imagi- nem bestia, eamq; animat
units.tr: VIII. Through the inhabitants of the earth it makes an image of the beast, and gives it life.

units.la: Hoc est, Imperiu vetus Romanum ita tractare fatagit, ut in federibus, bellis & transactionibus non nisi ab ipso animatum, & iuxta bullas suas & Nuntios a latere loquendum sit.
units.tr: That is, the old Roman Empire busies itself so that, in treaties, wars and agreements, nothing is to be done except what has been animated by the Pope himself, and what is to be spoken according to his bulls and his legates.

units.la: IX. Habet numerum 666. Quia primatus ille post Gregorium I. incepit cum Bonifacio III. circa annum Christi 600. quibus si addas numerum Bonifacii, qui excepto Petro (is enim Pontifex Rom. non fuit) est Papa 66. habes numerum 666.
units.tr: IX. It has the number 666. For that primacy began after Gregory I, with Boniface III, around the year of Christ 600. If you add to these the number of Boniface, who (excluding Peter, for he was not a Roman pontiff) was the 66th Pope, you have the number 666.

units.la: Hisce sic breviter delibatis (nam integrum tractatum postularent) apparet cur nostri pontifice Rom. pro Antichristo agnoverint. Et æquus lector iudicet an sine causa. Quod de Episcopis & Prælatis adiecit, non defendo; mancipia Pontificis à nostris sæpe appellantur, qui absque eo ne minimum quidem in religione docere audent. Si qui sint, qui aliter loquuntur, ipsi videriht.
units.tr: Having touched on these matters so briefly (for they would require a full treatise), it is clear why our people have recognised the Roman pontiff as Antichrist. Let the fair reader judge whether they did so without cause. What he added about bishops and prelates I do not defend. Our people often call them the slaves of the Pope, since without him they dare not teach even the smallest point of religion. If there are any who speak otherwise, let them see to it themselves.

units.la: IV. Quod omnes nullam ferunt con- stitutionem, nullas ecclesiæ catholicæ cere- monias.
units.tr: IV. That they bear no constitutions at all, and no ceremonies of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Loquitur procul dubio Jesuita de constitutionibus ecclesiæ Romanæ, de delectu ciborum, de festis ab ecclesia indictis, de baptismo campanarum, de imaginibus, de quadragesima, de horis canonicis, peregrinationibus, cereis & cineribus, & si quæ sint similes, quas debebat appellare papisticas non catholicas. Nam eam ob causam illas reiicimus, quòd contra scripturam sacram in ecclesiam introductæ sint, ad tentandum Deum, ut Apostoli loquebantur Act. 15: 10. cùm credamus, nos per gratiam Iesu Christi (absque illis) servatum iri ut ibidem docet Apostolus Petrus: Interim nos nullas constitutiones catholicae ecclesiae habere falsum est. Observamus diem dominicam ex institutione ecclesiae: in baptismo trinam aspersionem, baptismum parvulorum circa octavum diem. Habemus statas horas precum, item iuxta Augustini doctrinam, festum conceptionis, nativitatis, passionis, resurrectionis, ascensionis Christi in coelum, & missionis Spiritus sancti die pentecostes. Jeiunia etiam necessitatis tempore. An hoc est nullas constitutiones ecclesiae catholicae observare?
units.tr: Doubtless the Jesuit is speaking of the constitutions of the Roman Church: concerning the choice of foods, concerning feasts appointed by the Church, concerning the baptism of bells, concerning images, concerning Lent, concerning the canonical hours, pilgrimages, wax candles and ashes, and whatever else is similar, which he ought to have called Papistical rather than Catholic. For we reject them on this ground: that they were introduced into the Church contrary to holy Scripture, to tempt God, as the Apostles put it in Acts 15:10, since we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus (apart from them), as the Apostle Peter teaches in the same place. Meanwhile, we have no constitutions of the Catholic Church is false. We observe the Lord's day by the institution of the Church; in baptism we use threefold sprinkling, and we baptise infants around the eighth day. We have fixed hours of prayer; likewise, following the teaching of Augustine, the feast of the conception, nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension of Christ into heaven, and the sending of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. We also fast in times of necessity. Is this not observing the constitutions of the Catholic Church?

units.la: V. Quod omnes aeque oderunt & op- pugnant sacrificium Missae.
units.tr: V. That they all equally hate and oppose the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: De hoc multa dicenda forent, sed non permittit parvum hoc opusculum. Dicam paucis cur sacrificium missaticum a nostris ecclesiis reiectum sit & merito etiamnum reiiciatur.
units.tr: Much could be said about this, but this little work does not permit it. I will say briefly why the sacrifice of the Mass has been rejected by our churches, and why it is rightly rejected still.

units.la: I. Nomen Missae novum est, in scripturis non lectum, nec ante tertium seculum, id est, ante Ambrosii tempora in ecclesia auditum.
units.tr: I. The name Mass is new; it is not read in the Scriptures, and it was not heard in the Church before the third century, that is, before the time of Ambrose.

units.la: 2. Sacrificium Missæ est itidem novum inventum, sicut & totus canon Missæ. Etenim tempore Originis & Athanasii nulla adhuc fuerunt altaria, uti nec tempore Concilii Nicæni. mensis eo tempore utebantur in templis, iuxta morem Apostolicæ ecclesiæ. Unde per metonymiam, eucharistia mensa Domini appellata veteribus, & in actis synodi Nicænæ caput de eucharistia titulum habet ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΘΕΙΑΣ ΤΡΑΠΕΖΗΣ. 2. Circa annum 140. Alexander primus panem azymum & vinum aquâ dilutum instituit. Verba Platinæ sunt: voluit quoque aquam admisceri vinô in consecratione sanguinis & corporis Iesu Christi, quo significatur Christum ecclesiæ conjunctum esse. Oblationem quoque ex azymo, non autem ex fermentato ut antea fieri mandavit. Hic primùm fractio étio fuit omissa. 3. Transsubstantiatio verò longè post inventa à Johanne Damasceno circa annum 740, & postea 755, panis adoratio. De canonis missatici compilatione vide Polydorum Virgilium, de inventione rerum lib. 5. cap. 10. ubi docet, Celestinum instituisse introitum, cuius initium est, Iudica me Deus. Damasum, confessionem sacerdotis, cùm dicit, confiteor: Gregorium, antiphonam: Gregorium, gloriam in excelsis Deo. Gelasium, hymnos.
units.tr: 2. The sacrifice of the Mass is likewise a new invention, as is the whole canon of the Mass. For in the time of Origen and Athanasius there were as yet no altars, nor in the time of the Council of Nicaea; at that time they used tables in the churches, following the custom of the apostolic Church. Hence, by metonymy, the Eucharist was called by the ancients the table of the Lord, and in the acts of the Nicene Synod the chapter on the Eucharist bears the title Concerning the holy table [ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΘΕΙΑΣ ΤΡΑΠΕΖΗΣ]. 2. Around the year 140, Alexander I instituted unleavened bread and wine diluted with water. The words of Platina are: He also wished water to be mixed with the wine in the consecration of the blood and body of Jesus Christ, by which it is signified that Christ is joined to the Church. He also commanded that the oblation be made of unleavened bread, not of leavened bread as had been done before. Here the breaking of the bread was first omitted. 3. Transubstantiation was invented much later, by John of Damascus around the year 740, and afterwards, in 755, the adoration of the bread. On the compilation of the Mass canon see Polydore Vergil, On the Invention of Things, book 5, chapter 10, where he teaches that Celestine instituted the introit, whose beginning is Judge me, O God; Damasus the confession of the priest, when he says I confess; Gregory the antiphon; Gregory Glory to God in the highest; Gelasius the hymns.

units.la: 3. Res verò ipsa, id est, sacrificium Missæ secundùm omnes circumstantias sacrificio Christi in cruce perfecto contrariatur. Nam sacrificium Christi est 1. institutum secundùm ordinem Melchisedek. 2. est sacerdotium æternum & ἀπαραβατον nunquam transiturum. 3. non potest offerri, nisi à sacerdote qui sit sanctus, sine ullo vitio & segregatus à peccatoribus. 4. perfici debet ab eo, qui non habeat necesse pro propriis peccatis offerre. 5. semel tantum erat peragendum. Quod vocabulum ἐφ' ἅπαξ Apostolus in epistola ad Hebraeos ter repetiit, cum de sacrificio Christi locutus fuit. Atqui sacrificium missaticum non est secundum ordinem Melchisedeck, quia habet successores, quod de Melchisedeciano negat Apostolus. 2. Non est ἀπαξ-γάβατον, quia quotidie repetitur. 3. Conficitur à peccatore. 4. Qui necesse habet pro propriis peccatis offerre; videatur missale Romanum in praeparatione ad Missam, ad albam. 5. Non semel peragitur, sed quotidie. 6. Nec est coniunctum cum morte Christi & effusione sanguinis eius.
units.tr: 3. But the thing itself, that is, the sacrifice of the Mass, in all its circumstances is contrary to the sacrifice of Christ perfected on the cross. For the sacrifice of Christ is: (1) instituted according to the order of Melchizedek; (2) an eternal priesthood, inviolable [ἀπαράβατον], never to pass away; (3) it can be offered only by a priest who is holy, without any fault, and set apart from sinners; (4) it must be accomplished by one who has no need to offer for his own sins; (5) it was to be completed once only. The Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews repeated this word, once for all [ἐφ' ἅπαξ], three times, when he spoke of the sacrifice of Christ. Yet the sacrifice of the Mass is not according to the order of Melchizedek, because it has successors, which the Apostle denies of the Melchizedekian priesthood. (2) It is not inviolable [ἀπαξ-γάβατον], because it is repeated every day. (3) It is made by a sinner. (4) The priest who offers it needs to offer for his own sins; let the Roman Missal be consulted in the preparation for the Mass, at the alb. (5) It is not accomplished once, but every day. (6) Nor is it joined with the death of Christ and the shedding of his blood.

units.la: 4. Sacrificium Missae è diametro pugnat cum institutione Dominica sa- crae coenae.
units.tr: 4. The sacrifice of the Mass is diametrically opposed to the Lord's institution of the holy Supper.

units.la: Nam in institutione Dominica 1. iubentur omnes edere de fracto pane & bibere de poculo benedictionis: in missa sacerdos solus edit & bibit. 2. in institutione Christus mentionem facit fracti, id est, crucifixi corporis & effusi sanguinis: in missa negatur, quod Christus aliquid patiatur, & effusio sanguinis nulla est, unde vocant sacrificium incruentum. 3. Christus in institutione iussit commemorare mortem Domini donec venerit, in missa iteratur. 4. in coena Domini panis & vinum adsunt, sicuti in omni sacramento duo sunt, signum & res signata: in missa panem non adesse, est dogma catholicum, inquit Harscherus paulo infra.
units.tr: For in the Lord's institution, (1) all are bidden to eat of the broken bread and to drink from the cup of blessing; in the Mass the priest alone eats and drinks. (2) In the institution Christ speaks of the broken body, that is, the crucified body, and the poured-out blood; in the Mass it is denied that Christ suffers anything, and there is no shedding of blood, which is why they call it an unbloody sacrifice. (3) In the institution Christ commanded that the death of the Lord be remembered until he comes; in the Mass it is repeated. (4) In the Lord's Supper bread and wine are present, just as in every sacrament there are two things, the sign and the thing signified; in the Mass, that bread is not present is a Catholic dogma, says Harscher a little further on.

units.la: VI. Quod omnes ex ecclesia conantur omne sacerdotium profligatum atque sublatum. Varia nos habemus sacrificia, sine quibus religio Christiana subsistere non potest. Primum ac praecipuum sacrificium nostrum est sacrificium illud ἱλαστικόν (propitiatorium) quod Jesus Christus seipsum obtulit Deo Patri pro peccatis generis humani in ara crucis. Unde metonymice modò ἱλασμός propitiatio 1. Joh. 2: 2. modò propitiatorium in sanguine ipsius Rom. 3: 25. appellatur. Cuius olim typus fuit propitiatorium arcæ unà cum Cherubinis, Heb. 9: 5. hoc sacrificium nos in ecclesia nostra habemus & celebramus suo modo quotidie, quę cùm eleganter ex Augustino observarit Forbesius in instructionibus Historico-theologicis lib. XI. cap. 10. Verba ipsius hîc subiicere non piget, quondoquidem veterum Patrum quos citat, sententiis, nostrâ quoq; sententiam complectitur. Sic autè ille:
units.tr: VI. That all the Church's teachers try to overthrow and abolish the whole priesthood. We have various sacrifices, without which the Christian religion cannot stand. The first and chief of our sacrifices is that propitiatory sacrifice [hilastikon] which Jesus Christ offered himself to God the Father for the sins of the human race on the altar of the cross. Hence he is called by metonymy sometimes propitiation [hilasmos], 1 John 2:2, and sometimes the propitiatory in his blood, Rom. 3:25. Of this the propitiatory of the ark, together with the Cherubim, was once the type, Heb. 9:5. We have this sacrifice in our Church and celebrate it in our own way every day. Forbes has observed this elegantly from Augustine in his Instructiones historico-theologicae, book 11, chapter 10. It is not a trouble to set his words down here, since he embraces our view as well in the opinions of the ancient Fathers whom he cites. He writes thus:

units.la: Eucharistia non est verum & reale propitiatorium sacrificium (prout relativè veritas symbolo, res autem opponitur sacramento) sed symbolicum sacrificium seu ministerium, Dionys. de ecclesiast. hierarch. cap. 3. est sacramentum memoriæ. Augustinus: huius sacrificii caro & sanguis ante adventum Christi per victimas similitudinum promittebatur: in Passione Christi per ipsam veritatem reddebatur: post alcenium Christi per sacramentum memoriæ celebratur. lib. 20. cont. Faustum, cap 21. est immolatio Christi non in seipso, sed in sacramento. Augustinus: Nonne semel immolatus est Christus in ieipso, & tamen in sacramento non solùm per omnes Paschæ solennitates, sed omni die populo immolatur: nec utique mentitur, qui interrogatus, responderit immolari? Si enim sacramenta similitudinem earum rerum, quarum sacramenta sunt, non haberent, omninò sacramenta non essent. Ex hac autem similitudine plerumque etiam ipsarum rerum nomina accipiunt. Epist. 23. Quocirca non ineptè dici potest sacrificium sacramentale, quod in pane eucharistiæ,& poculo similiter eucharistiæ celebratur, Deo quidem in gratiarum actionem, nobis verò in fidem, in medelam, &c. In præcedenti sectione Eusebium & Chrysostomosoftomum citat, qui celebrationem coenæ vocant μνήμην ἀντὶ θυσίας; item μνημὴν τῆς μεγάλης θυμάτος, & ἀνάμνησιν θυσίας, ἣν πιστεύομεν.
units.tr: The Eucharist is not a true and real propitiatory sacrifice (for truth is opposed to a symbol in the way that the thing is opposed to the sacrament), but a symbolic sacrifice, or ministry, Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3; it is a sacrament of remembrance. Augustine: the flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before Christ's coming through victims as likenesses; in the Passion of Christ they were rendered through the truth itself; after the ascension of Christ they are celebrated through the sacrament of remembrance, book 20 against Faustus, chapter 21, is the immolation of Christ not in himself but in the sacrament. Augustine: Was Christ not sacrificed once in himself, and yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed to the people not only at all the Paschal solemnities but every day? Nor does he lie who, when asked, answers that he is sacrificed. For if sacraments did not have a likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they very often receive the names of the things themselves. Letter 23. Wherefore it may not inaptly be said that there is a sacramental sacrifice, which is celebrated in the bread of the Eucharist and likewise in the cup of the Eucharist, offered to God indeed in thanksgiving, but to us for faith, for healing, and so on. In the preceding section he cites Eusebius and Chrysostom, who call the celebration of the Supper a remembrance instead of a sacrifice [mnemen anti thysias]; likewise a remembrance of the great sacrifice [mnemen tes megales thymatos], and a remembrance of the sacrifice which we believe [anamnesin thysias, hen pisteuomen].

units.la: Reliqua sacrificia, quæ fideles tanquam sacerdotes Deo offerunt, sunt, primo, sacrificium laudis, sive labiorum celebrantium nomen Dei Heb 13: 15. sacrificium precum, quæ Oecumenius vocat ἀναμιμνήσκοντες θυσίας τὰς διὰ χειλέων. Secundo sacrificium sive victima beneficentiæ & communicationis, quo delectatur Deus ibid. v. 16. Tertio sacrificium fidei, per quam nos ipsos Deo offerimus, Phil. 2: 17. Quarto denique sacrificium nostri ipsius, quo quicquid in nobis est, Deo offerimus iuxta Apostoli hortationem Rom. 12: 1. Adhortor igitur vos fratres per miserationes Dei, ut sistatis corpora vestra, hostiam vivam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem illũ cultum vestrum. De quo David Propheta Psal. 51. 19. Sacrificia Dei sunt Spiritus fractus.
units.tr: The remaining sacrifices which the faithful, as priests, offer to God are, first, the sacrifice of praise, that is, the lips confessing the name of God, Heb. 13:15; the sacrifice of prayers, which Oecumenius calls remembering the sacrifices of the lips [anamimnaskontes thysias tas dia cheileon]. Second, the sacrifice or victim of beneficence and fellowship, in which God takes delight, ibid. v. 16. Third, the sacrifice of faith, by which we offer ourselves to God, Phil. 2:17. Fourth and finally, the sacrifice of ourselves, by which we offer to God whatever is in us, according to the Apostle's exhortation, Rom. 12:1: I exhort you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your rational service. Of this the prophet David says, Psalm 51:19: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.

units.la: Huiusce
units.tr: Of this kind.
