That a presbyter is not to be distinguished from a bishop by any difference. Bellarmine too says the same.

units.la: Deinde Melanchtonem accusat, quòd mala fide Epiphanii locum allegarit in apologia confessionis Augustanæ.
units.tr: Next he accuses Melanchthon of bad faith, because he cited the passage from Epiphanius in his Apology for the Augsburg Confession.

units.la: Animadverto ex Patrum lectione de Aerio distinctè loquendum esse. Considerandus enim, vel ut Ariana hæresi totaliter imbutus, qualis fuit etiam antequam Eustatius Episcopatum accepisset: vel ut dogmata quædam singularia fovens, quę demum post promotionem Eustatii tenuit & propósuit ex invidia, ob denegatum episcopatum. Qualia sunt, quæ de oblationibus pro mortuis, de statis ieiuniis & æqualitate presbyterorum & episcoporum docuit. Aerium autem damnatum fuisse (quatenus Arianus fuit, non est dubium: condemnatum fuisse propter privata dogmata ex nullo Concilio probari potest. Augustinus propter illa Aerium non refutavit. Hieronymus vero circa presbyterorum & episcoporum æqualitatem idem sentit quod Aerius.
units.tr: I observe from reading the Fathers that we must speak distinctly about Aerius. For he must be considered either as wholly steeped in the Arian heresy, as he was even before Eustathius had received the episcopate, or as one who cherished certain singular opinions, which he afterwards held and put forward, out of envy, after Eustathius was promoted and he himself was refused the bishopric. Such are the opinions he taught about oblations for the dead, about fixed fasts, and about the equality of presbyters and bishops. That Aerius was condemned, insofar as he was an Arian, is beyond doubt; that he was condemned for his private opinions cannot be proved from any council. Augustine did not refute Aerius on account of those opinions. Jerome, however, holds the same view as Aerius on the equality of presbyters and bishops.

units.la: Nec dissimulavit Medina, ut docet Valentia in disp. 9. Tomi IV. in tertiam Thomæ, docens multos ex Patribus cum Hieronymo sensisse. Errorem tamen appellat Medina in istis Patribus, nempe Hieronymo, Sedulio, Anshelmo, Augustino, Ambrosio, Chrysostomo. Ut videas reverentiam quam exhibent Pontificii S. Patribus. Sed, inquis, Epiphanius Aerii singularia illa dogmata refutavit. De hoc iterum distinctè. Primò quod superioritatem episcoporum, ratione ordinis & jurisdictionis simul, ut hodie pontificii docent, Epiphanius asseruerit, ex eodem Patre demonstrari non potest. Deinde quia Epiphanius tam prolixè differentiam episcoporum & presbyterorum asserit, sit certè hic error Epiphanio proprius. Quia autem quæstio nobis est de iure divino, non ecclesiastico, debebat Epiphanius ex scripturis illam differentiam demonstrare, quod non fecit, sed Aerio scripturam obiiciente, ipse ad ordinationem ecclesiae recurrit, dicens. Nam singula res non omnia ab initio habuerunt, sed progressu temporis ea quae ad necessariorum perfectionem requiruntur, parabantur.
units.tr: Medina did not conceal this, as Valentia teaches in disputation 9 of volume IV on the third part of Thomas, where he says that many of the Fathers agreed with Jerome. Yet Medina calls this an error in those Fathers, namely Jerome, Sedulius, Anselm, Augustine, Ambrose and Chrysostom. See the reverence the Papists show to the holy Fathers! But, you say, Epiphanius refuted those singular opinions of Aerius. On this point, again, let us be distinct. First, that Epiphanius asserted the superiority of bishops, both by reason of order and of jurisdiction together, as the Papists teach today, cannot be shown from the same Father. Next, since Epiphanius asserts the difference between bishops and presbyters at such length, this error is certainly peculiar to Epiphanius. But since our question concerns divine right, not ecclesiastical right, Epiphanius ought to have demonstrated that difference from the Scriptures. This he did not do; when Aerius objected Scripture, Epiphanius himself had recourse to the ordering of the Church, saying: For individual things did not all have everything from the beginning, but with the passage of time those things which are required for the perfecting of what is necessary were provided.

units.la: De ieiunio nos non Aerii sed Epiphanii doctrinam sequimur. Approbavit Aerius ea tantum ieiunia quae quilibet privatus sibi elegit, publica & ab ecclesia indicta ieiunia reiecit. Nos utraque approbamus. Nam habet ecclesia hanc facultatem, ut ingruentibus calamitatibus aut aliis de causis ieiunia praecipere possit, cuius mandato privatis hominibus fas non est contradicere. Quid autem nos in ieiuniis Papisticis desideremus postea dicam.
units.tr: As for fasting, we follow not the teaching of Aerius but that of Epiphanius. Aerius approved only those fasts which any private person chose for himself, and rejected public fasts appointed by the Church. We approve both. For the Church has this power: when calamities threaten or for other reasons, it may enjoin fasts, and it is not lawful for private persons to contradict its command. What we miss in the Papistical fasts I shall say afterwards.

units.la: Oblationum & precum pro mortuis mentionem facit Epiphanius in Anacephaleosi, lib. vero tertio de haeres. 75 precum tantum, quas scribit Aerium reiecisse. Ipse vero Epiphanius, in eodem loco preces pro demortuis asserit, sed ibidem de oblationibus ne verbum quidem. Quem locum forte inspexit Philippus Melanchton, adeo ut non magnam caussam habuerit Harfcherus calumniandi Philippum quasi mala fide Epiphanium citarit. Praesertim si oculum intendat ad disputationem, in qua versabatur Philippus. Nam permanens in statu controversiae scribit: Nos Aerio non patrocinamur, sed vobiscum litigamus qui haeresin manifeste pugnantem cum Prophetis, Apostolis & sanctis Patribus sceleste defenditis, videlicet quod missa ex opere operato justificet, quod mereatur remissionem culpae & poenae etiam injustis, pro quibus applicatur si non ponant obicem. Habuit ergo iustam caussam conqueredi Melanchton, quod falso citent adversarii damnationem Aerii, quia nihil horum quae in controversia sunt legitur in Epiphanio, nihil de missa, nihil de opere operato, nihil de remissione culpæ & pœnæ, nihil de obice.
units.tr: Epiphanius makes mention of oblations and prayers for the dead in his summary, but in the third book on heresies (heresy 75) he mentions only the prayers, which he writes that Aerius rejected. Yet Epiphanius himself, in the same place, asserts prayers for the departed, but says not a word about oblations there. Philip Melanchthon perhaps looked at this passage, so that Harscher had little reason for accusing Philip of citing Epiphanius in bad faith. This is especially so if one looks at the disputation in which Philip was engaged. For, keeping to the state of the controversy, he writes: We do not defend Aerius, but we contend with you, who wickedly defend a heresy manifestly at odds with the Prophets, the Apostles and the holy Fathers, namely that the Mass justifies by the work done, that it merits remission of guilt and punishment even for the unjust, for whom it is applied unless they place an obstacle. Melanchthon therefore had just cause to complain that the adversaries falsely cite the condemnation of Aerius, since none of these things at issue in the controversy is read in Epiphanius: nothing about the Mass, nothing about the work done, nothing about remission of guilt and punishment, nothing about an obstacle.

units.la: Nam hæc omnia sunt nova commenta. Ideo illud de omissione oblationum parvi momenti, quia de iis non erat quæstio. Nam nemo vel leviter in veterum historiis versatus, negabit oblationes apud ipsos in usu fuisse. Sed longè aliter quam hodie in Papatu. Ita ut qui illas concedit, has propterea non laudet. De utrisque & earum differentia breviter occasione citati loci ex Epiphanio differam.
units.tr: For all these things are recent inventions. As for the omission of oblations, that is of little weight, because there was no question about them. For no one who has read even slightly in the histories of the ancients will deny that oblations were in use among them. But they were very different from what they are today in Papacy. So one who admits oblations at that time is not for that reason to praise them now. I shall briefly discuss both, and their difference, on the occasion of the cited passage from Epiphanius.

units.la: Veterum preces & oblationes nihil aliud fuisse, quàm merum testimonium charitatis erga defunctos, historia nos docet, & consistebant in commemoratione defunctorum ad altare, ubi annuatim nomina martyrum legebantur, ut etiam aliorum sanctorum. Epiphanius hoc vocat memoriam facere & ὀνομαστίac dicit fieri pro Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, Evangelistis, Martyribus, Confessoribus, Episcopis, Anachoretis & universo ordine. Chrysostomus dicit fieri pro martyribus & omnibus defunctis fidelibus. Secundò commemorationi adiungebantur preces pro defunctis tam justis, quàm injustis. Harum precum utilitatem Epiphanius contra Aerium asserit, qui eam negabat; primò in viventibus, qui in hisce precibus fidem & spem suam de demortuis declarabant, quòd crederent pie defunctos & esse & vivere cum Domino, ut ipse loquitur. Precabantur etiam pro se, ut similem beatum exitum ex hac vita obtinere possent. Fiebant quoque pro iniustis, inquit Epiphanius, etiamsi non totam culpam abscindant. Precibus additæ oblationes, id est, sacrificia eucharistica, qualia fuerunt donaria, epulæ pauperibus præparatæ, donationes in usum pauperum, ecclesiæ & scholarum.
units.tr: History teaches us that the prayers and oblations of the ancients were nothing other than a plain testimony of love towards the departed. They consisted in commemorating the dead at the altar, where annually the names of martyrs were read, as also those of other saints. Epiphanius calls this making memory [ὀνομαστί] and says that it is done for the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Martyrs, Confessors, Bishops, Anchorites and the whole order. Chrysostom says it is done for the martyrs and all the faithful departed. Secondly, to the commemoration were added prayers for the departed, both just and unjust. Epiphanius asserts the usefulness of these prayers against Aerius, who denied it: first, for the living, who in these prayers declared their faith and hope concerning the departed, that they believed the piously departed both are and live with the Lord, as he himself puts it. They also prayed for themselves, that they might obtain a similar blessed end from this life. They were offered also for the unjust, says Epiphanius, even if they do not wholly remove their guilt. To the prayers were added oblations, that is, eucharistic sacrifices, such as gifts, meals prepared for the poor, and donations for the use of the poor, the Church and the schools.

units.la: Hic usus precum & oblationum an- tiquus
units.tr: This custom of prayer and oblation is ancient

units.la: tiquus est, sed non antiquissimus, nam 170. annis post natum Christum nullæ memoriæ celebratæ fuerunt sanctorum martyrum. Tertullianus (qui primus harum mentionem facit, nam Clementis constitutiones Bellarminus ipse reiicit & Dionysii lib. de Hierarch.) traditioni ecclesiasticæ eas tribuit, cùm scribit: harum disciplinarum si leges expostules scripturarum, nullam invenies, traditio tibi prætendetur. Lib. de corona milit. Si de caussa quæratur huius usus, non una fuit omnium temporum. Nam commemoratio Martyrum fiebat in ipsorum natalitijs (id est, die quo martyrium subiverunt, & recenter ingressi sunt ad vitam æternam) ut commonerentur superstites adhærere martyrum vestigiis. Hoc ex Augustino intelligi potest. Augustini quoquè tempore opinio obtinuit apud multos, animas beatorum non statim ingredi in cœlestia gaudia, sed in separato aliquo loco in quo securæ expectent iudicii diem ubi corpus recepturæ & angelis æquandæ sint, permanere: alii deinde putabant ex sanctis alios tardius resurrecturos. Hinc preces pro maturanda resurrectione & animarum cum corpore coniunctione. Imprimis autem respiciebant ad tremendam illam iudicii diem, quam omnibus demortuis felicë ac beatam apprecabantur. Unde adhuc illud à multis memorationi piè defunctorum additum, Gott wölle jhm ein fröliche aufferstendnuß verleyhen.
units.tr: It is ancient, but not the most ancient. For 170 years after the birth of Christ there were no recorded celebrations of the holy martyrs. Tertullian, who is the first to mention them (for Bellarmine himself rejects the Constitutions of Clement and the book of Dionysius on the Hierarchy), attributes them to ecclesiastical tradition when he writes: If you demand the laws of these observances from the Scriptures, you will find none; tradition will be put forward to you. De corona militis. If the reason for this custom is asked, it was not the same at all times. For the commemoration of the martyrs was made on their natal days (that is, the day on which they underwent martyrdom and newly entered eternal life), so that the survivors might be reminded to follow in the footsteps of the martyrs. This can be understood from Augustine. In Augustine's time too, many held the opinion that the souls of the blessed do not at once enter heavenly joys, but remain in some separate place where they wait safely for the day of judgment, when they are to receive their bodies and be made equal to the angels. Others then thought that some of the saints would rise later than others. Hence came prayers for hastening the resurrection and the reunion of souls with their bodies. But they looked chiefly to that dreadful day of judgment, and prayed that it would be happy and blessed for all the dead. Hence that addition, still made by many to the commemoration of the pious dead: Gott wölle jhm ein fröliche aufferstendnuß verleyhen.

units.la: Toto ergò cœlo differt praxis hodiernæ ecclesiæ Romanæ à veteris ecclesiæ consuetudine. Nam veteres precabantur pro sanctis omnibus, Pontificii pro peccatoribus quibusdam tantùm. Illi pro sanctis in æterna felicitate existentibus: hi pro miseris peccatoribus inter purgatorii tormenta versantibus. Illis nulla mentio purgatorii, eo tempore incogniti: his crebrò. Illis preces erant vota, his merita. Illis oblationes erant signa charitatis: his sunt redemptiones animarum, sed accedo ad
units.tr: Therefore the practice of the present Roman Church differs entirely from the custom of the ancient Church. For the ancients prayed for all the saints, while the Papists pray only for certain sinners. The ancients prayed for saints already existing in eternal happiness; the Papists pray for wretched sinners who dwell among the torments of purgatory. The ancients made no mention of purgatory, which at that time was unknown; the Papists mention it often. For the ancients, prayers were wishes; for the Papists, they are merits. For the ancients, oblations were signs of charity; for the Papists, they are redemptions of souls. But I come to

units.la: PARALLELUM I.
units.tr: PARALLEL I.

units.la: Calvinus lib. III. Instit. cap. 5:5. 10, 11. reiicit preces pro defunctis 1. quia destituuntur testimoniis & exemplis scripturae sacrae. 2. quòd veteres ipsi confitebantur. 3. quia quicquid hic factum ab antiquis, publico mori & vulgi imperitiae datum, aut amori defunctorum. Idcirco ad imitationem non esse trahendum.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes III.5.5, 10, 11, rejects prayers for the dead: (1) because they lack the testimony and examples of Holy Scripture; (2) because the ancients themselves confessed as much; (3) because whatever was done by the ancients was either a public custom, given to the ignorance of the common people, or an expression of love for the dead. For these reasons it is not to be taken up as an example to imitate.

units.la: At Harscherus contra instat & primò testimoniys scripturae nititur os obstruere Calvino. Deinde ex tribus hypothesibus Calvini & Orthodoxorum circa hanc quaestionem, doctrinam, in solidum everti, demonstrare conatur.
units.tr: But Harscher presses against him, and first strives to stop Calvin's mouth with the testimonies of Scripture. Then he tries to show that, from the three hypotheses of Calvin and the Orthodox on this question, the doctrine is overturned entirely.

units.la: De testimoniis scripturae primò.M
units.tr: First, on the testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: 1. Regum cap. ult. id est, cap. 31. v. 13, Habitatores Jabes Galaad ieiunaverunt mortuo Saule diebus septem.
units.tr: 1 Samuel (called 1 Kings in the Vulgate), last chapter, that is, chapter 31, verse 13: The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead fasted for seven days after Saul died.

units.la: 2. Regum cap. 1. David flevit & oravit pro Saule & Jonatha, & aliis occisis, quod idem fecit pro Abner. 2. Reg. c. 3. Hæc, inquit, luctui tantum & officio sepultura tribui, qua scriptura probat Calvinus? maxime cum venerabilis Beda in fine comment. in lib. I. Reg. hæc impetrationis gratia pro mortuis adhibita scribat.
units.tr: 2 Samuel (2 Kings in the Vulgate), chapter 1: David wept and prayed for Saul and Jonathan and the others who were slain, and he did the same for Abner. 2 Samuel chapter 3: "To what Scripture does Calvin appeal," he says, "to prove that these things were given only to mourning and the duty of burial? Especially since the venerable Bede, at the end of his commentary on 1 Samuel, writes that this was done as a means of obtaining grace for the dead."

units.la: Resp. A ieiunio ad preces pro defunctis afferendas inepta est consequentia, præsertim si nullum in textu appareat vestigium, quod talem interpretationem urgeat. Aliæ sunt causæ ieiuniorum Judaicorum, quas etiam in allegatis locis observare licet. Jeiunarunt olim Judæi publicè & privatim prout afflictiones & calamitates publicæ vel privatæ ipsis obvenerunt. Jeiunia publica fuerunt ea, de quibus Zacharias loquitur cap. 8: 9. ieiunium quarti mensis, & ieiunium quinti, & ieiunium septimi, ieiuniumque decimi. Jeiunium quarti mensis celebrabatur 17. die ad testandam tristitiam ac dolorem propter perruptam civitatem Hierofolymorum, Jer. 52: 7. propter fractas tabulas, propter cessationem jugis sacrificij, & quod idolum in templum sanctum positum fuisset: Jeiunium mensis quinti, die 9. quia eodem die templum Hierofolymitanum combustum. Jeiunium septimi mensis die 3. eiusdem, propter necem Gedoliæ Judæorum superstitum proregis, Jer. 41: 2. Tandem ieiunium decimi mensis, die decimo eiusdem celebratum, quia eodem die Rex Nebucadnezar incepit obsidere civitatem Hierusalem. Omnia ergo ieiunia instituta habitaque fuerunt, non nisi ob calamitates, pœnas & castigationes divinas commemorandas & in posterum præcavendas.
units.tr: Reply: The inference from fasting to the bringing forward of prayers for the dead is absurd, especially when no trace appears in the text that urges such an interpretation. The causes of Jewish fasts are different, as one may observe in the passages cited. The Jews once fasted publicly and privately, as public or private afflictions and calamities came upon them. The public fasts were those of which Zechariah speaks in chapter 8, verse 19: the fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth. The fast of the fourth month was kept on the 17th day to bear witness to the sorrow and grief over the breached city of Jerusalem (Jer. 52:7), on account of the broken tablets, the cessation of the continual sacrifice, and because an idol had been set up in the holy temple. The fast of the fifth month was on the 9th day, because on that day the temple of Jerusalem was burned. The fast of the seventh month was on the 3rd day of that month, on account of the murder of Gedaliah, the governor of the Jews who remained (Jer. 41:2). Finally, the fast of the tenth month was kept on the tenth day of that month, because on that day King Nebuchadnezzar began to besiege the city of Jerusalem. All these fasts, then, were instituted and observed only to commemorate God's calamities, punishments and chastisements, and to guard against them in future.

units.la: Sic certè ieiunarunt Jabefchitæ & merito ieiunarunt ob luctum & calamitatem publicam, quia perdiderunt regem suum & fortissimos Israëlis, maximo cum damno regni Israëlitici. Sic David ob eandem causam ieiunavit, quod exerte Spiritus sanctus docet: Et plangentes fleverunt jejunaveruntq; usq; ad vesperam propter Saulem & propter Jonathanem filium ejus, & propter populum Jehovæ, deniq; propter familiam Israëlis quod cecidissent gladio, non quod essent in purgatorio. Intolerabile vero est, quod homines illi tam impune & impudenter audent textui sacro addere aut detrahere pro libitu, quod hic facit Harfcherus, cum scribit, David flevit & oravit pro Saule. Ubi illud oravit pro Saule quaeso, aut in quo exemplari legitur?
units.tr: So certainly the men of Jabesh fasted, and rightly so, out of mourning and public calamity, because they had lost their king and the bravest of Israel, to the great loss of the kingdom of Israel. So too David fasted for the same reason, as the Holy Spirit plainly teaches: "And they wept and mourned and fasted until evening, for Saul and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the LORD, and finally for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword," not because they were in purgatory. It is truly intolerable that these men dare so freely and shamelessly to add to or take away from the sacred text at will, as Harscher does here when he writes, "David wept and prayed for Saul." Where, I ask, is that phrase "prayed for Saul", or in what copy is it read?

units.la: Addit Jesuita; Hæc tantum luctui & sepulturæ tribui, quâ scriptura probat Calvinus? Quasi vero hoc esset difficile. Inspiciat textum 2. Sam. 1: 12. Et quæ de morte Abneri leguntur 2. Sam. 3: 33, 34.
units.tr: The Jesuit adds: "To what Scripture does Calvin appeal to prove that these things were given only to mourning and burial?" As if this were difficult! Let him look at the text of 2 Samuel 1:12, and at what is read about the death of Abner in 2 Samuel 3:33, 34.

units.la: 33. 34. Lamentatus Rex Abnerum dixit; Ergo (ne) ut moritur sultus, mortuus fuerit Abner? Manus tua non (fuissent) ligata, & pedes tui æreis compedibus non fuissent admoti, ut cadit (quis) ante iniquissimos, cecidisti. Mors ergo insperata Abneri, caussa luctus & caussa ieiunii.
units.tr: Verses 33, 34: "The king lamented over Abner and said, 'Ought Abner to have died as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound, nor were your feet put into fetters of bronze; as one falls before the wicked, so you have fallen.'" Thus the sudden death of Abner was the cause of the mourning and the cause of the fast.

units.la: Illud verò lepidum quod addit Harscher, maximè cum venerabilis Beda hæc impetrationis gratiâ pro mortuis adhibitâ scribat. Emphaticum est adverbium maximè, quod Bellarminus non habet. Itaque (quantum quidem ego coniicere possum) hic sensus erit: etiamsi aliquid in textu pro sententia Calvini extaret, tamen contrarium afferendum fuisset propter authoritatem venerabilis Bedæ. Animadvertisne fundamentum fidei Pontificiæ? Sed cur solus Beda pro huius loci interpretatione citatur ab Harschero, Bellarmino & Cornelio à Lapide? Nempe quia nullus ita, ante Bedam. Ideo non ausi fuerunt Emanuel Sà & Mariana in notis suis ad hunc locum aliquid tentare* Lyranus verò insignis inter Pontificios sic locum interpretatur: jejunarunt sep-tem diebus in signum trisitiæ propter mortem Saul & filiorum ejus. Permittat ergo mihi dominatio Harscheri illud ingeminare: Iabeschitas & Davidem jejunasse pro animis defunctorum ex purgatorio liberandis quâ scriptura probat Harscherus?
units.tr: But that witty remark of Harscher is also worth noting, "especially since the venerable Bede writes that this was done as a means of obtaining grace for the dead." The adverb "especially" is emphatic, and Bellarmine does not have it. So (as far as I can guess) the sense will be this: even if something in the text supported Calvin's view, the contrary would still have to be asserted on account of the authority of the venerable Bede. Do you see the foundation of Papist faith? But why does Harscher, with Bellarmine and Cornelius a Lapide, cite Bede alone for the interpretation of this passage? Clearly because no one before Bede interpreted it so. That is why Emmanuel Sá and Mariana did not dare to attempt anything on this passage in their notes. Lyranus, however, an outstanding Papist, interprets the passage thus: "They fasted seven days as a sign of sorrow for the death of Saul and his sons." Let Harscher's lordship therefore permit me to repeat this: "That the Jabeshites and David fasted in order to free the souls of the dead from purgatory, what Scripture proves this, Harscher?"

units.la: Tobiæ. 4. Panem tuum & vinum super sepulturam justi constitue & noli ex eo manducare & bibere cum peccatoribus.
units.tr: Tobit 4: Set your bread and wine upon the grave of the just, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners.

units.la: Belle sibi caverunt & religioni suæ Pontificii quòd non tantùm libros sacros πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἀξίως obscuros, mancos, imperfectos, & consequenter articulis fidei decidendis insufficientes: contra libros τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ἀξίως, iisdem confirmandis idoneos, verùm etiam, versionem latinam corruptissimam eo-dem dem fine sibi eligendum putarunt. Ex his duo testimonia citat Harscherus. Primò ex Tobiæ cap. 4: 18. Panem tuum & vinum super sepulturam justi constitue, & noli ex eo manducare, & bibere cum peccatoribus. Nullo iure mihi succensere potest Harscherus, si hunc locum ex Græco textu & versione latina autoritate Sixti V. Pontificis Romani evulgatæ & Lutetiæ Parisiorum excusæ, corrigam. Sic illa habet: ἐηχθον Ἰὰς ἀρτας σὲ ὅτι τ τάφον τῶν δικαίων ἡ μὴ Θῶς τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς. Quod sic reddiderunt; effunde panes tuos super sepulturam justorum, & ne dederis peccatoribus. Animadvertendum igitur primò testimonium citatum corruptum esse vitio pleonastico, habet enim quod non est in Græco. Deinde interpretatio inepta est, orta ex ignorantia praxis Judaicæ circa sepulturam mortuorum. Luxerunt Judæi mortuos suos exemplo maiorum suorum per aliquot dies. In quibus amici & propinqui consfo-
units.tr: The Papists have been careful, and well for their religion, not only to choose as sacred books those that are obscure, defective, imperfect, and consequently insufficient for settling the articles of faith, but also to prefer, for the same purpose, the books that are worthy of all acceptance [πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἀξίως] and suitable for confirming those same articles, and to choose the very corrupt Latin version for the same end. Harscher cites two testimonies from these. First, from Tobit 4:18: "Set your bread and wine upon the grave of the just, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners." Harscher has no right to be angry with me if I correct this passage from the Greek text and from the Latin version, which was published by the authority of Pope Sixtus V and printed at Paris. It reads thus: "Ἐκχεον τοὺς ἄρτους σου ἐπὶ τὸν τάφον τῶν δικαίων, καὶ μὴ δῷς τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς" [pour out your bread upon the grave of the just, and do not give it to sinners]. They rendered this: "Effunde panes tuos super sepulturam justorum, et ne dederis peccatoribus." It must be noted, then, first, that the cited testimony is corrupted by a pleonastic fault, for it has something that is not in the Greek. Second, the interpretation is foolish, arising from ignorance of Jewish practice concerning the burial of the dead. The Jews mourned their dead for several days, following the example of their forefathers. During these days friends and relatives consoled the mourners with food and drink, whence the cup of consolations is spoken of by Jeremiah 16:7, and food for consolation, in the same place. This was a great office of humanity, and it was instituted only to lighten sorrow. In this fourth chapter, then, among other admonitions (for the whole chapter is instructive and moral [παιδευτικόν]), he enjoins his son not to neglect this duty of humanity and kindness, but to supply it generously to those who mourn. This precept, moreover, consists of pure rhetorical ornaments. Pour out (a metaphor), that is, bestow generously; your bread (a synecdoche of the species), that is, food and drink; upon the grave of the just (a metonymy of the subject), that is, upon the just who bury their parents or relatives. Here there is no trace of purgatory, and no trace of offerings for the dead.

units.la: consolabantur lugentes cibo & potu, unde poculum consolationum dictum a Jeremia cap. 16: 7. & cibus ad consolandum, ibidem. Hoc erat magnum humanitatis officium, & non nisi ad levandum luctum institutum. In capite ergo hoc quarto inter cæteras admonitiones (nam totum hoc caput est παιδευτικόν & morale) filio præcipit, ut hoc humanitatis & beneficentiæ officium non negligat, sed lugentibus copiosè e suo administret. Constat autem hoc præceptum meris ornamentis rhetoricis. Effunde (methaphora) id est, copiosè largire, panes tuos (synechdoche speciei) id est, cibum & potum: super sepulturam justorum (metonymia subiecti) id est, iustis sepelientibus parentes aut propinquos suos. Nullum hic vestigium purgatorii, nullum oblationum pro defunctis.
units.tr: They consoled the mourners with food and drink, whence the phrase a cup of consolations is used by Jeremiah in chapter 16, verse 7, and food for consolation in the same place. This was a great office of humanity, and it was instituted only to relieve grief. In this fourth chapter, then, among his other admonitions (for the whole chapter is instructive [παιδευτικόν] and moral), he instructs the son not to neglect this duty of humanity and kindness, but to supply it generously to the mourners from his own means. This precept, however, consists purely of rhetorical ornaments. Pour out is a metaphor, that is, bestow generously; your bread is a synecdoche of the species, that is, food and drink; upon the burial of the righteous is a metonymy of the subject, that is, upon righteous men burying their parents or kinsfolk. There is no trace of purgatory here, and no trace of offerings for the dead.

units.la: Deinde argumentatur ex 2. Mach. cap. 12. De quo libro Augustinus lib. 2. cap. 23. contra Gaudent. Hanc scripturam quæ appellatur Machabæorum non habent Iudæi sicut legem, & prophetas & psalmos, quibus Dominus testimonium perhibet tanquam testibus suis. Et tamen producunt Pontificii, quia non habent alium pro stabiliendo purgatorio suo. Duo citat ex eodem capite 1. ex v. 42. Atq; ita ad preces conversi rogarunt, ut id quod factum erat delictum oblivioni traderetur. 2. ex verf. 43. Iudam Machabæum duodecim millia drachmas argenti misisse Ierosolymam, ad offerendum pro peccatis mortuorum sacrificium. Quod autor librorum Machabæorum laudat, quia sancta & salubris est cogitatio pro defunctis exorare ut a peccatis solvantur.
units.tr: Next, they argue from 2 Maccabees chapter 12. Augustine, concerning this book, says in book 2, chapter 23, against Gaudentius: The Jews do not hold this writing, which is called that of the Maccabees, as they hold the law, the prophets and the psalms, to which the Lord bears witness as his witnesses. Yet the Papists produce it, because they have no other support for establishing their purgatory. They cite two passages from the same chapter: (1) from verse 42, And so, turning to prayer, they begged that what had been done might be consigned to oblivion as a sin. (2) From verse 43, that Judas Maccabeus sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to offer a sacrifice for the sins of the dead. The author of the books of the Maccabees praises this, because it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from their sins.

units.la: Nostri circa hunc locum (quamvis apocryphum) tria notant, vulgatæ versionis & textus Græci discrepantiam, autoris librorum Machabæorum errorem, & Pontificiorum falsam interpretationem. Quod primum concernit, omnia exemplaria græca, quæ ego vidi, etiam à Pontificibus approbata, habent ἀργυρέους δραχμὰς διςχιλίας argenti drachmas bis mille. E contra Vulgata habet duodecim millia. Quam multiplicationem suo commodo Jesuitæ studiosè retinent. Item; ἐξεγοντο γὴν ἀμαρτίας θυσίαν offerri pro peccatis sacrificium. Vulgatus autem offerri pro peccatis mortuorum sacrificium. Error compilatoris Maccabaicorum librorum notatur duplex. Unus quòd contra universam veteris Testamenti scripturam orationes & oblationes pro mortuis statuit. Alter, quòd scribit (contra mentem Judæ Machabæi) pecunias istas Hierosolymam missas ad instituendum sacrificium pro redimendo peccato demortuorum tantùm: Cùm id factum sit ad faciendum sacrificium pro toto exercitu, cuius magna pars ob peccatum contra legem Dei commissum, cecidit. Falsa denique què interpretatio Pontificiorum est, quòd hæc omnia interpretantur de purgatorio. Autor verò illius libri de purgatorio, poena in eo sustinenda & liberatione ex eo per oblationes & preces, ne minimum quidem. Imò si recte locus inspiciatur apparebit, illum doctrinam de purgatorio evertere.
units.tr: Our theologians note three things about this passage, although it is apocryphal: a discrepancy between the Vulgate version and the Greek text, an error of the author of the books of the Maccabees, and the Papists' false interpretation. As to the first, all the Greek copies I have seen, including those approved by the Papists, read two thousand silver drachmas [ἀργυρέους δραχμὰς διςχιλίας]. The Vulgate, by contrast, reads twelve thousand. The Jesuits eagerly keep this multiplication because it suits them. Again, the Greek reads a sacrifice offered [for] sin [ἐξεγοντο γὴν ἀμαρτίας θυσίαν], whereas the Vulgate reads a sacrifice offered for the sins of the dead. Two errors are noted in the compiler of the Maccabean books. First, he lays down prayers and oblations for the dead, contrary to the whole of Scripture of the Old Testament. Second, he writes (contrary to the mind of Judas Maccabeus) that the money sent to Jerusalem was for providing a sacrifice to redeem only the sin of the dead, whereas it was done to make a sacrifice for the whole army, a large part of which had fallen because of sin committed against the law of God. Finally, the Papists' interpretation is false in that they explain all of this as referring to purgatory. But the author of that book says nothing at all about purgatory, about punishment to be undergone there, or about deliverance from it through oblations and prayers. Indeed, if the passage is examined rightly, it will appear that it overturns the doctrine of purgatory.

units.la: Nam historicus docet Judam considerasse in hoc facto resurrectionem futuram, in qua ut demortui gratiam inveniant apud Deum, preces fieri voluisse.
units.tr: For the historian teaches that Judas, in this deed, had in view the future resurrection, and wished prayers to be offered so that the dead might find grace before God in that resurrection.

units.la: Ultimò argumentatur Harscherus ex cap. 10. prioris ad Corinthios, sed est error, leguntur enim cap 15. Verba Harscheri sunt huiusmodi. Alioquin quid facient, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si mortui non resurgent? ut quid baptizantur pro illis? ubi baptismus secundum legitimam huius loci interpretationem (quam afferunt Ephren in suo testamento, Petrus Cluniacensis lib. contra Petrobrusianos Dionysius, Hugo & alij) sumitur pro baptismo lachrymarum, & pœnitentia, qui suscipitur orando, jejunando, eleemosynas faciendo, &c.
units.tr: Lastly, Harscherus argues from chapter 10 of the first epistle to the Corinthians, but this is a mistake, for the words are found in chapter 15. Harscherus's words are these: Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise? Why are they baptized for them? Where baptism, according to the lawful interpretation of this passage (which Ephrem in his testament, Peter of Cluny in his book against the Petrobrusians, Dionysius, Hugo and others offer), is taken to mean the baptism of tears and repentance, which is undertaken by praying, fasting, giving alms, and so on.

units.la: Locus citatus est ex Διονυσίου Paulinis, de quibus Apostolus Petrus, posteriori epistola cap. 3: 16. Ideo tam variæ sententiæ veterum reperiuntur de eodem, quas collegit D. Pareus, Eas hic commemorabo.
units.tr: The passage cited is from the Pauline writings of Dionysius, of which the Apostle Peter speaks in his second epistle, chapter 3, verse 16. Therefore the opinions of the ancients on the same passage are very varied, and D. Pareus has gathered them. I shall mention them here.

units.la: Quid sit baptismus ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν scire non possumus, quia deficit historia, Alij tamen de sacramento baptismi intelligunt, alij de ablutione, quia verbum βαπτίζεσθαι & immersionem & aspersionem significat.
units.tr: We cannot know what baptism for the dead [ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν] is, because the history is lacking. Some, however, understand it of the sacrament of baptism, others of ablution, because the word βαπτίζεσθαι signifies both immersion and sprinkling.

units.la: Qui de baptismo intelligunt variè dissentiunt.
units.tr: Those who understand it of baptism differ widely.

units.la: 1. Baptizari pro mortuis aliquibus est vice & loco mortuorum baptizari, si qui enim morte præventi baptismum consequi non potuissent, solebant ad eorum lectulos vel ad sepulchrum pro ipsis, id est, ipsorum vice vice viventes baptizari. Chrysostomus & Epiphanius cont. Cerinth. hæres. 28. tribuunt Marcionitis & tanquam histrionicum lusum derident. Ambrosius etiam Christia- nus tribuit, addens Apostolum non morem laudare, sed intentionem. Sed sadus est baptismi abusus.
units.tr: 1. To be baptized for some dead people is to be baptized in the place and stead of the dead. For if those prevented by death could not receive baptism, they used to have the living baptized at their beds or at the grave on their behalf, that is, in their place the living being baptized in their stead. Chrysostom and Epiphanius, against Cerinthus, heresy 28, attribute this to the Marcionites and mock it as a theatrical game. Ambrose the Christian also attributes it to them, adding that the Apostle does not praise the custom but the intention. But it is a sad abuse of baptism.

units.la: II. Alij intelligunt de baptismo Clinicorum, qui moribundi demum in lectulis baptizari volebant, ne baptismi gratiam peccatis rursus effunderent. Hi igitur baptizabantur pro mortuis, id est, quasi mortui quia pro mortuis habebantur, Epiph. cont. Cerinth. Sed hic mos demum post Apostoli tempora superstitiosè inolevit.
units.tr: II. Others understand it of the baptism of the Cleansing ones, who, when dying, wished to be baptized in their beds, lest they pour out again the grace of baptism through sins. These, then, were baptized for the dead, that is, as if they were dead, because they were regarded as dead. Epiphanius against Cerinthus. But this custom grew up superstitiously only after the time of the Apostle.

units.la: III. Theodoretus & scholia Hieronymi, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, id est, Christo commortui, seu in mortem Christi.
units.tr: III. Theodoret and the scholia of Jerome: those who are baptized for the dead, that is, who are co-dead with Christ, or into the death of Christ.

units.la: IV. Chrysostomus: super fide resurrectionis mortuorum, quia baptizati prius recitabant symbolum Apostolicum, in cuius fine cum diceretur, credo resurrectionem mortuorum, super hac fide baptizabantur. Sed hæc duo omnibus baptizatis tribuuntur, cum Apostolus de speciali quodam baptismo loquatur.
units.tr: IV. Chrysostom: over the faith in the resurrection of the dead, because those baptized previously recited the Apostles' Creed, at the end of which, when it was said, I believe the resurrection of the dead, they were baptized upon this faith. But these two things are attributed to all the baptized, whereas the Apostle is speaking of a particular kind of baptism.

units.la: V. Thomas, pro mortuis, id est, pro peccatis mortalibus abluendis. Sed Apostolus non de peccatis, sed hominibus locutus est.
units.tr: V. Thomas: for the dead, that is, for the washing away of mortal sins. But the Apostle is speaking not of sins but of men.

units.la: VI. Lutherus, super mortuorum martyrum cæmiteriis ac sepulchris, ad testandam resurrectionis fidem. Sed historia est incerta.
units.tr: VI. Luther: over the cemeteries and graves of the dead martyrs, to bear witness to the faith in the resurrection. But the history is uncertain.

units.la: Qui de ablutione accipiunt varij sunt. Bezæ sententia approbanda donec melior proferatur, qui accipit pro ablutione mortuali, quâ Iudæi utebantur in spem futuræ resurrectionis. Vide Act. 9: 37.
units.tr: Those who take it of ablution are various. Beza's opinion, which takes it as a mortuary ablution, which the Jews used in hope of the future resurrection, is to be approved until a better one is put forward. See Acts 9:37.

units.la: Jesuitarum sententia de baptismo lachrymarum & ieiuniorum, præterquam quòd nihil ei faveat in tota illa disputatione Paulina de resurrectione mortuorum, nova est, unde nullum ex veteribus Pateribus producere potuit Harfcherus. Ephrem Syri fcripta quæ extant dubiæ fidei funt: & tamen loco â Jefuita citato explicatio illa non legitur. Petrus Cluniacenfis, & Hugo Cardinalis fufpecti. Cluniacenfis etiam Harfchero fufpectus effe debebat, qui lib. 1. epift. ad Petrobrufianos fcribit, Catholicos quofdam dubitaffe, an fit orandum pro mortuis. De quo Dionyfio loquatur Jefuita non fcio, Dionyfii Areopagitæ fcripta, id eft, quæ ipfius nomine circumferuntur fuppofititia effe plus quam decem rationibus alii probant, nec illa recipit Cardinalis Caietanus. Si intelligat Dionyfium Carthufianum, eius teftimonium non plus apud me valet, quàm Calvini apud Harfcherum.
units.tr: The Jesuits' opinion, of baptism of tears and fastings, is new, apart from the fact that nothing in the whole of that Pauline discussion of the resurrection of the dead favours it. Hence Harscherus could produce no support for it from the ancient Fathers. The writings of Ephrem the Syrian that survive are of doubtful authority, and yet that explanation is not read in the passage the Jesuit cites. Peter of Cluny and Cardinal Hugo are suspect. Harscherus too ought to have suspected Cluny, who writes in the first book of his letter to the Petrobrusians that certain Catholics doubted whether one ought to pray for the dead. I do not know what Dionysius the Jesuit means, since many have proved, on more than ten grounds, that the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite, that is, those circulating under his name, are spurious, and Cardinal Cajetan does not accept them either. If he means Dionysius the Carthusian, his testimony counts for me no more than Calvin's counts for Harscherus.

units.la: Ornament.
units.tr: Ornament.

units.la: GENERALE ARGUMENTUM Contra Calvinistas.
units.tr: GENERAL ARGUMENT Against the Calvinists.

units.la: NUnc ratione disputat ⸣ in qua sibi ita applaudit ac si de victoria nihil sit dubitandum: Audiamus.
units.tr: Now he argues by reason, and he congratulates himself as if there were no doubt about the victory. Let us hear him.

units.la: Calvinus lib.I. Instit. cap. 11. sect. 13. scribit, quingentis primis annis quibus magis adhuc florebat religio & sincerior doctrina vigebat, Christiana templa fuisse communiter ab imaginibus vacua, lib. IV. cap.2. §. 3. ait Calvinum asserere, à principio, usq; ad ætatem Irenæi, Tertulliani, Originis, Augustini nihil mutatum fuisse in doctrina. lib. IV. Instit. cap.9. §. 13. non omnibus seculis vel locis haberi Athanasios, Basilios, Cyrillos & similes veræ doctrinæ vindices, quos tunc Dominus excitavit.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes book 1, chapter 11, section 13, writes that during the five hundred years when religion still flourished more and sound doctrine was in vigour, Christian churches were generally free of images. Book 4, chapter 2, section 3, says that Calvin asserts that from the beginning, down to the age of Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen and Augustine, nothing was changed in doctrine. Book 4 of the Institutes, chapter 9, section 13, says that Athanasius, Basil, Cyril and similar defenders of true doctrine, whom the Lord then raised up, were not to be found in every age or place.

units.la: Ex his verbis tres maximas conficit.
units.tr: From these words he draws three very great propositions.

units.la: Prima; primis quingentis annis fuit in ecclesia adhuc florens religio, & vigens sincerior doctrina.
units.tr: First: in the first five hundred years there was in the Church a religion still flourishing and a purer doctrine thriving.

units.la: Secunda; Primis quadringentis annis certum est in doctrina nihil mutatum fuisse.
units.tr: Second: it is certain that within the first four hundred years nothing was changed in doctrine.

units.la: Tertia; Sancti, Athanasius, Basilius, Cyrillus fuerunt a Domino excitati verae doctrinae vindices.
units.tr: Third: the saints Athanasius, Basil and Cyril were raised up by the Lord as defenders of true doctrine.

units.la: Atque ex his tribus maximis dicit, tam efficaciter probari posse universam doctrinam christianam apostolicā Romanam, novamque Calvinisticam refutari, quàm veras illas Calvinus asseruit. Inanis pompa.
units.tr: And from these three very great propositions he says that the whole Christian doctrine, apostolic and Roman, can be proved as effectively as the new Calvinistic doctrine can be refuted, just as those true things were asserted by Calvin. Empty show.

units.la: Sub finem huius paralleli lectorem obtestatur & obsecrat, ut haec omnia Calvini dicta de veteribus scriptoribus & vetusta ecclesia conferat cum maximis Calvini, inde enim manifestum fore, quàm infami antilogia idem neget & asserat Calvinus princeps ecclesiarū reformatarum.
units.tr: Near the end of this parallel he begs and beseeches the reader to compare all these sayings of Calvin about the ancient writers and the old Church with Calvin's greatest statements; for from this it will become plain how shamefully the prince of the reformed Churches both denies and asserts the same thing.

units.la: N VidenVidendum primò quàm fideliter Jesuita ex Calvini verbis suas maximas exstruxerit. Deinde argumentum ipsum examinandum.
units.tr: First it must be seen how faithfully the Jesuit has built his greatest propositions from Calvin's words. Then the argument itself must be examined.

units.la: Cùm Calvinus disputasset lib. i. Instit. cap. ii. §. 13. An imagines in templis Christianis habere expediat? inter cætera ita scribit: Si quid nos movet veteris ecclesia authoritas, meminerimus quingentis circiter annis (Harscherus mutavit, scribens, primis annis) quibus magis adhuc florebat religio, & sincerior doctrina vigebat, Christiana templa communiter fuisse ab imaginibus vacua. Ratiocinatio Calvini in forma talis est. Quod factum in ecclesia Christi quingentis circiter annis, cùm magis adhuc florebat religio & sincerior doctrina vigebat, id hodie quoque fieri debet. Atqui quingentis circiter annis cùm adhuc, &c. templa ab imaginibus fuerunt vacua. Ergo adhuc hodie ab imaginibus vacua esse debent.
units.tr: When Calvin had discussed, in Institutes book 1, chapter 11, section 13, "Whether it is expedient to have images in Christian churches?", among other things he writes thus: If the authority of the ancient Church moves us, let us remember that for about five hundred years (Harscher changed this, writing "for the first years") when religion still flourished more and sound doctrine was in vigour, Christian churches were commonly free of images. Calvin's reasoning takes this form: what was done in the Church of Christ for about five hundred years, when religion still flourished more and sound doctrine was in vigour, ought to be done today too. But for about five hundred years, while still, etc., the churches were free of images. Therefore they ought to be free of images even today.

units.la: Harfcherus syllogismi maiorem & minorem concedit, ex quibus maximâ primam exstruxit & pro fundamento disputationis suæ posuit. Ergo conclusioni non poterit contradicere. Hoc primò notandum fuisset Harfchero,tanquam argumentum solidum, ad eliminandas imagines ex templis christianorum.
units.tr: Harscher grants the major and the minor of the syllogism, and from them he built the first proposition and laid it down as the foundation of his disputation. Therefore he will not be able to contradict the conclusion. This ought first to have been noted by Harscher, as a solid argument for removing images from the churches of Christians.

units.la: Verba vero ipsa Calvini quod concernit, non locutus est absolute (nam lib. III. Instit. cap. 5. quædam illo tempore in ecclesia introducta carpit) sed comparative respectu ecclesiæ subsequentis, in qua minùs sincera & pura religio quàm in prisca illa viguit. Hoc quivis poterit ex phrasibus observare. Nam dicit; magis adhuc, scilicet quàm postea temporibus subsequentibus. Ité sincerior (in comparativo) quàm in ecclesia seculis posterioribus. Ex quibus iudicare poterit lector de prima maxima Harfcheriana, in qua verba & sensum Calvini mutavit. Lib. IV. Instit. cap. 2. §. 3. instantiæ pontificiorum occurrit Calvinus, circa quæstionem de quinta nota ecclesiæ, quæ iuxta pontificios, est successio non interrupta episcoporum. Nostri disputant successione personalem non sufficere ad demonstrandam veram ecclesiam, cum hæc successio etiam esse possit in falsa ecclesia. Instant illi; Irenæum, Tertullianum, Originem & Augustinum, argumentum hoc à successione Episcoporum magni fecisse. Ad hoc Calvinus respondet loco ante citato, potuisse illos hoc facere, quia in doctrina eo tempore nihil fuit mutatum. Sensus est; valere argumentum à successione personali, si simul succedat ipsa pura doctrina. Harscherus unum hic arripit, quod putat facere ad suum propositum, nempe iuxta Calvini sententiam, tempore Tertulliani, Originis, Augustini, Irenæi, nihil in doctrina fuisse mutatum. Quæ Calvini verba cum mica salis, ut est in proverbio sumenda sunt. Nam non adeo fuit vir doctus in historia veteri caecus, ut non potuerit videre, iam statim post seculum III. haeresin Arianorum fere omnes ecclesias occupasse. Nec ignoravit Patrum naevos etiam vetustissimorum, de quibus passim ipsi Pontificii. Maldonatus Jesuita in cap. II. Matth. ita scribit: Iustinus quidem certe, aut quisquis ille fuit autor, & Tertullianus dicere non dubitant, vere de Christo Iohannem dubitasse. Pejus etiam quid Tertullianus adjungit, propterea dubitasse quod spiritus prophetiae ab eo in Christum recessisset. Illa nimirum aetate nondum satis culta Theologia hujusmodi aliquando spinas proferebat. Loquitur igitur Calvinus de ea doctrina, quam probare volebant contra haereticos. Quod si pontificii simili modo demonstrare possent doctrinam, de qua nobis est controversia simul cum episcopis suis a tempore Apostolorum nunquam mutatam fuisse, non video, quis tali argumento contradicere possset.
units.tr: As for Calvin's words themselves, he did not speak absolutely (for in Institutes book 3, chapter 5, he criticises certain things introduced into the Church at that time), but comparatively, with respect to the later Church, in which religion was less sincere and pure than it was in that ancient one. Any reader can observe this from the phrasing. For he says still more, namely than in the following times afterwards; likewise purer (in the comparative), than in the Church of later centuries. From these things the reader will be able to judge Harscher's first proposition, in which he has altered Calvin's words and meaning. In Institutes book 4, chapter 2, section 3, Calvin meets the objection of the Papists, concerning the fifth mark of the Church, which according to the Papists is an uninterrupted succession of bishops. Our side argues that personal succession is not sufficient to demonstrate the true Church, since this succession can also exist in a false Church. The Papists press: Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen and Augustine made great use of this argument from the succession of bishops. To this Calvin replies, in the passage cited above, that they could do this because nothing had been changed in doctrine at that time. The sense is: the argument from personal succession holds good if pure doctrine succeeds along with it. Harscher seizes on one point here, which he thinks serves his purpose, namely that according to Calvin's opinion, in the time of Tertullian, Origen, Augustine and Irenaeus nothing had been changed in doctrine. But Calvin's words must be taken with a grain of salt, as the proverb says. For he was not so blind a scholar in ancient history as not to see that, straight after the third century, the heresy of the Arians had occupied almost all churches. Nor was he unaware of the blemishes even of the most ancient Fathers, of which the Papists themselves often speak. The Jesuit Maldonatus, on Matthew chapter 2, writes thus: Justin, or whoever that author was, and Tertullian do not hesitate to say that John truly doubted about Christ. Tertullian adds something even worse, that he doubted because the spirit of prophecy had departed from him in regard to Christ. Certainly in that age theology was not yet sufficiently cultivated, and it sometimes brought forth such thorns. Calvin therefore speaks of the doctrine that they wished to prove against the heretics. But if the Papists could in a similar way demonstrate that the doctrine in dispute between us, together with their bishops, had never been changed from the time of the Apostles, I do not see who could contradict such an argument.

units.la: Tertiò, Calvinus Athanasium, Basilium, Cyrillum veræ doctrinæ vindices appellavit. Verè hic titulus ipsis competit. Vindicavit enim Athanasius doctrinam de persona Christi, veram & orthodoxam contra Arianos, Basilius contra Sabellianos, &c. Sed quomodo hæc omnia applicat Jesuita? Ponit
units.tr: Thirdly, Calvin called Athanasius, Basil and Cyril defenders of true doctrine. Truly this title belongs to them. For Athanasius defended the doctrine of the person of Christ, true and orthodox, against the Arians, Basil against the Sabellians, and so on. But how does the Jesuit apply all this? He sets down

units.la: [ornament]
units.tr: [ornament]

units.la: GENERALE ARGUMENTUM ad suffragia pro mortuis pro- banda. In forma tale.
units.tr: A GENERAL ARGUMENT to be proved for prayers for the dead. In the following form.

units.la: Quadringentis, quingentis à Christo annis erat florens adhuc religio, vigens sincerior doctrina, nihil à principio immutata, doctrina, inquam, vindicum veritatis. Quadringentis & quingentis illis annis homines orationibus, precibus, oblationibus vivorum juvabantur. Ergò cum homines defuncti juvabantur oblationibus, precibus, suffragiis, & vivorum, erat florens adhuc religio, sincerior doctrina, nihil à principio immutata, &c.
units.tr: Four and five hundred years after Christ, religion was still flourishing, and the purer doctrine was thriving, unchanged from the beginning: the doctrine, I say, of the defenders of the truth. In those four and five hundred years, men were helped by the prayers, supplications and oblations of the living. Therefore, since departed men were helped by the oblations, prayers and suffrages of the living, religion was still flourishing, the purer doctrine was unchanged from the beginning, etc.

units.la: Propositio maior prout Harfcherus eam tradit non est Calvini nec est universaliter vera, sed secundùm superiùs traditas limitationes intelligenda.
units.tr: The major premise, as Harfcherus gives it, is not Calvin's, nor is it universally true, but must be understood according to the limitations set out above.

units.la: Minor falsa est secundùm intellectû papistarum, quia oblationes, preces, in veteri ecclesia, non pro animabus ex purgatorio liberandis, sed alio fine institutæ fuerunt, de quo supra diximus, & ex veterum monumentis probavimus.
units.tr: The minor premise is false according to the understanding of the Papists, because the oblations and prayers of the ancient Church were instituted not for freeing souls from purgatory but for another end, which we have stated above and proved from the monuments of the ancients.

units.la: Probatio minoris, in qua totum præsidium caussæ Harfcherianæ situm, ad quam etiam diligenter perpendendam cum obsecratione invitat lectorem, parum aut nihil roboris habet, quia excepto Augustino, testimonia mera supposititia producit.
units.tr: The proof of the minor premise, on which the whole strength of Harfcher's cause rests, and which he urgently invites the reader to weigh carefully, has little or no force, because apart from Augustine, it produces nothing but spurious testimonies.

units.la: Primò Athanasii quæst. 34. ad Antiochum. Hunc librum Athanasii non esse docent Bellarminus, Possevinus & Maldonatus Iesuitæ. Nec desunt rationes. Nam in quæstione tertia citatur Epiphanius qui 50. annis post Athanasium vixit. Præterea numerus quæstionum varius est, quædam exemplaria habent quæstiones 162 quædam 46. ego in meo exemplari vetusto tantum 41.
units.tr: First, Athanasius, question 34, to Antiochus. That this book is not Athanasius's is taught by the Jesuits Bellarminus, Possevinus and Maldonatus. Nor are reasons lacking. For in question three Epiphanius is cited, who lived fifty years after Athanasius. Moreover, the number of questions varies: some copies have 162 questions, some 46; my old copy has only 41.

units.la: Secundò ex Basilii liturgia, quæ suppositicia est, quod D. Scultetus aliquot argumentis probat. 1. Quia nulla ejus apud vetustiores probata fidei scriptores fit mentio. 2. In antiquis exemplaribus nomina reperiuntur eorum, qui multis post annis vixerunt. 3. Non concordat per omnia cum Syriaca à Masio tralata. 4. Videtur pro peccatoribus in inferno orare. 5. Mariam vocat Deiparam, terminum ter sanctus usurpat, ignota Basilio vocabula, in cujus germanis scriptis nullum illius liturgiæ vestigium apparet. paret. 6. Preces concipit pro pijsimo Imperatore, quaeri autem jure potest quisnam pijsimus ille imperator fuerit, Constantinus ne Arianus, Iulianus ne Apostata, an Valens acerrimus Orthodoxorum persecutor? Sub his enim Basilius floruit. Obmutescent, inquit, omnes liturgiæ Basilianæ patroni, nisi forte ex veterum historiarum monumentis docuerint intra septem illos menses, quibus Iovinianus imperavit Liturgiam istam à Basilio fuisse fabricatam.
units.tr: Second, from Basil's liturgy, which is spurious, as D. Scultetus proves by several arguments. 1. Because no mention of it is found among the older writers of approved faith. 2. In ancient copies are found the names of men who lived many years later. 3. It does not agree in every point with the Syriac version translated by Masius. 4. It seems to pray for sinners in hell. 5. It calls Mary the Mother of God, uses the term "thrice holy," and employs vocabulary unknown to Basil, in whose genuine writings no trace of that liturgy appears. 6. It composes prayers for the most pious Emperor. But one may rightly ask who that most pious emperor was: Constantius the Arian, Julian the Apostate, or Valens, the fierce persecutor of the orthodox? For it was under these men that Basil flourished. All the defenders of the Basilian liturgy, he says, will be struck dumb, unless perhaps they can show from the records of ancient histories that within those seven months in which Jovian reigned this liturgy was composed by Basil.

units.la: Tertiò, ex Cyrilli Hierosolymitani catechesi mystagogica v. Putant quidam catecheses vulgò Cyrillo adscriptas, esse Iohannis Hierosolymitani, quod ego in medio relinquo, certum interim est, hasce catecheses variè à Monachis esse corruptas & quidem multis in locis, addita etiam aliqua quæ Cyrillo γνωσίω tribui non possunt. Sed sint hæc ipsius Cyrilli verba, quid hoc ad rem? Disputamus de precibus & oblationibus pro peccatoribus in purgatorio existentibus; testimonium allatum loquitur de orationibus, pro tranquillitate mundi, pro pace ecclefiæ, pro ægrotis, pro afflictis viventibus, pro Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, pro sanctis Patribus & Episcopis, & omnibus vitâ functis, quos in purgatorio minimè collocant pontificii. Sed de hoc more veteris ecclesiæ supra dixi.
units.tr: Third, from the Mystagogical Catechesis 5 of Cyril of Jerusalem. Some think the catecheses commonly ascribed to Cyril are by John of Jerusalem; I leave that question aside. It is certain, however, that these catecheses have been variously corrupted by monks, and indeed in many places, with some additions that cannot be attributed to the genuine Cyril [γνησίῳ]. But grant that these are Cyril's own words: what has this to do with the matter? We are disputing about prayers and oblations for sinners existing in purgatory. The testimony cited speaks of prayers for the tranquillity of the world, for the peace of the Church, for the sick, for the afflicted living, for the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, for the holy fathers and bishops, and for all who have departed this life, whom the Papists by no means place in purgatory. But I have spoken above of this custom of the ancient Church.

units.la: Quartò, ex Dionysii Pauli discipuli Hierarch. Ecclest. cap 7. p.3. Habent nostri invicta argumenta, quibus probant libros Dionysio à Paulo converso, adscriptos, ejus non esse. Leguntur ea apud Perkinsum in præparatione ad demonst. Problematis, 1. Ne uno quidem in loco Pauli mentionem facit, sed obscurum quendam Hierotheum Præceptorem suum appellat. 2. Plurimorum pontificum, præsulum, Sacerdotum, Monachorum &c. meminit, quorum præter quam Episcopi, Dionysii atatem nullum habuisse probari potest. 3. Eusebius & Hieronymus in Catalogo horum nullam faciunt mentionem, imo nullus ante Gregorium magnum, qui tamen citans hujus literas non judicat eum fuisse Dionysium Areopagitam. 4. Sixtus Senensis arbitratur Dionysii mysticaTheologiam tempore Athanasii fuisse ignotam, Biblioth. l. 4. Illyricus praeter haec, decem argumenta habet, quibus idem probat quod Perkinsus.
units.tr: Fourth, from the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 7, part 3, of Dionysius, the disciple of Paul. Our people have unanswerable arguments by which they prove that the books ascribed to Dionysius, the convert of Paul, are not his. These are read in Perkins, in the preparation to his Demonstration of the Problem: 1. He nowhere mentions Paul, but calls his teacher some obscure Hierotheus. 2. He mentions many pontiffs, prelates, priests, monks, etc., of whom it can be proved that none existed in Dionysius's time except bishops. 3. Eusebius and Jerome make no mention of these writings in their Catalogue of them; indeed no one before Gregory the Great mentions them, and even he, while citing his letters, does not judge that the author was Dionysius the Areopagite. 4. Sixtus of Siena thinks that the mystical theology of Dionysius was unknown in the time of Athanasius, Bibliotheca, book 4. Besides these, Illyricus has ten arguments by which he proves the same as Perkins.

units.la: Quintò, ex Chrysostomi homil. 69. ad populum Antiochenum. At non sunt illae homiliae Chrysostomi, sed ab alio aliquo hinc inde ex aliis autoribus consutae. Vides ergo quàm nihil sit sani, nihilque ponderis in hoc inflato argumento Jesuitico, si lector, ut ipse petit, dicta de vetusta ecclesia conserat cum verbis Calvini. Quod Augustinum attinet, approbat ille consuetudinem ecclesiae, ubi in precibus sacerdotis, quae Domino Deo ad eius altare funduntur, etiam locum habet commendatio mortuorum. Sed nihil hoc ad quæstionem. Fiebat in Augustini ecclesia commendatio mortuorum, id est, virtutum, fidei, charitatis, spei & constantiæ mortuorum, quâ membra ecclesiæ ad imitationem hortarentur. Secundò erat commemoratio, seu, ut ipse loquitur cap.4. in memoriam revocatio defunctorû, unde dicit sepulchra nominari monumenta. Tertiò, id ficbat promiscuè omnibus etiam sanctissimis, in beata vita existentibus. Quartò, commemorationem pro defunctis fecit tota ecclesia, id est, singula eius membra, ut Augustinus docet. Ultimò, non dissimulat Augustinus quid de istis precibus iudicet, cùm cap. 1. scribit: Meritum si nullum comparatum est in hac vita, frustra quaritur post hanc vitam. Hæc certè omnia nihil commune habent cum orationibus missaticis à solo sacerdote factis, pro defunctis ex purgatorio redimendis.
units.tr: Fifth, from Chrysostom's homily 69 to the people of Antioch. But those homilies are not Chrysostom's; they are patched together here and there from other authors. You see then how nothing sound and nothing weighty there is in this swollen Jesuit argument, if the reader, as the author himself asks, compares what is said about the ancient Church with the words of Calvin. As for Augustine, he approves the custom of the Church whereby, in the prayers of the priest poured out to the Lord God at his altar, the commemoration of the dead also has its place. But this has nothing to do with the question. In Augustine's Church there was a commendation of the dead, that is, of the virtues, faith, charity, hope and constancy of the dead, by which the members of the Church were exhorted to imitate them. Secondly, there was commemoration, or, as he himself says in chapter 4, the recalling of the departed to memory, which is why he calls tombs monuments. Thirdly, this was done indiscriminately for all, even the most holy, who exist in the blessed life. Fourthly, the whole Church, that is, each of its individual members, made commemoration of the dead, as Augustine teaches. Lastly, Augustine does not conceal what he thinks of these prayers, when in chapter 1 he writes: If no merit has been acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life. All these things certainly have nothing in common with the masses said by the priest alone for the dead, to redeem them from purgatory.

units.la: PARALLELUM II.
units.tr: Parallel II.

units.la: In hoc parallelo docet Harfcherus Calvinum & nostras ecclesias hæresi Aerianorum subscribere,in doctrina de ieiunio. Sic etiam Bellarminus. Anne hoc proprium est Jesuitis in quarto modo, de nobis scribere & fingere quod volunt? Nos certè nec ieiunia in fe improbamus, nec quatenus ab ecclesia sunt indicta, quod posterius fecit Aerius.
units.tr: In this parallel Harscher teaches that Calvin and our churches subscribe to the heresy of the Aerians in the doctrine of fasting. Bellarmine says the same. Is it a peculiarity of the Jesuits, in the fourth way, to write about us and invent whatever they wish? We certainly do not disapprove of fasts in themselves, nor of fasts as they have been appointed by the Church; it was Aerius who did the latter.

units.la: De primo ita Calvinus lib. IV. Inftit. cap. 12. §. 14. Hoc sanctum est & seculis omnibus salutare institutum, ut paftores ad publicum jejunium & extraordinarias preces plebem hortentur. Parag. 17. Legimus jejunasse in signum mœstitia non modo Israëliticam ecclesiam, verbo Dei formatam ac constitutam, sed Ninivitas quoq; qui nihil doctrina, praeter unicam sonam prædicationem habebant, quid caussa est est igitur cur non idem agamus? Parag. 16. Sic in summa habendum est: quoties de religione incidit controversia, quam vel ecclesiastico judicio finire oportet, quoties de eligendo ministro agitur, quoties deniq; tractatur res aliqua difficilis ac magni momenti: rursum cum apparent judicia ira Dei, ut sunt pestilentia & bellum & fames hoc sanctum esse & seculis omnibus salutare institutum, ut pastores ad publicum jejunium & extraordinarias preces hortentur.
units.tr: Concerning the first point, Calvin says in Institutes book 4, chapter 12, section 14: It is a holy institution, and one salutary in all ages, that ministers exhort the people to public fasting and extraordinary prayers. Paragraph 17: We read that not only the Israelite Church, formed and established by the Word of God, fasted as a sign of mourning, but also the Ninevites, who had no teaching beyond the one sermon. Why then should we not do the same? Paragraph 16: So in sum it must be held: whenever a controversy about religion arises, which ought to be settled by ecclesiastical judgment; whenever a minister is to be chosen; whenever some matter of difficulty and great importance is treated; and again, whenever the judgments of God's wrath appear, such as pestilence, war, and famine: it is a holy and salutary institution in all ages that ministers exhort the people to public fasting and extraordinary prayers.

units.la: De altero communiter omnes sentimus, habere ecclesiam potestate a Deo statuendi de iis, quae decenter in ecclesia fieri debent, cui quidem potestati nemo ius habet contradicendi, si illa nihil praecipiat contra Dei verbum. Quod si igitur stata ieiunia praecipiat iuxta Dei verbum, hoc praeceptum omnes obligat, quod Aerius negabat.
units.tr: On the second point we all commonly agree that the Church has from God the power to decide about those things which ought to be done decently in the Church. No one has a right to contradict this power, provided it commands nothing against the Word of God. If, therefore, it appoints fixed fasts in accordance with the Word of God, this command binds everyone. This is what Aerius denied.

units.la: Quid ergo est quod Reformati reprehendunt in ieiunio papistarum? Multa omnino, quae partim ex Calvino partim ex aliis nostrorum libris pervideri possunt.
units.tr: What then is it that the Reformed find fault with in the fasting of the Papists? Many things indeed, which can be seen partly in Calvin and partly in other books of ours.

units.la: 1. Quia ieiunium est abstinentia ab omni cibo, unde Græcis ἀ νῆ & ἰᾶϊεω dicitur, ipsi verò dicunt jejunare esse pisces edere.
units.tr: 1. Because fasting is abstinence from all food. Hence the Greeks call it nēsteia [νηστεία], and nēsteuein [νηστεύειν], whereas the Papists themselves say that "to fast is to eat fish."

units.la: 2. Quia ieiunia non definiunt ex sua natura, sed ex delectu ciborum.
units.tr: 2. Because they do not define fasts by their own nature, but by the choice of foods.

units.la: 3. Quia per totam quadragesimam exquisitissimis epulis, lautitiis, vino optimo, & omne genus piscibus apicianis artibus conditis, utuntur,
units.tr: 3. Because throughout Lent they use the most exquisite feasts, delicacies, the finest wine, and every kind of fish prepared with Apician arts.

units.la: 4. Quia ieiunium quadragesimale (quod dicunt fieri ad exemplum & imitationem Christi) incipiunt cum turpissimo boatu, lascivia, cursitationibus & potationibus ad exemplum & imitationem Ambubaiarum & Bachi mancipiorum,
units.tr: 4. Because they begin the Lenten fast (which they say is done after the example and imitation of Christ) with the most shameful shouting, wantonness, running about, and drinking, after the example and imitation of the dancing-girls and the slaves of Bacchus,

units.la: Orgia uti quondam Thyades celebrasse leguntur.
units.tr: Such orgies as the Thyades are read to have once celebrated.

units.la: Hoccine est Christum imitari?
units.tr: Is this to imitate Christ?

units.la: 5. Quia stata tempora ieiuniorum præcipiunt sub pœna peccati mortalis, quod non in scripturis, sed Montani schola fundamentum habet. Nam quibus dieb° non oporteat jejunare, & quibus oporteat, præcepto Domini non invenio definitum, inquit Augustinus epist. 86. contra Psychicos.
units.tr: 5. Because they prescribe fixed times of fasting under the penalty of mortal sin, which has its foundation not in the Scriptures but in the school of Montanus. For Augustine, in letter 86 against the Psychici, says: On which days one ought not to fast, and on which one ought, I do not find defined by the precept of the Lord.

units.la: 6. Quia ieiunium per se faciunt meritorium & satisfactorium pro pœnis temporalibus, cùm nihil aliud sit quàm medium, quo carnis lascivia retunditur, preces sanctius & ardentius concipiuntur, & humilitas nostra coram Deo declaratur.
units.tr: 6. Because they make fasting in itself meritorious and satisfactory for temporal punishments, whereas it is nothing other than a means by which the wantonness of the flesh is subdued, prayers are conceived more holily and ardently, and our humility before God is declared.

units.la: Non igitur ieiunia ipsa damnamus, sed eorum pravas appendices à Pontificibus successu temporis additas.
units.tr: We therefore do not condemn fasts themselves, but the perverse appendages which the Papists have added to them over time.

units.la: Scommaticè scribit Jesuita: Mirum! quod hoc saltem medio, nec Lutherus nec Calvinus, nec ullus successorum prædicantium & ministrorum usus sit, ad doctrinam nam nam suam, quam Deodidactam esse judicant, confirmandam & probandam, neque etiam Eliam veræ doctrinæ vindicem imitentur! Quasi vero regnum Dei sit esca & potus, aut ex his vera religio æstimanda? Jejunavit pharisæus ille, sed post jejunium illud descendit inanis & jejunij fructibus cassus. Publicanus non jejunavit, & pharisæum jejunantem præcesserit non jejunans; sunt verba Chrysostomi. Et cur hoc? Quia, ut idem Chrysostomus dicit, vita recta non est jejunandi labor, nec cineris ac cilicij lectulus, sed si charitate ardeas, famescentes pane tuo nutrias, si superior irâ fis, si gloriam inanem non concupiscas, si invidiâ non detinearis. Homil. 40. in Matth. Quàm apposite hæc de ieiuniis Monachorum! qui pharisæum, non publicanum imitantur.
units.tr: The Jesuit writes mockingly: Strange! that by this means at least, neither Luther nor Calvin, nor any of the successors, preachers and ministers, has used it to confirm and prove their doctrine, which they judge to be taught by God, and do not even imitate Elijah, the defender of true doctrine! As if the kingdom of God were food and drink, or true religion were to be judged by these! That Pharisee fasted, but after that fast he went down empty and bereft of the fruits of fasting. The publican did not fast, and the non-fasting publican preceded the fasting Pharisee; these are the words of Chrysostom. And why so? Because, as the same Chrysostom says, a right life is not the labour of fasting, nor a bed of ashes and sackcloth, but if you burn with charity, if you feed the hungry with your bread, if you are superior to anger, if you do not covet empty glory, if you are not held by envy. Homily 40 on Matthew. How aptly this is said about the fasts of the monks! They imitate the Pharisee, not the publican.

units.la: Præterea scomma hoc ipsos Apostolos attinet, non enim legimus, aut ullo idoneo testimonio probari potest, ipsos O ieiuniieiunium quadragesimale usurpasse. Contrarium innuit locus Matth. 9: 15. Et credo Jesuitas, si vixissent tempore Christi cum discipulis Johannis, instinctu pharisaeorum dicturos fuisse: Quare nos & pharisæi multum jejunamus, discipuli vero tui non jejunant? Matth.9: 14, 11. & de Christo ipso cum pharisæis, quare cum publicanis & peccatoribus edit Doctor vester, id est, Christus? Idcirco blasphemia est, quod ad marginem scribit Harscherus: Acatholici imitatores esse volunt Christi in canis. Id est, cupiunt laute vivere, ut Christus.
units.tr: Moreover this mockery touches the Apostles themselves. For we do not read, nor can it be proved by any suitable testimony, that the Apostles used the Lenten fast. Matthew 9:15 suggests the contrary. And I believe that the Jesuits, had they lived in the time of Christ with the disciples of John, would at the instigation of the Pharisees have said: Why do we and the Pharisees fast much, but your disciples do not fast? (Matthew 9:14). And of Christ himself with the Pharisees: Why does your Teacher eat with publicans and sinners? (Matthew 9:11). It is therefore blasphemy when Harscher writes in the margin: Non-Catholics want to be imitators of Christ in feasts. That is, they desire to live sumptuously, as Christ did.

units.la: Quod testimonia scripturæ attinet, quæ huic parallelo subiiciuntur, sunt illa sine omni delectu citata. Alia enim sunt, in quibus plane nihil de ieiunio. Alia quæ de ieiunio agunt, sed non ad scopum. Alia quæ pontificiorum sententiam evertunt.
units.tr: As for the testimonies of Scripture which are appended to this parallel, they are cited without any discrimination. For some have nothing at all about fasting; others deal with fasting but not to the point; others overthrow the opinion of the Papists.

units.la: Locus Gen. 2: 17. (de fructu vero arboris scientia boni & mali de isto ne comedas, nam quo die comederis de eo, utiq; moriturus es) nihil de ieiunio habet. Nam potest ne quis sibi persuadere, hominem in statu integritatis & felicitatis ieiunaffe, ut carnis lascivia retundereturs quando nondum peccavit? Non is fuit fcopus illius mandati, sed potius alius, de quo Augustinus de Gen. ad lit. lib. VIII. ut homo sciret fe sub Domino esse positum, cujus gratiam suâ obedientiâ promereri posset, vel inobedientiâ amittere. Praeterea quàm insulsum à prohibitione fructus arboris scientiæ boni & mali, ieiunium afferere? An idcirco Judæi perpetuò ieiunarunt, quod iussi sunt à carne suilla abstinere? Id hactenus inauditum per totam scripturam veteris Testamenti. Et fi ista abstinentia à fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali figura fuit ieiunii (ut scribit Jesuita) cur ergo non abftinent pontificii in suis ieiuniis à fructibus arborum? An datâ operâ volunt
units.tr: The passage Genesis 2:17 (but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat of it; for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die) has nothing about fasting. For can anyone persuade himself that man in the state of integrity and happiness fasted in order to subdue the wantonness of the flesh, when he had not yet sinned? That was not the aim of that command, but rather another, of which Augustine speaks in De Genesi ad litteram book 8: that man might know that he was placed under the Lord, whose grace he could earn by obedience, or lose by disobedience. Besides, how foolish it is to assert a fast from the prohibition of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil! Did the Jews then fast perpetually because they were commanded to abstain from swine's flesh? That has been unheard of throughout the whole Scripture of the Old Testament. And if that abstinence from the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a figure of fasting (as the Jesuit writes), why then do the Papists not abstain from the fruits of trees in their fasts? Do they wish, on purpose,

units.la: Evangelii. lunt imitari peccatum primorum parentum, quando scribunt fuisse figuram ieiunii & illi contrarium faciunt?
units.tr: to imitate the sin of our first parents, since they write that there was a figure of fasting and do the contrary?

units.la: Eiusdem commatis est testimonium ex Numero. cap. 6: 3. & seq. Nam fuit Naziraeatus singulare Dei institutum, in quo is qui Naziraeum se fore, vovit Jehovae, votum praestitit; se vinum aut potum inebriantem aut ex vite vinifera non bibiturum; uvas recentes & siccas non esurum: novaculum omnibus diebus Naziraeatus sui super caput ejus non transiturum, & ad cadaver emortui non accessurum. Hoc plane nihil commune habet cum ieiunio. Nam pontificii dum ieiunant in diebus Veneris & Sabbathi, in quadragesima, in ieiunio quatuor temporum, vinum bibunt & uvas tam recentes, quam siccas edunt. Male ergo applicatur Naziraeatus legalis ieiunio novi Testamenti: ceremonia Mosaica, Evangelio.
units.tr: Of the same kind is the testimony from Numbers 6:3 and following. For the Nazirite vow was a singular institution of God, in which he who vowed to be a Nazirite to Jehovah made the promise: that he would not drink wine or strong drink, nor drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat fresh or dried grapes; that no razor would pass over his head all the days of his separation, and that he would not come near a dead body.
