This plainly has nothing in common with fasting. For the Papists, while they fast on Fridays and Saturdays, in Lent, and in the Ember days, drink wine and eat grapes, both fresh and dried. It is therefore wrongly applied: the legal Nazirite vow to the fasting of the New Testament, a Mosaic ceremony to the Gospel.

units.la: Quod de Rechabitis citatur ex Jerem. 35: 6. iterum est ἐξαγώγιον. Jeiunium fuit particulare & politicum Rechabitis datum à Jonadab, ut tutius & commodius viverent inter populum, ubi erant inquilini.
units.tr: What is cited from the Rechabites in Jeremiah 35:6 is again an exagōgion [ἐξαγώγιον], a digression. Their fast was particular and political, given to the Rechabites by Jonadab, so that they might live more safely and conveniently among the people, where they were sojourners.

units.la: Reliqua testimonia ex Levit. 23, Esrae 8, Jerem. 36, Jonae. 3, Zach. 8. ut ex asse approbamus, sic nihil contra nos faciunt, modo tollatur quod ceremoniale est. Nam ut supra dixi, ieiunia etiam crebra urgemus & optamus. Illa vero ex Matth. 9. & ex Act. cap. 13, & 27. adducta sententiam nostrarum ecclesiarum de ieiunio confirmant, pontificiorum evertunt. Nam Christus noluit, ut discipuli sui se accommodarent ieiuniis discipulorum Johannis & pharisaeorum, imo plane noluit, ut ieiunarent. Ratio quod Christus esset cum ipsis, jejunaturos autem, ait, in diebus tribulationum. Quibus haud obscure docet ieiunia non debere esse stata, sed tempori accommodata, quod etiam observarunt discipuli Christi. Pontificii autem quia ordinationes suorum pontificum circa ieiunia observant, huic Christi doctrinae contraveniunt.
units.tr: We approve the remaining testimonies from Leviticus 23, Ezra 8, Jeremiah 36, Jonah 3, and Zechariah 8 wholly, and they do nothing against us, provided that what is ceremonial is set aside. For, as I said above, we also urge and desire frequent fasts. But those passages from Matthew 9 and from Acts chapters 13 and 27, which are adduced, confirm the opinion of our churches about fasting and overthrow that of the Papists. For Christ was unwilling that his disciples should conform themselves to the fasts of the disciples of John and of the Pharisees; indeed he plainly was unwilling that they should fast. The reason he gives is that the Bridegroom was with them, but the days would come when they would fast, in the days of tribulation. By this he quite clearly teaches that fasts ought not to be fixed, but suited to the time, which the disciples of Christ also observed. But the Papists, because they observe the ordinances of their popes concerning fasts, act against this doctrine of Christ.

units.la: Subiicit Harscherus testimonia patrum, primò Ignatii ex epistola ad philippenses, Quadragesimam nolite pro nihilo habere &c. Sed totus ille locus assutus est illi epistolae ex Clementis constitutionibus, ubi totidem verbis haec leguntur. Certè si fuisset constitutio apostolica, non minus apud Augustinum obtinuisset quàm Ignatium. Atqui Augustinus loco supra citato asserit, se non reperire apud Apostolos praeceptum Apostolorum, quando sit jejunandum.
units.tr: Harscher next cites the Fathers, first Ignatius from his letter to the Philippians: Do not hold the Quadragesima to be nothing, etc. But that whole passage was stitched into that letter from the Constitutions of Clement, where these very words are read. Certainly, if it had been an apostolic constitution, it would not have been less esteemed by Augustine than by Ignatius. Yet Augustine, in the place cited above, affirms that he does not find in the Apostles any precept of the Apostles as to when fasting is to be observed.

units.la: Secundò Irenaeum, qui varietatem jejunantium reprehendit. lib. de haeresibus. Apud Eusebium haec leguntur lib. 5. histor. Eccl. cap. 24. Sed hoc nihil ad nos. Habuerunt veteres varietatis metatis ieiunandi causa, quā Harscher legere potest apud Augustinum epist.86. In his rebus, de quibus nihil certi statuit scriptura divina, mos populi Dei vel instituta maiorum pro lege tenenda sunt. De quibus si disputare voluerimus, & ex aliorum consuetudine alios improbare, orietur interminata luctatio. Augustino certè ieiunandi tempus fuit indifferens. Et Irenæus loco citato scribit, istam dissonantiam jejunij consonantiam fidei non rupisse.
units.tr: Second, Irenaeus, who censures the variety among those who fast, in his book on heresies. This is read in Eusebius, Church History, book 5, chapter 24. But this has nothing to do with us. The ancients had a variety of customs in fasting, which Harscher may read about in Augustine, letter 86. In those matters about which Divine Scripture has laid down nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our forefathers must be held as law. If we wish to dispute about these things, and to condemn others by the practice of others, an endless wrangling will arise. Certainly for Augustine the time of fasting was a matter of indifference. And Irenaeus, in the place cited, writes that this dissonance in fasting had not broken the harmony of the faith.

units.la: Citat tertiò Basilium in hom. 2. de ieiunio, quadragesimæ ieiunium commendante. Quanquā forte homilia non est Basilii, si Erasmo credimus, qui graviter invehit in homines, qui notha & adulterina scripta sub magnorum virorum titulis obtrudunt orbi: tamen concedamus hæc Basilii esse verba, sicuti ieiunium quadragesimæ sinè controversia tempore Augustini in usu fuit. Quid autem hæc pro sententia Harscheri: aut quid pro sententia pontificiorum omnia illa testimonia tum scripturæ, tum patrum in præsenti parallelo citata? Non disputamus, non certamus inter nos de ieiunio ipso, sed de ieiunio qualiter â pontificiis hodie exercetur. Itaque debebat Harscherus ex scriptura & patribus probare, ieiunium consistere non in abstinentia ab omni cibo, sed à certis tantùm: licere in quadragesima etiam lautissimis cibis vesci, modò non adsit caro, aut lacticinia: licere quoque in nocte quadragesimam precedente, omnem nequitiam, & commessationes exercere: jejunia vetera sub pœna peccati mortalis fuisse præcepta: jejunia per se esse meritoria. Hæc fuissent, tanquam in controversia posita, ex scriptura probanda. Atqui ne verbum quidem de hisce, in omnibus illis testimoniis ab Harsehero allegatis.
units.tr: Third, he cites Basil in his second homily on fasting, which commends the fast of Lent. Yet perhaps the homily is not Basil's, if we believe Erasmus, who sharply inveighs against men who thrust spurious and adulterated writings on the world under the names of great men. Still, let us grant these to be Basil's words, just as the Lenten fast was without controversy in use in Augustine's time. But what do these things, or all those testimonies from Scripture and the Fathers cited in the present parallel, have to do with Harscher's position, or with the position of the Papists? We are not disputing, nor contending among ourselves, about fasting itself, but about fasting as it is practised today by the Papists. Harscher therefore ought to have proved from Scripture and the Fathers that fasting consists not in abstinence from all food, but only from certain foods; that in Lent it is lawful to eat even the most lavish dishes, provided there is no meat or dairy; that it is lawful also on the night before Lent to indulge in all wickedness and revelry; that the old fasts were enjoined under pain of mortal sin; that fasts are meritorious in themselves. These points, as things placed in controversy, would have needed proof from Scripture. Yet there is not a word about them in all those testimonies Harscher has alleged.

units.la: Obiicit postremò, Calvinistas sua jejunia, egregiâ instructa mensâ, lixis & assis finire. Fieri potest ut ditiores inter nos (nam de pauperibus non est quæstio) quando integrum diem absque ullo cibo & potu, precibus & auditione verbi Dei consumpserunt sub vespera circa sextam carne utantur, quia Domino edunt & gratias agunt Deo. Rom. 14: 6. Scientes nihil esse impurum per se, Rom. 14: 14. Idcirco nihil quod ingreditur in os polluere hominem. Matth. 15: 11. Verè autem possum hîc Monachis applicare illud Christi, quod in eodem capite legitur v. 7. 8. hypocritæ bene de vobis prophetavit Esajas, dicens, appropinquat mihi populus hic ore suo, & labijs me honorant, cor autem eorum procul abest à me. Nam ecce hypocrisin claustralem. 1. Non abstinent à cibo & potu cùm ieiunant. 2. Tempus ieiunio quadragesimali destinatû, mutaverunt. Veteres enim dixerunt finiri jejunium circa nonam quæ est nostra tertia pomeridiana (habebant enim horas χεῳνικὰς, quas auspicabantur ab ortu solis, & finiebant in eius occasu) vel ad vesperam quando cœnabant. Sic Cornelius usq; ad horam nonam jejunavit. Act. 10. 30. Israelitæ ad vesperam usq;: Iud. 20: 26. Et 2. Sam. 1: 12. plangentes fleverunt, jejunaverunq; usq; ad vesperam. Id Bellarminus non diffitetur lib. 2. de bonis operibus in partic. cap. 2. Bernhardi tempore non placuit amplius mos ieiunandi ad nonam tantùm horam, serm. 3. de quadrage. quia secundùm canonem concilii Cabilonensis, jejunare nullatenus credebantur, si ante manducaverint, quàm vespertinum celebretur officium, quod iuxta Bellarminum celebrandum hora duodecima inæquali, id est, sexta nostra. Hodierni verò pontificii in quadragesima vesperâ mutant in meridiem, ac officium vespertinum celebrant hora undecima ante meridiem, & sole in summo cœlo splendente canunt hymnum vespertinum.
units.tr: Lastly he objects that the Calvinists end their fasts with a splendid table, with boiled and roasted meats. It may be that some richer men among us (for the poor are not in question) who have spent a whole day without any food or drink, in prayers and in hearing the Word of God, eat meat towards evening, around six o'clock, because they eat to the Lord and give thanks to God (Rom. 14:6), knowing that nothing is unclean in itself (Rom. 14:14), and therefore that nothing which goes into the mouth defiles a man (Matt. 15:11). But I may truly apply to the monks that saying of Christ, read in the same chapter, v. 7–8: Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, saying, This people draws near to me with its mouth, and honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. For behold the cloistral hypocrisy: (1) they do not abstain from food and drink when they fast; (2) they have changed the time appointed for the Lenten fast. For the ancients said that the fast ends about the ninth hour, which is our three in the afternoon (for they had seasonal hours [ὡρικάς], which they began at sunrise and ended at sunset), or else at evening, when they dined. So Cornelius fasted until the ninth hour (Acts 10:30); the Israelites until evening (Judg. 20:26); and in 2 Sam. 1:12, they mourned, wept and fasted until evening. Bellarmine does not deny this, in book 2 on good works, chapter 2 in particular. In Bernard's time the custom of fasting only until the ninth hour no longer pleased, sermon 3 on Lent, because according to the canon of the council of Chalon, they were not thought to fast at all if they ate before the evening office was celebrated, which, according to Bellarmine, was to be celebrated at the twelfth unequal hour, that is, our sixth. But today the Papists in Lent move vespers to midday, and celebrate the evening office at eleven in the morning, and while the sun shines high in the sky they sing the evening hymn:

units.la: Tetrum chaos illabiturSol recedit igneusInfunde lumen cordibus.
units.tr: The dreadful chaos will fall in. The fiery sun withdraws. Pour light into our hearts.

units.la: Ac tum horâ duodecima meridiana prandent, vel verius cœnant. Deum immortalem! quanta est in religione pontificia perversitas? quantum ludibrium Dei & ecclesiæ? In ipsâ meridie ad Deum clamare; sol recedit igneus? vesperam mutare in meridiem, ut ventri satisfacere possint? An non venter ipsorum Deus est, in cuius gratiam officium vespertinum celebrant in meridie? Et tamen illi Censores qui omnia nostra carpunt, hanc consuetudinem laudant. Sic enim Bellarminus, lib. 2. de bonis operibus in particulari, cap. 2. licèt jejuniorum severitas nostro tempore sit aliquantum relaxata: tamen ideò reprehendi non posse populos christianos, qui morem introductum atq; à patribus vel probatum vel permissum velint sequi.
units.tr: And then at twelve noon they dine, or rather sup. Immortal God! How great is the perversity of the papal religion? How great is the mockery of God and the Church? To cry out to God at midday, the fiery sun withdraws? To move evening to midday, so that they may satisfy their belly? Is not their belly their god, for whose sake they celebrate the evening office at midday? And yet those critics who pick at everything of ours praise this custom. For thus Bellarmine, book 2 on good works in particular, chapter 2: Although the severity of the fasts has been somewhat relaxed in our time, nevertheless Christian peoples who wish to follow a custom introduced and either approved or permitted by the Fathers cannot be blamed.

units.la: Hi nunc cœnam habent in meridie, ubi lautius vivunt, quàm in diebus in quibus caro licita est. 3. Sub vesperam datur signum ad collationem, & hic iterum lautè.
units.tr: These now have their supper at midday, where they live more lavishly than on the days when meat is permitted. (3) Towards evening the signal is given for the collation, and here again they feast lavishly.

units.la: Nam Prælatis & Canonicis apponuntur confectiones, ficus, placentæ, boleti, dactyli: aliis placentæ, poma, pyra, nuces, uvæ, cum vino generoso aut cerevisia. De his recte Augustinus in Domin. in octavam Paschæ: Sunt quidam observantes quadragesimæ, delitiosi potius, quàm religiosi, exquirentes novas suavitates magis quàm veteres concupiscentias castigantes, qui pretiosis copiosisque diversorum, fructuum apparatibus aliorum ciborum sapores superare contendunt. Vasa in quibus coctæ sunt carnes, tanquam immunda formidant, & in carne sua ventris & gutturis luxuriam non formidant.
units.tr: For the prelates and canons are served with confections, figs, cakes, mushrooms and dates; for others, cakes, apples, pears, nuts and grapes, with fine wine or beer. Augustine rightly says of these in his sermon on the octave of Easter: There are some who observe Lent who are self-indulgent rather than devout, seeking new sweetnesses rather than chastising old desires, who strive to surpass the flavours of other foods with costly and abundant preparations of various fruits. They dread the vessels in which the meats were cooked as unclean, and in their own flesh they do not dread the lust of belly and throat.

units.la: Ut ergò olim pharisæus dixerat; jejuno bis in sabbatho: Sic Jesuita dicere potest: ego edo bis in jejunio. Apud reliquos autem in papatu sicuti septuagesimæ terminus à quo, sunt bacchanalia, sic terminus ad quem sunt tympana, saltationes & luxuriæ.
units.tr: So just as the Pharisee once said, I fast twice on the Sabbath, so the Jesuit may say, I eat twice in the fast. And among the rest, in popery, just as Septuagesima is the starting point, the bacchanals are its beginning, so the end is the drums, dancing and lusts.

units.la: Sicuti igitur iam olim de ieiunio pontificio communis erat gnoma: unum jejunium triplex crapula: ita recte de quadragesima dici potest: Una quadragesima, duo Dionysia-
units.tr: Therefore, just as even long ago the saying was common about the papal fast, one fast, a threefold gluttony, so rightly it may be said of Lent: One Lent, two Dionysia.

units.la: Nihil horum, per Dei gratiam in Ecclesiis reformatis.
units.tr: None of these things, by the grace of God, occur in the reformed Churches.

units.la: AETIANI.
units.tr: AETIANI.

units.la: A B Aetio Syro appellati, qui prater Arianam haresin docebat nullum peccatum, quantumlibet grave, imputari in fide manentibus, solamq; fidem absq; ullo alio opere satis esse ad vitam æternam consequendam. Affirmabat quoq; qua Deus concessit Apostolis, sibi revelata fuisse. Vide tripart. histo. lib. 5. cap. 42.
units.tr: Called after Aetius the Syrian, who, besides the Arian heresy, taught that no sin, however grave, is imputed to those who remain in the faith, and that faith alone, without any other work, is enough to obtain eternal life. He also affirmed that what God granted to the Apostles had been revealed to him. See Tripartite History, book 5, chapter 42.

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATIO.

units.la: De Aetio Syro cur multa dicam nulla est necessitas: Arianus fuit, quem secutus est Eunomius, à quo postea Eunomiani appellati fuerunt illi qui Aetii hæresin sequebantur. Eius doctrina in synodo Constantinopolitana fuit damnata, utpote quæ non ex sacra scriptura, sed ex dialectico fastu & syllogistica vanitate, ut Epiphanius loquitur, ortum habuit. Præter Arianam hæresin etiam alia dogmata divulgavit, de quibus Augustinus, Sozomenus, Epiphanius & Nicephorus. Harscherus relictis cæteris unum falsò arripit, & dicit Aetium docuisse: nullum peccatum quantumlibet grave, imputari in fide manentibus, solamque fidem absque ullo alio opere satis esse ad vitam æternam consequendam.
units.tr: Why should I say much about Aetius the Syrian? There is no need: he was an Arian, and Eunomius followed him, and from Eunomius those who followed the heresy of Aetius were afterwards called Eunomians. His teaching was condemned at the Synod of Constantinople, since it arose not from Holy Scripture but from dialectical pomp and syllogistic vanity, as Epiphanius puts it. Besides the Arian heresy he also spread other doctrines, which Augustine, Sozomen, Epiphanius and Nicephorus record. Harscher, leaving the rest aside, falsely seizes upon one point and says that Aetius taught that no sin, however grave, is imputed to those who remain in the faith, and that faith alone, without any other work, is enough to obtain eternal life.

units.la: Quæso quid speres de istis hominibus, penes quos nulla fides, nullus candor? qui historias veterum & sententias Patrum mutant, mutilant, & corrumpunt pro lubitu. Aetius (inquit Jesuita Harscherus) docebat, nullum peccatum quantumlibet grave imputari in fide manentibus, solam fidem absq; ullo alio opere satis esse ad vitam aeternam consequendam. E contra Augustinus antiqua fide: Fertur etiam usq; adeo fuisse bonis moribus inimicus, ut asseveraret, quod nihil cuiquam obesset quorumlibet perpetratio, ac perseverantia peccatorum. SI HUIUS QUAE AB ILLO DOCEBATUR FIDEI PARTICIPES ESSENT. De haeres. ad quod vult Deum, haeres. 54. Epiphanius in Anaceph. Caeterum aberrare aliquem in scortatione aut alio peccato, nihil esse ajunt, nihil enim quaerit Deus, dicunt, quam ut sit quis solum in ipsorum fide. Quis non videt apertam fraudem? Annon aliud est in fide Christi esse, & esse in fide ac religione Aetii? Pergo ad
units.tr: What can you hope for from these men, who have neither faith nor candour? They change, mutilate and corrupt the histories of the ancients and the opinions of the Fathers as they please. Aetius, says the Jesuit Harscher, taught that no sin, however grave, is imputed to those who remain in the faith, and that faith alone, without any other work, is enough to obtain eternal life. On the contrary, Augustine, in the old faith: It is said that he was so hostile to good morals that he asserted that the commission and persistence of whatever sins harmed no one, IF THEY WERE PARTAKERS OF THIS FAITH WHICH WAS TAUGHT BY HIM. Augustine, On Heresies, against the one who is willing God, heresy 54. Epiphanius, in the Anacephalaeosis: Moreover, they say that to go astray in fornication or some other sin is nothing, for God seeks nothing, they say, except that someone be in their faith alone. Who does not see the open fraud? Is it not one thing to be in the faith of Christ, and another to be in the faith and religion of Aetius? I pass on to

units.la: PARALLELUM.
units.tr: PARALLEL.

units.la: Ut Calvinum possit Aetianae haeresis sews reū facere Jesuita, scribit ipsum lib. III. Inst. cap. 4. S. 28. docere: fidelium peccata venialia esse, non quia mortem non mereantur, sed quia nulla est condemnatio ijs, qui sunt in Christo Iesu: quia non imputantur: quia venia delentur. Quid hoc ad hæresin Aetianam? An his verbis docet Calvinus, nihil obesse quorumlibet peccatorum perpetrationem modò quis maneat in fide & religione Calvini? Atqui sic loquendum fuisset, alias nullus est parallelismus.
units.tr: So that the Jesuit may make Calvin guilty of the Aetian heresy, he writes that Calvin teaches, in Institutes book III, chapter 4, section 28: that the sins of believers are venial, not because they do not deserve death, but because there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus; because they are not imputed; because they are blotted out by pardon. What does this have to do with the Aetian heresy? Does Calvin by these words teach that the commission of any sins does no harm, provided one remains in the faith and religion of Calvin? Yet it would have had to be put that way, otherwise there is no parallel.

units.la: Obiiciet Harscherus; sit homonymia in vocabulo fidei, attamen dicit Calvinus, si quis maneat in fide, nullam esse ei condemnationem etiamsi peccet, annon hoc Aetianum, aut secundum Bellarminum Eunomianum est? Respondeo, non esse. Ratio est, quia Aetius homo (secundùm Augustinum) bonis moribus inimicus docuit, perpetrationem quorumlibet peccatorum & perseverantiam in ijsdem, non nocere, sic Calvinus nunquam docuit, nec nos docemus, sed ita.
units.tr: Harscher will object: there is an equivocation in the word faith; yet Calvin says that if anyone remains in faith, there is no condemnation for him even if he sins. Is this not Aetian, or according to Bellarmine Eunomian? I answer: it is not. The reason is that Aetius, a man (according to Augustine) hostile to good morals, taught that the commission of any sins, and perseverance in them, does no harm. Calvin never taught this, nor do we; we teach the opposite.

units.la: Primò, Primo in fide esse, seu esse in Christo est ambiguum. Dicuntur enim aliquando in fide seu in Christo esse illi, qui ore saltem & externa professione Christum confitentur fide temporariâ, de quibus loquitur Christus Luc. 8: 4. seq. Hi sunt palmites infructuosi, qui exscinduntur & in ignem proiiciuntur. Joh. 15: 6. Sunt pisces putres in lagena, & zizania in agro ecclesiæ. Secundo, dicuntur in fide seu in Christo esse, qui non tantum fide temporariâ Christum profitentur, sed etiam verâ & salvificâ fide & firmâ fiduciâ Christum novi foederis intercessorem, omnia quæ ipsius beneficia amplectuntur. De posterioribus Calvino tantum est sermo. Deinde de his non pronuntiat, quòd nullum peccatum quantumlibet grave ipsis imputetur, & quod sola fides absque ullo alio opere satis sit ad vitam æternam consequendam. Annon peccatum adulterii & homicidii fuit imputatum Davidi, quando propheta Nathan ei dixit: non amovebitur gladius à domo tua usque in seculum, eò quòd sprevisti me, ut acciperes uxorem Uriæ Chythæi quæ esset tibi uxor, sic ait Iehova, ecce ego suscitaturus sum contra te malum è domo tua &c. 2. Sam. 12: 10, 11. An non etiam eidem imputatum est peccatum, quando numeravit populum? Sic etiam omnibus fidelibus peccata imputantur. Quomodo autem eadem non imputentur ad mortem (licèt omnia sint mortalia) idem exemplum Davidis nos docet, quando ad confessionem peccati Davidis, dixit propheta: etiam Iehova transtulit peccatum tuum, non es moriturus. Sic verè in Christum credentes, sciunt si peccent, se habere advocatum apud Deum Iesum Christum justum, qui factus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris.
units.tr: First, to be in faith, or to be in Christ, is ambiguous. For those are sometimes said to be in faith or in Christ who confess Christ at least with the mouth and by outward profession, with a temporary faith. Of these Christ speaks in Luke 8:4 ff. These are unfruitful branches, which are cut off and cast into the fire, John 15:6. They are rotten fish in a jar, and tares in the field of the Church. Secondly, those are said to be in faith or in Christ who profess Christ not only with a temporary faith, but with true and saving faith, and with firm trust embrace Christ as the mediator of the new covenant and all his benefits. It is only of these latter that Calvin speaks. Then, of these he does not pronounce that no sin, however grave, is imputed to them, and that faith alone, without any other work, is enough to obtain eternal life. Was not the sin of adultery and murder imputed to David, when the prophet Nathan said to him: the sword shall not depart from your house for ever, because you have despised me and taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife; thus says the LORD, behold, I will raise up evil against you from your own house, etc., 2 Sam. 12:10, 11? Was not sin also imputed to the same man when he numbered the people? So also sins are imputed to all believers. How they are not imputed unto death, although all sins are mortal, the same example of David teaches us, when, on David's confession of sin, the prophet said: "The LORD also has taken away your sin; you shall not die." Thus those who truly believe in Christ know that if they sin, they have "an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the propitiation for our sins," 1 John 2:1, 2.

units.la: 1. Joh. 2: 1, 2. & ad se pertinere vocem de foederatis pronuntiatam: ero propitius iniquitatibus eorum, & peccatorum eorum & iniquitatum non recordabor amplius. Heb. 8: 12. Idcircò peccata sua conficonfitentur, & gratiâ Spiritus sancti resurgunt, rogantque ut per meritum Jesu Christi peccata sibi remittantur, quod etiam obtinent, quia si confitemur peccata nostra fidelis est Deus & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata & emundet nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. 1: 9. Atque hoc est, quod Calvinus voluit, quando dixit omnia peccata in se esse mortalia, fieri autem venialia per misericordiam Dei, peccata propter meritum, justitiam & satisfactionem Christi, nobis condonantis. Vasquesius Jesuita scribit fuisse ex catholicis viros graves & pios, Gersonem, Almarium, Rossensem, qui idem docuerint, quod Calvinus, Tom. III. disp. II. §. 4. Perseverantibus autem in peccatis nulla spes veniæ & remissionis peccatorum est exspectanda.
units.tr: They also know that the word spoken about those in covenant applies to them: "I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins and iniquities no more," Heb. 8:12. Therefore they confess their sins, and, raised up again by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they ask that their sins be forgiven them through the merit of Jesus Christ. This they also obtain, because "if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness," 1 John 1:9. This is what Calvin meant when he said: all sins are in themselves mortal, but they become venial through the mercy of God, sins being pardoned on account of the merit, righteousness and satisfaction of Christ, which is bestowed upon us. The Jesuit Vasquez writes that among the Catholics there were grave and pious men, Gerson, Almain and Rossensis, who taught the same as Calvin, Tom. III, disp. II, §4. But for those who persevere in sins, no hope of pardon and remission of sins is to be expected.

units.la: Ex quibus apparet luculentissime falsa esse, quæ nobis attribuit Harscherus, quasi doceremus, nullum peccatum esse iis, qui in fide manent, ut ipse loquitur.
units.tr: From these things it appears most clearly that what Harscher attributes to us is false, as if we taught that there is no sin for those who remain in faith, as he himself puts it.

units.la: Sed & illud falsum est quod de perseverantia in fide subiungit ex Calvini lib. III. Instit cap. 22: §. 7. ac si illa in electis perseverantibus efficeret talem persectionem, ut peccare amplius non possint. Non ea est doctrina nostra, nec Calvini. Etiamsi enim asseramus, fidem iustificam semel acceptam (propter inhabitantem Spiritum 1. Cor. 3: 16. per quem obsignantur usque in diem redemptionis, Eph. 4: 30. propter fidelitatem Dei, qui suos non sinit tentari supra vires, 1. Cor. 10: 13. qui opus suum inchoatum perficit usque ad diem Jesu Christi, Phil. 1: 6. propter potentiam Dei Patris & Filii ex quorum manibus nemo poterit oves Christi rapere, Joh. 10: 20. propter preces Christi nunquam non a Patre exauditi, Joh. 17. toto, propter arctissimam unionem fidelium cum capite Christo: propter naturam regenerationis spiritualis, quae non minus semel fit, quam ipsa haec nostra generatio naturalis in hunc mundum) totaliter & finaliter amitti non posse: tamen neutiquam asserimus in homine fideli idcirco peccatum non esse. Quamdiu vivis, inquit Augustinus tract. 42. in Joh. necessum est peccatum esse in membris tuis, & quisquis se inculpatum dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est.
units.tr: But what he adds about perseverance in faith, from Calvin's Institutes book III, chapter 22, §7, is also false: as if that perseverance produced in the elect such perfection that they could no longer sin. That is neither our doctrine nor Calvin's. For although we assert that justifying faith, once received, cannot be lost totally and finally, we do so on these grounds: because of the Spirit dwelling within (1 Cor. 3:16), by whom believers are sealed until the day of redemption (Eph. 4:30); because of the faithfulness of God, who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond their strength (1 Cor. 10:13), and who completes the work he has begun until the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6); because of the power of God the Father and the Son, out of whose hands no one can snatch the sheep of Christ (John 10:20); because of the prayers of Christ, which are always heard by the Father (John 17 throughout); because of the most intimate union of believers with Christ their head; and because of the nature of spiritual regeneration, which happens no less once than this natural birth of ours into this world. Nevertheless, we by no means assert that there is therefore no sin in the believing man. "As long as you live," says Augustine, tract. 42 on John, "sin must be in your members, and whoever says he is blameless is either proud or a fool."

units.la: Confitemur itaque (1) electos fide praeditos in gravissima peccata labi, (2) praesentiam Spiritus sancti efficacem ad tempus amittere, (3) & fidem ipsorum maximopere labefactari, (4) imo etiam ad ellychnium fumigans, & ignem sub cineribus latentem pervenire posse, adeo ut propter peccata commissa cogantur cum Davide clamare, omnes irrumpentes fluctus tui (irae tuae) & undae tuae super me transeunt.
units.tr: We therefore confess that (1) the elect, endowed with faith, can fall into most grave sins; (2) the efficacious presence of the Holy Spirit can be lost for a time; (3) their faith can be greatly shaken; and (4) it can even come down to a smoking wick and a fire hidden under the ashes, so that on account of the sins committed they are compelled to cry out with David: "All your billows and waves have gone over me."

units.la: Interim nihil ipsis timendum si Dei auxilium implorant, quia per mortem Christi, aculeus mortis, legis & peccati ademptus est, & Christus arundinem quassatam non frangit, & ellychnium sumigans non extinguit: Esa. 42: 3. Hæc constans est scripturæ sacræ sententia, & tamen errorem appellat Harscherus, & exinde consequentiam talem struit: Si fides semel habita nunquam amitti potest, sequitur manifeste, fidelem quicquid agat, quantacunq; scelera committat, quantumcunq; impœnitens vivat atq; etiam moriatur, semper esse & manere justum, peccata nihil obesse ejus saluti, nihil afferre damnationis. Quod est viam facere & impunitatem promittere omnibus flagitijs &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile they have nothing to fear, if they implore God's help, because through the death of Christ the sting of death, of the law and of sin is taken away, and Christ does not break a bruised reed, nor quench a smoking wick (Isa. 42:3). This is the constant sentence of Holy Scripture, and yet Harscher calls it an error, and from it he constructs this consequence: If faith once had can never be lost, it manifestly follows that the believer, whatever he does, however many crimes he commits, however impenitently he lives and even dies, is always and remains righteous; sins do nothing to harm his salvation and bring nothing of damnation. This is to open the way and promise impunity for all wickedness, etc.

units.la: Si hominem christianum fidelem definiremus, ut Canisius suum catholicum Romanum, haberet certè Harscherus rationem non condemnandam, huiusmodi consequentias formandi. Verum catholicum Romanum Canisius definit qui credit quodcunque ecclesia romana credit, sive id in scriptura expresse scriptum sit sive non scriptum. Nihil Canisius de bonis operibus, fidem caecam requirit tantum, quam Bellarminus per ignorantiam rectius definiri posse contendit, quam per notitiam.
units.tr: If we defined the Christian believer as Canisius defines his Catholic Roman, Harscher would certainly have a reasonable ground for forming such consequences, and one not to be condemned. But Canisius defines the Roman Catholic as one who believes whatever the Roman Church believes, whether or not it is expressly written in Scripture. Canisius requires nothing about good works, only blind faith, which Bellarmine contends can be defined more rightly by ignorance than by knowledge.

units.la: Nos vero christianum vere credentem esse membrum Iesu Christi afferimus, & unctionis illius participem, ut sanctum nomen Christi portet ac confiteatur, seq; Christo sistat vivam gratitudinis hostiam, (non conformando se seculo isti, sed transformando se per renovationem mentis Rom. 12: 1, 2.) & ut in hac vita contra peccatum & Satanam liberâ & bonâ conscientiâ pugnet, & postea aeternum cum Christo regnum in omnes creaturas teneat.
units.tr: But we assert that the Christian who truly believes is a member of Jesus Christ and a partaker of his anointing, so that he bears and confesses the holy name of Christ, and presents himself to Christ as a living sacrifice of gratitude (not conforming himself to this age, but being transformed by the renewing of his mind, Rom. 12:1, 2), and that in this life he fights against sin and Satan with a free and good conscience, and afterwards holds, with Christ, an eternal kingdom over all creatures.

units.la: Requirimus sanè fidem in homine christiano, quia accedentem ad Deum oportet credere, Heb. 11: 6. Sed quid credere oportet? omnia quae Deus in verbo suo patefecit; utpote Deum esse, & esse non tantum misericordem, sed etiam iustum & sanctum, cujus voluntas sit sanctificatio nostri 1. Thess. 4: 3. & ut ei serviamus cum sanctitate & justitia cunctis vitæ nostræ diebus Luc. 1: 75. Imò eum in finem illuxisse gratiam Dei salutiferam in Christo, ut abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, sapienter, juste & pie vivamus in præsenti seculo Tit. 2: 11, 12.
units.tr: Indeed we require faith in the Christian man, because whoever comes to God must believe (Heb. 11: 6). But what must one believe? All that God has revealed in his Word: namely, that God exists, and that he is not only merciful but also just and holy, whose will is our sanctification (1 Thess. 4: 3), and that we should serve him in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life (Luke 1: 75). Indeed, the saving grace of God has appeared in Christ for this end, that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age (Titus 2: 11, 12).

units.la: Quæ omnia quia ignorat vel dissimulat Harscherus, fit ut huiusmodi ἀθεολόγικς διαλογισμὸς proponat in suis disputationibus. Nam in postremo argumento manifeste subordinata disiungit & ἀσύνγατα coniungit, siquidem impossibile est, ut is qui per fidem Christo est insitus, non fructus ferat gratitudinis. Qui in me manet, inquit Christus, Joh. 15: 5. & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructum multum. Quisquis natus est ex Deo, peccato non dat operam, 1. Joh. 3: 9. Absit enim ut qui mortui sunt peccato, adhuc in eo vivant, Rom. 6: 2.
units.tr: Since Harscher ignores or dissembles all of this, he comes to put forward such an atheological reasoning [ἀθεολόγικος διαλογισμός] in his disputations. For in his last argument he manifestly separates what is subordinate and joins unconnected things [ἀσύναπτα] together, since it is impossible that one who has been grafted into Christ through faith should not bear the fruit of gratitude. He who abides in me, says Christ (John 15: 5), and in whom I abide, the same bears much fruit. Whoever is born of God does not devote himself to sin (1 John 3: 9). Far be it that those who have died to sin should still live in it (Rom. 6: 2).

units.la: Ad scripturæ testimonia ab Harschero adducta nunc respondendum. Quia autem ipse ne quidem ut explorator in castra nostra venit, ut cognoscat, quæ nostra sit fides & religio, necessum est, ut pauca hic præmittam.
units.tr: Now I must answer the testimonies of Scripture which Harscher has adduced. But since he has not even come into our camp as a spy, to learn what our faith and religion are, I must first set down a few things here.

units.la: Doctrinam enim de perseverantia sanctorum in fide distincte proponimus, distinguentes perseverantiam, credentes, fidem. Nomine perseverantiæ non intelligimus talem, quâ electi in gravissima peccata labi nequeant: quâ fides eorum non labefactetur: quâ spiritus sancti efficax præsentia ad tempus amitti non possit: sed quâ (fide etiam aliquando ad exiguam scintillam redactâ) penitus tamen excidere non possunt.
units.tr: For we set forth the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints in faith distinctly, distinguishing perseverance, believers, and faith. By perseverance we do not mean that by which the elect cannot fall into the gravest sins, by which their faith is not weakened, or by which the effective presence of the Holy Spirit cannot be lost for a time; but that by which, even when their faith has been reduced at times to a small spark, they nevertheless cannot utterly fall away.

units.la: Per credentes, primò, non temporarios notamus, qui externâ tantùm prosessione ad tempus Christum amplectuntur, sed qui verè Christo sunt insiti. Nec secundò loquimur de Angelis, qui proprie ad ecclesiam militantem non spectant. Nec tertiò de iis qui sub sedere operum: sed qui sub sedere gratiæ sunt, quod priore nobiliores habet conditiones.
units.tr: By believers, first, we do not mean temporary ones, who embrace Christ for a time only by outward profession, but those who are truly grafted into Christ. Nor do we speak, second, of the angels, who do not properly belong to the Church militant. Nor, third, of those who are under the covenant of works, but of those who are under the covenant of grace, which has the nobler conditions.

units.la: Per fidem in hac disputatione non intelligimus fidem temporariam, quæ ad tempus durat, mox sub persecutionibus exarescit: nec fidem quam credimus, quæ est ipsa doctrina apostolica, nam ab hac multi deficiunt quotidiè 1. Tim. 1: 19. Sed fidem quâ credimus ab Apostolo Paulo, electorum dicta Tit. 1: 1. quæ est pretiosa & constans acquiescentia in promissionibus divinis, de remissione peccatorum per sanguinem Christi. Basilius hanc ob insignem eius præstantiam & efficientiam vocat τ̂ ἐκκλησίας στέφανον, τ̂ ψοθεσίας ὑπομνήσιον, τῆς τῶ χριστῶ μαθητῶν τὸ ὠφέλημον, ecclesiæ coronam, adoptionis nostræ fundamentum, & discipulorum Christi ornamentum.
units.tr: By faith in this disputation we do not mean temporary faith, which lasts only for a time and soon withers under persecutions; nor the faith which we believe, which is the apostolic doctrine itself, for many daily fall away from this (1 Tim. 1: 19). But we mean the faith by which we believe, which Paul the Apostle calls the faith of God's elect (Titus 1: 1), and which is a precious and steadfast resting upon the divine promises concerning the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ. On account of its remarkable excellence and efficacy, Basil calls it the crown of the Church, the foundation of our adoption, and the ornament of Christ's disciples [τὸ στέφανον τῆς ἐκκλησίας, τὸ ὑπόθεμα τῆς υἱοθεσίας ἡμῶν, τὸ ὠφέλημα τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ μαθητῶν].

units.la: Hisce sic præmissis non est difficile ad argumenta Harscheri, ex scriptura adducta, respondere. Primum est Gen. 3. Adamus fidelis tale peccatum admisit, quo non tantùm se sed omnes omninò involuit, ideoq; gravissimis pœnis subjectus fuit.
units.tr: With these things premised, it is not difficult to answer Harscher's arguments drawn from Scripture. The first is Gen. 3: Adam, a faithful man, committed such a sin that he involved not only himself but absolutely all, and therefore was subjected to the gravest punishments.

units.la: Nihil ad scopum. Primò, Adamus & Eva non fuerunt sub sedere gratiæ, sed operum. Secundò, non habuerunt fidem iustificantem, sed generalem quoad promissionem benedictionis per arborem vitæ designatam. Tertiò, non habuerunt promissionem perpetuæ assistentiæ, ut fideles sub gratiæ sedere.
units.tr: This is beside the point. First, Adam and Eve were not under the covenant of grace but of works. Second, they did not have justifying faith, but only a general faith regarding the promise of blessing signified through the tree of life. Third, they did not have the promise of perpetual assistance, which the faithful have under the covenant of grace.

units.la: II. Lib. 2. Regum cap. 12.
units.tr: II. Book of Kings, chapter 12.

units.la: David utiq; fidelis admisso adulterio & homicidio, suâ etiam sententiâ dignum se morte pronuntiat, quam subivisset æternam, nisi pœnitentia peccatum delevisset, Psal. 6. & 37. meritus est furorem, quem tam calidis lachrymis pœnitentiæq; operibus studet mitigare.
units.tr: David, being faithful, after committing adultery and murder, himself pronounces that he deserves death by his own sentence, which he would have undergone eternally unless repentance had blotted out the sin (Psal. 6 and 37). He deserved the wrath, which he strives to mitigate with such warm tears and works of repentance.

units.la: Davidem Regem commisisse peccatum mortale nos non negamus, neque hoc est contra fidei nostræ articulos: amisisse eum quoque cordis lætitiam, & conscientiæ puritatem non diffitemur. Sed eundem Davidem plena voluntate & elata, quod dicitur, manu peccasse scriptura non testatur. Credibile magis est fuisse in ipso tanquam homine secundum cor Dei, luctum carnis & spiritus in hoc peccato perpetrando, ubi autem est luctus carnis & spiritus Dei, ibi plene spiritus non auffertur. Id quod etiam de Davide scriptura testatur. Nam non petit a Deo, ut reddat spiritum sanctum, sed ne auferat eum, Psal. 51: 13.
units.tr: We do not deny that King David committed a mortal sin, nor is this against the articles of our faith; nor do we deny that he lost the joy of his heart and the purity of his conscience. But Scripture does not testify that David sinned with full and deliberate will, with what they call a high hand. It is more credible that in him, as a man after God's own heart, there was a struggle of flesh and spirit in committing this sin; and where there is a struggle of the flesh and the Spirit of God, the Spirit is not wholly taken away. Scripture itself testifies to this of David. For he does not ask God to restore the Holy Spirit to him, but that he not take it away (Psal. 51: 13).

units.la: Illud vero, Davidem poenitentia delevisse peccata sua, directe est contra textum. Cur non Harscherus cum Davide, Deo gloriam tribuit? Nam David clamat: Expiato me hyssopo ut mundus sim: abluito me, ut prae nive albescam: facito ut audiam gaudium & laetitiam: omnes iniquitates meas dele: absconde iratam faciam tuam a peccatis meis &c. III. Lib.
units.tr: But that David blotted out his sins by repentance is directly against the text. Why does Harscher not give glory to God with David? For David cries: Purge me with hyssop that I may be clean; wash me that I may be whiter than snow; let me hear joy and gladness; blot out all my iniquities; hide your angry face from my sins, etc. III. Lib.

units.la: III. Lib. 3. Regum cap. II. scribitur de Salomone: averterunt mulieres cor ejus &c. quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: III. Lib. 3. Regum cap. II. is written of Solomon: "His wives turned away his heart," and what follows.

units.la: Vult Jesuita cum Bellarmino & aliis, Salomonem Regem fidem iustificantem & Spiritum sanctum amisisse in eo, quod factus sit idolatra & insignis peccator. Id quidem ego de homine, qui typum Christi gessit, propheta Dei fuit, & libros canonicos scripsit non ausim affirmare. Præcipuè cum Deus per prophetam Nathanem de Salomone locutus sit: Ego ero illi Pater & ipse erit mihi filius, qui cum perverse egerit, ego corripiam eum virgâ hominum & plagis humanis: & benignitas mea non amovebitur ab eo. Fuit itaque Salomon ad tempus emansor, sed non defertor. Quanquam itaque cum Hieronymo dicendum, Salomonem divitijs confisum per mulieres offendisse Deum, ab eo tamen spiritum sanctum totaliter sublatum esse superius vaticinium non permittit. Observandum itaque in hac controversia quod Gregorius dicit Hom.5. in Ezech.
units.tr: The Jesuit, with Bellarmine and others, holds that Solomon, the king, lost justifying faith and the Holy Spirit when he became an idolater and a notorious sinner. I would not venture to affirm this of a man who bore the type of Christ, was a prophet of God, and wrote canonical books, especially since God spoke through the prophet Nathan about Solomon: "I will be his Father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the children of men; but my mercy shall not depart from him." Solomon, then, was for a time a stray, but not a deserter. Although, then, we must say with Jerome that Solomon, trusting in his riches, offended God through women, the foregoing prophecy does not allow that the Holy Spirit was wholly taken from him. In this controversy, therefore, we should observe what Gregory says in Homily 5 on Ezekiel:

units.la: Spiritum sanctum in sanctorum cordibus juxta quasdam virtutes semper permanere, juxta quasdam autem recessurum venire & venturum recedere.
units.tr: "The Holy Spirit always remains in the hearts of the saints according to certain virtues, but according to certain others he comes and goes, departing and returning."

units.la: IV. Ezech. cap. 18. Cùm averterit se justus à justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem morte morietur. Quô ha[?] mina, si justus & fidelis non potest nec justitiam amittere, nec peccatum, quò moriatur, perpetrare. Locus ipse nihil concludit pro pontificiis. Primò quia in eo agitur de moraliter iusto, quem describit v. 7. qui neminem oppresserit, pignus suum debitori reddiderit, rapinam non rapuerit, panem suum esurienti dederit & nudum operuerit veste. Talis si deficiat dicitur sibi videri habuisse quod revera non habuit, Luc. 8: 18. quicunque non habet, etiam quod videtur habere ab ipso tolletur. Nos loquimur de evangelicè iusto. Locus ergo alienus. Deinde conditionalis hæc nihil ponit inesse, non magis quàm si quis ex illo Gal. 1: 8. Si angelus è cœlo evangelizet vobis præter id, quod vobis evangelizavimus, anathema esto, concludere vellet: Ergò Angelus è cœlo potest fieri anathema, aut potest evangelizare aliud evangelium.
units.tr: Ezekiel 18: "When the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in it." To what end, then, these threats, if the righteous and faithful man can neither lose righteousness nor commit sin so as to die? The passage itself proves nothing for the Papists. First, because it treats of a man righteous in the moral sense, whom verse 7 describes: "who has oppressed no one, has restored the pledge to the debtor, has robbed no one by violence, has given his bread to the hungry and covered the naked with a garment." If such a man fails, he is said to seem to himself to have had what in truth he never had, as in Luke 8:18: "whoever has not, even that which he seems to have shall be taken from him." We speak of a man righteous in the evangelical sense. The passage, therefore, is foreign to the question. Next, this conditional clause asserts nothing as present, no more than if someone wished to conclude from Galatians 1:8, "If an angel from heaven preach to you any other gospel than that which we have preached to you, let him be accursed," that therefore an angel from heaven can become accursed, or can preach another gospel.

units.la: Quod verò Jesuita quærit: quo hæ minæ, si justus & fidelis non potest nec justitiam amittere, nec peccatum quò moriatur patrare dico, interrogatione ista opus non esse apud eum qui cognitionem habet rerum theologicarum. Nam omninò iustus & fidelis potest iustitiam amittere, potest peccatum patrare ut moriatur, si consideretur in se, & secundùm vires suas: quod autem non potest, fit, quia cum cadit justus non prosternitur, quia Iehova sustentat manum ejus. Psal. 37: 24. Fiunt ergo huiusmodi admonitiones, ut fideles admoneantur propriæ fragilitatis, excitentur quinetiam ad vigilantiam & preces, quæ vera sunt perseverantiæ media.
units.tr: As for the Jesuit's question, "To what end these threats, if the righteous and faithful man can neither lose righteousness nor commit sin so as to die?", I say that this question is unnecessary for anyone who has knowledge of theological matters. For the righteous and faithful man can altogether lose righteousness and can commit sin so as to die, if he is considered in himself and according to his own strength. That he does not do so is because "though the righteous fall, he shall not be utterly cast down, for the LORD upholds his hand" (Ps. 37:24). Such admonitions are therefore given so that the faithful may be reminded of their own frailty and roused also to watchfulness and prayer, which are the true means of perseverance.

units.la: V. Exemplum Petri Apostoli gravi- ter lapsi adducit Harscherus de quo Luc. 22: 57. & seq.
units.tr: V. Harscher adduces as an example "the Apostle Peter, who fell grievously," from Luke 22:57 ff.

units.la: Graviter lapsum esse Petrum nemo inficiari potest: fidem in corde amisisse negatur. Nam recte Augustinus: defecit professio in ore, non fides in corde. Quî sic? Quia Christus Matth. 22: 32. dixit, ego rogavi pro te ne deficiat fides tua. Videatur Bellarminus lib. IV. de Pontifice Rom. cap. 3. qui ibidem ex Augustino, Chrysostomo, Theophylacto & aliis prolixè probat Petrum à fide non defecisse. VI. Locus ex epist. ad Rom. cap. 5. est {ξ}ἐξαγώγιος, quia agit de Adamo in statu integritatis constituto, de quo supra diximus.
units.tr: No one can deny that Peter fell grievously; that he lost faith in his heart is denied. For Augustine rightly says: "His profession failed in his mouth, not his faith in his heart." How so? Because Christ said (Matt. 22:32, as cited), "I have prayed for you that your faith fail not." Let Bellarmine be consulted, Book 4 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 3, where he proves at length from Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact and others that Peter did not fall away from faith. VI. The passage from Romans 5 is [exagogios], because it deals with Adam placed in a state of integrity, of whom we spoke above.

units.la: VII. Fideles erant Galatæ de quibus Paulus ad Galatas (cap. 5: 4.) evacuati estis à Christo, qui in lege justificamini, à gratia excidistis.
units.tr: VII. "The Galatians were believers, of whom Paul writes to the Galatians (5:4): 'You are severed from Christ, you who are justified by the law; you have fallen from grace.'"

units.la: In hac sententia apostolica phrases obseruandæ & modus loquendi. Καταργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ hypallage est, usitata Apostolo Paulo, pro ὁ Χριστὸς ὑμῖν καταργήσει Christus vobis inutilis factus est & inanis. Τὸ χάρειτος ἐξέπεσατε, per χάριν hic intelligitur gratia Christi in Evangelio oblata, per quam credentibus offertur remissio peccatorum per mortem & meritum eius, absque lege operum. Modus loquendi desumptus est ex communi hominum usu, cum aliquid dissuadere volunt. Exempli gratia, dissuasurus ne quis mari se committat aut in militiam proficiscatur, dicit, si abis, mortuus es, e vita discessisti. Sic Apostolus Paulus dissuadens circumcisionem Galatis dicit: si circumcidamini, Christus vobis inanis factus est, ex gratia excidistis, id est, gratia Evangelij ad vos non spectat. Uno verbo, repetit hic Apostolus, quod verf. secundo brevius dixit: Si circumcidamini, nihil prodest vobis Christus. Nihil ergò locus hic de gratia electionis, iustificationis & cum Christo unionis electorum, de qua controvertitur.
units.tr: In this apostolic sentence the phrases and the manner of speaking must be observed. [Katargēthēte apo tou Christou] is a hypallage, usual with the Apostle Paul, for [ho Christos hymin katargēsei], "Christ has become useless and empty to you." [To charitos exepesate]: by "grace" is here understood the grace of Christ offered in the Gospel, through which remission of sins is offered to believers by his death and merit, apart from the works of the law. The manner of speaking is taken from common human usage when people wish to dissuade someone. For example, one who wishes to dissuade a man from committing himself to the sea or setting off to war says, "If you go, you are dead; you have departed from life." So the Apostle Paul, dissuading the Galatians from circumcision, says: "If you are circumcised, Christ has become empty to you; you have fallen from grace," that is, "the grace of the Gospel does not concern you." In a word, the Apostle here repeats what he said more briefly in verse two: "If you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing." Therefore this passage says nothing about the grace of election, of justification, or of union with Christ of the elect, which is what is in dispute.

units.la: VIII. De fidelibus peccatoribus loquitur Apostolus ad Hebræos: sed impossibile eos, qui semel sunt illuminati, gustaverunt etiam donum cœleste, & participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti, gustaverunt nihilominus bonum Dei verbum, virtutemq; seculi venturi & prolapsi sunt, renovari iterum ad pœnitentiam.
units.tr: VIII. "The Apostle to the Hebrews speaks of faithful sinners: 'For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have nevertheless tasted the good Word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance.'"

units.la: Illustris est hic locus dignus qui accuratius explicetur. Sed primò de verbis Jesuitæ. Dicit de fidelibus peccatoribus loquitur Apostolus ad Hebræos. Quàm inepta phrasis & in scriptura nusquam usitata illa, de fidelibus peccatoribus. Nunquam enim hæc duo coniunguntur fideles peccatores, sed fidelis & dilectus in Domino 1. Cor. 4: 17. vocati electi & fideles Apoc. 17: 14. fideles & dilecti, 1. Tim. 6: 2. phrasis congruit sententiæ. Deinde verum est, alloquitur Apostolus Hebræos, nempe iuxta communem consuetudinem Apostolis usitatam, qui sine distinctione verba ad omnes dirigunt, ac si eiusdem essent conditionis, cùm tamen magna sit distinctio. In priori ad Corinthios & epistola ad Galatas omnes reprehendit communiter, cùm procul dubio multi inter ipsos reprehensione ista indigni fuerint. Idem dicendum de epistola ad Hebræos.
units.tr: This is a notable passage that deserves a more careful explanation. But first, concerning the Jesuit's words. He says, "The Apostle to the Hebrews speaks of faithful sinners." How inept is that phrase, "faithful sinners," which is nowhere used in Scripture! For these two words are never joined as "faithful sinners," but "faithful and beloved in the Lord" (1 Cor. 4:17), "called, chosen and faithful" (Rev. 17:14), "faithful and beloved" (1 Tim. 6:2). The phrase does not fit the sense. Next, it is true that the Apostle addresses the Hebrews, according to the common custom of the Apostles, who direct their words without distinction to all, as though they were of the same condition, although there is in fact a great distinction. In the earlier letter to the Corinthians and in the letter to the Galatians he rebukes all in common, although without doubt many among them were unworthy of that rebuke. The same must be said of the letter to the Hebrews.

units.la: Locum ipsum Apostoli quod concernit, explicatio eius ex antecedentibus est desumenda. Capite quinto v. 12. incepit Apostolus disputare de Hebræorum in fide Evangelica institutione, dicens, ipsos equidem de Christo Pontifice nostro satis instilutos fuisse, ita ut pro temporis ratione oportuerit ipsos esse Doctores: sed tamen propter segnitiem factos esse ἀπείρως λόγω δικαιοσύνης. Exprobrationi huic subiicit adhortationem verf. 1. capitis sexti, his verbis: Feramur ergo ad perfectionem non jacientes rursum fundamentum refipiscentiae ab operibus mortuis & fide in Deum, &c. Hortatio proponitur axiomate discreto, cuius pars consequens explicatur per membra, posteriori colo v. 1. & v. 2. integro. Dum ostendit, in quibus fundamentum religionis, quod supra rudem sermonem vocavit, & in quo illi instituti erant, consistat. Nempe in doctrina 1. refipiscentiae ab operibus mortuis, 2. fidei in Deum, 3. baptismi, 4. manuum impositionis, 5. resurrectionis mortuorum, & 6. iudicii aeterni.
units.tr: As for the Apostle's passage itself, its explanation must be drawn from what precedes. In chapter 5, verse 12, the Apostle began to discuss the instruction of the Hebrews in the Evangelical faith, saying that they had indeed been well instructed about Christ our High Priest, so that, given the time, they ought to have become teachers themselves; but because of sloth they had become [apeirōs logō dikaiosynēs], "unskilled in the word of righteousness." To this rebuke he adds an exhortation in verse 1 of chapter 6, in these words: "Let us therefore be carried on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, etc." The exhortation is set forth in a distinct axiom, whose consequent part is explained by its members, the latter clause in verse 1 and verses 2 entire, while he shows in what the foundation of religion consists, which above he called "the rudimentary word," and in which they had been instructed. Namely, in the doctrine of 1. repentance from dead works, 2. faith in God, 3. baptism, 4. the laying on of hands, 5. the resurrection of the dead, and 6. eternal judgment.

units.la: Hanc doctrinam semel suscepta m, dicit, non saltem non deserendam sed ab hac ad perfectionem tendendum esse v. 1.
units.tr: Having once received this doctrine, he says, they must not only not abandon it, but must press on from it to perfection (verse 1).

units.la: Id probat argumento ex hac ipsa doctrina desumpto, sed mutatis phrasibus. Versiculo enim 1, & 2. causas, versiculo vero 4. & 5. effecta tradit.
units.tr: He proves this by an argument drawn from this very doctrine, but with changed phrases. For in verses 1 and 2 he gives the causes, and in verses 4 and 5 the effects.

units.la: Dicit semel illuminati & intelligit semel baptizatos. Ita Syrus, qui semel ad baptismum descenderunt. Nam veteres baptismum φώτισμα appellabant, & baptizatos φωτιζομένους, ut est apud Clementem Alexandrinum. Unde Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus conciones suas ad baptizatos vocavit catecheses φωτιζομένων. Rationem huius nomenclaturæ reddit Iustinus Martyr Apol. pro Christia. Καλεῖται τοῦτο τὸ λούτρον φωτισμός, ὡς φωτιζομένων τ διάνοιαν τῆς ταυτα μαν-θανόντῶν, vocatur autem lavacrum hoc illuminatio, quod eorum qui hæc discunt mentes illuminentur. Huc etiam spectat doctrina de operibus mortuis, v. 1. ut & Rom. 6: 11. quia, qui baptizantur peccato moriuntur & vivunt Deo per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: He says "once enlightened" and means "once baptized." So the Syriac has "who once went down to baptism." For the ancients called baptism phōtisma [φώτισμα], and the baptized photizomenous [φωτιζομένους], as in Clement of Alexandria. Hence Cyril of Jerusalem called his sermons to the baptized the catecheses of the enlightened [φωτιζομένων]. Justin Martyr gives the reason for this name in his Apology for the Christians: "This washing is called illumination, since the minds of those who learn these things are enlightened" [Καλεῖται τοῦτο τὸ λούτρον φωτισμός, ὡς φωτιζομένων τὴν διάνοιαν τῶν ταῦτα μανθανόντων]. To this also pertains the doctrine of dead works, v. 1, as also Rom. 6:11, because those who are baptized die to sin and live to God through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Gustaverunt donum cœleste) id est, fidem in Deum, ut est verf. 1. vel fidem symboli apostolici, quod gustasse dicuntur, quia addidicerunt initia eloquiorum Dei, & lac verbi Dei gusta. runt per catechismi institutionem.
units.tr: "Have tasted the heavenly gift": that is, faith in God, as in v. 1, or the faith of the Apostles' Creed, which they are said to have tasted, because they learned the rudiments of God's oracles and tasted the milk of God's word through instruction in the catechism.

units.la: Participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti, nempe per impositionem manuum. Nam ut ex Cypriano addisci potest, obtinuit in ecclesia, iam a tempore Apostolorum ritus, quo baptizatis catechumenis, cum oratione & manuum impositione benedictio data, & preces habitae, ut infunderetur super ipsos Spiritus sanctus. Vide de hoc ritu Apostolis usitato, Act. 8: 17.
units.tr: "Were made partakers of the Holy Spirit," namely through the laying on of hands. For, as can be learned from Cyprian, a rite had prevailed in the Church already from the time of the Apostles: after the catechumens were baptized, a blessing was given with prayer and the laying on of hands, and prayers were offered that the Holy Spirit might be poured out upon them. On this rite, used by the Apostles, see Acts 8:17.

units.la: Cognoverant etiam virtutes futuriseculi per doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum & aeterno iudicio, v. 2.
units.tr: "Had also tasted the powers of the age to come," through the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment, v. 2.

units.la: Ex hisce Apostolus argumentatur in hunc modum: si qui post baptismalem regenerationem semel illuminati: si qui per impositionem manuum donorum Spiritus sancti participes: si qui per institutionem, Dei verbum & virtutes futuri seculi gustarunt, lapsi, ad resipisresipiscentiam non renovantur, necessum habetis ut ad perfectionem feramini. Prius verum est. Minor syllogismi est v. 4, 5. probata comparatis dissimilibus, v. 7, 8.
units.tr: From these things the Apostle argues in this way: if those who have once been enlightened after baptismal regeneration, if those who through the laying on of hands have become partakers of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, if those who through instruction have tasted God's word and the powers of the age to come have fallen away, they are not renewed to repentance; you must be carried on to perfection. The first premise is true. The minor premise of the syllogism is proved in vv. 4, 5 by comparing dissimilar things, vv. 7, 8.

units.la: Nullo vero modo sequitur, quod qui tales sunt, statim etiam sint fideles, electi & vera ac salvifica fide praediti, ut adversa pars concludit. Ratio, quia semen bonum etiam cadit super petrosam, ubi radicem habere non potest Matth. 13: 20.
units.tr: But it by no means follows that those who are such are at once also believers, elect, and endowed with true and saving faith, as the opposing party concludes. The reason is that the good seed also falls on stony ground, where it cannot take root, Matt. 13:20.

units.la: Credunt etiam & baptizantur quorum cor non est rectum in Dei conspectu, qualis fuit Simon Magus Act. 8: 13, 21. Imbrem etiam Evangelij imbibere potest terra reproba, ἀδόκιμος, Heb. 6: 8.
units.tr: Some also believe and are baptized whose heart is not right in the sight of God, such as Simon Magus, Acts 8:13, 21. "Even reprobate land, which drinks in the rain of the Gospel" [ἀδόκιμος], Heb. 6:8.

units.la: Habent enim hypocritae dona quaedam cum electis communia, sed ad veram regenerationem & fidem salvisicam non pertingentia, qualia sunt externa vitae correctio, pristinae impuritatis desertio, externa quoque ergá Evangelium obedientia, evanidum & non diu permanens gaudium, ex Evangelii luce ortum. A quibus, si prolabuntur, dicuntur redire ad vomitum, ut canes, & ad volutabrum cæni, ut sues lotæ, 2. Pet. 2: 22. Hi sunt servi illi ignavi & mali, qui talentum unum acceperunt, propter cuius abusum id ab ipsis tollitur, illi verò tanquam inutiles eiiciuntur in tenebras extimas, Matth. 25: 24, 28, 30. quia impossibile est, ut ad resipiscentiam renoventur, nam talentum ablatum est. Hinc Apostolus Petrus dicit, conditionem illorum ultimam priore esse deteriorem, 2. Pet. 2: 20. Peccant enim peccatum, pro quo non est orandum, 1. Joh. 5: 16. quia non remittitur hominibus, Matth. 12: 31. Ex hisce apparet quàm longè aberrent à scopo illi, qui hunc locum de verè electis & verè regeneratis ac fide salvifica præditis ditis intelligunt. In quos peccatum in Spiritum sanctum cadere non potest.
units.tr: For hypocrites have certain gifts in common with the elect, but these do not reach to true regeneration and saving faith. Such are outward correction of life, abandonment of former impurity, and also outward obedience to the Gospel, and a joy that is fleeting and does not last long, arising from the light of the Gospel. From these, if they fall away, they are said to return to their vomit, like dogs, and to the wallowing of mire, like washed pigs, 2 Pet. 2:22. These are the wicked and slothful servants who received one talent, and because of its abuse it is taken from them, while they are cast out as useless into outer darkness, Matt. 25:24, 28, 30. It is impossible for them to be renewed to repentance, because the talent has been taken away. Hence the Apostle Peter says that their last state is worse than the first, 2 Pet. 2:20. For they sin a sin for which one should not pray, 1 John 5:16, because it is not forgiven to men, Matt. 12:31. From this it is clear how far from the mark those are who understand this passage of those who are truly elect, truly regenerate, and endowed with saving faith, into whom the sin against the Holy Spirit cannot fall.

units.la: Ultimò exemplum Episcopi Ephesini subiicit his verbis: Episcopus Ephesinus retinens fidem, & primam charitatem relinquens monetur unde exciderit, jubetur agere pœnitentiam, alias candelabrum movendum e loco suo, Apoc. cap. 2.
units.tr: Finally, he adds the example of the Bishop of Ephesus in these words: "The Bishop of Ephesus, retaining faith but leaving his first love, is warned whence he has fallen, is bidden to do repentance, otherwise the candlestick is to be moved out of its place, Rev. ch. 2."

units.la: Disputat Jesuita fidem salvificam amitti posse, hoc ut demonstrare possit, producit exemplum illius qui fidem retinuit non amisit. Es sieht dem Pater Harscher sehr übel an ex scriptura zu argumentieren. Quid amiserit Lyranus docet in hunc locum: Charitatem amisisti, id est, opera charitatis, qua habuisti in principio tua conversionis. Consueverunt enim sustentare pauperes Christianos ferventer & devote, & eleemosynam mittere in Hierusalem habitantibus. Refrigeratus erat ab hoc fervore: ideo non dici-turtur, quòd reliquerit simpliciter charitatem, sed primam, id est, fervoris gradum prius habitum. Ergo nec fidem nec charitatem amisit. Quid ergo exemplum hoc ad rem?
units.tr: The Jesuit disputes that saving faith can be lost, and to demonstrate this he produces the example of one who retained faith and did not lose it. It looks very bad for Father Harscher to argue from Scripture in this way. What he lost, Lyra teaches on this passage: "You have lost charity, that is, the works of charity which you had at the beginning of your conversion. For they were accustomed to support poor Christians fervently and devoutly, and to send alms to those living in Jerusalem. He had cooled from this fervour; therefore it is not said that he left charity simply, but his first, that is, the earlier degree of fervour." Therefore he lost neither faith nor charity. What, then, is this example to the point?

units.la: ANTIDICOMARIANI.
units.tr: ANTIDICOMARIANI.

units.la: TEste Hosio & Lindano Beatam virginem Mariam non sustinent audire Dei genetricem; Christum fingentes ut unius personæ, sic unius naturæ: Virginitatem ejusdem Matris Virginis calumniantur & abnegant &c.
units.tr: On the testimony of Hosius and Lindanus, the Antidicomarians do not allow the Blessed Virgin Mary to be heard as the Mother of God; feigning Christ to be of one person and therefore of one nature, they calumniate and deny the virginity of the same Virgin Mother, etc.

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATION.

units.la: Sed cur ex Lindano & Hosio Antidicomarianitarum hæresin proponit? cur non ex Epiphanio, qui longam epistolam de hac hæresi conscripsit ad Arabes, eamque Panariis inseruit? Nempe quia ibi leguntur quæ parum pro papistis faciunt circa Beatæ Virginis adorationem. Admirati sumus, inquit, cum audivissemus, alios ita desipere, ut in tractatione de ipsa sancta semper virgine, pro Deo hanc introducere studuerint & adhuc studeant. Et Paulò post: Sive mortua est sancta virgo & sepulta, in honore ipsius dormitio, & in castitate mors, & in virginitate corona, sive sublata est velut scriptum est, animam ejus pertransibit gladius, inter martyres est ipsius gloria, & in laudibus sanctum ipsius corpus & non convenit colere sanctos ultra decorum, sed honorare ipsorum Dominum. Cessetitaq; error seductorum, non enim Deus est Maria. Item Hæresi seq. 79. Revera sanctum erat corpus Mariæ non tamen Deus. Revera virgo erat ipsa virgo & honorata, sed non ad adorationem data, sed ipsa adorans eum, qui ex ipsa, carne genitus est, de cœlis vero ex finibus paternis accessit. Et propterea Evangelium munit nos, dicens quòd ipse Dominus dixerit, quid mihi & tibi cura est mulier, nondum venit hora mea: quo quò non putarent aliqui magis eximiam esse sanctam virginem, mulierem eam appellavit, velut prophetans qua futura essent in terra, sectarum & haereseon gratia, ut ne aliqui nimium admirati sanctam in hanc haeresin, ejusque deliramenta dilabantur. Qua Scriptura de hoc narravit? Quis Prophetarum praecepit hominem adorare, nedum mulierem? Haec & similia Epiphanii dicta quamvis antiqui Patris, parùm apta videbantur pro sententia Pontificia afferenda idcircò commodum magis erat ex propriis authoribus quamvis suspectis rem proponere.
units.tr: But why does he take the heresy of the Antidicomarianites from Lindanus and Hosius? Why not from Epiphanius, who wrote a long letter on this heresy to the Arabians and inserted it into his Panarion? Clearly because there are things in it that do little to help the Papists regarding the adoration of the Blessed Virgin. We were amazed, he says, when we heard that some are so foolish that, in treating of the holy ever-virgin herself, they have sought, and still seek, to introduce her as God. And a little later: Whether the holy virgin died and was buried, so that her falling asleep is for her honour, her death in chastity and her crown in virginity, or whether she was taken up, as it is written, "a sword shall pass through her soul," her glory is among the martyrs, and her holy body is to be praised in hymns. Yet it is not fitting to worship the saints beyond what is seemly, but to honour their Lord. Let then the error of the deceived cease, for Mary is not God. Likewise in heresy 79 that follows: Truly the body of Mary was holy, yet not God. Truly the virgin was a virgin and honoured, but she was not given for adoration; rather she herself adores him who was born of her flesh and came down from the heavens, from the paternal borders. And therefore the Gospel warns us, saying that the Lord himself said, "What is it to me and to you, woman? My hour is not yet come," so that some might not think the holy virgin more eminent, he called her woman, as prophesying what would be on earth for the sake of sects and heresies, so that some, too much amazed at the holy one, might not slide into this heresy and its ravings. What Scripture has told of this? Which of the prophets commanded a man to be adored, let alone a woman? These and similar sayings of Epiphanius, though of an ancient Father, seemed little suited to bring forward in support of the Papist opinion; it was therefore more convenient to set out the matter from their own authors, though they are suspect.

units.la: Quod verò rem ipsam concernit, dicit; Antidicomarianos non sustinere Beatam virginem Mariam Dei genetricem. Sed an nos similiter? Falsissimum esse dico, si afferat Harscherus. Quomodo enim non esset Dei-genetrix de qua Angelus dixerat, paries filium & vocabis nomen ejus Iesum, hic erit Magnus & filius Altissimi vocabitur, Luc. 1: 31, 32. Et quæ genuit Deum qui proprio sanguine ecclesiam acquisivit, Act. 20:28. Quocirca Cyrilli anathematismum adprobamus in synodo Ephesina tertia, cui ille præsedit, propositum: si quis non confitetur Immanuelem verum Deum esse, ἡ διὰ τῆτο Θεοτόκον τ ἁγίαν παρθένον, genuit enim illa incarnatum Dei verbum, anathema sit.
units.tr: As for the matter itself, he says that the Antidicomarianites do not allow the Blessed Virgin Mary to be the Mother of God. But do we do likewise? I say it is most false, if Harscherus asserts it. For how would she not be the Mother of God, of whom the angel had said, "You will bear a son and call his name Jesus; he will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High" (Luke 1:31, 32)? And she who bore him "who obtained the Church with his own blood" (Acts 20:28)? Therefore we approve the anathematism of Cyril, proposed in the third Synod of Ephesus over which he presided: "If anyone does not confess Immanuel to be true God, and on that account the holy Virgin to be Theotokos [διὰ τοῦτο Θεοτόκον τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον], for she bore the incarnate Word of God, let him be anathema."

units.la: Alterum, quod dicit Antidicomarianitas Christum finxisse, ut unius persona, sic unius natura, quæ hæresis Eutychetis fuit, itidem à nobis alienum. Confitemur enim Filium Dei, secundam Deitatis personam verè assumsisse naturam humanam in unitatem personæ, ita ut sit in una persona Θεάνθρωπος.
units.tr: The other point, that he says the Antidicomarianites feigned Christ as one person, so one nature, which was the heresy of Eutyches, is likewise alien to us. For we confess that the Son of God, the second Person of the Deity, truly assumed human nature into the unity of his person, so that in one person there is the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος].

units.la: Tertium; Nos virginitatem MatrisVirginis calumniari & abnegare, tantum à nobis abest, ut existimemus virginitatem Beatæ virginis negantes simul negare praecipuum symboli apostolici & verae religionis articulum, & omnes Matrem Domini calumniantes gravissimâ poenâ afficiendos esse. Ut autem sciant Jesuitae quae nostra sit circa Beatissimam semper-virginem Mariam sententia, breviter dico, nos asserere; de illa non nisi sanctè cogitandum & loquendum honorificè, cum agnitione beatitudinis ejus & eximiae eminentiae: interim à nemine religiosè adorandam aut invocandam esse.
units.tr: Third: that we calumniate and deny the virginity of the Virgin Mother. So far is this from us that we think those who deny the virginity of the Blessed Virgin at the same time deny a chief article of the Apostles' Creed and of the true religion, and that all who calumniate the Mother of the Lord are to be punished with the gravest penalty. So that the Jesuits may know what our opinion is about the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, I say briefly that we assert: of her we must think and speak only holily and honourably, with acknowledgement of her blessedness and her exceptional eminence; meanwhile she is to be adored or invoked religiously by no one.

units.la: Duo tamen videtur Harscherus nobis obiicere, unde putat nostros Beatâ Virginem calumniari & virginitatem eius negare. Unum quod scribant illam ab omni peccato non fuisse immunem, alterum, quod Christus ex eadem natus sit utero aperto.
units.tr: Yet Harscherus seems to object two things to us, from which he thinks ours calumniate the Blessed Virgin and deny her virginity. One is that they write she was not free from every sin; the other is that Christ was born from the same womb, opened.

units.la: De hisce duobus agit in sequenti parallelo.
units.tr: He deals with these two in the following parallel.

units.la: PARALLELUM.
units.tr: PARALLEL.

units.la: Calvinus in Antidoto Concilij Tridentini scribit: De speciali Virginis Mariæ privilegio cùm cœleste diploma protulerint credemus quod jactant, ubi etiam S. Augustinum (licèt expressis verbis protestantem, & mentem suam verbis explicantem in l. de natura & gratia contra Pelagianos his verbis: Cum de peccatis agitur de S. V. Maria propter honorem Domini nullam prorsus habere volo quæstionem) suæ blasphemiæ facit authorem. Ecclesiæ certè, inquit, membrum erat Augustinus, qui tametsi amoliendæ invidiæ caussa, vult alicubi de B. Virgine silere, passim tamen sine ejus exceptione totum Adæ genus peccato involuit. Et in cap. 1. Luc. non magnopere, ait, laborandum est, ut Mariam purgemus ab omni vitio.
units.tr: Calvin, in his Antidote to the Council of Trent, writes: "Concerning the special privilege of the Virgin Mary, we shall believe what they boast of when they have produced the heavenly charter. There too he makes Saint Augustine the author of their blasphemy, although Augustine, in his book On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians, expressly protests and explains his mind in these words: 'When the question is about sins, I wish to have no question at all concerning the holy Virgin Mary, for the honour of the Lord.' Augustine was certainly a member of the Church, and although for the sake of removing odium he wishes to be silent about the Blessed Virgin in one place, nevertheless he everywhere involves the whole race of Adam in sin without any exception for her. And in chapter 1 of Luke: 'We need not labour greatly to cleanse Mary from every fault.'"

units.la: Calvinum inter hæreticos recenset, quod de peccato originali disputans contra Patres Concilii Tridentini, B. Virginem eo non eximit. Verùm si propterea Calvinus est hæreticus, hæretici quoquè erunt omnes veteres patres, præcipui ex Doctoribus Pontificiis, & Dominicani omnes. Ita enim Melchior Canus Loc. Theol. lib. 7. c. 5. Quod ex loco ad Romanos cap. 5. sancti omnes uno ore asseverarint Beatam Virginem in peccato Originali conceptam fuisse, Chrysostomus, Eusebius, Remigius, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Bernhardus, Beda, Anselmus, Erardus Martyr, sanctus Antonius, Bonaventura, Aquinas, Vincentius, Hugo de sancto Victore, & quod nullus autor contra venerit. Johannes de Turre cremata scribit se centum autores pro hac sententia collegisse, quod incredibile non est, quia ante Scotum, circa annum 1150, nemo aliter sensit.
units.tr: They count Calvin among the heretics because, in disputing about original sin against the Fathers of the Council of Trent, he does not exempt the Blessed Virgin from it. But if Calvin is therefore a heretic, then all the ancient Fathers will be heretics too, along with the chief Papist teachers and all the Dominicans. For Melchior Canus says this in Loci Theologici, book 7, chapter 5: "That all the saints with one voice have asserted, from the passage in Romans 5, that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in original sin, namely Chrysostom, Eusebius, Remigius, Ambrose, Augustine, Bernard, Bede, Anselm, Erardus Martyr, Saint Antonine, Bonaventure, Aquinas, Vincent, Hugh of Saint Victor, and that no author has spoken against it." John de Turrecremata writes that he had collected a hundred authors for this opinion, which is not incredible, since before Scotus, about the year 1150, no one thought otherwise.
