units.la: Cur ergo non observant Jesuitæ, regulam Salmeronis socii, cùm scribit: Dogma illud fidem in ecclesia catholica facere, quod à Doctoribus universali consensu vel fere ab omnibus magna constantia est traditum. Sed hic non placet. Atqui debuissent Thomæ Aquinatis doctrinam admittere, quandoquidem ille omnia sua scripta B. Virginis imagini obtulit, & quæsivit an rectè de ea scripserit, & imago Virginis respondit, rectè de me scripsisti Thoma. Sed hic iterum non placet.
units.tr: Why, then, do the Jesuits not observe the rule of Salmeron, their fellow member, when he writes: "That dogma makes a matter of faith in the Catholic Church which has been handed down by the teachers with universal consent, or almost by all with great constancy." But this rule does not suit them. Yet they ought to admit the teaching of Thomas Aquinas, since he offered all his writings to an image of the Virgin and asked whether he had written rightly about her, and the image of the Virgin replied: "You have written rightly about me, Thomas." But here again the rule does not suit them.

units.la: Calvinum interea accusat Harscherus quod Augustinum suæ blasphemiæ faciat autorem. Non est blasphemia, quod scriptura asserit. Nam si stipendium peccati mors est, ut Apostolus docet, Rom. 6: 23. Et Catholica ecclesia Romana nullam de obitu Dei genetricis dubitationem admittit, sed quam novit humanæ naturæ fuisse consortem, humanam pariter moriendi necessitatem expertem affirmat, ut Cardinalis Baronius docet ad A. C. 48. quid ambigunt amplius Jesuitæ? Deinde, quod Augustinum attinet,
units.tr: Meanwhile Harscher accuses Calvin of making Augustine the author of his blasphemy. It is no blasphemy to assert what Scripture asserts. For if the wages of sin is death, as the Apostle teaches (Rom. 6:23), and "the Roman Catholic Church admits no doubt about the death of the Mother of God, but affirms that she, who is known to have shared in human nature, was likewise free from the necessity of dying as human beings are," as Cardinal Baronius teaches at the year of Christ 48, why do the Jesuits still hesitate? Next, as for Augustine,

units.la: R tinet, quem Calvinus recte citavit, ita lib. de perf. Justit. disertis verbis: Legitur sane homo sine crimine, legitur sine querela, at non legitur sine peccato, nisi filius hominis UNUS, itemq; Dei Filius unicus. Et ferè sub finem in eodem libro: Quisquis ergo fuisse vel esse in hac vita aliquem hominem vel aliquos homines putat, excepto uno mediatore Dei & hominum, quibus necessaria non sit remissio peccatorum contrarium est divinæ scripturæ. Certè Maria in cantico Luc. 1: 47. exultavit super Deo servatore suo. Atqui dicat Harscherus; hoc est, Filium Dei ignominiâ afficere. Respondeo, non est. Audi, quid dicat Bernhardus epist. 174. Dico Mariam Virginem peperisse, non partam esse à Virgine. Solus Iesus de Spiritu sancto conceptus, quia solus ante conceptum sanctus: hac prærogativa prolis Dom. est, hanc B. Mariæ tribuere non est honorare Virginem, sed honori detrahere, de alijs omnibus verum est, quod cecinit propheta Psal. 51. in iniquitatibus concepit me mater mea.
units.tr: he is rightly cited by Calvin, who says in plain words in his book On the Perfection of Justice: "Indeed we read of a man without crime, we read of one without complaint, but we do not read of one without sin, except the one Son of Man, and likewise the only Son of God." And almost at the end of the same book: "Whoever therefore thinks that any man or men have been, or are, in this life, apart from the one Mediator between God and men, for whom forgiveness of sins is not necessary, is contrary to divine Scripture." Certainly Mary in the Canticle of Luke 1:47 "rejoiced in God her Saviour." But let Harscher say: "This means putting a stigma on the Son of God." I answer: it does not. Hear what Bernard says in letter 174: "I say that the Virgin Mary bore a child, not that she was herself born of a virgin. Jesus alone was conceived of the Holy Spirit, because alone holy before conception; this prerogative belongs to the Lord's offspring. To attribute this to the Blessed Mary is not to honour the Virgin but to detract from her honour. Of all others it is true what the prophet sang in Psalm 51: 'In iniquities did my mother conceive me.'"

units.la: Reliqua verba à Jesuita adiecta (quasi Augustin9 lib.de Natura & Grat. contra Pelagianos contrarium sentiret, quando scribit; cum de peccatis agitur de sancta Virgine Maria, de qua propter honorem Domini nullam prorsus habere volo quæstionem) nihil impediunt quò minus Calvini sententiæ sua constet veritas. Ratio, quia Dominicus à Soto, quem Gregorius de Valentia autorem imprimis gravem appellat, non male observavit 1. Augustinum in illo loco non agere de peccato originali, quod verum est, & ex antecedentibus facile evincitur. 2. Nihil quicquam affirmasse vel negasse, sed propter honorem Domini, noluisse de ea quæstionem moveri. In quo prudenter & piè fecit Augustinus. Et nos de ea nihil quicquam moveremus propter eundē Domini honorem nisi nos importunè cogerent adversariorum disputationes.
units.tr: The remaining words added by the Jesuit (as if Augustine, in his book On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians, held the contrary opinion, when he writes: "When the question is about sins, concerning the holy Virgin Mary, for the honour of the Lord, I wish to have no question at all") do not prevent the truth of Calvin's opinion from standing. The reason is that Dominic Soto, whom Gregory of Valencia calls an especially weighty author, observed well: (1) that Augustine in that passage is not treating of original sin, which is true and is easily proved from what precedes it; (2) that he affirmed or denied nothing, but for the honour of the Lord he was unwilling that a question should be raised about her. In this Augustine acted prudently and piously. And we too would raise no question about her for the same honour of the Lord, unless the disputations of our adversaries compelled us importunately.

units.la: Alterum de virginitatis Mariæ negatione obiectat Bezæ, quod L. de omnipræsentia Christi, neget Christum per non apertum B. Virginis uterum penetrasse, sed aperto & corrupto utero natum, adeoque in partu virginem non mansisse, affirmet. Christum aperto utero Mariæ natum esse fatemur omnes, quod in partu virgo non manserit, nec Beza, nec nos unquam diximus, nec dicemus, si sani, si orthodoxi sumus. Quicquid Bellarminus, Maldonatus & alii clamitent.
units.tr: Another objection concerns the denial of Mary's virginity: Beza, in his book on the omnipresence of Christ, is charged with denying that "Christ passed through the Blessed Virgin's womb unopened, but was born with the womb opened and corrupted, and so affirms that the Virgin did not remain a virgin in childbirth." We all confess that Christ was born with the womb of Mary opened; but that the Virgin did not remain a virgin in birth, neither Beza nor we have ever said, nor shall we say, if we are sound and orthodox. Whatever Bellarmine, Maldonado and others may cry out.

units.la: Sed videndum Jesuitarum argumentum. Sic illi: Quæcunque gignit utero aperto, ea in partu Virgo non manet. Atqui B. Maria secundum Calvinianos Christum genuit utero aperto. Ergo in partu Virgo non mansit. Nos universalitate maioris negamus, non enim omnis fœmina, quæ utero aperto gignit virginitatem amittit, sed ea demum cuius uterus aperitur per virum. Bellarminus & Toletus Jesuitæ, etiam in casu pudendo virginitatem amitti negant, cum nimirum fœmina non consentit. Sed hæc sententia exsibilanda. Nunc minorem negamus, quod B. Mariæ uterus per virum fuerit apertus. Nam virum non cognovit Luc. 1: 34. Virgo igitur permansit. Ita Veteres quoq; docente Jansenio Episcopo Gandavensi, Harmon: Evang. cap. 10. ad verba Evangelistæ, Luc.2: 22.23. & cum impleti fuissent dies purgationis Mariæ secundùm legem Mosis adduxerunt eum Hierosolymam, ut sisterent eum Domino, prout scriptum est in lege Domini omnis masculus adaperiens vulvam, &c. Alii hanc legem proprie ad Christum pertinuisse asserunt, eò quòd ipse solus aperuit vulvam matris suæ, cum aliis aperiat vir uterum, quæ est sententia Theophylacti super hoc loco. Similiter & Ambrosii sic scribentis: non enim virilis coitus vulvæ virginalis secreta reseravit, sed immaculatum semen inviolabili utero Spiritus sanctus infudit. Hic ergo solus sibi aperuit vulvam. Nec mirum, qui enim dixerat ad Prophetam: priusquam te formarem in utero novite, & in vulva matris sanĉlisanctificavi te: qui ergo vulvam sanctificaverat alienam, ut nasceretur Propheta, est qui aperuit matris suae vulvam, ut immaculatus exiret. Similia habet Origines Hom. 14. super Lucam: sacratum, inquit, quippiam sonat. Quemadmodum enim de utero effusum marem dixeris, non sic aperit matris suae vulvam, ut Dominus Iesus, quia omnium mulierum non partus infantis, sed coitus viri vulvam reserat.
units.tr: But let us examine the Jesuits' argument. They argue thus: whatever woman bears a child with an opened womb does not remain a virgin in childbirth. But according to the Calvinists the Blessed Mary bore Christ with an opened womb. Therefore she did not remain a virgin in childbirth. We deny the universality of the major premise: not every woman who bears with an opened womb loses her virginity, but only the one whose womb is opened by a man. Bellarmine and the Jesuit Toledo deny that virginity is lost even in a shameful case, when, of course, the woman does not consent; but that opinion is to be hissed off. Now we deny the minor premise, that the womb of the Blessed Mary was opened by a man. For he did not know a man (Luke 1:34). The Virgin therefore remained a virgin. So too the ancients, as Jansen, Bishop of Ghent, teaches in his Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 10, on the words of the Evangelist, Luke 2:22-23: "When the days of Mary's purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord, every male that opens the womb, etc." Others assert that this law pertained properly to Christ, because he alone opened the womb of his own mother, whereas a man opens the womb of others; this is the opinion of Theophylact on this passage. Similarly also Ambrose, who writes thus: "For the marital union did not unseal the secrets of the virginal womb, but the Holy Spirit poured an unstained seed into the inviolable womb." So he alone opened his own womb. Nor is this strange: for he who had said to the Prophet, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you," he who had sanctified another's womb so that the Prophet might be born, is the one who opened his mother's womb so that he might come forth unstained. Origen has similar words in Homily 14 on Luke: "'Holy' is the sense of the word," he says. "For just as you would say that a male was poured out of the womb, so the Lord Jesus did not open his mother's womb as all women's wombs are opened, not by the birth of an infant, but by the intercourse of a man."

units.la: Subiicit postea Janfenius suam opinionem, nimirum ut non negemus Christum aperuisse uterum matris suae, nam omnino videri Lucam sic legem adduxisse, quasi etiam ad Christum pertinentem, & tamen etiam asseramus clauso utero Virginis natum esse, quia scilicet sic per naturalis generationis membra natus est, ut virginalis pudicitia claustra nascendo non convelleret, nec dolorem parturienti adferret, quem necesse est esse in hujusmodi uteri apertione, quali nascuntur reliqui.
units.tr: Janssen afterwards adds his own opinion: "Namely, that we do not deny that Christ opened his mother's womb, for Luke clearly seems to have cited the law as pertaining also to Christ; and yet we also assert that he was born with the Virgin's womb closed, because he was so born through the members of natural generation that in being born he did not break the bars of virginal chastity, nor bring to the mother the pain which is necessary in such an opening of the womb as that by which the rest are born."

units.la: Hoc postea explicat similitudine, quòd
units.tr: He afterwards explains this by a comparison, namely that

units.la: quòd Christus per uterum clausum dicatur exivisse: quemadmodum per portam Orientalem semper clausam, solus Pontifex ingredi & egredi dicitur: Id est, ante natum Christum clausum, in nativitate apertum, & postea iterum clausum. Quæ Episcopi Gandavensis sententia, non video cur ampleƈtenda non sit, si prout verba sonant intelligatur.
units.tr: Christ is said to have come forth through a closed womb, just as through the Eastern Gate, which was always shut, only the High Priest is said to enter and leave. That is, before Christ's birth the womb was closed, at his birth it was opened, and afterwards it was closed again. I do not see why the opinion of the Bishop of Ghent should not be embraced, if it is understood as the words sound.

units.la: Ecclesiæ enim nostræ communiter credunt Mariam ante partum, in partu & post partum virginem mansisse. Et Beza quem accusat Jesuita: Itaque Jesus Christus, verus Deus & verus homo natus est, ex ea ipsa virgine, virgine, inquam, & ante, & post partum, Confess.art.23. Nam cur non ille unigenitus a Patre ab æterno, & primogenitus inter multos fratres adoptivos, non esset quoque unigenitus a Matre? cur non pietas Josephi ipsi dictasset, abstinendum esse homini peccatori a templo Spiritus sancti?
units.tr: For our churches commonly believe that Mary remained a virgin before, in and after the birth. And Beza, whom the Jesuit accuses, says: Thus Jesus Christ, true God and true man, was born of that same virgin, a virgin, I say, both before and after the birth, Confession, art. 23. For why should that only-begotten Son, from the Father from eternity, and firstborn among many adoptive brothers, not also be the only-begotten of his Mother? Why would the piety of Joseph not have dictated to him that a sinful man should abstain from the temple of the Holy Spirit?

units.la: Atque unica hæc confessio nostra nos absolvere potest ab Helvidij & Antidicomarianitarum errore, de quibus Augustinus cap. 84. de hæres. quòd Mariæ virginitati usq; adeo contradixerint, ut assirmarint eam post Christum natum viro suo fuisse commixtam, quod nos non dicimus. Credimus ergo corde, & ore confitemur, Beatam virginem sine corruptione virginitatis ut virginem concepisse, ut virginem peperisse, ut virginem in utero gestasse, ut virginem lactasse, quæ omnia uteri apertio nihil impedit, quæ vel virginibus naturaliter accidere potest, manente virginitate, si Fernelio, reliquisque Medicis fides habenda. Cætera verò quæ superstitio peperit & simplicitas retinuit, de cantu Angelorum in nativitate Mariæ, educatione eius in templo inter virgines per Zachariam, de translatione ædium Mariæ per Angelos Loretum usque, ut destituta omni fundamento historiæ & scripturæ sacræ merito reiicimus. Maximè ximè verò eiusdem B. Virginis Θεοτόκου, imperium ei tributum super filium, quod ne quidem in statu exinanitionis admittere voluit Christus, Ioh. 2:4. redemptionis generis humani gloriam, imperium in cœlo, & titulos soli Deitati competentes, quæ omnia Pontificii B. Virgini attribuunt. Ac si Deus abdicasset omne imperium & abiecto sceptro supremæ maiestatis, ancillæ (Luc. 1:38.) potestatem tradidisset universi.
units.tr: This one confession of ours can absolve us from the error of Helvidius and the Antidicomarianites, concerning whom Augustine says in chapter 84 of On Heresies, that they so contradicted the virginity of Mary as to affirm that after the birth of Christ she was joined with her husband, which we do not say. We therefore believe in our heart and confess with our mouth that the Blessed Virgin conceived as a virgin without corruption of her virginity, bore as a virgin, carried the child in her womb as a virgin, and nursed as a virgin. The opening of the womb hinders none of this, and such a thing can happen naturally even to virgins while their virginity remains, if we trust Fernel and the other physicians. But the rest, which superstition has produced and simplicity has retained, we rightly reject as destitute of all foundation in history and Holy Scripture: the song of the angels at Mary's birth, her upbringing in the temple among virgins under Zechariah, and the transport of Mary's house by angels as far as Loreto. Above all, the title Theotokos of the same Blessed Virgin; the dominion granted to her over her Son, which Christ himself would not admit even in the state of his humiliation (John 2:4); the glory of the redemption of the human race; dominion in heaven; and titles belonging to Deity alone. All of these the Papists attribute to the Blessed Virgin, as if God had abdicated all dominion, cast aside the sceptre of supreme majesty, and handed over the power of the whole universe to a handmaid (Luke 1:38).

units.la: Unicum illud testimonium ex Luc. cap. 1. citatum, quando Evangelista scribit: Ingressus igitur Angelus ad eam, dixit: Ave gratis dilecta, seu (ut vulgatus habet) gratia plena, Dominus tecum. Item: ne metuas Maria, invenisti enim gratiam apud eum, ecce concipies in utero & paries filium, & vocabis nomen ejus Iesum, hic erit magnus & filius altissimi vocabitur, & quæ sequuntur, non magnopere iuvat Pontificios.
units.tr: As for that single testimony cited from Luke chapter 1, where the Evangelist writes: The angel, entering to her, said: Hail, highly favoured, or (as the Vulgate has it) full of grace, the Lord is with you. Likewise: Fear not, Mary, for you have found grace with him; behold, you shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; he shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High, and what follows, this does not greatly help the Papists.

units.la: Duo urgent in præsenti loco Pontificii pro afferenda Beatæ Virginis intemerata conceptione 1. quòd ab Angelo gratiâ plena. 2. â cognata Elisabetha benedicta inter mulieres dicitur.
units.tr: In the present passage the Papists press two arguments in favour of the immaculate conception of the Blessed Virgin: first, that she is called full of grace by the angel; second, that she is called blessed among women by her kinswoman Elizabeth.

units.la: Primum argumentum quod concernit parum roboris habet, sive textum Græcum sive Latinum consideremus. Græcus habet: χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη. Theophylactus ex Patribus græcis illud κεχαριτωμένη per subsequentia explicat & dicit κεχαριτωμένος esse, invenire gratiam apud Deum & ἀφίσωεν Θεῷ. Quod merito Angelus supremi decreti præco de Maria dicere potuit, utpote quæ inter omnes mulieres sola istam gratiam nacta, ut vocari possit mater Filii Dei.
units.tr: The first argument, whether we consider the Greek or the Latin text, has little force. The Greek reads: "Hail, you who have been graced" [χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη]. Theophylact, following the Greek Fathers, explains κεχαριτωμένη by what follows, and says that it means to have found grace with God. The angel, herald of the supreme decree, could rightly say this of Mary, since she alone among all women obtained that grace, to be called the mother of the Son of God.

units.la: Janfenius quoque Gandavensis Episcopus considerans vim participii græci κεχαριτωμένη sic locum explicat: Graecè est κεχαριτωμένη participium passivum, à verbo χαρίζω, quod est gratifico vel gratum facio, proinde ad verbum sonat gratificata, hoc est, quam Deus singulari & gratuito favore suo sibi gratam fecit & gratam habet. Pro gratificata tamen melius est, fi dicatur & vertatur gratiosa. Gratiosi enim dicuntur latinis, quibus favetur singulari aliquo animi studio. Hæc ex Erasmo habet Gandavensis.
units.tr: Jansenius, the Bishop of Ghent, also considers the force of the Greek participle κεχαριτωμένη and explains the passage thus: "In Greek, κεχαριτωμένη is a passive participle from the verb χαρίζω, which means to show favour or to make pleasing. Literally, then, it means 'made gracious', that is, one whom God, by his singular and gratuitous favour, has made pleasing to himself and holds in favour. Yet for gratificata it is better to say and translate gratiosa. For in Latin those are called gratiosi who are favoured by some singular affection of mind." The Ghent man has this from Erasmus.

units.la: Quod fi eidem Janfenio & Bedæ credimus, Johannes Zachariæ filius eodem nomine appellatus quo B. virgo nempe gratiosus. Est enim Johannes origine hebræum nomen, יוחנן vel יהוחנן compositum ex יהו & חן gratia quod est à radice חנן gratiosus fuit, quia parentibus à Deo gratis datus, & gratiâ plenus fuit, Israelitis quoque salutem & gratiam per Christum annuntiavit. Sic Maria κεχαριτωμένη, quia ex misericordia Dei electa fuit, ut esset Mater Domini. Nam supplendum ὁ ἄγγελος. Eodem loquendi modo Epiphanius Mosen vocat σωσέσει ἐν θεῷ κεχαριτωμένον.
units.tr: If we believe the same Jansenius and Bede, John, the son of Zechariah, was called by the same name as the Blessed Virgin, namely gratiosus. For John is a Hebrew name in origin, יוחנן or יהוחנן, compounded of יהו and חן (grace), from the root חנן. He was gratiosus because he was given freely by God to his parents, and was full of grace, and he also announced salvation and grace through Christ to the Israelites. So Mary is κεχαριτωμένη, because she was chosen by the mercy of God to be the Mother of the Lord. The word ὁ ἄγγελος must be supplied. In the same manner of speaking, Epiphanius calls Moses [σωσέσει ἐν θεῷ κεχαριτωμένον].

units.la: Atqui (obiiciunt Adversarii) vulgata versio habet gratia plena, quomodo etiam Syrus vertit, & Tremellius iuxta Syri versionem. Sic legunt Patres, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus. Respondeo. Si Pontificii phrasin intelligerent iuxta scripturam, & Patrum explicationem, nullam de hac re litem ipsis moveremus. De Stephano protomartyre dicit scriptura, quod fuerit plenus Spiritu sancto, Act. 7: 55. quod Vasquesio idem est, quod plenus gratiâ. Philippenses dicuntur pleni fructibus iustitiæ, Phil. 1: 11. hæc enim dicuntur de iis, qui maiore mensurâ præ cæteris hominibus dona Spiritus sancti acceperunt. In quo sensu hominibus attribui posse aliquando plenitudinem gratiæ non negamus. Quamvis Patres ad hanc gratiæ rationem non respexerint, sed potiùs ad Christum plenum gratiæ & veritatis, Joh. 1: 14. Unde Ambrosius in Luc. cap. 2. Maria gratiâ plena dicta, quia repleta fuit autore gratia. Et Hieronymus in expos. Psal. 44. Sancta Maria Maria plena gratiâ salutatur, quia concepe-rat eum, in quo omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitat corporaliter.
units.tr: But (the Adversaries object) the Vulgate version has gratia plena, as the Syriac also translates it, and Tremellius follows the Syriac version. So the Fathers read it: Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine. I reply: if the Papists understood the phrase according to Scripture and the explanation of the Fathers, we would not raise any dispute with them on this matter. Scripture says of Stephen the protomartyr that he was full of the Holy Spirit, Acts 7:55, which to Vasquez is the same as full of grace. The Philippians are said to be filled with the fruits of righteousness, Phil. 1:11. For these things are said of those who have received the gifts of the Holy Spirit in a greater measure than other men. In this sense we do not deny that fullness of grace can sometimes be attributed to men. Although the Fathers did not look to this sense of grace, but rather to Christ, full of grace and truth, John 1:14. Whence Ambrose on Luke chapter 2: Mary was called full of grace because she was filled by the author of grace. And Jerome, in his exposition of Psalm 44: Holy Mary is greeted as full of grace, because she had conceived him in whom all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.

units.la: Alterum, quod dicitur Benedicta inter mulieres, non est magni ponderis pro afferenda immunitate à peccato, quia Elisabetha non aliam ob causlam cognatam Mariam benedictam inter mulieres appellat, quàm ob singulare hoc beneficium, quod inter omnes mulieres sola esset mater Domini. Quomodo ob insignia & peculiaria dona, Jahel benedicta inter mulieres quoque dicitur, Judi. 5: 24.
units.tr: The second argument, that she is called blessed among women, is of no great weight for proving immunity from sin. Elizabeth calls her kinswoman Mary blessed among women for no other reason than this singular benefit, that she alone among all women was the mother of the Lord. In the same way, Jael is also called blessed among women, Judg. 5:24, on account of her outstanding and peculiar deeds.

units.la: Jesuita contentus unico hoc testimonio, accedit ad testimonia humana, ac primùm adducit Concilium Ephesinum his verbis: Concilium Ephesinum ex primis quatuor, congregatum est ad tuendam Matris Dei dignitatem contra Nestorium. In quo tam multa dicta sunt de laudibus Virginis, ut vix aliquid addi posse videatur. At primò Concilium Ephesi-
units.tr: The Jesuit, content with this single testimony, turns to human testimonies, and first adduces the Council of Ephesus in these words: The Council of Ephesus, the first of the four, was gathered to defend the dignity of the Mother of God against Nestorius. In it so many things were said in praise of the Virgin that hardly anything seems able to be added. But first, the Council of Ephesus

units.la: fuerit non fuit congregatum ad tuendam matris Dei dignitatem, sed conNestorii hærefin, qui ἕνωσιν φυσικὴν κατ' ὑσίαν in Christo, uti patres loquantur, negabat, & unitionem duarum personarum talem in Christo aliquam esse, quam ille fraudulenter vocabat ἕνωσιν κατ' ὑπόστασιν, alio sensu, quàm orthodoxi patres. Voluit nempe verbum in assumpto homine habitasse seclusum gratiam, affectum & societatem, & consequenter non rectè dici Dei esse natum, nec Mariam Θεοτόκον. Uno verbo statuit duas personas in Christo. Deinde non viquæ laudes B. Virgini in Concilio -sino tributæ, ut vix aliquid addi videatur. In anathematismo Cyrilli vocatur Θεοτόκος & ἁγία παρplures ei non tribuuntur. Non -n nego posteriori tempore, quamperstitio crevit, plures titulos eitos fuisse, ut tandem Deo Patri adæquata, Filio longè prælata.
units.tr: was not gathered to defend the dignity of the Mother of God, but against the heresy of Nestorius, who denied the natural union in Christ according to substance, as the Fathers speak, and held that there was no union of two persons in Christ of the kind which he fraudulently called union according to hypostasis, in a sense other than that of the orthodox Fathers. For he wished the Word to have dwelt in the assumed man only by grace, affection and fellowship, and consequently that it was not rightly said that God was born, nor that Mary was Theotokos. In a word, he asserted two persons in Christ. Next, not so many praises were given to the Blessed Virgin in the Council that hardly anything seems to be added. In the anathematism of Cyril she is called Theotokos and holy [ἁγία], but many other titles are not attributed to her. I do not deny that at a later time, when superstition grew, many titles were added, so that at last she was made equal to God the Father and far preferred to the Son.

units.la: Ex Patribus profert Basilium, Athanasium, deinde Sophronium, Methodium, Petrum Damiani, Anshelmum, Bernhardum. Sed responsio ad hæc facilis est. Primo Basilii Liturgiam & Athanasii lib. de Deipara supposititia scripta esse superius probavimus. Reliqui omnes sunt neoterici, qui vixerunt in ea ætate, quando idololatria iam in ecclesia incepit obtinere.
units.tr: Out of the Fathers he brings forward Basil, Athanasius, then Sophronius, Methodius, Peter Damian, Anselm and Bernard. But the reply to these is easy. First, we have proved above that Basil's Liturgy and Athanasius' book on the Mother of God are spurious writings. All the rest are modern writers who lived in the age when idolatry had already begun to prevail in the Church.

units.la: SECVLVM V. PELAGIANI.
units.tr: CENTURY V. THE PELAGIANS.

units.la: PElagiani â Pelagio monacho, ex magna Britannia oriundo, dicti, qui etiam Coelestini â Coelestio Pelagij affectatore nominati sunt) docent, naturalibus viribus, solius liberi arbitrij vi, sine Dei gratia justitiam Dei consequi nos posse. Pueros non egere baptismo ad deletionem peccati originalis, quòd ante baptismum nullum habeant peccatum. Traditiones respuunt, referente D. Aug. lib. de natura & gratia cap. 39. in hac verba. Credamus igitur quod legimus, & quod non legimus nefas credemus astruere, quod de cunctis etiam dixisse sufficiet.
units.tr: The Pelagians, so called from Pelagius, a monk born in Great Britain (who are also called Coelestians from Coelestius, Pelagius' follower), teach that by natural powers, by the power of free will alone, without the grace of God, we can attain the righteousness of God. Boys do not need baptism for the removal of original sin, since before baptism they have no sin. They reject traditions, as D. Augustine reports in On Nature and Grace, ch. 39, in these words: "Let us therefore believe what we read, and we shall deem it wrong to assert what we do not read; it will suffice to have said this of all things."

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATION.

units.la: Progreditur Jesuita ad seculum quintum, & in eo Pelagianis primum locum assignat. De Pelagii ortu, patria, & pernitiosa hæresi, contra quam Hieronymus scripsit in Oriente, Augustinus in Africa circa A. D. 411. & quæ in concilio Carthaginensi & Milevitano cui interfuit Augustinus damnata fuit, prolixè non differam. Harscherus tria de Pelagianis commemorat: Primò, quòd docuerint, hominem viribus naturalibus solius liberi arbitrii, sine Dei gratia iustitiam consequi posse. Secundò, pueros non egere baptismo ad deletionem peccati originalis, quòd ante baptismum nullum habeant peccatum. Tertiò, quod traditiones reiecerint.
units.tr: The Jesuit proceeds to the fifth century and gives the Pelagians first place in it. I will not go at length into the origin and homeland of Pelagius, or into his pernicious heresy, against which Jerome wrote in the East and Augustine in Africa around AD 411, and which was condemned at the councils of Carthage and Milevis, in which Augustine took part. Harscher mentions three things about the Pelagians: first, that they taught that man can attain righteousness by the natural powers of free will alone, without the grace of God; second, that boys do not need baptism for the removal of original sin, since before baptism they have no sin; third, that they rejected traditions.

units.la: De primo nihil Iesuita in parallelis tractat, quia procul dubio novit Theologos Orthodoxos, Pelagianam hanc sententiam de viribus liberi arbitrii detestari, de quo passim eorum scripta loquuntur. É contra Pontificios Doctores maximè in doctrina de libero arbitrio in eam inclinare, exiguo discrimine, unde à nostris Semi-Pelagiani non immerito appellantur. Quia autem ipse hanc controversiam non attingit, nec ego eam hic prolixius tractabo.
units.tr: On the first point the Jesuit says nothing in the Parallels, because he doubtless knows that orthodox theologians detest this Pelagian opinion about the powers of free will, as their writings speak of everywhere. On the contrary, the Papist doctors incline towards it, especially in their doctrine of free will, with only a slight difference, and for this reason they are not unfairly called Semi-Pelagians by our side. But since he himself does not touch this controversy, I too will not treat it at greater length here.

units.la: Quod secundo de baptismo puerorum, ex mente Pelagianorum disserit, de eo Augustinus multis in locis disputat. Perspicue in lib. de Haref. ad quod vult Deum, haeresi 88. Parvulos etiam negant secundum Adam carnaliter natos, contagium mortis antiquae prima nativitate contrahere. Sic enim eos sine ullo peccati originalis vinculo asserunt nasci, ut prorsus non sit, quod eis oporteat secunda nativitate dimitti, sed eos propterea baptizari, ut regeneratione adoptati, admittantur ad regnum Dei, de bono in melius translati, non ista renovatione ab aliquo malo obligationis veteris absoluti.
units.tr: As to the second point, about infant baptism in the mind of the Pelagians, Augustine discusses it in many places. Plainly in the book On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus, heresy 88: "They also deny that infants born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of the ancient death at their first birth. For they assert that they are born without any bond of original sin, so that there is nothing that must be remitted to them by a second birth; but they are baptized so that, adopted by regeneration, they may be admitted to the kingdom of God, being transferred from good to better, not absolved by this renewal from some evil of an old obligation."

units.la: Duo itaque Pelagiani docuerunt. Primo, infantes sine peccato originali nasci a parentibus. Secundo eam ob causam baptismum ipsis neutiquam esse necessarium. Utrumque nos haereticum esse asserimus, utrumquè longissimè abesse â fide nostra.
units.tr: Thus the Pelagians taught two things. First, that infants are born from their parents without original sin. Second, for that reason baptism is in no way necessary for them. We assert that both are heretical, and that both are far removed from our faith.

units.la: De primò sic docenus, confess. Helv. pag. 27. Agnoscimus in omnibus esse originale peccatum. Catech. Heidel. quæst. 7. Unde existit natura pravitas?
units.tr: On the first point we teach as follows, in the Confession of Helvetia, p. 27: We acknowledge that original sin is in all. Heidelberg Catechism, Question 7: Whence comes this corrupt nature?

units.la: Resp. Ex lapsu & inobedientia primorum parentum Adam & Eva, hinc natura nostra ita est depravata, ut omnes in peccatis concipiamur & nascamur.
units.tr: Answer: From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve; hence our nature is so depraved that we are all conceived and born in sins.

units.la: Calv. lib. II. c. 1 §. 5. Sicut spiritualis Adæ vita erat manere opifici suo conjunctij & devinctus: ita alienatio ab eo fuit animæ interitus. Nec mirum si genus suum pessumdedit sua defectione, qui totum naturæ ordinem pervertit in cœlo & in terra. Ingemiscunt omnes creaturæ, inquit Paulus, corruptioni obnoxiæ non volentes, si caussa quæritur non dubium est quin partem sustineant ejus pœnæ, quam promeritus est homo, in cujus usum conditæ fuerant. Quum ergo sursum & deorsum ex ejus culpa fluxerit maledictio quæ grassatur per omnes mundi plagas, nihil à ratione alienum, si propagata fuerit ad totam ejus sobolem. Postquam ergo in eo obliterata fuit cœlestis imago, non solus sustinuit hanc pœnam, ut in locum sapientia, virtutis, sanctitatis, veritatis, (quibus ornamentis vestitus fuerat) teterrimi cederent pestes, cæcitas, impotentia, impuritas, vanitas, justitia: sed ijsdem quoq; miseriis implicuit suam progeniem & immersit.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes II, ch. 1, §5: As the spiritual life of Adam was to remain joined and bound to his Maker, so alienation from him was the death of the soul. Nor is it surprising that by his defection he ruined his own race, he who overturned the whole order of nature in heaven and on earth. "All creatures groan," says Paul, "subject to corruption, not willingly"; if the cause is sought, there is no doubt that they bear a part of the punishment which man, for whose use they were made, has deserved. Since therefore a curse has flowed upward and downward from his fault, spreading through all the corners of the world, it is not at all unreasonable that it has been propagated to his whole posterity. Therefore, after the heavenly image was effaced in him, he not only underwent this punishment, that in place of wisdom, virtue, holiness and truth (the ornaments with which he had been clothed) the most foul plagues took their place: blindness, impotence, impurity, vanity, injustice; but he also entangled and immersed his progeny in the same miseries.

units.la: Hæc Erbsünde hæreditaria corruptio, quam peccatum originale veteres nuncuparunt.
units.tr: This Erbsünde is hereditary corruption, which the ancients called original sin.

units.la: Sic communiter omnes Theologi orthodoxi peccatum originale non solum infantibus, sed etiam homini vixdum concepto & nondum nato inesse, & ut rapacitatem in catulis luporum se magis magisque exerere. Hæc de primo.
units.tr: Thus all orthodox theologians commonly teach that original sin is present not only in infants, but also in a human being scarcely conceived and not yet born, and that it grows more and more, like the rapacity in the whelps of wolves. This is what I have to say on the first point.

units.la: Baptismi necessitatem nunquam negavimus sensu Pelagiano, quasi Baptismus idcirco necessarius non sit, quia infantes absque peccato nascantur, nam
units.tr: We have never denied the necessity of baptism in the Pelagian sense, as though baptism were on that account not necessary, because infants are born without sin, for

units.la: argumentum hoc antea reiecimus. Nec sensu Quintilianorum, qui (referente Tertulliano) idcirco baptismi necessitatem negarunt, quòd fides satis sit: nam & Abraham nullius aqua, nisi fidei Sacramento Deo placuisse. Sed urgemus necessitatem Baptismi cum Tertulliano, quia lex tingendi nobis est à Domino imposita & forma præscripta. Interim verum est, nos peremptoriam necessitatem baptismi negare, ac si regno Dei excluderentur credentes, qui non fuerint aquâ externâ tincti. Quia Deus ad media non est astrictus. Medium, inquam, est ordinarium & præcepti Christi causâ necessarium, nunquam negligendum & expetendum semper, si verò ad id pervenire non possunt infantes propter præmaturam mortem, tum Bernhardi regula nos docet: Non privationem, sed contemptum damnare.
units.tr: we have rejected this argument before. Nor do we deny it in the sense of the Quintilians, who (as Tertullian reports) therefore denied the necessity of baptism because faith is enough; for Abraham pleased God by no water, but by the sacrament of faith. But we press the necessity of baptism with Tertullian, because the law of baptizing has been imposed on us by the Lord and its form prescribed. Meanwhile it is true that we deny a peremptory necessity of baptism, as if believers who had not been washed with external water were excluded from the kingdom of God, because God is not bound to means. The means, I say, is ordinary and necessary by Christ's command, never to be neglected and always to be desired; but if infants cannot reach it because of premature death, then Bernard's rule teaches us: to condemn not the deprivation, but the contempt.

units.la: Tertium quod attinet de reiectis â Pelagianis traditionibus ex Augustino citatum, quàm illud inepte huic loco accommodatur? Nam Augustinus Pelagii verba non intelligit de scriptis divinis. Unde ita respondet: Non omnia, quæ legimus credere nos debemus propter illud, quod Apostolus ait: omnia legite, quæ bona sunt tenete, & aliquid astruere, etiam quod non legimus nefas non est. Possumus enim aliquid bona fide testibus astruere, quod experti sumus, etiamsi forte non legimus. Potuit ne Augustinus scribere, non omnia quæ legimus in Dei verbo credenda esse? Infidelitatis argumentum est, inquit Basilius serm. de fidei confess. & signum superbiæ certissimum si quis eorum, quæ scripta sunt, aliquid velit reycere. De fide ergo humana locutus est Augustinus. Idcirco excipit & dicit, hic fortasse respondet: Ego cum hæc dicerem de scripturis sanctis agebam. Audi nunc quid ad hæc Augustinus, o utinam (inquit) non dicat aliud, quàm in illis literis legit. Quâ unica responsione omnes traditiones de fide ad salutem non scriptas in verbo Dei, reiecit. Videamus nunc ex sequentibus tribus parallelis
units.tr: As for the third point, the traditions rejected by the Pelagians, cited from Augustine, how inappropriately is that applied to this place! For Augustine does not understand Pelagius' words as referring to the divine writings. Hence he answers thus: We ought not to believe everything we read, on account of what the Apostle says, "read all things, hold fast what is good"; and it is not wrong to assert something even if we do not read it. For we can assert in good faith, on the testimony of witnesses, something we have experienced, even if perhaps we have not read it. Could Augustine have written that not everything we read is to be believed in God's Word? It is an argument of unbelief, says Basil in his sermon on the confession of faith, and a most certain sign of pride, if anyone wishes to reject anything of what has been written. So Augustine was speaking of human faith. Therefore he adds, and says, perhaps someone will reply: I was speaking of the holy Scriptures. Hear now what Augustine says to this: Would that he might say nothing other than what he reads in those letters. By this one answer he rejected all traditions concerning faith unto salvation that are not written in the Word of God. Let us now see from the following three parallels...

units.la: PARALLELUM PRIMUM.
units.tr: The First Parallel.

units.la: Calvinus in Antidoto concilij Tridentini ad seff. 6. cap. 5. & lib. 4. Inslit. cap. 16. §. 24. & 25. docet parvulos fidelium etiam sine baptismo esse sanctos & membra ecclesiae & si moriantur salvari, verba Calvini sunt priori loco. Quasi vero de nihilo dictum sit nasci sanctos, qui ex fidelibus nascantur; imo quo jure eos ad baptismum admittimus, nisi quod promissionis sint haredes? nisi enim jam ante ad eos pertineret vitae promissio baptismum profanaret, quisquis illis daret. Et: Non a baptismo igitur initium habet ipsorum salus, sed quae jam in verbo fundata erat, obsignatur. Posteriori loco infans haereditario jure secundum promissionis formulam jam a matris utero in sedere continetur.
units.tr: Calvin, in his Antidote to the Council of Trent, on session 6, chapter 5, and in Institutes book 4, chapter 16, §§ 24 and 25, teaches that the infants of believers, even without baptism, are holy and members of the Church, and that if they die they are saved. These are Calvin's words in the former place: As if it had been said for nothing that those are born holy who are born of believers. Indeed, by what right do we admit them to baptism, unless because they are heirs of the promise? For unless the promise of life already pertained to them, baptism would profane whoever gave it to them. And: Therefore their salvation does not have its beginning from baptism, but what was already founded in the Word is sealed. In the latter place the infant is already contained in the womb by hereditary right, according to the formula of the promise.

units.la: Antea dixi Calvinum confiteri omnes infantes Christianorum cum peccato originali nasci, & esse filios irae, naturae vitio. Quod adeo verum, ut illud ne quidem per baptismum tolli afferat. Hoc Bellarminum caeterosque Jesuitas non latet, nam idcirco ipsi litem movent. Calumniantur tamen, ut vexent. Quod si quis obiiciat, quomodo simul stare possint duo opposita, sanctum esse, & originali vitio inquinatum? Respondeo optime posse, quia non quaevis sanctitas peccato originali opponitur. Triplex enim est sanctitas, prima est sanctitas federalis quae est omnium federatorum communiter, omnium inquam ad quos foederis promissiones pertinent, quae non est aliqua inhaerens qualitas, sed extrinsecus adhaerens privilegium, quod ad omnes pertinet, qui in populo & ecclesia Dei censentur. Hoc titulo ornavit Deus Israelitas Deut. 7. 8. Populus sanctus es Jehovae Deo tuo, te selegit. Huius sanctitatis respectu Apostolus liberos Corinthiorum vocat Sanctos, 1. Cor. 7: 14. Qui sanctitate federali sanctus est opponitur βεβήλῳ profano, qui extra fedus Dei est, & ad ecclesiam non spectat. Secunda est sanctitas sacramentalis, quâ per baptismum foederatis externâ aquæ aspersione remissio peccatorum per sanguinem Christi & regeneratio per Spiritum sanctum, item per usum Eucharistiæ participatio corporis & sanguinis Christi obsignatur. Hæc superiore illa strictior est, reprobis tamen quoque competit, cuius obsignationis respectu dicuntur ab Apostolo Paulo illuminati, & per Christi sanguinem sanctificati, adeò, ut hisce mediis abutentes, dicantur Filium Dei conculcare & sanguinem foederis, per quem fuerant (sacramentali sanctitate) sanctificati, prosanare, Spiritumque gratiæ (obsignatæ) contumeliâ afficere, Heb. 10: 29. Tertia est sanctitas spiritualis & interna regenerationis, quæ est qualitas electis inhærens, effecta à Spiritu sancto in cordibus eorum, quâ vitiositas nativa destruitur, & imago Dei restauratur.
units.tr: Above I said that Calvin confesses that all the infants of Christians are born with original sin and are children of wrath through the corruption of nature. This is so true that he does not even claim it is removed by baptism. Bellarmine and the other Jesuits are not unaware of this; for that reason they stir up the quarrel. Yet they slander him in order to harass him. But if someone objects, how can two opposites stand together: to be holy, and to be defiled by original sin? I answer that it is entirely possible, because not every kind of holiness is opposed to original sin. For holiness is threefold. The first is federal holiness, which belongs in common to all who are in covenant, to all, I say, to whom the promises of the covenant pertain. It is not some inhering quality but an externally adhering privilege, which belongs to all who are reckoned in the people and Church of God. God adorned the Israelites with this title, Deut. 7:8: "You are a holy people to Jehovah your God; he has chosen you." With respect to this holiness the Apostle calls the children of the Corinthians holy, 1 Cor. 7:14. The one who is holy by federal holiness is opposed to the profane [βεβήλῳ], who is outside God's covenant and does not belong to the Church. The second is sacramental holiness, by which, through baptism, those in covenant are sealed, by the external sprinkling of water, with the remission of sins through the blood of Christ and regeneration through the Holy Spirit; likewise, through the use of the Eucharist, with participation in the body and blood of Christ. This is stricter than the former, yet it also belongs to the reprobate. With respect to this sealing the Apostle Paul says they are enlightened and, through the blood of Christ, sanctified. So much so that those who abuse these means are said to trample underfoot the Son of God, to profane the blood of the covenant through which they had been sanctified (with sacramental holiness), and to insult the Spirit of grace (who has been sealed), Heb. 10:29. The third is spiritual and inward holiness of regeneration, which is a quality inhering in the elect, effected in their hearts by the Holy Spirit, by which native corruption is destroyed and the image of God is restored.

units.la: Sanctitas ista est electorum tantùm Theologis personalis & habitualis dicta opposita peccato originali, quod in regeneratis paulatim abolet. Sciendum itaque Calvinum quando docet infantes fidelium nasci sanctos, non loqui de sanctitate regenerationis, personali & habituali, cùm hac enim sanctitate nemo nascitur, nec illa à parentibus in filios propagatur, ut apparet in Ismaël, Esau, Manasse & aliis, est enim ex gratia speciali à Spiritu sancto infusa. Quemadmodum enim Doctor, non gignit Doctorem aut Medicus Medicum, sic nec sanctus gignit sanctum. Falsa ergò sunt illa Jesuitæ de Calvino dicta: Calvinus facit pueros sine baptismo hæreditario jure sanctos. Nec loquitur Calvinus de sanctitate sacramentali ut notum est. Sed de sanctitate federali, quæ ita dicitur phrasi hebræa, & est jus federale, dignitas federalis, jus civitatis Dei, quod alii extra civitatem non habent: Hæc sanctitas federalis & ius civitatis transit à parentibus in liberos, sicuti iura civitatis transeunt à parentibus in filios. Ut civis gignit civem, ita christianus christianum. Atque hæc est caussa cur christianorum infantes in ecclesia nati baptizentur, Mahumetanorum & Ethnicorum non item. Nemo ergo improbabit Calvini dicta, cum ait: Infans hæreditario jure secundum promissionis formulam jam à matris utero in sedere continetur. Item; quo jure fidelium infantes ad baptismum admittimus, nisi quod promissionis sint hæredes, nisi enim jam ante ad ipsos pertineret vitæ promissio, baptismum prophanaret, quisquis illis daret. Nam hoc argumento utitur Apostolus Petrus apud suos auditores in concione die Pentecostes habita Act. 2. Baptizetur unusquisq; vestrum
units.tr: This holiness, which theologians call personal and habitual, belongs only to the elect and is opposed to original sin, which it gradually abolishes in the regenerate. It must therefore be understood that when Calvin teaches that the infants of believers are born holy, he is not speaking of the holiness of regeneration, personal and habitual; for no one is born with this holiness, nor is it propagated from parents to children, as appears in Ishmael, Esau, Manasseh and others, since it is infused by the Holy Spirit by special grace. For just as a teacher does not beget a teacher, or a physician a physician, so a holy person does not beget a holy one. Therefore those words the Jesuits attribute to Calvin are false: "Calvin makes infants holy without baptism by hereditary right." Nor does Calvin speak of sacramental holiness, as is well known; but of federal holiness, which is so called in the Hebrew idiom, and which is federal right, federal dignity, the right of the city of God, which others outside the city do not have. This federal holiness and right of citizenship passes from parents to children, just as rights of citizenship pass from fathers to sons. As a citizen begets a citizen, so a Christian begets a Christian. And this is the reason why the infants of Christians born in the Church are baptized, but those of Muslims and heathens are not. No one, therefore, will disapprove of Calvin's words when he says: "The infant is contained in the womb by hereditary right, according to the formula of the promise." Likewise: "By what right do we admit the infants of believers to baptism, unless because they are heirs of the promise? For unless the promise of life already pertained to them, baptism would profane whoever gave it to them." For the Apostle Peter uses this very argument with his hearers in the sermon he gave on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2: "Let each of you be baptized"

units.la: Ioan. 3. vestrum v. 38. cur? Quia vobis facta est promissio & liberis vestris v. 39. Ratiocinatio talis est: Quibus facta est promissio, illi debent & possunt baptizari. Atqui vobis & liberis vestris facta est promissio. Ergo vos & liberi vestri debetis baptizari. In quo argumento Calvini verba fundantur. Hæc omnia (quamvis iuxta veritatem scripturæ di� cta) eludunt Jesuitæ, obiicientes, neminem nasci Christianum: & promissionem istam nihil conferre, quia nemo sit in fede re Dei absq; fide, quâ Infantes destituuntur. Ad hæc respondeo: 1. Nos libenter concedere liberos fidelium antequam baptizentur de facto nondum esse Christianos, quia per baptismum nondum sunt inscripti in sanctam militiam Christi, ut habet Helvetica consessio. Sunt tamen Christiani de iure, quia ius habent, ut inscribantur, quod non omnibus concessum. Atquè sic loquitur Calvinus locis supra citatis: Infans jure hæreditario: Quo jure fidelium infantes &c. 2. Promissionem istam equidem non conferre gratiam regenerantem, conferre autem gratiam federalem, id est, ius illud & privilegium introeundi in fedus, ita ut nemo illis Sacramentum sederis denegare audeat, etiam fi vellet. Atque hoc multum est & insignis gratia. Hanc gratiam Ephesii non habebant ante vocationem gentium, ut docet Apoftolus cap. 2. 11, 12. Nam sicuti extranei erant, quoad federa promissionis, ita etiam erant alieni a circumcisione in carne 3. Fidelium infantes ante baptismum in sedere esse eo modo quo sunt Christiani, id est, de iure: de facto in eodem esse postquam per baptismum recepti, sese Deo obstrinxerunt ad novam obedientiam & mortificationem carnis. Similiter ut feudatarii alicuius filius natus, ius habet ad accipiendum feudum, de facto autem id non accipit nisi praestiterit homagium. Nec impedit, quòd fidem non habent, sufficit quod non sint infideles. Cùm enim infidelitas duplex sit, una negativa, quæ est fidei vacuitas, privativa altera, quæ habet contrarii habitus positionem, infantes Christianorum ante baptismum hoc posteriori modo infideles dici non possunt, tales quippe sunt infantes Turcarum & Judæorum, quibus idcirco baptismus non debetur. Licet autem fide actuali careant, nihil hoc impedit, quia Deus fidem (cuius per naturam nondum sunt capaces) ab ipsis non poltulat.
units.tr: Acts 2, "of you," v. 38. Why? "For the promise is made to you and to your children," v. 39. The reasoning runs thus: those to whom the promise was made ought to be baptized, and can be. But the promise was made to you and to your children. Therefore you and your children ought to be baptized. On this argument Calvin's words are founded. The Jesuits mock all these things, although they are spoken according to the truth of Scripture, objecting that no one is born a Christian, and that this promise confers nothing, since no one is in the covenant of God without faith, of which infants are destitute. To these objections I reply: 1. We gladly concede that the children of believers, before they are baptized, are not in fact yet Christians, because through baptism they have not yet been enrolled "in the holy militia of Christ," as the Helvetic Confession has it. Yet they are Christians by right, because they have the right to be enrolled, which is not granted to everyone. And so Calvin speaks in the places cited above: "by hereditary right," "by what right do the infants of believers," and so on. 2. That promise indeed does not confer regenerating grace, but it does confer federal grace, that is, the right and privilege of entering into the covenant, so that no one dares to deny them the sacrament of the covenant, even if he wished to. This is a great thing and a notable grace. The Ephesians did not have this grace before the calling of the Gentiles, as the Apostle teaches in chapter 2, verses 11 and 12: "For just as they were strangers with respect to the covenants of promise, so also they were aliens from circumcision in the flesh." 3. The infants of believers are in the covenant before baptism in the same way they are Christians, that is, by right; in fact they are in it only after they have been received through baptism and have bound themselves to God to new obedience and the mortification of the flesh. It is similar to the son of some vassal who, once born, has a right to receive the fief, but in fact does not receive it unless he has performed homage. Nor does it hinder that they lack faith; it is enough that they are not unbelievers. For since unbelief is twofold, one negative, which is the absence of faith, and the other privative, which involves the positive presence of a contrary habit, the infants of Christians before baptism cannot be called unbelievers in the latter sense. Such, indeed, are the infants of Turks and Jews, to whom baptism is therefore not owed. Although they lack actual faith, this does not stand in the way, because God does not require faith from them, since by nature they are not yet capable of it.

units.la: II. Zvvinglius lib. de vera & falsa Religione negat baptismum esse necessarium, quòd nihil sit nisi externum symbolum.
units.tr: II. Zwingli, in his book On the True and False Religion, denies that baptism is necessary, because it is nothing but an external sign.

units.la: Quid? Zvvinglius scripsit Baptismum esse nudum symbolum? & idcirco non necessarium? an ille fidem orthodoxam aut confessionem Helveticam aut propria sua scripta abnegavit? Hoc nemo sanus dixerit. An ergo hoc Jesuitæ mendacium? plane pro more. Est baptismus lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. 3: 5. est ablutio peccatorum, Act. 22: 10. id est, eiusmodi divinum symbolum ac pignus, quo Deus certum facit nos non minùs verè à peccatis nostris interna lotione ablui, quàm externa & visibili aquâ abluti sumus, ut habet Cathechismus nostrer. Aut, ut confessi Helveti. art. XX. Nascimur omnes in peccatorum sordibus & sumus filij irae. Deus autem, ut qui dives est misericordia, purgat nos à peccato gratuitò, per sanguinem Filij sui, & in hoc adoptat nos in filios, adeoque sedere sancto nos connectit, & variis donis ditat, ut possimus novam vivere vitam. Obsignantur haec omnia baptismo. An hoc est, esse nudum symbolum? quod praeter significationem etiam exhibet, applicat, & obsignat remissionem peccatorum per sanguinem Christi? De necessitate baptismi quid iudicarit Zwinglius mihi ignotum non est. In lib. verò de vera & falsa religione cum necessitatem baptismi negavit, videndum de quo baptismo locutus sit, id ex ipsius verbis manifestum fiet. Nam ita loquitur Zvvinglius in loco prædiɖto: Spiritus sanƈti baptismus duplex est alter, quo omnes irrigantur interne, qui Christo fidunt, ad eum enim nemo venit, nisi quem pater traxerit. Ioh. 6. Alter Spiritus sanƈti baptismus est æque ac baptismus aquæ. Quo compunƈti aliquando pij ceperunt linguis loqui peregrinis quæ res signum fuit aliis potius quàm iis qui loquebantur. Atqƒ iste posterior Spiritus sanƈti baptismus non est necessarius, sed superior est necessarius, ut nisi detur nemo salvus fiat. Vides cuius baptismi necessitatem negarit Zvvinglius? nempe non baptismi fluminis, sed flaminis.
units.tr: What? Did Zwingli write that baptism is a bare sign, and therefore not necessary? Or did he renounce the orthodox faith, the Helvetic Confession, or his own writings? No sane person would say so. Is this, then, a lie of the Jesuits? Certainly, as is their custom. Baptism is the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5) and the washing away of sins (Acts 22:10). That is, it is a divine sign and pledge by which God assures us that we are no less truly cleansed from our sins by an inward washing than we are bathed with external and visible water, as our Catechism says. Or as the Helvetic Confession says in article XX: We are all born in the filth of sin and are children of wrath. But God, who is rich in mercy, cleanses us from sin freely, through the blood of his Son, and in this adopts us as sons, joins us to the holy seed, and enriches us with various gifts, so that we may live a new life. All these things are sealed by baptism. Is this to be a bare sign? Does it not, beyond signifying, also exhibit, apply and seal the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ? What Zwingli judged about the necessity of baptism is not unknown to me. But in his book On the True and False Religion, when he denied the necessity of baptism, it must be seen which baptism he was speaking of; this will become clear from his own words. For Zwingli speaks thus in the place cited: There are two baptisms of the Holy Spirit. The first, by which all who trust in Christ are inwardly watered, for no one comes to him unless the Father draws him (John 6). The other baptism of the Holy Spirit is like the baptism of water. By it devout men, pricked in their hearts, sometimes began to speak in foreign tongues, which was a sign to others rather than to those who spoke. And this latter baptism of the Holy Spirit is not necessary, but the former is necessary, so that unless it is given, no one is saved. Do you see whose baptism Zwingli denied to be necessary? Namely, not the baptism of water, but of the Spirit.

units.la: Subnectit his Jesuita duo argumenta historica, unum, ex Adriani Jungii lib. 3. de doƈtr. & moribus Evangelicorum; Alterum forte ex Utopia.
units.tr: The Jesuit adds to these two historical arguments, one taken from the third book of Adrian Junius's work on the doctrine and morals of the Evangelicals, and the other perhaps from Utopia.

units.la: Prius est quod in synodo Vilnæ habita anno 1589. Calvinista decreverint, ne quis parvulos illegitimè natos baptizare audeat. Posterius, In Palatinatu disseminatos fuisse articulos anno 1587, quorum secundus ita habet: Infantes, qui ex illegitimo thoro nascuntur, æternæ perditionis & damnationis obnoxij sunt, nec per baptismum juvari possunt. Utrumque parvi momenti. Nam vix reperies scriptorem pontificium, qui vero animi candore sententias nostrorum cum omnibus circumstantiis proferat. Sit ita scripserint synodici Vilnenses, ne quis parvulos illegitimè natos baptizare audeat, nisi prius rem ad superiores retulerit, de utroque parente inquisiverit, & de sponsoribus certus sit, an idcirco, simpliciter baptismum illegitimè natorum ab ipsis prohiberi concludendum est? Horum enim baptismum probat praxis omnium ecclesiarum reformatarum, qui infantes ex illegitimo thoro prognatos, baptizare consueverunt.
units.tr: The first is that in the synod held at Vilna in the year 1589 the Calvinists decreed that no one should dare to baptize children born out of wedlock. The second: In the Palatinate, in 1587, articles were circulated, of which the second reads: Infants who are born of an illegitimate bed are liable to eternal perdition and damnation, and cannot be helped by baptism. Both are of little weight. For you will hardly find a Papist writer who sets out the opinions of our people, with all their circumstances, with genuine candour. Suppose the Vilna synodists did write that no one should dare to baptize children born out of wedlock unless he first referred the matter to his superiors, inquired about both parents, and was certain of the sponsors. Is it therefore to be concluded that they simply forbade the baptism of children born out of wedlock? For the practice of all the Reformed churches, which are accustomed to baptize infants born of illegitimate unions, proves that their baptism is allowed.

units.la: T
units.tr: T

units.la: Calvinus ad quæstionem ab amico propositam; An idololatrarum & excommunicatorum liberos ad baptismum admittere liceat? respondet suo & ecclesiæ Genevensis nomine, omnino licitum esse, modo parentes aut cognati spondeant pro fide infantis, secus lusoriam fore actionem baptismi. Sententiæ suæ rationem hanc tradit; quia non recipitur quisquam ad baptismum unius duntaxat patris sui respectu vel favore, sed propter continuum Dei fedus: & unius parentis odio aut vitio ab ecclesia ingressu prohiberi infantes, nullam rationem pati.
units.tr: Calvin, answering a question put to him by a friend, Is it permissible to admit to baptism the children of idolaters and excommunicated persons?, replies in his own name and in the name of the Church of Geneva: It is altogether lawful, provided the parents or relatives stand surety for the faith of the infant; otherwise the action of baptism would be a mockery. He gives this reason for his opinion: because no one is received to baptism out of regard or favour to one parent alone, but on account of the continuing covenant of God; and infants should not be kept from entering the Church on account of the hatred or vice of one parent; there is no reason for this.

units.la: Bucanus nostram sententiam de baptizandis ex adulterio natis deducit ex sequentibus rationibus 1. quia parentum impietas liberis in ecclesia natis fraudi esse non debet, Ezech. 18: 4. 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Hic rectè ab ipso applicatum illud Augustini, de excommunicatorum liberis: qui non sunt participes cri-minis minis, non sunt participes excommunicationis, epist. 75. ad Auxilium Episc. 2. quia non est spectanda proximorum parentum impietas, sed pietas ecclesiæ, in qua nati sunt, quæ est ceu ipsorum mater, & maiorum suorum, qui pie vixerunt. 3. quia nec impiorum Judæorum liberis denegata fuit circumcisio. Instit. Theol. loc. 47. quæst. 33.
units.tr: Bucanus derives our opinion about baptizing children born of adultery from the following reasons. (1) Because the impiety of parents should not harm children born in the Church: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:4, 20). Here Augustine's words about the children of excommunicated persons are rightly applied by him: those who are not partakers of the crime are not partakers of the excommunication (Epistle 75 to Auxilius, the bishop). (2) Because the impiety of the nearest parents is not to be regarded, but the piety of the Church in which they are born, which is as their mother, and of their ancestors, who lived piously. (3) Because circumcision was not denied to the children of the impious Jews. Institutes of Theology, loc. 47, quest. 33.

units.la: De disseminatis articulis in Palatinatu nullum authorem producit. Fieri autem omninò potuit, ut tales articuli à malevolis & maleferiatis hominibus sparsi fuerint in contemptum ecclesiæ Palatinæ, sicuti hodie sparguntur in Helvetia nostra, parallela evangelica falsa, mendacia, eodem fine, non tamen credendum Palatinos orthodoxos erroneam istam sententiam fovi-se. An enim illi qui spurios sub spe regenerationis per Spiritum sanctum & iustificationis per Christum baptizant, ad sacramentum eucharistiæ admittunt, per baptismum eosdem iuvari non posse & æternæ damnationi obnoxios esse, credere possunt?
units.tr: He produces no author for the articles scattered in the Palatinate. It was entirely possible, however, that such articles were spread by malicious and mischievous men to bring the Palatine Church into contempt, just as false, lying evangelical parallels are spread today in our Helvetia for the same end. Yet we must not believe that the orthodox Palatines fostered that erroneous opinion. For can those who baptize spurious children in the hope of regeneration by the Holy Spirit and justification through Christ, and admit them to the sacrament of the Eucharist, believe that these same children cannot be helped by baptism and are liable to eternal damnation?

units.la: Atqui, inquit, hoc videtur aperte sequi ex principijs Calvini, promissionem Abrahæ factam ad jus hæreditarium alligantis. Lepidus disputator. Promissio Abrahæ hæreditario iure ad omnes ipsius posteros pertinet: Ergo spurii in novo Testamento non sunt baptizandi, sunt æternæ damnationi obnoxii. Baculus stat in angulo, ergo Cæsar vicit Pompeium. Debebat contrarium concludere, ergo æternæ damnationi non sunt obnoxii, sunt baptizandi, quia in veteri Testamento illegitimè nati, à circumcisione non arcebantur, propter promissionem Abrahæ factam. Infans Davidi natus ex Bath-schebah, thoro illegitimo, circumcisus fuit, & cum mortuus esset, dixit David servis suis, ego sum abiturus ad ipsum, & ipse non est reversurus ad me, 2. Sam. 12: 29. Sed ad hæc, ut & plurima alia levioris momenti argumenta respondere, est bonum tempus male collocare.
units.tr: But, he says, this seems clearly to follow from the principles of Calvin, who binds the promise made to Abraham to a hereditary right. A witty disputant! The promise made to Abraham by hereditary right pertains to all his posterity. Therefore spurious children are not to be baptized in the New Testament; they are liable to eternal damnation. The staff stands in the corner, therefore Caesar defeated Pompey. He ought to have concluded the contrary: therefore they are not liable to eternal damnation, and they are to be baptized, because in the Old Testament children born out of wedlock were not excluded from circumcision, on account of the promise made to Abraham. The child born to David from Bathsheba, of an illegitimate bed, was circumcised; and when he died, David said to his servants, I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me (2 Sam. 12:23). But it would be a poor use of time to answer these and many other arguments of lesser weight.

units.la: Pro absoluta necessitate baptismi duo argumenta inartificialia huic parallelo subiicit Jesuita. Unum ex scriptura, alterum ex Augustino. Illud legitur Joh. 3: 5. Hoc in epistolis Augustini ad Innocentium Papam & Hieronymum. Item in lib. 3. de origine animæ cap. 9.
units.tr: For the absolute necessity of baptism the Jesuit adds two non-technical arguments to this parallel. One is from Scripture, the other from Augustine. The first is found in John 3:5; the second in the epistles of Augustine to Pope Innocent and to Jerome, and likewise in the third book On the Origin of the Soul, chapter 9.

units.la: Verba Christi ad Nicodemum huiusmodi sunt: Nisi quis genitus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Bellarminus cæteriquę Jesuitæ ex his verbis statuunt baptismum ad salutem necessarium esse necessitate medii simpliciter. Nos necessitatem regenerationis per Spiritum sanctu absolutam agnoscimus, parem necessitatem baptismi aquæ cum eadé non credimus licet hic à Christo coniungantur. tur. Sententiam nostram confirmant locorum parallelorum collatio, adversariorum confessio & veterum interpretatio. Ad Philipp. 1: 9. dicit Apostolus, novi enim fore, ut hoc mihi cedat in salutem per vestram deprecationem & suppeditationem Spiritus Iesu Christi. Coniunguntur hîc duo salutis media, deprecatio Philippensium & Spiritus Jesu Christi suppeditatio, sed dispari necessitate. Quando Bellarminus verba Christi explicat, si non lavero te, non habebis partem mecum, nullam absolutam necessitatem externæ lotionis pedum agnoscit, unde dicit ecclesiam Romanam hac ceremoniâ nunquam usam fuisse: internæ verò lotionis, quam â Christo accipimus necessitatem absolutam requirit, lib. 2. de Sacram. essectu cap. 2.
units.tr: The words of Christ to Nicodemus are these: Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Bellarmine and the other Jesuits conclude from these words that baptism is simply necessary to salvation by a necessity of means. We acknowledge an absolute necessity of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, but we do not believe that the necessity of water-baptism is equal to it, although Christ joins them here. The comparison of parallel passages, the admission of our opponents, and the interpretation of the ancients confirm our opinion. In Philippians 1:19 the Apostle says: For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Here two means of salvation are joined, the prayer of the Philippians and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, but with unequal necessity. When Bellarmine explains the words of Christ, If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me, he recognizes no absolute necessity of the external washing of feet, whence he says that the Roman Church never used this ceremony; but of the internal washing, which we receive from Christ, he requires an absolute necessity (On the Effect of the Sacraments, book 2, chapter 2).

units.la: Præterea si quis conferat confessionem Pontificiorum cum principio Thomæ Aquinatis, animadvertet Jesuitas nullo iure sententiam noftram de difpari neceffitate baptifmi & regenerationis per Spiritum fanctu reiicere poffe. Illud eft, inquit Thomas, ad finem aliquem confequendum fimpliciter neceffarium neceffitate medij, fine quo non poteft habere finis. Atqui dicunt Pontificii Doctores vitam æternam haberi & obtineri poffe absque baptifmo, nempe per fupplementum baptifmi sanguinis & flaminis. Ergo baptifmus fluminis non eft fimpliciter neceffarius neceffitate medii. Ita quidem Pontificii. Sed Auguftinus magis ad orthodoxiam cum fcribit: Invenio non tantum paffionem pro nomine Christi, id quod ex baptifmo deerat poffe fupplere, fed etiam per fidem conversionemq; cordis, fi forte ad celebrandum myfterium baptifmi in angustiis temporum fuccurri non poteft. Lib. 4. cap. 12. de baptifmo. Idcirco recte Lombardus Magifter fententiarum de loco Johannis: intelligendum esse de ijs qui possunt & contemnunt baptizari quantum ad visibile sacramentum, quamvis absolute intelligendum sit quantum ad regenerationem spiritualem. Lib. 4. sententidistinct. 4. Et Theophylactus ex veteribus in tertium caput Johannis, duplicem facit τῆς γεννήσεως Τεσσάρων, unum aquæ visibiliter acceptæ ad corporis puritatem, alterum Spiritus ad invisibilis animæ regenerationem. Non autem eiusdem sunt necessitatis ad salutem corporis ablutio & animæ regeneratio. Concludamus ergo verbis Johannis Feri Pontificii Francisçani in hunc locum: Deus non alligavit potentiam suam sacramentis. Ordinata quidem voluntate dat gratiam per sacramenta, nihilominus tamen potest sine sacramentis eam dare. Quæ est sententia nostra.
units.tr: Moreover, if anyone compares the confession of the Papists with the principle of Thomas Aquinas, he will see that the Jesuits have no right to reject our view of the disparity between the necessity of baptism and regeneration by the Holy Spirit. "That is," says Thomas, "simply necessary for attaining some end by necessity of means, without which the end cannot be had." But the Papist teachers say that eternal life can be had and obtained without water baptism, namely through the supplement of baptism of blood and of fire. Therefore water baptism is not simply necessary by necessity of means. So far the Papists. But Augustine writes more in keeping with orthodoxy: "I find that suffering for the name of Christ can supply what was lacking from baptism, and also faith and conversion of heart, if perhaps in the straits of the times no help can be had for celebrating the mystery of baptism." Book 4, chapter 12, on baptism. Therefore Lombard, the Master of the Sentences, rightly says concerning the passage of John: it must be understood of those who can be baptized and despise it, as regards the visible sacrament, although it must be understood absolutely as regards spiritual regeneration. Book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 4. And Theophylact, among the ancients on the third chapter of John, makes a twofold [τῆς γεννήσεως] birth: one of visibly received water for the purity of the body, the other of the Spirit for the invisible regeneration of the soul. But the washing of the body and the regeneration of the soul are not of the same necessity for salvation. Let us conclude, then, with the words of the Papist Franciscan John Ferus on this passage: God has not bound his power to the sacraments. By his ordained will he gives grace through the sacraments, yet nevertheless he can give it without the sacraments. This is our view.

units.la: Nunc ad Augustini testimonia accedo, ab Harschero citata, quorum primum habetur in epistola 90, & 92, ad Innocentium Papam. His verbis: parvulos etiam propter salutem, quæ per salvatorem Christum datur, baptizandos negant ac sic eos mortifera ista doctrina in aeternum necant, promittentes, etiamsi non baptizentur, habituros vitam aeternam, nec pertinere ad eos de quibus Dominus ait: venit filius hominis quaerere, quod perierat, neque est quod in eis salvetur. Et infra: Sed multi, qui eorum perhibentur esse vel fuisse discipuli haec mala quibus fundamenta christianae fidei conantur evertere quantumcunque possunt, affirmare non cessant. Et Paulo post: Quicunque negat parvulos per baptismum Christi a perditione liberari, & salutem percipere sempiternam, anathema sit.
units.tr: Now I come to the testimonies of Augustine cited by Harscher, the first of which is found in letters 90 and 92 to Pope Innocent. In these words: They deny that infants are to be baptized even for the salvation which is given through the Saviour Christ, and so by this deadly doctrine they destroy them forever, promising that even if they are not baptized they will have eternal life, and that those of whom the Lord says, "The Son of man came to seek that which was lost," do not pertain to them, and that there is nothing in them to be saved. And below: But many who are said to be or to have been their disciples do not cease to affirm these evils, by which they try to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith as far as they can. And a little after: Whoever denies that infants are freed from perdition through the baptism of Christ and receive everlasting salvation, let him be anathema.

units.la: Et epist. 92. Ut ergo alia omittamus, quae contra sacras scripturas plurima differunt, haec interim duo, quibus omnino totum, quod christiani sumus, niituntur evertere, quae fidelia corda sustinent, non esse rogandum Deum, ut contra peccati malum, atque ad operandam justitiam sit noster adjutor & non opitulari parvulis ad consequendam vitam aeternam christiana gratia sacramentum.
units.tr: And in letter 92: To pass over the many other points which differ from the holy Scriptures, these two things, by which they try utterly to overthrow the whole of what we Christians are, which faithful hearts sustain: that God is not to be asked to be our helper against the evil of sin and to work righteousness, and that the sacrament of Christian grace does not help infants to obtain eternal life.

units.la: Quid verò prodest testimonia ἀπὸ δόξης & à quæstione aliena (quibus indoctos decipere possunt Jesuitæ, doctos non possunt) in medium producere? qualia sunt illa ex duabus epistolis Augustini citata. Accusat Augustinus in locis allegatis Pelagium & Cœlestinum 1. quòd negant parvulos propter salutem quæ per salvatorem Christum datur baptizandos esse 2. quòd promittunt, parvulos vitam æternam habituros, etiamsi non baptizentur. 3. quòd dicunt, ad infantes non pertinere, de quibus Dominus ait: Venit filius hominis quærere & salvare quod perierat. Ratio, quia isti non perierant (inquiunt) nec est quod in iis salvetur, vel tanto pretio redimatur, quia nihil est in eis vitiatum, nihil tenetur sub Diaboli potestate captivum nec pro eis fusus est sanguis, qui fusus est in remissionem. 4. quòd statuunt, sacramentum christianæ gratiæ parvulis non opitulari ad consequendam dam vitam æternam. Hæc omnia nos cum ecclesia Carthaginensi & Augustino iudicamus esse hæretica, fidei & religioni nostræ contraria.
units.tr: But what is the use of bringing forward into the open testimonies taken out of context and from a question unrelated to the matter (with which the Jesuits can deceive the unlearned, but not the learned)? Such are those cited from two letters of Augustine. In the places alleged, Augustine accuses Pelagius and Celestius: first, that they deny infants are to be baptized for the salvation which is given through the Saviour Christ; second, that they promise infants will have eternal life even if they are not baptized; third, that they say the words of the Lord, "The Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost," do not apply to infants. The reason, they say, is that these infants had not perished, and there is nothing in them to be saved or redeemed at so great a price, because nothing in them is corrupted, nothing is held captive under the power of the devil, and the blood which was shed for the remission of sins was not shed for them. Fourth, they maintain that the sacrament of Christian grace does not help infants to obtain eternal life. We, together with the Church of Carthage and with Augustine, judge all these things to be heretical and contrary to our faith and religion.

units.la: Nam credimus 1. parvulos omninò baptizandos esse, ut ipsis salus per Christum parta obsignetur. 2. non promittimus infantibus vitā æternam, etiamsi ex contemptu Pelagiano non baptizentur. Nam huiusmodi contemptus damnat. 3. afferimus ad infantes pertinere suavem illam consolationem: venit filius hominis servare quod perierat. Nam perierunt omnes peccato originali vitiati: omnes coguntur fateri cum Davide: En in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato fovit me mater mea, Psal. 51: 7. 4. nisi fusus fuisset sanguis Christi pro infantibus in æternum perirent, quia omnes sunt sub Diaboli potestate captivi. Quæ cùm ita sint, nullius omninò ponderis sunt allegationes antiquorum patrum, quas contra nos producunt. Sunt tormenta, quæ fragorem efficiunt, hostes non lædunt.
units.tr: For we believe: first, that infants must by all means be baptized, so that the salvation won through Christ may be sealed to them. Second, we do not promise eternal life to infants, even if they are not baptized through Pelagian contempt; for such contempt condemns.
