Third, we assert that the sweet consolation "the Son of man came to save that which was lost" pertains to infants. For all who are tainted by original sin have perished; all are compelled to confess with David: "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me," Psalm 51:7. Fourth, unless the blood of Christ had been shed for infants, they would perish forever, since all are held captive under the power of the devil. Since these things are so, the allegations of the ancient Fathers which they bring against us have no weight at all. They are cannons that make a noise but do not wound the enemy.

units.la: Illud magis ad scopum quod ex lib. 3. de origine animæ cap. 9. citat: noli credere, noli dicere, noli docere infantes antequâ baptizentur morte præventos pervenire posse ad originalium indulgentiam peccatorum si vis esse catholicus. Eiusdem sensus est testimonium sequens ex epistola Augustini 20. ad Hieronymum, citatum, ut exemplar Harscherianum habet, sed est epistola 28. Quisquis dixerit, quòd in Christo vivificabuntur etiam parvuli, qui sine sacramenti ejus participatione de vita exeunt, hic profecto & contra apostolicam prædicationem venit, & totam condemnat ecclesiam, ubi propterea cum baptizandis parvulis festinatur & curritur, quia sine dubio creditur, aliter eos in Christo vivificari omninò non posse.
units.tr: More to the point is what they cite from book 3, On the Origin of the Soul, chapter 9: Do not believe, do not say, do not teach that infants who die before they are baptized can attain the forgiveness of original sins, if you wish to be catholic. Of the same meaning is the following testimony from Augustine's letter 20 to Jerome, cited as the Harsch copy has it, but it is letter 28: Whoever shall say that even infants who depart this life without participation in his sacrament will be made alive in Christ, he certainly contradicts apostolic preaching and condemns the whole Church, where for this reason haste and running are made to baptize infants, because without doubt it is believed that they cannot in any other way be made alive in Christ.

units.la: Jam non nego Augustinum in ea fuisse sententia, ut existimarit, baptismum absolutè esse ad salutem necessarium, quia Christus dixit Nicodemo: Nisi quis genitus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Sicuti etiam pertinaciter docuit, infantes non posse salutem æternam consequi, nisi eucharistiam percipiant, ex verbis Christi Joh. 6: 53. Nisi ederitis carnem filij hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem non habebitis vitam in vobis. De peccat. meri. & remiss. lib. 1. c. 20. & 24. Quanquam autem posteriorem sententiam pari fervore disputarit Augustinus, hodie tamen nemo ex Pontificiis eius opinionem probat. In priori autem illa de baptismi necessitate absoluta tam fuit perplexus, ut ad Hieronymum scripserit & edoceri ab ipso voluerit, ubi contraxerit anima reatum, quo trahatur in condemnationem etiam infantis morte praeventi, si ei per sacramentum, quo etiam parvuli baptizantur Christi gratia non subvenerit? Imò, infantes igne aeterno puniendos & in ultimo judicio haedis annumerandos censet, quod Pighius vester vocat sententiam scripturæ & ecclesiasticæ authoritati contrariam.
units.tr: Now I do not deny that Augustine held the view that he judged baptism to be absolutely necessary for salvation, because Christ said to Nicodemus: Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Just as he also stubbornly taught that infants cannot obtain eternal salvation unless they receive the Eucharist, from the words of Christ in John 6:53: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you. On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, chapters 20 and 24. Yet although Augustine argued the latter view with equal fervour, today none of the Papists approves his opinion. In that former view about the absolute necessity of baptism, however, he was so perplexed that he wrote to Jerome and wished to be taught by him: where the soul contracts the guilt by which it is dragged into condemnation, even of an infant who dies before grace has helped him through the sacrament, by which infants too are baptized in Christ? Indeed, he judges that infants are to be punished with eternal fire and numbered among the goats at the last judgment, which your Pighius calls a doctrine contrary to Scripture and to ecclesiastical authority.

units.la: Alibi tamen satis rotundè de hac quæstione scribit: Quantum itaq; valeat etiam sine visibili sacramento baptismi quod ait Apostolus corde creditur ad justitiam ore autem confessio fit ad salutem in illo latrone declaratum est, sed tunc impletur invisibiliter, cum mysterium baptismi non contemptus religionis, sed articulus necessitatis excludit. Lib. 4. de Baptis. cont. Donat. cap. 22.
units.tr: Elsewhere, however, he writes quite plainly on this question: How much, then, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, is worth what the Apostle says, "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation," is declared in that thief; but then it is fulfilled invisibly, when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt of religion but by the article of necessity. Book 4 On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 22.

units.la: Quam doctrinam de non absoluta necessitate baptismi alii quoquè docuerunt, Ambrosius, Bernhardus, Gerson, Hugo de sancto Victore, Lombardus, Bonaventura, Caietanus, magni Pontificii.
units.tr: Other writers also taught this doctrine of the non-absolute necessity of baptism: Ambrose, Bernard, Gerson, Hugh of Saint Victor, Lombard, Bonaventure, Cajetan, great Papists.

units.la: PARALLELUM II.
units.tr: PARALLEL II.

units.la: In hoc parallelo secundo præsumit Harscherus ex Calvino & Zwinglio demonstrare, quòd cum Pelagio negent peccatum originale, cùm tamen nihil magis sit ab iis alienum. Consessioni gallicæ subscripsit Calvinus, in qua articulus X. sic habet: Credimus totam Adami sobolem hac contagione infectam esse quam peccatum originale vocamus, vitium videlicet ex propagatione manans, non autem ex imitatione duntaxat, sicuti Pelagiani senserunt, quorum omnes errores detestamur. Et articulus XI. Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis, adhuc in utero matris delitescentibus æternæ mortis reos peragat.
units.tr: In this second parallel Harscher presumes to demonstrate from Calvin and Zwingli that they deny original sin along with Pelagius, although nothing is more foreign to them. Calvin subscribed the French Confession, in which article X reads: We believe that the whole offspring of Adam is infected with this contagion which we call original sin, namely a vice flowing from propagation, and not from imitation alone, as the Pelagians thought, whose errors we all detest. And article XI: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes all and each of mankind, not even infants excepted, still hidden in their mothers' wombs, liable to eternal death.

units.la: Zwinglius subscripsit confessioni Helveticæ, in cuius articulo octavo hæc leguntur: Peccatum originale intelligimus esse esse nativam illam hominis corruptionem ex primis illis nostris parentibus in nos omnes derivatam vel propagatam, quâ concupiscentijs pravis immersi & à bono aversi, ad omne verò malum propensi, pleni omni nequitiâ, diffidentiâ, contemptu & odio Dei nihil boni ex nobis ipsis facere, imò ne cogitare quidem possumus. Et Paulò post: Agnoscimus ergò in omnibus hominibus esse originale peccatum.
units.tr: Zwingli subscribed the Helvetic Confession, in whose eighth article these words are read: We understand original sin to be that native corruption of man, derived or propagated to all of us from our first parents, by which, immersed in wicked desires and turned away from good, and inclined to every evil, full of all wickedness, distrust, contempt and hatred of God, we can do nothing good of ourselves, indeed we cannot even think it. And a little later: We acknowledge, therefore, that original sin is in all men.

units.la: Sed Pater Harscher, ut est subtilis disputator, hoc ex Calvini & Zvvinglii scriptis per consequentiam concludit, sicuti videbimus.
units.tr: But Father Harscher, being a subtle disputant, concludes by inference from the writings of Calvin and Zwingli, as we shall see.

units.la: Calvinus lib. 2. Instit. cap. 1. §. 8. peccatum originale definit hoc modo: videtur ergò peccatum originale hæreditaria natura nostra pravitas & corruptio in omnes animæ partes diffusa, qua primùm facit reos iræ Dei, tum etiam opera in nobis profert, quæ scriptura vocat opera carnis, atq; id est, quod à Paulo sæpius peccatum nominatur, ad Rom. 6. Et infra: Qui dixerunt esse esse concupiscentiam non nimis alieno verbo usi sunt, si modo adderetur (quod minimè conceditur à plerisq;) quicquid in homine est ab intellectu ad voluntatem, ab anima ad carnem hac concupiscentiâ inquinatum, refertumq; esse, aut ut brevius absolvatur, totum hominem non aliud ex seipso esse quam concupiscentiam.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes, book 2, chapter 1, §8, defines original sin in this way: original sin is therefore hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, spread through all parts of the soul, which first makes us liable to the wrath of God, and then also produces in us those works which Scripture calls the works of the flesh; and this is what Paul often calls sin, Rom. 6. And further on: Those who have said that it is concupiscence have not used too alien a word, provided it is added (which is by no means conceded by most) that whatever is in man, from the intellect to the will, from the soul to the flesh, is polluted and filled by this concupiscence; or, to conclude more briefly, that the whole man is nothing of himself but concupiscence.

units.la: Hæc sunt verba Calvini ab Harschero citata. Unde ita concludit: Atqui concupiscentia hæc non est peccatum, vix est in parvulis, major in uno reperitur, quàm in altero. Ergò peccatum originale non est peccatum, vix est in parvulis, majus est in uno, quàm in altero.
units.tr: These are the words of Calvin cited by Harscher, from which he concludes thus: But this concupiscence is not sin; it is scarcely in infants; it is greater in one person than in another. Therefore original sin is not sin; it is scarcely in infants; it is greater in one than in another.

units.la: Duplex locus allegatur. In primo Calvinus peccatum originale describit 1. à forma, quòd sit pravitas & corruptio totius hominis, 2. à subiecto, quòd sit diffusum in omnes partes animæ, intellectum, voluntatem & appetitum, unde in scriptura ὀικοῦσα ἁμαρτία, inhabitans peccatum, Rom. 7: 17. &
units.tr: Two passages are alleged. In the first, Calvin describes original sin 1. from its form, in that it is the depravity and corruption of the whole man; 2. from its subject, in that it is spread through all parts of the soul, the intellect, the will and the appetite; whence in Scripture it is called oikousa hamartia [ὀικοῦσα ἁμαρτία], sin dwelling within, Rom. 7:17, and

units.la: V
units.tr: V

units.la: n ἡ ἐνπερίσατος ἁμαρτία undiq; circumstans peccatum dicitur Heb. 12:1. 3. ab essecto duplici, primò facit omnes homines reos irae Dei, de quo Apostolus disputat Rom. 5. capite, secundò, efficit omnia peccata actualia, quorum est causa & radix: Unde ab Apostolo valdè emphaticè appellatur ἁμαρτία καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς, peccatum summè peccans. In his nihil desiderat Harscherus, Calvinum sine censura dimittit.
units.tr: hē euperistatos hamartia [ἡ ἐνπερίσατος ἁμαρτία], sin that surrounds us on every side, Heb. 12:1. 3. from its double effect: first, it makes all men liable to the wrath of God, of which the Apostle treats in Rom. chapter 5; second, it produces all actual sins, of which it is the cause and root. Hence the Apostle very emphatically calls it hamartia kath' hyperbolēn hamartōlos [ἁμαρτία καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς], sin sinning beyond measure. In these points Harscher finds nothing to object to, and lets Calvin pass without censure.

units.la: In altero Calvinus docet, illos qui peccatum originale concupiscentiae nomine appellârunt, tolerari posse, modò concupiscentiae vocabulum latius sumant, ut intellectui etiam & voluntati tribuatur.
units.tr: In the second passage Calvin teaches that those who have named original sin by the name of concupiscence may be tolerated, provided they take the word concupiscence more broadly, so that it is attributed also to the intellect and the will.

units.la: Hoc carpit nunc Jesuita, clamans Calvinum peccatum originale negare, quia concupiscentia non sit peccatum, nec insit parvulis, sit etiam in alio maior, in alio minor. Quae tria de peccato originali dici non possint. Sed debebat Profeffor controversiarum suos discipulos de vero controversiæ statu fideliter instituere, quod cùm non fecerit, ego id pro declaratione & defenfione sententiæ orthodoxæ hoc loco faciam. Nam non tantùm Harfcherus, sed & Bellarminus & Becanus hic fraudulenter agunt.
units.tr: This is what the Jesuit now carps at, shouting that Calvin denies original sin because concupiscence is not sin, and is not in infants, and is greater in one person and less in another. These three things cannot be said of original sin. But the Professor of controversies ought to have faithfully instructed his disciples on the true state of the controversy; since he has not done so, I shall do it here, for the explanation and defence of the orthodox opinion. For not only Harscher, but also Bellarmine and Becanus act fraudulently here.

units.la: Observandum igitur, quid orthodoxi nominibus peccati originalis & concupiscentiæ intelligant. Peccati originalis nomine intelligunt naturalem hominis vitiositatem, depravationem & corruptionem, omnibus hominibus naturaliter ex Adamo descendentibus inexistentem, immissam posteris propter reatum peccati Adami. Corruptio illa partim privativa partim positiva est.
units.tr: It must therefore be observed what the orthodox mean by the terms original sin and concupiscence. By the name of original sin they understand the natural vitiation, depravity and corruption of man, existing in all men who naturally descend from Adam, and transmitted to their posterity on account of the guilt of Adam's sin. That corruption is partly privative and partly positive.

units.la: Privativa corruptio est, quâ in homine lapso dona tum naturalia corrupta sunt, tum supernaturalia sublata.
units.tr: The corruption is privative by which, in fallen man, natural gifts are corrupted and supernatural gifts are taken away.

units.la: Nam licet intellectus, voluntas & appetitus permanserint, est tamen intellectus obtenebratus, voluntas depravata, & inferior appetitus totaliter vitiatus, supernaturalia autem penitus sunt sublata, nempe intellectûs claritas, voluntatis rectitudo & appetitus cum ratione conformitas.
units.tr: For although the intellect, the will and the appetite have remained, nevertheless the intellect is darkened, the will is depraved, and the lower appetite is wholly vitiated; but supernatural gifts are utterly taken away, namely the clarity of the intellect, the rectitude of the will, and the conformity of the appetite with reason.

units.la: Positiva corruptio est, quâ præter illam iustitiæ originalis carentiam homo iam propensus est ad omne malum, id est, ad odium Dei & proximi. Scholastici vocant inordinatam dispositionem animæ. Thomas habitum corruptum. Huius pravæ dispositionis respectu Augustinus peccatum originale vocat vitium, quo claudicat omne humanum genus; utriusque respectu appellat cœnum, quo omnes nascuntur squalidi. Sacra vero scriptura eandem, concupiscentiam, nominat. Jacob. 1: 14,15.
units.tr: The corruption is positive by which, besides that lack of original righteousness, man is now inclined to every evil, that is, to hatred of God and of neighbour. The Schoolmen call it an inordinate disposition of the soul; Thomas calls it a corrupt habit. With respect to this depraved disposition, Augustine calls original sin a vice, by which the whole human race limps; with respect to both, he calls it a filth, in which all are born squalid. Holy Scripture names the same thing concupiscence. James 1:14, 15.

units.la: Concupiscentiæ (ἐπιθυμίας) vocabulum ambiguum est, significat enim physicè, tùm facultatem naturalem concupiscendi & appetendi,tum actum ex facultate illa procedentem. Illa vocatur potentia concupiscibilis, barbarè concupiscibilitas, Græcè [illegible, ~6 letters]: hæc actualis concupiscentia. Sunt autem actus illi vel primi, vel secundi, qui boni & ordinati dicuntur, si sint consentanei legi divinæ respectu obiecti, modi & finis. Atquè hæc concupiscentia fuit in Adamo ante lapsum, cuius autor fuit Deus, & etiamnum in homine est, pertinens ad naturæ constitutionem, nisi quòd nunc post lapsum vitiata est. In se autem spectata sinè adiacente vitiositate peccatum omninò non est, neque Calvinus aut alius ullus ex orthodoxis Theologis hac significatione eam peccatum appellavit. Quia hac ratione Deus autor peccati statueretur, quod longè à nobis absit. Alio igitur modo eam considerant nimirum ethicè seu moraliter respectu obiecti circa quòd versatur & modi secundum quem ut & finis propter quē concupiscentia agit, quorum respectu illa vel ordinata vel inordinata dicitur. Ordinata, cum fertur in obiectum licitum & lege Dei non prohibitum, modo licito & ad Dei gloriam. Inordinata vero cum fertur in res legibus divinis prohibitas, modo excessivo vel defectivo.
units.tr: The word concupiscence (epithymias [ἐπιθυμίας]) is ambiguous, for physically it signifies both the natural faculty of desiring and longing, and the act proceeding from that faculty. The former is called the concupiscible power, in barbarous Latin concupiscibility, in Greek [illegible in the scan]; the latter is actual concupiscence. These acts are either first or second acts, and are called good and ordered if they accord with the divine law as regards object, mode and end. This concupiscence was in Adam before the fall, and God was its author, and it is still in man, belonging to the constitution of nature, except that now after the fall it is vitiated. Considered in itself, without an adhering vitiosity, it is by no means sin, and neither Calvin nor any other of the orthodox theologians has called it sin in this sense. For in this way God would be made the author of sin, which is far from us. They consider it, therefore, in another way, namely ethically or morally, with respect to the object with which it is concerned, and the mode according to which it acts, and the end for the sake of which concupiscence acts; with respect to these it is called either ordered or inordinate. It is ordered when it is directed to a lawful object not forbidden by the law of God, in a lawful manner and to the glory of God. It is inordinate when it is directed to things forbidden by the divine laws, in an excessive or defective manner.

units.la: De ordinata illa iterum nulla quæstio habetur, nam procul dubio peccatum Calvino non est. Quando itaque Orthodoxi concupiscentiam peccatum appellant, intelligunt concupiscentiam illam inordinatam legi Dei contrariam, quâ caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, Gal. 5: 17. omni homini vel potentialiter vel actualiter inexistentem. Quæ tamen concupiscentia totum peccatum originale non est, sed eius pars, post lapsum facultati naturali subintroducta. Peccatum autem illam appellant, cùm scriptura sacra, quæ de peccato non tantùm formaliter sed etiam materialiter loquitur. Nam peccatum non habet propriam ὑπόστασιν, aut ὁσὶν ἀνυπόστατον, ut Basilius docet, ideo est in subiecto veluti quædam διάθεσις, hinc fit ut sæpè subiectum simul cum peccato, peccati nomine veniat. Unde Augustinus peccatum definivit, voluntatem retinendi vel consequendi, quod justitia vetat.
units.tr: Concerning the ordered kind there is again no question, for undoubtedly it is not sin to Calvin. When therefore the orthodox call concupiscence sin, they mean that inordinate concupiscence contrary to the law of God, by which the flesh lusts against the Spirit, Gal. 5:17, existing in every man either potentially or actually. Yet this concupiscence is not the whole of original sin, but a part of it, introduced into the natural faculty after the fall. They call it sin, however, since Holy Scripture speaks of sin not only formally but also materially. For sin has no proper hypostasis, or is anhypostaton [ἀνυπόστατον], as Basil teaches; therefore it exists in a subject as a certain diathesis [διάθεσις]; hence it happens that often the subject, together with the sin, comes under the name of sin. Whence Augustine defined sin as the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids.

units.la: Atquè hæc corruptio naturalis concupiscendi adversùs legem Dei non saltem est in inferiori animæ parte, quam Scholastici sensualitatem vocant, sed etiam in superiori, putà in intellectu & voluntate, quod scriptura multis in locis docet, cuius authoritate convictus Bellarminus scribit non negandum esse in parte superiore simile etiam vitium inveniri. Et probat verbis Apostoli in epistola ad Gal. 5: v. 17. & sequentibus, ubi Apostolus carnis concupiscentiæ obiecta etiam facit idoidolatriam, hæresin, invidiam & inimicitiam. Becanus quoque id apertis verbis confitetur. Nec obstat, quòd carnis concupiscentia vocatur, quia caro hic accipitur pro toto homine ex anima & corpore constante, quod non negat Maldonatus Jesuita, in comment. cap. 3. in Johann. Quòd autem scriptura concupiscentiam carni tribuit, fit, quia respicit ad generationem & propagationem carnalem ex Adamo, ex quo uno homine peccatum in mundum introiit, Rom. 5: 12. Hinc etiam homo consideratus iuxta generationem carnalem per Spiritum sanctū nondum regeneratus, carnalis dicitur, qui non intelligit, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, 1. Cor. 2.
units.tr: And this natural corruption of desiring against the law of God is not only in the lower part of the soul, which the Schoolmen call sensuality, but also in the higher part, namely in the intellect and the will, which Scripture teaches in many places; Bellarmine, convinced by its authority, writes that a similar vice is not to be denied to be found also in the higher part. And he proves it by the words of the Apostle in the epistle to the Galatians 5:17 and following, where the Apostle also reckons among the objects of the lust of the flesh idolatry, heresy, envy and enmity. Becanus also confesses this in plain words. Nor does it stand in the way that it is called the lust of the flesh, because flesh here is taken for the whole man consisting of soul and body, which the Jesuit Maldonatus does not deny, in his commentary on John chapter 3. But that Scripture attributes concupiscence to the flesh is because it looks to carnal generation and propagation from Adam, through whom alone sin entered the world, Rom. 5:12. Hence also man, considered according to carnal generation and not yet regenerated by the Holy Spirit, is called carnal, who does not understand the things of the Spirit of God, 1 Cor. 2.

units.la: Ut ergò breviter concludam, respondeo ad verba Harscheri scribentis primò, atqui concupiscentia hæc non est peccatum, verum esse quatenus est facultas à Deo creata, aut actus legi Dei conformis, secundum modum & finem eius: est autem peccatum, materialiter simul cum inordinata dispositione consideratā, quatenus est contraria legi Dei. Secundò, vix est in parvulis, respondeo, imò in omnibus est æqualiter, secundùm potentiam seu in actu primo, vix dum conceptis & nondum natis, ut rapacitas in catulis luporum, quæ crescente ætate se magis magisquè exerit. Hinc Psalmista confitetur: En in iniquitate conceptus sum, & in peccato me fovit mater mea, Psal. 51: 7. Tertiò major in uno reperitur quàm in altero, respondeo, quo ad actum secundum concedo, nego quo ad potentiam, aut actum primum.
units.tr: To conclude briefly, I reply to the words of Harscher, who first writes: but this concupiscence is not sin. This is true insofar as it is a faculty created by God, or an act conformable to the law of God according to its mode and end. But it is sin, materially considered together with the disordered disposition, insofar as it is contrary to the law of God. Second, he says it is scarcely in infants. I reply that it is indeed in all equally, according to power or in first act, even in those who are scarcely yet conceived and not yet born, as rapacity is in wolf cubs, which grows and shows itself more and more as age advances. Hence the Psalmist confesses: Behold, I was conceived in iniquity, and in sin my mother cherished me, Ps. 51:7. Third, he says it is found greater in one than in another. I reply that as to second act I concede this, but as to power or first act I deny it.

units.la: Pergit nunc Jesuita & accusat Zwinglium his verbis: Zwinglius lib. de baptismo tract. 3. in digressione de peccato originali sic scribit: Theologi morbum hunc & contagionem animæ nostræ hereditariam peccatum originale vocare consueverunt, Pauli Apostoli dictum, quo utitur ad ad Rom. 5. minùs probè intelligentes. Qui enim fieri potest, ut quod morbus & contagio est, peccati nomen mereatur, vel peccatum veré sit? Item in declaratione de peccato originis initio. Quid brevius aut clarius dici potuit, quàm originale peccatum, non esse peccatum sed morbum, & Christianorum liberos propter morbum istum non addici æterno supplicio? Contra verò quid imbecillius dici potuit & à canonica scriptura alienius, quàm baptismi lavacro hanc calamitatem levari, & non tantùm esse morbum sed etiam reatum. Et infra: Hoc volo culpam originalem non veré sed metonymicè à primi parentis admisso, culpam vocari, esse autem nihil aliud, quàm conditionem miseram illam quidem & multò leviorem quàm crimen mereatur. Et inferius: Est ergò ista ad peccandum amore sui propensio peccatum originale, qua quidem propensio non est proprie peccatum, sed fons quidam & ingenium. Hæc Zvvinglii verba sunt, quibus addit Pater Harscher iudicium proprium; Itaq; Zvvinglius glius negat peccatum originale esse peccatum, negat originale tolli aut deleri.
units.tr: The Jesuit now goes on and accuses Zwingli in these words: Zwingli, in his book on baptism, tract 3, in the digression on original sin, writes thus: Theologians have been accustomed to call this disease and hereditary contagion of our soul original sin, using the saying of the Apostle Paul in Romans 5, understanding it rather poorly. For how can that which is a disease and a contagion deserve the name of sin, or truly be sin? Likewise in the declaration on the origin of sin, at the beginning: What could be said more briefly or more clearly than that original sin is not sin but a disease, and that the children of Christians are not doomed to eternal punishment because of this disease? On the contrary, what could be said more feebly, and more alien to canonical Scripture, than that this calamity is lightened by the washing of baptism, and that it is not only a disease but also guilt? And below: I wish to say that original guilt is called guilt not truly but metonymically, from the offence of our first parent, and that it is nothing other than that wretched condition, indeed much lighter than a crime deserves. And further on: Therefore this propensity to sin out of self-love is original sin, which propensity is properly not sin but a certain source and inclination. These are the words of Zwingli, to which Father Harscher adds his own judgment: "Thus Zwingli denies that original sin is sin, and denies that original sin is taken away or blotted out."

units.la: Zwinglium ita locutum esse non diffiteor. Sed videndum, quo sensu & modo ita sit locutus.
units.tr: I do not deny that Zwingli spoke in this way. But we must consider in what sense and manner he spoke thus.

units.la: Peccatum originis in quo omnes homines nascuntur, plures habet respectus. Nam primo si consideratur respectu peccati Adami, est reatus, quo nascentes propter lapsum Adami, rei sunt irae Dei & mortis aeternae. Apostolus eam ob causam omnes homines vocat filios irae, non solum facto nostro sed etiam naturae vitio. Sic est poena peccati primi. Secundo, Quatenus est carentia iustitiae originalis debitae inesse, ut Anshelmus imperfecte peccatum originale definit, quam scriptura vocat caecitatem mentis 2. Cor. 3: 14. & desectionem gloriae Dei Rom. 3: 23. Sic mera est privatio. Tertio, Quatenus, intellectum, voluntatem & appetitum contrario habitu afficit, qui in locum originalis iustitiæ successit, qui in scripturis appellatur figmentum cordis Gen. 6: 5. præputium cordis, Deut. 10: 16. & concupiscentia carnis 1. Joh. 2: 16. sic est aliquid positivum, inordinata nimirum dispositio proveniens ex dissolutione harmoniæ superiorum & inferiorum facultatum animæ, in qua ratio originalis iustitiæ consistebat. Quarto, quatenus est radix omnium peccatorum actualium, sic est mater concipiens, pariens & gignens peccatum. Non autem est peccatum tale quale produxit, id est, consummatum, ut Jacobus docet, Jacob. 1: 15. quia causa non est effectum: seu non est actuale dictum aut factum contra legem Dei. Est tamen suo modo peccatum, quia est ἀνομία, legi Dei non conformis. Propter varios hosce respectus variè etiam Theologi orthodoxi peccatum originale definiverunt. Zvvinglius considerans peccatum originale, quatenus est pravitas quædam naturæ, desectio iustitiæ originalis & mala difpositio : considerans etiam ftrictiorem definitionem peccati, quâ definitur, quo in cogitationibus, dictis aut factis lex Dei violatur, scripsit peccatum originale non esse peccatum, nempe eo modo quo peccatum actuale peccatum dicitur. Sed esse morbum & contagionem animæ. A' quo loquendi genere non abhorret Becanus in manuali. Interea non negat Zwinglius, quòd plane non sit peccatum, cùm expresse scribat tale esse peccatum, ut quicunque in eo nascuntur hostes sint & adversarii Dei.
units.tr: The sin of origin, in which all men are born, has several aspects. For first, if it is considered with respect to the sin of Adam, it is guilt, by which those who are born, because of the fall of Adam, are liable to the wrath of God and to eternal death. For this reason the Apostle calls all men children of wrath, not only by our deed but also by the vice of nature. Thus it is the punishment of the first sin. Second, insofar as it is the lack of the original righteousness that ought to be present, as Anselm imperfectly defines original sin, which Scripture calls blindness of mind, 2 Cor. 3:14, and the falling short of the glory of God, Rom. 3:23. Thus it is pure privation. Third, insofar as it affects the intellect, will and appetite with a contrary habit, which succeeded in the place of original righteousness, and which in the Scriptures is called the imagination of the heart, Gen. 6:5, the foreskin of the heart, Deut. 10:16, and the concupiscence of the flesh, 1 John 2:16. Thus it is something positive, namely a disordered disposition arising from the dissolution of the harmony of the superior and inferior faculties of the soul, in which the order of original righteousness consisted. Fourth, insofar as it is the root of all actual sins, thus it is the mother that conceives, bears and begets sin. Yet it is not sin in the form that it produces, that is, fully completed, as James teaches, James 1:15, because the cause is not the effect; nor is it an actual word or deed against the law of God. Nevertheless it is sin in its own way, because it is lawlessness [ἀνομία], not conformable to the law of God. Because of these various aspects, orthodox theologians have also defined original sin in various ways. Zwingli, considering original sin insofar as it is a certain corruption of nature, a defect of original righteousness and a bad disposition, and also considering the stricter definition of sin, by which sin is defined as that in which the law of God is violated in thoughts, words or deeds, wrote that original sin is not sin, namely in the way in which actual sin is called sin; but that it is a disease and contagion of the soul. Becanus in his Manual does not shrink from this way of speaking. Meanwhile Zwingli does not deny that it is plainly sin, since he expressly writes that it is such a sin that all who are born in it are enemies and adversaries of God.

units.la: Simili modo Hieronymus ex Cypriano dicit lib. 3. adversùs Pelag. Infans recens natus nihil peccavit, nisi quod secundùm Adam carnaliter natus, contagium mortis antiquæ prima nativitate contraxit. Et Augustinus lib.I.cont.Julianum cap.2.scribit: Iohannes Constant. dixisse, parvulos non habere peccata nempe, propria. Et addit Augustinus: comparans ergo eos Iohannes majoribus, quorum propria peccata dimittuntur in baptismo, dixit eos non habere peccata.
units.tr: In a similar way Jerome, following Cyprian, says in book 3 against the Pelagians: A newly born infant has sinned nothing, except that, being born carnally according to Adam, he contracted by his first birth the contagion of ancient death. And Augustine, in book 1 against Julian, chapter 2, writes: John of Constantinople said that infants do not have sins, namely their own. And Augustine adds: Comparing them therefore with adults, whose own sins are forgiven in baptism, he said that they do not have sins.

units.la: Uterque ergo tum Calvinus tum Zwvinglius peccatum originale confessus est, in quo omnes carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendentes nascantur. Zwvinglius vero negans peccatum originale esse peccatum, voluit non esse peccatum definitione illa, qua peccatum actuale peccatum esse dicitur. Vide Zwvingl. Decl. peccat. origin. pag. 116.
units.tr: Both Calvin and Zwingli therefore confessed original sin, in which all who descend from Adam by carnal propagation are born. But Zwingli, in denying that original sin is sin, meant that it is not sin by that definition by which actual sin is said to be sin. See Zwingli, Declaration on original sin, p. 116.

units.la: Testimonia scripturae, quae pro confirmatione peccati originalis a Jesuita Harschero huic parallelo subiiciuntur, ex asse laudamus, nam sunt illa ex quibus nos peccatum originale afferimus, utpote Rom. 5: 12. 17. 2. Cor. 5: 15. Psal. 50: 7. Job. 14: 5. Sed non scio an parem gratiam meruerit apud reliquos Jesuitas, quia testimonia talia sunt, ut nulla ratione B. Virgo a peccato originali eximi possit.
units.tr: The testimonies of Scripture which the Jesuit Harscher adds to this parallel in support of original sin we praise without reserve, for they are those from which we too derive original sin, such as Rom. 5:12, 17; 2 Cor. 5:15; Ps. 50:7; Job 14:5. But I do not know whether he has earned the same favour among the other Jesuits, because such testimonies are of a kind that by no reasoning can the Blessed Virgin be exempted from original sin.

units.la: Sub finem tamé duo argumenta proponit, Calvini sententiæ, ut ille putat, opposita, quibus vult probare concupiscentiam non esse peccatum, ut contendit Calvinus. Primum est Jacobi, qui cap. 1: 15, 16. ita scribit: Unusquisque tentatur dum a propria cupiditate (concupiscentia suâ) abstrahitur & inescatur. Deinde concupiscentia postquam concepit, parit peccatum, peccatum autem cum consummatum fuerit parit mortem. Hæc verba, inquit, sic exponit Augustinus lib. 6. cont. Julianum cap. 5. profectò in his verbis partus à pariente discernitur, pariens enim est concupiscentia, partus peccatum.
units.tr: Toward the end, however, he puts forward two arguments, which, as he thinks, are opposed to Calvin's view, by which he wishes to prove that concupiscence is not sin, as Calvin maintains. The first is from James, who in chapter 1:15-16 writes thus: Each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire (his own concupiscence). Then concupiscence, after it has conceived, brings forth sin, and sin, when it is fully grown, brings forth death. These words, he says, Augustine expounds thus in book 6 against Julian, chapter 5: Surely in these words the offspring is distinguished from the parent, for the parent is concupiscence, the offspring sin.

units.la: Vult Harscherus cum omnibus aliis Jesuitis, concupiscentiam non esse peccatum, quia pariens non est partus ipse, caussa non est effectus.
units.tr: Harscher, with all the other Jesuits, wishes to maintain that concupiscence is not sin, because the parent is not the offspring itself, the cause is not the effect.

units.la: Verba Jacobi non sunt propria sed modificata, metaphorica, inquani, metaphora â pariente muliere deduēta. Quemadmodum enim illa primò semen concipit, deinde iusto tempore parturit: ita inquit Jacobus, concupiscentia carnis (non facultas illa naturalis physicè considerata, sed inordinata illa cupiditas, quâ caro concupiscit adversùs spiritum) quæ est matrix omnium peccatorum, concipit semen peccati vel per sensus externos, vel per Diaboli suggestiones, & postea ex hoc impuro semine peccatum tanquam impurus fœtus gignitur. Sicuti ergò mater non est ipse filius, aut semen conceptum homo perfectus: ita libenter concedo, concupiscentiam illam pravam, quam peccatum originale vocamus, non esse ipsum peccatum consummatum, quod Jacobus voluit, sed tamen peccatum esse suo modo, nemo inficias ibit. Nam quia simile generat sibi simile, fieri non potest, quin concupiscentia illa sit corrupta & peccatum, quia fœtus id est peccatum consummatum peccatum quoque est. Huc respexit Jobus cap. 14. 5. quis edat mundum ex immundo. Augustinus valde eleganter pro hac explicatione: Quis tam imprudens, impudens, insanus, qui cum peccata mala esse fateatur, neget malam esse concupiscentiam peccatorum? cont. Julia. lib. 6. cap. 5.
units.tr: The words of James are not literal but figurative, I say, a metaphor drawn from a pregnant woman. For as she first conceives seed and then at the proper time gives birth, so, says James, the concupiscence of the flesh (not that natural faculty considered physically, but that disordered desire by which the flesh lusts against the spirit), which is the womb of all sins, conceives the seed of sin either through the external senses or through the suggestions of the Devil, and afterwards from this impure seed sin is begotten like an impure offspring. Just as, therefore, the mother is not the son herself, nor the conceived seed a complete man, so I willingly concede that that corrupt concupiscence, which we call original sin, is not sin fully completed, as James meant, but nevertheless that it is sin in its own way; no one will deny this. For since like begets like, it cannot be that that concupiscence is not corrupt and sin, because the offspring, that is, completed sin, is sin also. Job looked to this in chapter 14:4: who brings a clean thing out of an unclean? Augustine, very elegantly, in support of this explanation: Who is so imprudent, shameless and insane that, while confessing that sins are evil, he denies that the concupiscence of sins is evil? Against Julian, book 6, chapter 5.

units.la: Alterum testimonium est Pauli Apostoli Rom. 8: 1. Nulla igitur condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Harscherus ita ratiocinatur: Nihil est condemnationis iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu: Sed concupiscentia est in iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Ergo concupiscentia non est aliquid damnationis.
units.tr: Another testimony is that of the Apostle Paul, Rom. 8:1. Therefore there is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. Harscher reasons thus: There is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus; but concupiscence is in those who are in Christ Jesus. Therefore concupiscence is not anything of condemnation.

units.la: Respondeo. Propositionem maiorem esse sophistice propositam, ut sallere posset lectorem. Nam non dicit Apostolus, nihil esse damnationis in iis qui sunt in Christo Jesu, sed nullam esse condemnationem iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Graece οὐδὲν (neutrum adiectivum) χρίμα, nulla condemnatio, ut Erasmus habet, & ineptè Vulgatus adverbialiter per nihil interpretatur. Ideo est aperta falsatio textus. Nam Apostolus qui fuit in Christo Iesu & damnationem non metuit, ut in hoc ipso capite testatur v. 34. Quis est qui condemnet? tamen in se sensit, sibi adjacere malum, & in membris suis esse legem belligerantem adversus legem mentis suae, & captivum reddentem se lege peccati.
units.tr: I answer that the major premise is sophistically framed, so as to be able to deceive the reader. For the Apostle does not say that there is nothing of condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus, but that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. In Greek it is οὐδὲν κρίμα [ouden krima], "no condemnation" (οὐδὲν being a neuter adjective), as Erasmus renders it. The Vulgate translator, clumsily, renders it adverbially by nihil. So this is a plain falsification of the text. For the Apostle, who was in Christ Jesus and did not fear condemnation, as he attests in this same chapter at v. 34, Who is he that condemneth?, nevertheless perceived in himself that evil lay close to him, and that in his members there was a law warring against the law of his mind, making him captive to the law of sin.

units.la: Si quis obiiciat concupiscentiam pravam semper esse damnabilem, si ergo illa in renatis manet quomodo illos non potest manere damnatio?
units.tr: If someone objects that wicked concupiscence is always blameworthy, and that if it remains in the regenerate, condemnation cannot fail to remain in them as well, how is that possible?

units.la: Resp. Concupiscentiam malam in se absolutè spectatam omninò damnabilem esse etiam in renatis, fieri autem indamnabilem per accidens propter iustificationem Christi. Unde Paulus Rom. 8: 33, 34. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est qui justificat. Quis Quis est qui condemnet? Christus est qui mortuus est, &c. Certè si concupiscentia illa peccatum non esset in renatis, nemo renatorum peccaret, quia sublata caussa tollitur effectus. At nullus homo, quamvis magna sanctitate praeditus absque peccato existit, ut Augustinus multis in locis docet. Videatur etiam Hieronymus lib. 3. adversus Pelagianos.
units.tr: I answer: concupiscence, considered absolutely in itself, is wholly blameworthy even in the regenerate, but it becomes non-blameworthy by accident, on account of the justification of Christ. Hence Paul, Rom. 8:33, 34: Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, etc. Surely if that concupiscence were not sin in the regenerate, none of the regenerate would sin, since the effect is removed when the cause is removed. But no man, however great his holiness, exists without sin, as Augustine teaches in many places. See also Jerome, book 3 against the Pelagians.

units.la: PARALLELUM III.
units.tr: PARALLEL III.

units.la: Calvinus lib. 4. Instit. cap. 8. §. 8. Ēsto igitur hoc firmum axioma, non aliud habendum esse Dei verbum, cui detur in ecclesia locus, quàm quod lege primùm, deinde scriptis Apostolicis continetur.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes book 4, ch. 8, §8: Let this therefore be a firm axiom: that no other word of God is to be held as having a place in the Church than that which is contained first in the law and then in the apostolic writings.

units.la: Et hic Pelagianizare Calvinum vult Harscherus. Sed si diligenter inspicias utrumque locum Calvini & Pelagii, videbis haec parùm παραλλήλως dicta esse. Nam Pelagius loco ab Harschero citato, non docet quidnam pro verbo Dei habendum, quod facit Calvinus, sed quomodo ex Dei verbo argumentandum sit. Voluit enim Pelagius nihil esse credendum, aut asserendum, nisi quod expressis & perspicuis verbis scripturæ continetur. Sic enim ille apud Augustinum ratiocinabatur: Si Abel peccasset scriptura hoc dixisset (nempe expressis verbis.) Atqui non dixit scriptura Abelem peccasse. Ergo Abel non peccavit. Hæc argumentandi ratio longè abest à Calvino & Orthodoxis, utpote qui Nazianzeni regulam sequuntur, qui docet quædam in scriptura esse, quæ non dicuntur. Ideo Augustino assurgunt nostri, ad minorem Pelagiani syllogismi respondenti, argumentando à genere ad speciem, hoc modo: Si illa sententia Apostoli, (per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines pertransiit, in quo omnes peccarunt,) & antiquos & recentiores & & nos & posteros nostros complectitur, sequitur etiam Abelem peccasse. Nullus itaque hic est parallelismus.
units.tr: Here too Harscher wishes to charge Calvin with Pelagianism. But if you examine both passages carefully, Calvin's and Pelagius', you will see that these things are said not at all in parallel [παραλλήλως]. For Pelagius, in the place Harscher cites, does not teach what is to be held as the word of God, which is what Calvin does, but how one ought to argue from the word of God. Pelagius wished that nothing be believed or asserted except what is contained in Scripture in express and plain words. For so he reasoned, as Augustine reports: If Abel had sinned, Scripture would have said so (namely in express words). But Scripture does not say that Abel sinned. Therefore Abel did not sin. This mode of arguing is far from Calvin and the Orthodox, who follow the rule of Nazianzen, who teaches that there are some things in Scripture which are not said. Hence our writers rise up for Augustine, answering the minor premise of the Pelagian syllogism by arguing from genus to species, in this way: If that saying of the Apostle, (through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned) embraces ancients and more recent, and us and our posterity, it follows that Abel also sinned. So there is no parallel here.

units.la: Interim non diffiteor Calvinum & cum ipso Theologos Orthodoxos traditiones dogmaticas, quas Pontificii praeter & contra scripturam urgent, & ecclesiae tanquam ad salutem necessarias obtrudunt, reiicere. Nam traditiones cum verbo conjungere est miscere aquam cum vino, inquit Irenæus lib 3. cap. 1. Et graviter Hieronymus in Agg. c. 1. Quae absque authoritate & testimoniis scripturarum quasi apostolica traditione sponte reperiunt & confingunt percutit gladius Dei. Cùm itaque Bellarminus fateatur traditiones non fuisse scripturae committendas, quòd mysteria sint populo non divulganda, & hac ratione in scriptura non contineantur, sequitur secundùm Hieronymi iudicium illas gladio Dei percutiendas esse.
units.tr: Meanwhile I do not deny that Calvin, and with him the Orthodox theologians, reject the dogmatic traditions which the Papists press beside and against Scripture, and thrust upon the Church as necessary to salvation. For to join tradition to the word is to mix water with wine, says Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 1. And Jerome, sharply, on Haggai ch. 1: Those things which they devise and invent of their own accord, without the authority and testimonies of Scripture, as if they were apostolic tradition, the sword of God strikes down. Since therefore Bellarmine admits that traditions were not to be committed to Scripture, because the mysteries are not to be divulged to the people, and for this reason are not contained in Scripture, it follows, by Jerome's judgment, that they are to be struck down by the sword of God.

units.la: Sed contra hanc sententiam nostram disputat Harscherus Jesuita, & primò testimonia scripturæ, deinde Basilium citat, tertiò exempla profert eorum quæ creduntur nec leguntur, & denique D. Molinæi argumentum examinat. De singulis ordine.
units.tr: But against this view of ours the Jesuit Harscher disputes. He first cites testimonies of Scripture, then Basil, thirdly brings examples of things that are believed but not read, and finally examines the argument of D. Molinaeus. I take them in order.

units.la: Testimonia scripturæ sunt, Psal. 44. Deus auribus nostris audivimus, patres nostri annuntiaverunt nobis, opus quod operatus es in diebus eorum, & in diebus antiquis. Psal. 77: Quanta mandavit patribus nostris nota facere filiis suis, ut cognoscat generatio altera, filii qui nascuntur & exurgent & narrabunt filiis suis. Act. 15. Perambulabat autem (Paulus) Syriam & Ciliciam confirmans ecclesias, præcipiens custodire præcepta Apostolorum & seniorum. Et cap. 16. Cùm autem pertransirent civitates, tradebant eis custodire dogmata, quæ erant decreta ab Apostolis & senioribus, qui erant Ierosolymis.
units.tr: The testimonies of Scripture are: Psalm 44: We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work that thou didst in their days, in the times of old. Psalm 77: What he commanded our fathers, that they should make known to their children, so that the generation to come might know them, the children who shall be born, and arise and declare them to their children. Acts 15: And he (Paul) went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches, commanding them to keep the precepts of the apostles and elders. And ch. 16: And as they went through the cities, they delivered to them to keep the decrees that were decided by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem.

units.la: Mirabilis plane philosophia est philosophia Jesuitica. In qua nunc valet posito uno subordinatorum removere reliqua, contra tritissimum canonem; subordinata non pugnant. Quasi vero ea quae à patribus nuntiantur filiis, non etiam possint esse scripta? Aut quae ab Apostolis viva voce praedicata non potuerint in scripturam postea referri? An ergo, si ego aut alius aliquis annuntiet posteris omnia mendacia illa, quibus religionem nostram conspurcant Jesuitae in suis libris illa propterea non sunt scripta? An nulla possumus commemorare historica lecta?
units.tr: Truly the Jesuit philosophy is a marvellous philosophy. In it, it now holds that once one of the subordinates is posited, the rest may be removed, against the most trite canon: subordinates do not contradict. As if indeed those things which the fathers announce to their children could not also be written? Or those things preached by the apostles by living voice could not afterwards be recorded in Scripture? Then if I, or anyone else, should announce to posterity all those lies with which the Jesuits defile our religion in their books, are those not written for that reason? Or can we not record historical matters that have been read?

units.la: Et, ut videat, lector quàm appositè illa testimonia proferantur producam integra loca. Psal. 44. clamat ecclesia tempore psalmistae: ô Deus auribus nostris audivimus, majores nostri narraverunt nobis opus, quod operatus es in diebus eorum? Quodnam verò est opus illud? Hoc psalmista addit: te manu tua gentes expulisse & plantasse ipsos, malo affecisse nationes, & propagasse ipsos. Non enim gladio suo hereditario jure possederunt terram, & brachium eorum non dedit salutem eis.
units.tr: And so that the reader may see how aptly those testimonies are brought forward, I shall produce the passages entire. In Psalm 44 the Church, in the psalmist's time, cries: O God, with our ears we have heard; our elders have told us the work which thou didst in their days? What, then, is that work? The psalmist adds this: how thou by thy hand didst drive out the nations and plant them, didst afflict the peoples and spread them abroad. For they did not possess the land by their own sword, by hereditary right, and their arm did not give them salvation.

units.la: Haec omnia scripta sunt in libro secundo Moisis, quem Exodum appellamus, & libro Josuae. Lyra: opus quod operatus es in diebus eorum, id est, Moisis, Josuae & aliorum patrum. Manus tua gentes disperdidit. i. e. quae habitabant in terra promissionis. Et plantasti eos, id est, filios Israelis in eadem terra.
units.tr: All these things are written in the second book of Moses, which we call Exodus, and in the book of Joshua. Lyra: the work which thou didst in their days, that is, of Moses, Joshua and the other fathers. Thy hand destroyed the nations, i.e. those who dwelt in the land of promise. And thou didst plant them, that is, the sons of Israel in the same land.

units.la: Psal. 77. Praecepit majoribus nostris, nota facere filiis ipsorum, ut sciat generatio posteta, &c. Quaenam vero sunt illa? hoc in sequentibus versiculis docet: Miracula quae fecerat coram majoribus eorum, terra AEgypti & agro Tanitico, Diffiderat mare, ut traduceret eos, statuens aquas tanquam acervum. Deduxerat eos nube interdiu, & totam noctem lucente igne. Fiderat rupes in deserto, &c. Haec a Mose fidelissimo Dei amanuensi perscripta sunt. Vide quam ridiculi fiant homihomines illi in argumentationibus suis. Dum enim de traditionibus non scriptis disputant, illi mera scripta protulerunt.
units.tr: Psalm 77: He commanded our fathers to make them known to their children, that the generation to come might know, etc. But what are those things? He teaches this in the following verses: The miracles which he had done before their fathers, in the land of Egypt and the field of Tanis. He divided the sea to lead them through, and made the waters stand like a heap. He led them by a cloud in the daytime, and all the night by a light of fire. He clave the rocks in the wilderness, etc. These things were written down by Moses, God's most faithful amanuensis. See how ridiculous these men become in their arguments. For while they dispute about unwritten traditions, they have produced plain writings.

units.la: Quod ex actis Apostolicis cap. 15. de Paulo in Syria & Cilicia ecclesias confirmante & praecipiente praecepta Apostolorum & seniorum custodire, scribit, in nullis graecis codicibus legitur. Ad alterum vero, ex cap. 16. de Paulo & Timotheo tradentibus servanda instituta & decreta Apostolorum & Presbyterorum, adductum, respondeo, illa esse instituta & decreta synodica Apostolorum & seniorum descripta cap. 15:28,29. Visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis, ne quid amplius imponeremus vobis oneris praeter necessaria ista; ut abstineatis ab iis, quae sunt immolata simulachris, & sanguine, & suffocatis rebus, & scortatione, a quibus si vobis caveritis bene agetis. Hoc recte observavit Lyranus in notis ad hunc locum: praecipiens custodire praecepta Apostolorum posita posita cap. praecedente, ad unionem gentilium & Iudaeorum.
units.tr: As for the claim, drawn from Acts ch. 15, that Paul, confirming the churches in Syria and Cilicia, commanded them to keep the precepts of the apostles and elders, it is not read in any Greek manuscripts. As for the other passage, adduced from ch. 16, where Paul and Timothy delivered for observance the institutions and decrees of the Apostles and Presbyters, I answer that these were the synodical institutions and decrees of the apostles and elders, set down in ch. 15:28, 29: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Lyra rightly observed this in his notes on this passage: commanding the keeping of the precepts of the apostles, set down in the preceding chapter, for the union of Gentiles and Jews.

units.la: Pergit Jesuita 1. Cor. 11. Laudo autem vos, quòd per omnia mei memores estis, & sicuti tradidi vobis praecepta mea tenetis. Et in fine capitis, cum plura de communione celebranda scripsisset subdit; cetera vero cum venero disponam 2. Thess. cap. 2 Itaque fratres state & tenete traditiones, quas didicistis sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam.
units.tr: The Jesuit goes on: 1 Cor. 11. "Now I praise you, brethren, that you remember me in all things, and keep the precepts as I delivered them to you." And at the end of the chapter, after writing at length about celebrating the communion, he adds: "The rest I will set in order when I come." 2 Thess. 2: "So then, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle."

units.la: Ad haec testimonia toties nostris obiecta, iam dudum sufficienter fuit responsum. Ego breviter dico. Primo, duplicem fuisse praedicandi Evangelii modum per Apostolos usurpatu, quod Clem. Alexandrinus erudite observavit, δια λόγου [?] & δι᾽ ἐπιστολῆς. Quemadmodum autem non sequitur; haec in epistolis scripta sunt, ergo non fuerunt viva voce praedicata: ita non licet concludere, haec praedicata sunt viva voce, ergo non sunt in epistolas relata. Nam hi modi non opponuntur. Hinc fit, quòd
units.tr: To these testimonies, which have so often been objected to us, a sufficient answer was given long ago. I will say briefly. First, the Apostles used a twofold mode of preaching the Gospel, which Clement of Alexandria observed learnedly: by word [διὰ λόγου] [?] and by letter [δι᾽ ἐπιστολῆς]. Just as it does not follow that, because these things were written in epistles, they were not preached by living voice, so it is not permissible to conclude that, because these things were preached by living voice, they were not committed to epistles. For these modes are not opposed to each other. Hence it comes about that

units.la: Note: the Greek words in the printed line are read with doubt and marked accordingly. quòd orationes Petri ad populum habitæ viva voce, nunc scriptæ reperiantur à Luca in Actis apostolicis. Committunt ergo Pontificii elenchum oppositorum, quotiescunque negant ea, quæ sermone fuerunt ab Apostolis tradita, scripta non esse. Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 1. adversùs Hæresf. monet, Apostolos Evangelium primò prædicniavisse, postea per Dei voluntatem in scriptis nobis tradidisse. Quapropter Chrysostomus ad locum 1. Cor. 11. scribit, Apostolum ea, quæ ante admonuerat præsens, per epistolam nunc tanquam doctum medicum infundere.
units.tr: the speeches of Peter delivered to the people by living voice are now found written down by Luke in the Acts of the Apostles. The Papists therefore commit the fallacy of opposites whenever they deny that what the Apostles handed down in speech was written. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1, against heresies, warns that the Apostles first preached the Gospel and afterwards, by God's will, handed it down to us in writings. Wherefore Chrysostom, on 1 Cor. 11, writes that the Apostle, having been present, now pours into a letter what he had earlier admonished, like a learned physician.

units.la: Hæc sufficere possent omnibus tribus locis explicandis. Sed præterea dico 1. Non posse Pontificios quicquam solidi ex hisce locis concludere, nisi αὐθεντικῶς demonstrent se habere illas ipsas traditiones, de quibus hîc fit sermo, & quas illi asserunt, scriptas non esse. 2. Non esse verosimile Pontificios præcepta ἀγραφα Apostoli Pauli habere, primò quia traditiones Pontificiæ pleræque, de quibus disputamus, sunt traditiones Ethnicorum, quales procul dubio Apostoli non tradiderùt, secundò quia successu temporis in Ecclesiam sunt introductæ omnes illorum traditiones, unde sequitur aut non esse apostolicas, aut summam fuisse negligentiam Pontificum Romanorum, quòd non citius eas Ecclesiæ præceperint, tertiò, Concedere nos libëter, fuisse rituales aliquas seu ecclesiasticas traditiones illis ecclesiis particulares, ad illarum ἐνωσεξίαν facientes, de quibus nulla est controversia, quia ad salutem non faciebant.
units.tr: These points might suffice for explaining all three passages. But I further say: 1. The Papists cannot conclude anything solid from these passages unless they demonstrate authentically [αὐθεντικῶς] that they possess those very traditions under discussion, which they assert were not written. 2. It is not likely that the Papists have the unwritten precepts [ἀγραφα] of the Apostle Paul. First, because most of the Papist traditions in dispute are traditions of the heathen, which the Apostles certainly did not hand down. Second, because all their traditions were introduced into the Church over the course of time, from which it follows either that they are not apostolic, or that the Roman Pontiffs were most negligent in not having them taught to the Church sooner. Third, we readily concede that there were some ritual or ecclesiastical traditions particular to those churches, serving their unity [ἐνωσεξίαν], about which there is no controversy, because they did not bear on salvation.

units.la: Accedit ad Basilii locum lib. de spirit. S cap. 27. Quem Bellarminus, Bailius, Becanus, & omnes alii traditionum non-scriptarum Patroni, veluti Achillis clypeum nobis opponunt. Is ita ab Harschero citatur: Dogmata quæ in Ecclesia seruantur ac prædicantur, partim ex conscripta doctrina habemus, partim ex Apostolorum traditione ad nos delata, in mysterio recipimus, quae utraque eandem ad pietatem vim habent, & nemo his contradicit, qui vel modicam saltem ecclesiasticorum juris experientiam habet: si enim aggrederemur non scripto proditas consuetudines, velut non magnam vim habentes reicere, imprudenter etiam ipsis principalibus evangelij partibus damnum inferremus, imo potius ipsam Evangelij praedicationem ad nudum nomen contraheremus; veluti verbi gratia, ut ejus quod primum & communissimum est, primam mentionem faciam: figura crucis signare eos, qui in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi spem habent, quis scripto docuit? ad orientem conversos esse nos dum oramus, quae scriptura docuit? Invocationis verba, dum conficitur panis eucharistiae & poculum benedictionis, quis sanctorum nobis reliquit? non enim his contenti sumus quorum Apostolus, aut Evangelium mentionem fecit, sed & ante & postea alia quaedam dicimus, velut magnum robur ad mysteria habentia, ex doctrina scripta non prodita, assumpta. Benedicimus aquam baptismatis & oleum unctionis, insuper illum qui baptizatur ex quibus scriptis? nonne tacita & arcana traditione? Ipsam vero olei illitionem, qua doctrina scripto docuit?
units.tr: Next comes the passage of Basil, in his book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 27, which Bellarmine, Bailly, Becanus and all the other patrons of unwritten traditions oppose to us like Achilles' shield. Harscher cites it thus: "The dogmas which are kept and proclaimed in the Church, partly from written teaching we have, partly we receive in mystery, handed down to us from the tradition of the Apostles; both have the same force for piety, and no one contradicts these who has even a modest experience of ecclesiastical law. For if we were to undertake to reject customs handed down unwritten, as not having great force, we would imprudently inflict harm even on the principal parts of the Gospel; indeed we would reduce the preaching of the Gospel to a bare name. For example, to mention first what is first and most common: who taught in writing to sign with the cross those who hope in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ? Who taught in Scripture that we turn towards the east when we pray? Who of the saints left us the words of invocation while the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing is made? For we are not content with those things of which the Apostle or the Gospel made mention, but both before and after we say certain other things, as having great weight for the mysteries, taken from unwritten, not published, teaching. We bless the water of baptism and the oil of anointing, and moreover the one who is baptized: from what writings? Is it not from silent and secret tradition? And the very anointing with oil: what written teaching taught it?"

units.la: Theologi Orthodoxi hic notant loci Basiliani dubiam fidem, versionem latinam corruptam & falsam Pontificiorum interpretationem.
units.tr: Orthodox theologians here note the doubtful trustworthiness of the passage of Basil, the corrupt and false Latin version, and the false interpretation of the Papists.

units.la: Dubiam huius loci fidem faciunt, Basilii confessio contraria, Erasmi observatio, Apostoli Pauli & Pontificiorum praxis, ut & scripturae sacrae authoritas.
units.tr: What makes the trustworthiness of this passage doubtful is Basil's contrary confession, Erasmus' observation, the practice of the Apostle Paul and of the Papists, and also the authority of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Basilius alibi traditiones scripturae sacrae assutas magno zelo reiicit. De vera fide: Haud dubia manifestissimum infidelitatis argumentum est, & signum superbiae certissimum, si quis eorum quae scripta sunt, aliquid velit reicere, aut eorum quae non scripta sunt introducere, cum Dominus noster Iesus Christus dixerit, oves mea vocem meam audiunt, alienorum vocem non sequuntur. Apostolus sumpto ex hominibus exemplo vehementissimè interdicit, ne quid eorum, quæ in divinis literis habentur dematur, aut quod absit addatur. In reg. brevi. reg. 95. Quæ ad usum pertinentia sunt, ea ut unusquisq; ex divinis literis ediscat & rectum & necessarium est, tum ad majorem expletionem animi in pietate, tùm etiam ut ne humanis constitutionibus assuescat. In his & aliis locis Basilius ea reiicit, quæ extra scripturam credenda proponuntur.
units.tr: Basil, elsewhere, rejects with great zeal traditions stitched on to Holy Scripture. On the true faith: "Without doubt it is a most manifest argument of unbelief, and a most certain sign of pride, if anyone wishes to reject any of the things that are written, or to introduce any of the things that are not written, since our Lord Jesus Christ said: my sheep hear my voice, and they do not follow the voice of strangers. The Apostle, taking an example from men, most vehemently forbids that anything of those things which are contained in the divine letters be removed, or, far be it, added." In the Short Rules, rule 95: "It is both right and necessary that each person learn from the divine letters those things which pertain to use, both for the fuller perfecting of the soul in piety, and also so that he does not become accustomed to human constitutions." In these and other places Basil rejects those things which are proposed to be believed outside Scripture.

units.la: Unde Erasmo de libro Basilii ab Harschero Jesuita allegato scribit in epist. ad Episcopum Culmensem: se in eo vertendo deprehendisse phrasin alium referre parentem, aliumq; spirare genium, nempe studiosum quempiam, & quidem eum qui doctissimis Athanasii libellis de spiritu suas loquaces & elumbes attexit nænias.
units.tr: Hence Erasmus, writing in his letter to the Bishop of Culm about the book of Basil cited by the Jesuit Harscher, says: that in translating it he had detected a style that refers to another parent and breathes another genius, namely some studious person, and indeed one who attached his garrulous and feeble trifles to the most learned little books of Athanasius on the Spirit.

units.la: Prœterea praxis Pontificiorum docet traditiones à Basilio recęsitas, aut apostolicas non esse, aut graviter ipsos peccare, dum eas non observant. Nam Basilius inter traditiones apostolicas numerat trinam immersionem baptizandorum, & quòd diebus dominicis à pascha usque ad pentecosten stantes orare debeant Christiani. Neutrum faciunt Pontificii. Imò ne Paulus Apostolus hoc posterius fecit, qui paucis diebus ante pentecosten oravit flexis genibus, Act.20, 26. Quomodo ergo potuit esse institutio apostolica? Quàm verò illud parum pietatis habet, quod Basilii corruptor dicit esse traditionem apostolicam, ut orantes se vertant versus orientem? nempe quia paradysum quaerimus, hortum Edenis, qui in oriente fuit? Quasi verò nos quaeramus paradysum terrestrem, & non potius superna ubi Christus sedet ad dextram Dei Patris? An non Antiocheni à Deo exauditi, qui versus occidentem precabantur, ut Socrates docet? Apostolus nos de loco & tempore monet, precandum esse omni in loco & semper. Ad quam plagam mundi, non docet. Idcirco Theophylactus in cap. sextum Matth. recte monet quod τεχπος καὶ σπουδὴς orationis, non τόπος observandus sit.
units.tr: Moreover, the practice of the Papists shows that the traditions recalled by Basil are either not apostolic, or else they sin gravely in not observing them. For Basil counts among the apostolic traditions the threefold immersion of those to be baptized, and that Christians should pray standing, from Easter to Pentecost, on the Lord's days. The Papists do neither. Indeed the Apostle Paul did not even do the latter, who a few days before Pentecost prayed with bended knees, Act. 20, 26. How then could it be an apostolic institution? How little piety, moreover, is there in what the corrupter of Basil calls an apostolic tradition, that those praying should turn towards the east! Surely because we seek paradise, the garden of Eden, which was in the east? As if we sought an earthly paradise, and not rather the heavenly places where Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father! Were not the Antiochenes heard by God, who prayed facing the west, as Socrates teaches? The Apostle admonishes us concerning place and time: that we must pray in every place and always. He does not teach towards which quarter of the world. Therefore Theophylact rightly observes, on Matthew 6, that the time and zeal [τεχπος καὶ σπουδὴς] of prayer, not the place [τόπος], is to be observed.

units.la: Falsa loci Basiliani versio latina & falsa Pontificiorum interpretatio observatur, quod interpres scribit; dogmata quae in ecclesia servantur & praedicantur. Ubi utrumque verbum ad unum refertur, nempe dogmata, quasi illa partim scripta essent partim non scripta. Cum in Basilio legatur, τῆς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ πιστευομένων δογμάτων ἢ κηρυγμάτων, servatorum in ecclesia dogmatum & praedicationum. Ita ut, quod interpres in consequente axiomatis habet, sit ad antecedens referendum. Nam distinguit Basilius, dogmata & praedicationes statim in sequentibus verbis, & per dogmata intelligit ritus ecclesiasticos, per praedicationes vero articulos fidei. Quod cum non observassent Pontificii, sequentia sequnntia verba, τὰ μὲν ἐν τῷ ἐγχειρίδιῳ διδασκαλίας ἔχομεν, τὰ δὲ ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀποστόλων παραδόσεως, ad articulos fidei retulerunt, quasi eorum aliquos ex scriptura, alios ex traditione non scripta haberemus, cùm Basilius illud non scriptum ad ritus (quos ipse dogmata vocat) scriptum verò ad prædicationes, id est, articulos fidei referat.
units.tr: The false Latin version of the passage of Basil and the false interpretation of the Papists are seen in the translator's words: "the dogmas which are kept and proclaimed in the Church." Here both words are referred to one thing, namely the dogmas, as if some of them were written and some not written. Yet Basil reads: "of the dogmas and proclamations believed and kept in the Church" [τῆς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ πιστευομένων δογμάτων ἢ κηρυγμάτων]. So what the translator has in the consequent part of the sentence is to be referred to the antecedent. For Basil distinguishes dogmas from proclamations in the words that follow at once: by dogmas he means ecclesiastical rites, and by proclamations the articles of faith. Since the Papists did not observe this, they referred the words that follow, "some we have in the written teaching, others in the tradition of the Apostles" [τὰ μὲν ἐν τῷ ἐγχειρίδιῳ διδασκαλίας ἔχομεν, τὰ δὲ ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀποστόλων παραδόσεως], to the articles of faith, as if we had some of them from Scripture and others from unwritten tradition. Whereas Basil refers the unwritten to the rites (which he himself calls dogmas) and the written to the proclamations, that is, to the articles of faith.

units.la: Ornament
units.tr: Ornament

units.la: EXEMPLA EORVM quæ non scripta creduntur & tenentur.
units.tr: EXEMPLA EORVM quæ non scripta creduntur & tenentur.

units.la: INCIPIT nunc veterem-novam cantilenam Jesuiticam, de creditis non lectis canere, quâ Bellarminus, Eckius, Becanus, Bailius Jesuitæ, & nuperus apostata Daniel Martinius Bearnensis mirè sibi placent, eamque plus delicatè habent, quam simia suum fœtum. Ego rideo & sperno. Nam quæcunque illi proseproferunt, aut ad salutem non sunt absolute necessaria & fide salvifica non credenda, aut in scripturis habentur quoad sensum & solida consequentia ex illis deduci possunt, aut sunt nuda vocabula, aut ritus ecclesiastici per se indifferentes & pro ratione loci & temporis mutabiles.
units.tr: Now the old-new Jesuit tune begins, to sing of things believed but not read. Bellarmine, Eck, Becanus, Bailly the Jesuits, and the recent apostate Daniel Martinius of Béarn are very pleased with it, and they cherish it more delicately than a monkey cherishes its young. I laugh at it and scorn it. For whatever they bring forward is either not absolutely necessary to salvation and not to be believed with saving faith, or it is found in Scripture as to its sense and can be deduced from it by solid consequence, or it is mere words, or it is ecclesiastical rites that are indifferent in themselves and changeable according to place and time.

units.la: Nos autem cum de scripturae sacrae sufficientia disputamus, loquimur 1. de rebus, & dicimus cum Epiphanio haeref. 69. in sacra scriptura mirabiliter ad nostram salutem omnia scripta sunt & persecta. Cum Tertulliano adoramus scripturarum plenitudinem, adverf. Hermog. 2. Quoad modum rerum in scriptura contentarum, observamus Nazianzeni regulam: quaedam in scriptura sunt, & dicuntur, quaedam sunt, & non dicuntur.
units.tr: But when we dispute about the sufficiency of Holy Scripture, we speak (1) concerning things, and we say with Epiphanius (Haer. 69): in holy Scripture all things for our salvation are written down wonderfully and perfectly. With Tertullian we revere the fullness of the Scriptures (Against Hermogenes, bk. 2). As to the manner of the things contained in Scripture, we observe the rule of Nazianzen: some things are in Scripture and are said; some things are, and are not said.

units.la: Sed videamus Harfcherum, is partim de principio conclusionum theologicarum, partim de conclusionibus loquitur. De illo quærit: Ubi sit scriptus numerus librorum canonicorum? Et quæ scriptura doceat, Evangelia Matthæi, Marci, &c. esse verbum Dei: Evangelia verò S. Andreæ, Thomæ, Bartholomæi esse apocrypha?
units.tr: But let us look at Harscher. He speaks partly about the principle of theological conclusions and partly about the conclusions themselves. About the former he asks: Where is the number of the canonical books written? And what Scripture teaches that the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, etc. are the Word of God, but the Gospels of St. Andrew, Thomas and Bartholomew are apocryphal?

units.la: Respondeo quoad primum, numerum librorum canonicorum, ut & capitum librorum, non esse articulum fidei, nec fide salvificâ credendum. Dominus Pareus duabus regulis proponit, quarum posterior priori est subordinata.
units.tr: I answer, as to the first point, that the number of the canonical books, as also the number of the chapters of the books, is not an article of faith, nor to be believed with saving faith. Lord Pareus proposes two rules, the latter of which is subordinate to the former.

units.la: Prima: numerum ac seriem librorum canonicorum item capitum singulorum, ut nunc habentur in bibliis tenemus fide tantum historicâ. Cujus ignoratio non damnat, dubitatio insciitiam & infirmitatem arguit, negatio hæreticum facit per accidens.
units.tr: The first: We hold the number and order of the canonical books, and likewise of the individual chapters, as they now stand in the Bibles, by historical faith only. Ignorance of this does not condemn; doubt indicates ignorance and weakness; denial makes one a heretic only by accident.

units.la: Secunda: quòd liber aliquis in particulari, puta Hosèas, Matthæus, sit Hosèa, Matth. &c. fide tantum historica tenemus. Cujus ignoratio non damnat, negatio est haeresis saltem per accidens.
units.tr: The second: That some particular book, for example Hosea or Matthew, is the book of Hosea or of Matthew, we hold by historical faith only. Ignorance of this does not condemn; denial is heresy at least by accident.

units.la: Ad secundum respondeo, id ex scriptura sacra ipsa haberi, licet non expresse scriptum. De hoc iterum duae regulae D. Parei observandae.
units.tr: As to the second point, I answer that this is found in Holy Scripture itself, although not expressly written there. On this, two rules of Pareus are to be observed.

units.la: Prima; qua scriptura habet titulum veri Prophetae & Apostoli, vera autem divinae scripturae νεστηεια non habet, qualia sunt doctrinae genus divinum, styli divina majestas, & doctrinae divinus consensus, illa nec divina est nec pro divina & canonica habenda.
units.tr: The first: Where a Scripture bears the title of a true prophet or apostle, but does not have the marks of divine Scripture, such as a divine character of doctrine, the divine majesty of style, and the divine agreement of doctrine, that writing is neither divine nor to be held as divine and canonical.

units.la: Secunda; scripturae titulum veri Prophetae aut Apostoli pro se ferentes & illa divinae scripturae νεστηεια evidenter etiam habentes, indubitatè pro divinis & canonicis haberi debent.
units.tr: The second: Scriptures that bear the title of a true prophet or apostle, and also clearly have the marks of divine Scripture, must without doubt be held as divine and canonical.

units.la: Ex priori regula iudicamus, Evangelia Thomae, Thaddaei, Andreae, Nicodemi esse apocrypha. Ex posteriori Evangelia Matthæi, Marci, Lucæ, Johannis esse divina & canonica.
units.tr: By the former rule we judge that the Gospels of Thomas, Thaddeus, Andrew and Nicodemus are apocryphal. By the latter we judge that the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are divine and canonical.

units.la: De conclusionibus varia habet P. Harscher, de iis autem quia quærit & edoceri cupit recte facit, licet iam societatis Jesu Theologus, nam optime Ambrosius, erubescat senectus quæ emendare se non poterit. Deducam ergo ipsum ad Doctores quorum doctrinam & institutionem non poterit reiicere, nempe ex Apostolis, Patribus & Pontificiis præcipuos.
units.tr: Harscher has various things to say about conclusions, but since he asks and desires to be taught, he does well, although he is now a theologian of the Society of Jesus; for Ambrose rightly says: let old age blush, which cannot correct itself. I shall therefore bring him to teachers whose doctrine and instruction he cannot reject, namely the chief of the Apostles, the Fathers and the Papists.

units.la: Quæret ergo P. Harscher, & Doctores respondebunt.
units.tr: Harscher will ask, and the teachers will answer.

units.la: Harscher Jes. Vbi est scriptum Spiritum sanctum à Patre & Filio procedere? Bellarmine doce: Respondeo, ex scripturis ostenditur Spiritum sanctum à Filio procedere, Joh. 16: 15. Joh. 17: 10. Rom. 8: 9. Gal. 4: 6. Lombarde doce: Quod autem Filius ab utroque procedat multis divinorum eloquiorum testimoniis probari potest, Part. i. d. ii. Thoma doce: Licèt per verba non inveniatur in sacra scriptura quòd Spiritus sanctus procedit à Filio, invenitur tamen quoad sensum i. part. q. 36. art. 2.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where is it written that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son? Bellarmine teaches: I answer, it is shown from the Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, John 16:15; John 17:10; Rom. 8:9; Gal. 4:6. Lombard teaches: That the Son proceeds from both may be proved by many testimonies of the divine oracles, Part 1, d. 11. Thomas teaches: Although it is not found in words in Holy Scripture that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, it is nevertheless found as to the sense, Part 1, q. 36, art. 2.

units.la: Harscher Jes. Ubi est scriptum duas naturas in una verbi hypostasi divina subsistere, divinam scilicet verbi & humanam in Christo?
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where is it written that two natures subsist in one divine hypostasis of the Word, namely the divine nature of the Word and the human nature in Christ?

units.la: Quæstio omnibus doctis merito odiosa. Quid enim iudicabimus de sanctis Patribus qui de hac ipsa quæstione magno zelo contra Nestorianos, Eutychianos & Monothelitas disputarunt? An illos absque fundamento scripturæ sacræ hoc fecisse credendum est?
