Veruntamen Augustine doce: In terra loquebatur, & in cœlo se esse dicebat, quo id pertinet, nisi ut intelligamus unam personam esse Christum, Deum & hominem, non duas, ne fides nostra non sit trinitas, sed quaternitas. Christus ergo unus est. Tract. 27. in Joh. Salmero Jesuita doce: Ea quæ necessariæ consequentiæ vi ex scripturis derivantur sunt pro traditionibus scriptis habenda. Atqui Christus dicitur unus Mediator, & Emanuel Deus nobiscum: ergo Deus & homo in una persona.
units.tr: This question is rightly hateful to all learned people. For what shall we judge of the holy Fathers who disputed with great zeal about this very question against the Nestorians, Eutychians and Monothelites? Are we to believe that they did this without the foundation of Holy Scripture? Nevertheless Augustine teaches: He was speaking on earth, and said that he was in heaven; what does this mean, unless we understand that Christ is one person, God and man, not two, lest our faith be not a Trinity but a quaternity. Christ is therefore one. (Tractate 27 on John.) The Jesuit Salmeron teaches: Those things which are derived from Scripture by the force of necessary consequence are to be held as written traditions. But Christ is called the one Mediator, and Emmanuel, God with us; therefore God and man are in one person.

units.la: Harscher Jes. ubi est scriptum, an sint duo sacramenta, an tria, an septem, an nullum? Augustine doce: Percussum est Christi latus, ut Evangelium loquitur, & statim manavit sanguis & aqua, quæ sunt Ecclesiæ gemina sacramenta, lib. 2. de symb. ad catech. cap. 6.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where is it written whether there are two sacraments, or three, or seven, or none? Augustine teaches: The side of Christ was pierced, as the Gospel tells, and immediately blood and water flowed out, which are the twin sacraments of the Church (Book 2 on the Creed to the Catechumens, ch. 6).

units.la: Harscher Jes. Vbi est scriptum quod Infantes sint baptizandi? Catechisme Romane doce: Credendum est noluisse Christum Domini baptismi sacramentum & gratiam pueris denegari, de quibus dicebat: finite puerulos & nolite eos prohibere ad me venire, talium enim est regnum cœlorum, quos amplexabatur super quos manus imponebat, & quos benedicebat. Bellarmine doce: infantes posse baptizari deducitur evidenter ex scripturis 1, 1. de Sacram. Baptif. c. 9.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where is it written that infants are to be baptized? The Roman Catechism teaches: It must be believed that Christ the Lord did not wish the sacrament and grace of baptism to be denied to children, of whom he said: "Suffer the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven," and whom he embraced, upon whom he laid his hands, and whom he blessed. Bellarmine teaches: That infants can be baptized is evidently deduced from Scripture (1, 1, On the Sacrament of Baptism, ch. 9).

units.la: Harfcher Jef. ubi scriptum infantes esse baptizandos nomine imposito, adhibitis patrinis, recitato Pater noster & symbolo Apostolico? Augustine doce: electa sunt quæ scriberentur, quæ saluti credentiü sufficere videbantur, tract. 49. in Joh. Quid verò hoc ad salutem, utrum hic Claudius an Pancratius appelletur? an vicinam an nobilem aliam pro commatre habeas? ô cæcitas! Cùm quæritur de articulis fidei, illi has extravagantias meditantur.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where is it written that infants are to be baptized with a name given, with godparents present, with the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed recited? Augustine teaches: Those things were chosen to be written which seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers (Tractate 49 on John). But what does it matter to salvation whether this one is called Claudius or Pancratius? Or whether you have a neighbour or some noble woman as co-mother? O blindness! When the question is about the articles of faith, they devise these trifles.

units.la: Harfcher Jef. ubi leges Christum vel cum pane dedisse corpus suum, vel dedisse illud tantùm in figura, non realiter præsens? nusquam leges. Augustine doce; Non dubitavit Christus dicere corpus meum, cum signum dedisset corporis sui. Cont. Adimantum, cap. 12.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where do you read that Christ gave his body with bread, or gave it only in a figure, not really present? You read it nowhere. Augustine teaches: Christ did not hesitate to say "my body" when he had given a sign of his body (Against Adimantus, ch. 12).

units.la: Harscher Jef. quænam scriptura habet de commutato sabbatho in diem dominicam, & quænam concedit sabbathum tam severè præceptum, profanare, ejusq; loco diem dominicam tam religiosè observare?
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: What Scripture has the sabbath changed to the Lord's Day, and what Scripture allows the sabbath, so strictly commanded, to be profaned, and the Lord's Day to be observed so religiously in its place?

units.la: Ribera Jesuita doce: Apoc. 1. 10. fui correptus die dominica, videmus tempore Apostolorum mutatam esse sabbathi solennitatem & diei dominicæ celebritatem consecratā, cuius meminit Paulus, 1. Cor. 16. monens, ut illo die collectæ fiant, quoniam tum omnes conveniebant solennitatis diei causa Com. in Apoc, Esti doce: Diei dominicæ observationem apostolicā constat ex scriptura. In Epist. ad Gal. cap. 4. De non observatione diei sabbathi Doctor Gentium doceat: Ne quis vos damnet ob cibum vel potum aut respectu festi aut novilunii aut Sabbathorum. Col. 2. 16.
units.tr: Ribera the Jesuit teaches: Rev. 1:10, I was caught up in the Lord's Day. We see that in the time of the Apostles the solemnity of the sabbath was changed and the celebration of the Lord's Day consecrated, of which Paul makes mention, 1 Cor. 16, admonishing that collections be made on that day, since then all assembled because of the solemnity of the day (Commentary on the Apocalypse). Estius teaches: The observance of the Lord's Day is clear from Scripture by apostolic practice (On Galatians, ch. 4). Concerning the non-observance of the sabbath day, the Doctor of the Gentiles teaches: "Let no one condemn you in food or drink, or with respect to a feast or a new moon or sabbaths" (Col. 2:16).

units.la: Harscher Jef. ubi legis contra quartadecimanos Pascha esse celebrandum dominica die post lunam decimam quartam conseconsequente? Quid hoc ad articulos fidei de quibus disputamus? sed Lindane doce: Paschae celebrandae illa olim variata per regiones diversitas, nihil fidei officiebat. Panopl. lib. 4.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where do you read against the Quartodecimans that Easter is to be celebrated on the Sunday after the fourteenth moon? What does this have to do with the articles of faith we are disputing about? But Lindanus teaches: The diversity of the celebration of Easter, which varied of old from region to region, did no harm to the faith (Panoplia, bk. 4).

units.la: Harscher Jes. qua scriptura continet symbolum apostolicum, symbolum Athanasianum, Nicaenum & Constantinopolitanū? qua plures adversarij recipiunt. Uti etiam prima quatuor Concilia, Nicaenum, Constantinopolitanum, Ephesinum & Calcedonense? Thoma de Aquino doce: Necessarium fuit, ut ex sententiis sacrae scripturae aliquid manifestum summarie colligeretur, quod proponeretur omnibus ad credendum, quod quidem non est additum sacrae scripturae, sed potius ex sacra scriptura desumtum. Sum. p. 2. q. 1. art. 9.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Which Scripture contains the Apostles' Creed, the Athanasian Creed, the Nicene and the Constantinopolitan? Which many of our opponents accept? Likewise the first four Councils, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon? Thomas Aquinas teaches: It was necessary that something plain should be briefly gathered from the sayings of Holy Scripture and proposed to all for belief. This was not added to Holy Scripture but rather drawn from it. Summa, pt. 2, q. 1, art. 9.

units.la: Reliqua symbola & Concilia sunt symboli Apostolici explicationes, quae non est necessum, ut verbotenus in scriptura habeantur. Revera hae quaestiones vix sunt hominis sanæ mentis? An enim vult Jesuita ut omnes commentarii & conciones verbotim in scriptura sacra contineantur? Nos recipimus Augustini libros, Hieronymi, Athanasii, Chrysostomi, an ergo omnes illi libri in scriptura sacra quærendi? An si non reperientur, reiiciendi? Nugæ.
units.tr: The remaining creeds and Councils are explanations of the Apostles' Creed, and they need not be contained in Scripture word for word. Truly, these questions are hardly those of a sane man. Does the Jesuit really want all commentaries and sermons to be contained word for word in Holy Scripture? We accept the books of Augustine, Jerome, Athanasius and Chrysostom. Must all those books therefore be sought in Holy Scripture? And if they are not found there, must they be rejected? Trifles.

units.la: Harscher Jesuita: quæ scriptura tollit gravissimam illam prohibitionem, comedendi cum sanguine aut suffocato, quæ habetur Gen. 9. Levit. 17. Actor. 15? Quam perfunctorie omnia! Quid hoc rei comedendi cum sanguine? aut suffocato? Deus prohibet comedere sanguinem: Apostoli comedere suffocatum, sed Harscherus scribit prohibitionem factam esse comedendi cum sanguine, prorsus ineptè. Sed tamen Baroni Cardinalis & Jesuita doce: Quid si dicant id ipsum reverentia Apostolorum servandum esse: certè universam ecclesiam catholicam iam senescentem iis vinculis alligare, quis non censeat esse dementiæ? cum præstet apostolico spiritu libertatem indictam sequi, ut manducans manducantem non spernat, Rom. 14: 3. & non manducans minimè spernere debeat manducantem. A. D. 692. f. 30.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Which Scripture removes the most serious prohibition, of eating with the blood or of what is strangled, which is found in Gen. 9, Lev. 17 and Acts 15? How superficially everything is done! What has eating with the blood to do with the matter, or with what is strangled? God forbids eating blood; the Apostles forbade eating what is strangled. But Harscher writes that the prohibition was of eating "with the blood," which is utterly absurd. But still, Baronius the Cardinal and the Jesuit teach: What if they say that this very thing must be kept out of reverence for the Apostles? Surely to bind the whole Catholic Church, now growing old, with such chains, who would not judge this to be madness? Since it is better to follow the freedom enjoined by the apostolic spirit, that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not eat (Rom. 14:3), and the one who does not eat should by no means despise the one who eats. A.D. 692, f. 30.

units.la: Harfcher Jef. Ubi legebant Iudæi remedium peccati originalis pro fœminis? pro pueris ante octavum diem morientibus? pro iis qui non erant ex posteris Abrahami, qualis fuit Iob, vir simplex & rectus ac timens Deum & recedens à malo? Pereri Jesuita doce: Quoniam peccatum originis non per fœminas, sed per masculos transfundebatur in posteros, sacramentum quod in eius remedium dabatur, voluit Deus esse peculiare virorum, fœminarum autem tollendo peccato originali alia ratione consultū fuit, coment.in cap.4.Rom.Quâ alia ratione? Thoma de Aquino doce: Sicuti ante institutionem circumcisionis sola fides Christi futuri iustificabat tam pueros, quàm adultos: ita etiam circumcisione data. Cum itaque Abrahamus pater sit credentium, & fœminæ quoq; sint filiæ Abrahæ, Luc. 13. 16. rectè scripsit Thomas, quòd hæ per fidem in Christum servatæ fuerint, idquè sine circumcisione, quia etiam & ipsi Abrahamo cum esset adhuc in præputio fides fuit imputata ad iustitiam absquè circumcisione, docente Apostolo Rom. 4: 10. de Jobo idem est iudicium, qui cap. 19: 25, 26. dicit, ego novi redemptorem meum vivere, & posteriorem super pulverem resurrecturum, & postquam vermes confoderint illud, evigilante me tum carne mea me visurum esse Deum. Lyranus ad hunc locum: Redemtorem dicit Dei Filium incarnandum, qui ab æterno in Deitate vixit secundum quod dicitur Heb. 6. Jesus Christus heri & hodie idem in secula.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where did the Jews read of a remedy for original sin for women? For boys dying before the eighth day? For those who were not descendants of Abraham, such as Job, a man simple and upright, who feared God and turned from evil? Pererius the Jesuit teaches: Because original sin was transmitted to posterity not through women but through men, God willed that the sacrament given as its remedy should be peculiar to men. But for women the removal of original sin was provided for by another way, in his commentary on chapter 4 of Romans. By what other way? Thomas Aquinas teaches: Just as before the institution of circumcision faith in the coming Christ alone justified both children and adults, so it was also after circumcision was given. Therefore, since Abraham is the father of believers, and women too are daughters of Abraham (Luke 13:16), Thomas rightly wrote that these were saved through faith in Christ, and this without circumcision, because faith was reckoned to Abraham himself for righteousness while he was still uncircumcised, as the Apostle teaches (Rom. 4:10). The same judgment holds for Job, who says in chapter 19, verses 25 and 26: I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he will rise last upon the dust; and after worms have destroyed this body, I shall see God in my flesh. Lyra on this passage: He calls the Redeemer the Son of God, who was to be made flesh, who from eternity lived in the Godhead, according to what is said in Heb. 6: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.

units.la: Illi qui non fuerunt ex posteris Adami aut proselyti fuerunt, aut omnino extra populum Dei. De proselyto dixit Deus, esto ipse sicuti indigena terræ, Exod 12: 48. Reliqui erant extra promissionis fœdera spem non habentes, Eph. 2: 13.
units.tr: Those who were not from the posterity of Adam were either proselytes or wholly outside the people of God. Of a proselyte God said: Let him be as one born in the land (Exod. 12:48). The rest were strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope (Eph. 2:13).

units.la: Harscher Jef. ubi fideles ab Abraham usq; ad Mosen suas scripturas sacras habue- runt? ubi legerunt ea, quæ crediderunt?
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where did the faithful have their sacred Scriptures from Abraham to Moses? Where did they read what they believed?

units.la: Placuit Deo, pro sapientissimo suo consilio, ecclesiam suam secundùm varias eius ætates aliter atq; aliter administrare, cuius quidem administrationis quatuor distinctas formas observamus. Prima est ab Adamo ad Abrahamum, quæ facta est verbis illis brevissimis promissionis; semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. Secunda est ab Abrahamo ad Mosen, in qua duo adiecta, expressum obsequium seu obedientia tanquam altera fœderis pars, & sacramentum circumcisionis. Tertia à Mose ad Christum, quæ plurimis sacrificiis, typis, & praecipuè sacramento Paschae fuit aucta. Quarta à Christo ad finem usquè mundi, in qua Deo placuit per verbum scriptum, vivamque praedicationem ecclesiam suam instituere. Jam autem ab una administrationis forma ad alteram, nulla ratione valet consequentia, nisi quis libertatem Dei & πολυπoίκιλον eius σοφίαν sub rationis humanae censuram vocare velit. Quemadmodum igitur ineptae fuissent quaestiones si quis tempore Abrahami quaesivisset, ubi ante Patrem nostrum Abrahamum fuit circumcisio? aut tempore Mosis; ubi cùm Patres nostri vixissent Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus, fuit Pascha, ubi iugé sacrificium, ubi festa clangoris, tabernaculorum? &c. Ita certè ridiculum est, ex administratione ecclesiae quarta, velle de prima iudicare, aut vice versâ. Nam illo tempore Deus ecclesiam suam aliter instituit, nempe vel per somnia, vel per visiones, vel per alloquium oris ad os, vel per institutiones paternas, quia ecclesia tantum erat in quibusdam familiis: in quorum locum Deus ecclesiæ iam adultæ verbum suum scriptum tradidit. Theophylacte igitur doce non tantum deproximis duabus quæstionib⁹, sed etiā de subsequente, cùm Harscherus quærit: primi Christiani, ubinam fidem christianam & dogmata necessaria legerunt antequam à sacris scriptoribus perscriberentur? hæc tamen non scripta crediderunt, Theophylactus: Ii quidem, qui ante legem vixerunt viri divini absquè literis & libris docebantur, sed munda præditi mente sancta spiritus illuminatione illustrabantur, atq; in hunc modum Deo ipsis ore ad os colloquente, eius voluntatem cognoscebant. Huiusmodi erat Noe, Abraham, Job, Moses. At postquam deteriores facti sunt homines, atquè indigni qui illuminarentur, & docerentur à Spiritu sancto, dedit misericors Deus scripturas, ut saltem per eas divinæ voluntatis admonerentur.
units.tr: It pleased God, in his most wise counsel, to administer his Church differently in its various ages. We observe four distinct forms of this administration. The first runs from Adam to Abraham, and was made by those very brief words of promise: the seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. The second runs from Abraham to Moses, in which two things were added: an express obedience or obedience as the other part of the covenant, and the sacrament of circumcision. The third, from Moses to Christ, was increased by very many sacrifices, types and especially the sacrament of the Passover. The fourth, from Christ to the end of the world, is that in which God has willed to establish his Church through the written Word and living preaching. Now, from one form of administration to another, no consequence holds, unless someone wishes to call God's freedom and his very manifold wisdom under the judgment of human reason. Therefore, just as the questions would have been absurd if someone in Abraham's time had asked where circumcision was before our father Abraham, or in Moses' time, where the Passover was, when our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had lived, where the continual sacrifice was, where the feasts of trumpets and of tabernacles were, and so on, so it is surely ridiculous to judge the first administration from the fourth, or the reverse. For at that time God instituted his Church differently, namely either through dreams, or through visions, or through speaking mouth to mouth, or through paternal instruction, because the Church then existed only in certain families. In their place God gave to the now-grown Church his written Word. Theophylact, then, teaches not only concerning the two preceding questions but also concerning the following one, when Harscher asks: Where did the first Christians read the Christian faith and the necessary doctrines before they were written down by the sacred writers? Yet they believed these things unwritten. Theophylact: Indeed, those who lived before the Law, holy men, were taught without letters and books, but endowed with a pure mind they were illuminated by the sacred enlightenment of the Spirit, and in this way, God speaking to them mouth to mouth, they knew his will. Such were Noah, Abraham, Job and Moses. But after men became worse and unworthy to be enlightened and taught by the Holy Spirit, merciful God gave the Scriptures, so that at least through them they might be reminded of the divine will.

units.la: Z
units.tr: Z

units.la: Sic etiam Christus Apostolis quidem in propriis personis constitutis collocutus est, misitque Spiritus gratiam magistra. Verùm quoniam haereses pullulaturi erant, & mores nostri corrumpendi, placuit ei, ut scriberentur Evangelia.
units.tr: So also Christ spoke with the Apostles, who were established in their own persons, and sent the grace of the Spirit as teacher. But since heresies were about to spring up and our morals were to be corrupted, it pleased him that the Gospels should be written.

units.la: Harscher Jef. ubi leguntur scripta illa adversariorum maxima? Quæ? 1. Nihil esse credendum, nisi quod scriptum est. Paulus Apostolus docet; hæc autem fratres figurâ quâdam transfluli ad me ipsum & Apollo propter vos, ut in omnibus discatis supra id, quod scriptum non sapere. 2. Bonis operibus nihil nos mereri? Christus Jesus docet: quum feceritis omnia, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus, nam quod debuimus facere, fecimus Luc. 17. 10. Doctor Gentium docet: & comperiar in eo non habens meam justitiam, quæ est ex lege, sed eam, quæ per fidem est Christi, Philip. 3: 9. gratiâ estis servati per fidem, & hoc non est ex vobis, Dei donum est. Non ex operibus ne quis glorietur, Eph. 2: 8, 9. scientes non justificari hominem ex operibus operibus legis, sed per fidem Iesu Christi, propterea quod non justificabitur ex operibus legis ulla caro, etiam nos in Jesum Christum credidimus, ut iustificaremur ex fide Christi & non operibus legis. 3. Pontificem Romanum esse Antichristum? Hoc ex scripturis habemus, quemadmodum Judaei ex veteri Testamento sciverunt Jesum Mariae filium esse Messiam mundi. Nam nullibi in veteri Testamento αὐτολεξεὶ lectum, Mariae filius est Messias mundi. Eundem tamen Messiam esse solidissime cognoverunt ex vaticiniorum impletione hoc modo: Messias debuit Bethlehemi nasci Mich. 5:2. Nazarethae educari, Esa. 11:1. Hierosolymam stante templo secundo ingredi Zach. 9:9. Sceptro a Judaeis penitus sublato Gen. 49:10. Atqui Mariae filius Bethlehemi natus fuit Matt. 2:1. Nazarethae educatus, Matt. 2:21. Hierosolymam stante templo secundo ingressus, Matt. 21:10. Sceptro a Judaeis sublato, Luc. 2:1. Ergo Mariae filius est Messias mundi. Simili modo argumentamur de Pontifice Romano. Jesuita legere potest, quæ supra de hac materia scripsimus. 4. Fide sola, & peccata, & pœnas omnes omninò deleri? Apostolus Paulus doceat: justificati ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Rom. 5: 1. Ubi autem est pax erga Deum ibi & peccatum est deletum, & pœna non extimescenda. 5. Fidelium peccata omnia esse venialia? Christus doceat: propterea dico vobis quodvis peccatum & blasphemia remittetur hominibus, blasphemia autem in Spiritum non remittetur hominibus, Matt: 12:31. Evangelista Johannes doceat: si confiteamur peccata nostra fidelis est & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra & purget nos ab omni iniquitate, 1. Joh. 1: 9. 6. Purum putum verbum Dei & Evangelium haberi apud Lutheranos & Calvinistas? Quia hoc nullibi iisdem verbis scriptum est in Dei verbo, quæro ego vicissim ex qua traditione Apostolica Harscherus possit probare, purum putum evangelium apud Lutheranos & Calvinistas non esse? Nullibi scriptum erat Paulum & Silam habere purum putū Evangelium, sed Beroënses conferentes Pauli & Silæ dicta cum scriptura deprehenderunt hos viros apostolicos veritatis esse prædicatores. Sic quævis religio pro lydio lapide habet scripturam sacram, cum qua si consentiat vera est, si dissentiat falsa. Quocirca Irenæe doce: Hi qui sunt à Valentino,id quod ab Apostolis scriptū non est veritatis evangelium titulant, in nihilo conveniens Apostolorum evangeliis, si enim quod ab eis profertur veritatis est evangeliū, dissimile autem hoc est illis, quæ ab Apostolis nobis tradita sunt, qui volunt possunt discere, quemadmodum ex ipsis scripturis ostenditur, iam non esse id quod Apostolis traditum est, veritatis evangelium. Lib. 3. adverss. hæress. cap. II. 7. Ecclesiam Christi defecisse, ita ut non semper à Christo fuerit vera fide- Z lium ecclesia. De ecclesia militante particulari nobis est quæstio, nam aliâs nunquam ecclesia Christi deficiet sive pateat sive lateat. De priore ergo Christus ipse sponsus Ecclesiæ doceat: Filius hominis cùm venerit num reperturus est fidem in terra? Janseni Episcope quomodo hæc intelligis? doce; de paucitate hominum qui reperientur vivi in novissimis.
units.tr: Harscher the Jesuit: Where are read those greatest sayings of our opponents? Which? (1) Nothing is to be believed unless it is written. The Apostle Paul teaches: These things, brethren, I have figuratively transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes, that in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written (1 Cor. 4:6). (2) That we merit nothing by good works? Christ Jesus teaches: When you have done all that is commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; for we have done only what we ought to have done (Luke 17:10). The Apostle of the Gentiles teaches: And be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ (Phil. 3:9); by grace you are saved through faith, and this is not of yourselves; it is the gift of God; not of works, lest anyone should boast (Eph. 2:8, 9); knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified; we also have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by the works of the law. (3) That the Roman Pontiff is Antichrist? We have this from Scripture, just as the Jews knew from the Old Testament that Jesus, the son of Mary, was the Messiah of the world. For nowhere in the Old Testament is it read in these very words, The son of Mary is the Messiah of the world. Yet they most firmly knew that he was the same Messiah from the fulfilment of the prophecies in this way: the Messiah had to be born at Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2), be brought up at Nazareth (Isa. 11:1), enter Jerusalem while the second temple stood (Zech. 9:9), and the sceptre be wholly taken from the Jews (Gen. 49:10). But the son of Mary was born at Bethlehem (Matt. 2:1), was brought up at Nazareth (Matt. 2:21), entered Jerusalem while the second temple stood (Matt. 21:10), and the sceptre was taken from the Jews (Luke 2:1). Therefore the son of Mary is the Messiah of the world. We argue in a similar way about the Roman Pontiff. The Jesuit can read what we have written above on this matter. (4) That by faith alone sins and all punishments are wholly blotted out? The Apostle Paul teaches: Justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). But where there is peace with God, there sin is also blotted out, and punishment is not to be dreaded. (5) That all sins of the faithful are venial? Christ teaches: Therefore I say to you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men (Matt. 12:31). The Evangelist John teaches: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). (6) That the pure and simple Word of God and the Gospel are held to be among the Lutherans and Calvinists? Since this is nowhere written in God's Word in these same words, I in turn ask: from what apostolic tradition can Harscher prove that the pure and simple Gospel is not among the Lutherans and Calvinists? It is nowhere written that Paul and Silas had the pure and simple Gospel, but the Bereans, comparing the words of Paul and Silas with Scripture, found that these apostolic men were preachers of the truth. Thus every religion has holy Scripture as its touchstone: if it agrees with that, it is true; if it disagrees, it is false. Therefore, Irenaeus, teach: Those who are from Valentinus call the Gospel of truth that which was not written by the Apostles, agreeing in nothing with the Gospels of the Apostles. For if what is brought forward by them is the Gospel of truth, but this is unlike what was handed down to us by the Apostles, let those who wish learn how, from the Scriptures themselves, it is shown that what is not what was handed down by the Apostles is not the Gospel of truth. Book 3 against heresies, ch. 11. (7) That the Church of Christ has failed, so that it was not always the true Church of the faithful under Christ? We have a question about the Church militant in particular, for otherwise the Church of Christ will never fail, whether it is seen or hidden. Concerning the former, let Christ himself, the Bridegroom of the Church, teach: When the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth? Bishop Jansen, how do you understand this? Teach: Concerning the small number of men who will be found alive at the last times.

units.la: At Harscherus in præterito locutus? Ergò verax ille testis in apocalypsi doceat: & percussa est tertia pars solis, & tertia pars lunæ, & tertia pars stellarum, ita ut obscuraretur tertia pars eorum, & diei non luceret pars tertia & noctis similiter. Apoc. 8: 12. Augustine doce, ecclesia est sol & luna & stellæ, quando sol obscurabitur, luna non dabit lucem, stellæ cadent è cœlo, ecclesia tùm non apparebit. Atquè hoc impletum est partim in ecclesiis orientalibus ab ipsis Apostolis plantatis, quæ factæ sunt Mahumetanæ, partim in ecclesiis occidentalibus, quæ factæ sunt Papisticæ. Obiiciet Harscherus: has Doctorum institutiones nihil ad rem facere, se enim quaerere ubi hæc nostra dogmata formalibus verbis in scriptura contineantur? exempli gratia, ubi his verbis scriptum sit; tantum sunt duo Sacramenta novi Testamenti non plura; Item ista, vos debetis infantes baptizare, &c. Respondeo ego, Jesuitam sibi singere adversarios quos non habet. Nam nemo ex Theologis reformatis unquam asseruit, quòd omnia credenda κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, in scriptura sacra contineantur, sed disiunctivè loquuntur, quòd in eadem vel contineantur expressis verbis, vel solidâ consequentiâ inde deducantur. Utrumque satis evidenter demonstratum est ab allegatis Doctoribus.
units.tr: But has Harscherus spoken only in the past tense? Then let that truthful witness in the Apocalypse teach: and the third part of the sun was smitten, and the third part of the moon, and the third part of the stars; so that the third part of them was darkened, and the day shone not for a third part of it, and the night likewise. Rev. 8:12. Augustine, teach us: the Church is the sun, the moon and the stars; when the sun is darkened, the moon gives no light, and the stars fall from heaven, then the Church does not appear. And this has been fulfilled partly in the eastern churches planted by the Apostles themselves, which became Mahometan, and partly in the western churches, which became Papistical. Harscherus will object: these teachings of the Doctors have nothing to do with the matter, for he seeks where our doctrines are contained in Scripture in formal words; for example, where is it written in these words: there are only two sacraments of the New Testament, not more; likewise this: you ought to baptize infants, etc. I answer that the Jesuit invents for himself adversaries whom he does not have. For no theologian of the Reformed churches has ever asserted that all things to be believed are contained in Holy Scripture κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν [according to the letter], but they speak disjunctively: that they are contained in it either expressly in words, or are deduced from it by solid consequence. Both have been shown quite clearly by the Doctors cited.

units.la: Præterea hæ Jesuiticæ sive obiectiones sive quæstiones desumptæ sunt ex schola Sadducæorum, qui quod non expressis verbis in libris Mosis (nam hos solos admittebant) exstaret fore universalem mortuorum resurrectionem, eandem negabant. Quos Christus docuit quomodo articulus ille fidei per consequentiam ex Dei verbis eruendus sit. Dicit enim: de resurrectione vero mortuorum, non legistis quod vobis dictum est à Deo, dicente, ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci & Deus Iacob, Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed viventium, Matt. 22: 31, 32. Ad quae verba ita Janse-nius Episcopus Gandavensis: tale profert (Christus) testimonium, quod per se quidem resurrectionem non asseruit, sed tantum ex consequenti, ostendens suam in scripturarum intelligentia, sapientiam, & docens quanta cum attentione & expensione sint scriptura legenda & tractanda, ut non haec tantum sint spectanda, quae in eis aperte pronuntiantur, nec per aperta tantum testimonia agendum contra haereticos, sed & per ea quae argumentatione non coacta & consequentia necessaria eorum destruunt errorem. Sic & noštri. Quæstionibus suis de creditis non lectis subiicit Jesuita disputationem Illustrissimorum Principum Badensium, Vaudimontii & Marchionis Durlacensis, illius Pontificii, huius Lutherani. Quam ego in medio relinquo, ne limites meos transiliam, in proloquio primæ disputationis propositos. Idcirco pergo ad nostros.
units.tr: Moreover, these Jesuit objections or questions are taken from the school of the Sadducees, who denied that the universal resurrection of the dead would occur, because it was not expressly stated in the books of Moses (for they admitted only these). Christ taught them how that article of faith is to be drawn by consequence from the words of God. For he says: but as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living, Matt. 22:31, 32. On these words Janssen, bishop of Ghent, says thus: Christ brings forward such a testimony, which does not indeed assert the resurrection by itself, but only by consequence, showing his wisdom in understanding the Scriptures, and teaching with how great attention and weighing the Scriptures are to be read and handled, so that not only those things are to be regarded which are plainly pronounced in them, nor is one to contend against heretics only by plain testimonies, but also by those things which, by an argument not forced and by necessary consequence, destroy their error. So also our men. After his questions about things believed which are not read, the Jesuit subjoins the disputation of the most illustrious princes of Baden, Vaudémont and the Margrave of Durlach, the one Papist, the other Lutheran. I leave this aside, lest I overstep my limits, which I set out in the preface to the first disputation. Therefore I proceed to our men.

units.la: Sic ergò porrò Harscherus.
units.tr: Thus, therefore, Harscherus goes on.

units.la: RETORSIO ADVERSARIORUM.
units.tr: THE ADVERSARIES' OWN ARGUMENTS TURNED BACK ON THEM.

units.la: Petrus du Moulin in scuto fidei, in libello quem inscripsit: Fuites & Euasions du Sieur Arnou Iesuite, hoc est, effugia Domini Arnoux Iesuita sol. 805. & sequentibus recenset XVII. quæstiones, quas vult Catholicos probare ex sacra scriptura, quasq; nunquam probare possint. Non officit ergo vera fidei aliqua credere, quæ ex scripturis probari non possint, vel hoc etiam officiet fidei Catholicæ Romanæ ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Peter du Moulin, in his Shield of the Faith, in the little book he entitled Fuites & Euasions du Sieur Arnoux Jesuite (that is, the evasions and escapes of Father Arnoux the Jesuit), at pages 805 and following, lists seventeen questions which he wants the Catholics to prove from Holy Scripture, and which they can never prove. So it does no harm to the true faith to believe some things that cannot be proved from Scripture; and yet this would harm the Catholic faith of the Roman Church.

units.la: Cùm Ministri Gallicani, & inter hos doctissimus Molinæus, sæpiùs ad certamen provocarentur â Jesuitis, experti sunt hi tantum nostrorum acumen, & in refutandis opinionibus pontificiis tantam dexteritatem & soliditatem, ut cogitandū ipsis esset quâ aliâ viâ (quia hac non succedebat) aggredi possent, Cauterius Jesuita pro sua subtilitate suasit suis Pontificiis, ne in posterum dogmata Romanæ ecclesiæ in disputationibus defenderent, viderent potiùs quâ ratione nostros ad probanda fidei nostræ dogmata ex puris scripturæ verbis, adigere possent. Hoc stratagema, tanquam omnium tutissimum Jesuitæ ambabus ulnis amplexi sunt, eaque uti cœperunt in Gallia contra Molinæum & alios ecclesiæ ministros, quibus quæstiones hinc inde anquisitas obiecerunt ex scripturis demonstrandas. Huius praxin suaserunt Jesuitæ Principi Vaudimontio contra Illust. Marchionem Badensem. Eo etiam usus est Harscherus, ut ex antecedentibus quæstiunculis videndum. Ministri ecclesiarum gallicanarum volebant ἀμεῖβἰᾶς, & Jesuitis vicissim septendecim quæstiones sequentes proposuerunt.
units.tr: When the French ministers, and among them the most learned Molinaeus, were often challenged to dispute by the Jesuits, these found our men so sharp and so skilful and firm in refuting Papist opinions that they had to think about some other way of attack, since the first did not succeed. The Jesuit Cauterius, proud of his cleverness, advised his Papists not to defend the dogmas of the Roman Church in future disputations, but rather to consider how they might force our men to prove the dogmas of our faith from the bare words of Scripture. The Jesuits embraced this stratagem with both arms, as the safest of all, and began to use it in France against Molinaeus and the other ministers of the Church. They put to them questions, gathered from here and there, which they said were to be demonstrated from Scripture. The Jesuits also advised this method to Prince Vaudemont against the illustrious Margrave of Baden. Harscher too used it, as may be seen from the little questions above. The ministers of the French churches wanted a reciprocal exchange [ἀμοιβάς], and in turn they proposed to the Jesuits the following seventeen questions.

units.la: I. In quo scriptura loco Deus præceperit sanctos demortuos invocare?
units.tr: I. In what passage of Scripture has God commanded that the holy dead be invoked?

units.la: II. Ubi scriptum sit in Dei verbo, sacrosanctam Trinitatem in lapide aut in pictura exprimendam esse?
units.tr: II. Where is it written in the Word of God that the most holy Trinity is to be represented in stone or in painting?

units.la: III. Quo in loco sacra scriptura præcipiatur cultus imaginum sanctorum, aut adoratio eorundem, sicut in concilio Nicæno traditum?
units.tr: III. In what place does Holy Scripture command the worship of images of the saints, or the adoration of them, as the Council of Nicaea handed down?

units.la: IV. Quis locus sacra scriptura doceat, sacrificandum esse corpus Christi in eucharistia, & ubi Christus sacerdotes sui corporis instituerit?
units.tr: IV. What passage of Holy Scripture teaches that the body of Christ is to be sacrificed in the Eucharist, and where has Christ appointed priests of his body?

units.la: V. Item in quo loco scriptura Deus præceperit laicis poculum eucharisticum eripere?
units.tr: V. Likewise, in what passage has God commanded that the cup of the Eucharist be taken away from the laity?

units.la: VI. In quo loco scripturæ sacræ Episcopus Romanus confirmatus sit successor S. Petri, sub titulo capitis ecclesiæ?
units.tr: VI. In what passage of Holy Scripture has the Roman Bishop been confirmed as successor of St. Peter, under the title of head of the Church?

units.la: VII. Ubi scriptum, quòd Deus mandaverit, in ecclesia scripturam sacram legendam, linguâ populo ignotâ?
units.tr: VII. Where is it written that God has commanded that Holy Scripture be read in the Church in a language unknown to the people?

units.la: VIII. Ubi Deus præceperit se invocare linguâ incognitâ, quam ne ipse quidem qui orat, intelligat?
units.tr: VIII. Where has God commanded us to call upon him in an unknown tongue, which even the one who prays does not understand?

units.la: IX. In quo sacra scriptura loco legatur, quòd mors & passio Iesu Christi satisfecerit pro culpa & pœna peccatorum ante baptismum perpetratorum, & quòd pro pœnâ peccatorum post baptismum satisfaciendum sit justitiæ Dei, vel in hac vita, vel in purgatorio?
units.tr: IX. In what passage of Holy Scripture is it read that the death and passion of Jesus Christ satisfied for the guilt and punishment of sins committed before baptism, and that for the punishment of sins committed after baptism satisfaction must be made to the justice of God, either in this life or in purgatory?

units.la: X. Ubi Deus prohibuerit matrimonium sacerdotibus aut Monialibus?
units.tr: X. Where has God forbidden marriage to priests or to nuns?

units.la: XI. Item in quo loco scripturæ præceptum, adorare reliquias sanctorum?
units.tr: XI. Likewise, in what passage of Scripture is there a command to adore the relics of the saints?

units.la: XII. Ubi legatur in Dei verbo de Lymbo Infantum? XIII. Ubi
units.tr: XII. Where is the Limbo of infants read of in the Word of God? XIII. Where

units.la: XIII. Ubi scriptum sit in scriptura, quod ecclesia Romana sit infallibilis judex controversiarum fidei, & quòd illa errare non possit?
units.tr: XIII. Where is it written in Scripture that the Roman Church is the infallible judge of controversies of faith, and that it cannot err?

units.la: XIV. In quo loco scriptura, virgo Maria appelletur regina cæli?
units.tr: XIV. In what passage of Scripture is the Virgin Mary called Queen of Heaven?

units.la: XV. Quo testimonio scriptura probari possit, lectionem sacræ scripturæ populo seu laicis esse prohibitam absq; speciali permissione?
units.tr: XV. By what testimony of Scripture can it be proved that the reading of Holy Scripture is forbidden to the people or the laity without special permission?

units.la: XVI. In quo loco scriptura sacræ potestas data sit Pontifici Romano colligendi in thesaurum ecclesiæ satisfactiones supererogationum sanctorum & Monachorum, easq; convertendi in satisfactiones aliorum, & distribuendi per indulgentias?
units.tr: XVI. In what passage of Scripture has power been given to the Roman Pontiff to gather into the treasury of the Church the satisfactions of the supererogations of the saints and of the monks, and to convert them into the satisfactions of others and distribute them through indulgences?

units.la: XVII. Tandem, ubi & quando Deus Papæ potestatem dederit deponendi Reges, liberandi animas ex purgatorio, & concedendi peccata per septingenta aut octingenta millia annorum?
units.tr: XVII. Finally, where and when has God given the Pope the power to depose kings, to free souls from purgatory, and to grant pardon for sins for seven or eight hundred thousand years?

units.la: Has quæstiones proposuerunt Arnoldo Jesuitæ, cum hac moderatione & animi candore, se usquè adeo non requirere hàrum quæstionum formalia verba, contentos se fore, si demonstrare possint, illas vel quoad sensum in scriptura contineri, vel bonâ consequentiâ ex illa deduci posse.
units.tr: The Jesuits proposed these questions to Arnoux with this moderation and candour of mind: that they did not require the formal words of these questions, and would be content if they could show that they are contained in Scripture, either in sense, or can be deduced from it by a good inference.

units.la: Arnoldus effugia quæsivit & respondit. 1. non esse penes ipsos (pastores) de fide & religione sua quærere. 2. petitionem fore tolerabilem aliquo modo si coram iudice tali proponerent, cui ius esset iudicandi de controversiis. 3. nondum sibi satisfactum esse ad sua quæsita, proinde stultitiam fore si talem μεταβασιν permitteret. 4. si tamen rotundè confiteri velint, quòd de verbo Dei amplius gloriari nolint, confessionem fidei orthodoxæ annihilare, & eius plané nunquam amplius mentionem facere velint, tum se paratum esse ad respondendum. 5. quæstiones illas moveri non posse ab iis, qui norunt Pontificios purum Dei verbum non admittere (quod faciunt orthodoxi) sed ad traditiones non scriptas consugere.
units.tr: Arnoux looked for escapes and replied: (1) that it is not for the ministers to ask about their own faith and religion; (2) that the request would be tolerable in some measure if they put it before a judge who had the right to decide controversies; (3) that he was not yet satisfied with their questions, and that it would be folly to allow such a change of ground; (4) that if, however, they were willing to confess frankly that they no longer wished to boast about the Word of God, and wanted to annul the confession of orthodox faith and never again make any mention of it, then he was ready to answer; (5) that those questions could not be raised by men who know that the Papists do not admit the pure Word of God (as the orthodox do), but take refuge in unwritten traditions.

units.la: Ecce lepidas istas excusationes. Harscherus (Arnoldum obliquè castigans) respondet. Sed ne videatur genium & ingenium suum mutasse, primò Molinæo mendacium affingit, quasi ita doctissimus vir argumentatus fuisset:
units.tr: See these pretty excuses. Harscher, while obliquely rebuking Arnoux, replies. But, lest he seem to have changed his character and disposition, he first attributes to Molinaeus a falsehood, as if that most learned man had argued thus:

units.la: Si non officit ecclesiæ pontificiæ, quòd illius Doctores aliquas quæstiones ex scripturæ probare non possunt. Ergò nec veræ fidei officit quoq; etiamsi quasdam quæstiones ex scriptura demonstrare non possint orthodoxi. Quod fictum plane est mendacium, & ratiocinatio, quæ Molinæo nunquam in mentem venit. Nunc respondet & dicit:
units.tr: If it does no harm to the Papist Church that its teachers cannot prove some questions from Scripture, then it does no harm to the true faith either, even if the orthodox cannot demonstrate certain questions from Scripture. This is plainly a fabricated lie, and an argument that never came into Molinaeus's mind. Now Harscher replies and says:

units.la: Est ignorantia elenchi. Non est quæstio apud Catholicos, an aliquid credant aut credere. credere debeant, quod in scriptura sacra expresse & in specie non sit descriptum. Confitentur enim credenda omnia, quae Deus revelavit, sive scripta sint, sive non sint. Pluraque non esse explicite descripta, quae habeamus ex verbo Dei tradito. Unde miror hujus Achillis Calvinistici pugnas aerem verberantis, & suis verba inania dantis.
units.tr: It is a case of ignorance of the point at issue. Among Catholics the question is not whether they believe, or ought to believe, something that is not expressly and specifically described in Holy Scripture. For they confess that all things are to be believed which God has revealed, whether they are written or not. Many things are not explicitly described that we have from the handed-down Word of God. Hence I wonder at the battles of this Calvinist Achilles, who beats the air and gives empty words to his own side.

units.la: Resp. Non est ignorantia elenchi in argumento Molinaei, sed ignorantia in Harschero, qui verum disputandi modum ignorat. Non enim in disputationibus respiciendum, quamnam adversarius obstinate teneat sententiam, sed quam omnino tenere debeat. Secus in omnibus disputationibus perpetuam committemus ignorationem elenchi. Exempli gratia: Ego firmiter credo nullum esse purgatorium. Quod si Harscherus contra opponeret, & ego responderem, Harscherum committere ignorationem elenchi cum probe sciat apud orthodoxos non esse quæstionem an sit purgatorium. Quàm ridiculum hoc foret. Quanta ergo hæc est stultitia respondere, esse ignorantiam elenchi, cùm Catholici confiteantur credenda omnia quæ Deus revelavit, (intelligo quæ verè revelavit) sive scripta sint, sive non sint. Rectius itaq; Harscherus fecisset, si cum Arnoldo tacuisset. Ista bella responsio vix meruit tantam præsumptionem, ex qua Jesuita scribit: unde miror hujus Achillis Calvinistici pugnas aërem verberantis, & suis inania verba dantis.
units.tr: Reply. There is no ignorance of the point at issue in Molinaeus's argument, but ignorance in Harscher, who does not know the true manner of disputing. For in disputations we must look not at what an adversary obstinately holds, but at what he ought altogether to hold. Otherwise we shall commit a perpetual ignorance of the point at issue in every disputation. For example: I firmly believe that there is no purgatory. If Harscher were to object to this, and I were to answer that Harscher commits an ignorance of the point at issue, since he knows full well that among the orthodox the question is not whether there is a purgatory, how ridiculous that would be. How great, then, is the folly of answering that there is ignorance of the point at issue, when Catholics confess that all things are to be believed which God has revealed (I mean, which he has truly revealed), whether they are written or not. Harscher would have done better to keep silent with Arnoux. That fine answer scarcely deserved such presumption, from which the Jesuit writes: Hence I wonder at the battles of this Calvinist Achilles, who beats the air and gives empty words to his own side.

units.la: Certavit Molinæus cum acutissimis Jesuitis, eques & pedes, id est, ore & calamo eminùs & cominùs, summa cum laude, ut testabitur Gallia, qui certè has exiguas Harscherianas pagellas, criminationes & nugaces ratiunculas ex alto despiceret, quantumcunque Harscherus contemptim de eo hic loquatur. Sed restat argumentum catholicorum examinandum. Sic Jesuita:
units.tr: Molinaeus fought with the keenest Jesuits, on horse and on foot, that is, with mouth and pen, at long range and at close quarters, with the highest praise, as France will bear witness. He certainly would look down from a height on these meagre little Harscherian pages, accusations and trifling little arguments, however contemptuously Harscher speaks of him here. But the argument of the Catholics still remains to be examined. The Jesuit says:

units.la: Hoc est catholicum argumentum: Quod non est scriptum in sacra scriptura non est credendum. Sed superius enarrata exempla non sunt scripta in sacra scriptura. Ergo superius enarrata exempla non sunt credenda. Major (inquit) est maxima adversariorum, minor patet ad oculum. Consequentia legitima. Addit; quia majorem propositionem concedunt adversarij, catholici autem eam negent, inde illud adversus catholicos esse plumbeum, adversus Calvinistas adamantinum.
units.tr: This is the Catholic argument: What is not written in Holy Scripture is not to be believed. But the examples set out above are not written in Holy Scripture. Therefore the examples set out above are not to be believed. The major premise, he says, is the maxim of our opponents, and the minor is plain to see. The consequence is valid. He adds: Because our opponents concede the major premise, but the Catholics deny it, therefore this argument is leaden against the Catholics, and adamantine against the Calvinists.

units.la: Non est nobis quaerendus sanguis hircinus, qui nobis solvat hunc Adamantem, res est facilis negotii. Quod orthodoxos attinet, respondent illi ad maiorem, & dicunt illam esse ambiguam. Dicitur enim aliquid esse vel contineri in sacra scriptura duobus modis, vel <bl>αὐτολεξεὶ</bl> vel <bl>κατὰ τὸ πραγμα</bl>, seu <bl>κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν</bl> vel <bl>κατὰ τ᾽ διάνοιαν</bl>. Hoc est, conclusiones vel totidem verbis in scriptura expressae sunt, vel in scriptura præpræmissas habent, ex quibus vi necessariæ consequentiæ deducuntur.
units.tr: There is no need for us to seek goat's blood to dissolve this adamant; the matter is easy. As for the orthodox, they answer the major premise and say that it is ambiguous. For something is said to be, or to be contained, in Holy Scripture in two ways: either [αὐτολεξεί] word for word, or [κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα] according to the thing, that is, [κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν] according to the words or [κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν] according to the sense. That is to say, conclusions are either expressed in Scripture in so many words, or they have their premises in Scripture, from which they are drawn by the force of necessary consequence.

units.la: Doctissimus Rivetus orthodoxorum sententiâ perspicuè proponit & authoritatibus confirmat, eius verba idcirco huc reponâm: Cum dicimus, omnia quæ ad salutem necessaria plenè & perfectè in scriptura continentur, id non est intelligendum, ac si expressis verbis habentur in scriptura quacunque credimus; sed quia expresse in ea leguntur, vel ex expressis legitimâ deductione eruuntur, idq; necessaria & evidenti consequentiâ. Quæ tamen cùm evidens est, eodem loco habenda est conclusio, ac si αὐτοπξει in sacra scriptura haberetur, quia etiamsi non sit in scripturis quoad γράμματα inest tamen quoad σφάγμα, juxta regulam Nazianzeni: quædam in scripturis sunt & dicuntur, quædam in ijs sunt etsi non dicuntur. Isagoge ad script f. p. 244.
units.tr: The most learned Rivetus sets out the orthodox opinion clearly and confirms it with authorities, so I will quote his words here: When we say that all things necessary to salvation are fully and perfectly contained in Scripture, this is not to be understood as if everything we believe were there in express words; rather, they are either read there expressly or are brought out from what is expressed by a legitimate deduction, and that by a necessary and evident consequence. Although such a conclusion is not in Scripture as to the letter, yet when it is evident it is to be held in the same place as if it were in Scripture [αὐτοπξει], since it is in Scripture as to the spirit [πνεῦμα], according to the rule of Nazianzen: some things are in the Scriptures and are said there, and some things are in them even though they are not said. Isagoge ad Script., p. 244.

units.la: Hanc sententiam probat autoritate tum Patrum tum Pontificiorum. Primò
units.tr: He proves this opinion by the authority both of the Fathers and of the Papists. First,

units.la: ex Nazianzeni lib. 5. de Theol. ubi vocabula ingenitum & anarchum ex scripturis haberi dicit & scribit: Nonne perspicuum est hac de ijs scripta esse ex quibus colliguntur, tametsi minime dicantur? Addit Nazianz. Quod si te bis quinque aut bis septem dicente, decem aut quatuordecim ex verbis tuis colligerem, aut ex eo quod animal ratione praditum & mortale diceres, hominem esse concluderem, an tibi nugari viderer? nequaquam profecto eum tua dicerem.
units.tr: from Nazianzen, book 5 of his work on theology, where he says and writes that the words unbegotten and without beginning are found in Scripture: Is it not clear that things have been written about these from which they are gathered, even though they are not named at all? Nazianzen adds: If, when you say two times five or two times seven, I were to gather ten or fourteen from your words, or if, when you call man a rational and mortal animal, I were to conclude that he is a man, would I seem to you to be talking nonsense? By no means, surely, would I be saying what you say.

units.la: Deinde ex Ambrosio lib. de fide cont. Arianos cap. 5. Cum hanc unitatem substantia in Patre & Filio non solum prophetica, sed etiam evangelica agnoscat authoritas, quomodo dicis in scripturis divinis ὁμοούσιον non inveniri? quasi aliud sit homousion quàm quod dicit, ego de Deo Patre exivi, & ego & pater unum sumus.
units.tr: Second, from Ambrose, in his book on the faith against the Arians, chapter 5: Since the Scripture, both prophetic and evangelical, acknowledges this unity of substance in the Father and the Son, how can you say that homoousion is not found in the divine Scriptures? As if homoousion meant anything other than what it says: "I came out from God the Father," and "I and the Father are one."

units.la: Tertiò ex Augustino epist. 178. etsi verbum ipsum in lege scriptum non invenitur, res tamen ipsa invenitur.
units.tr: Third, from Augustine, letter 178: Even if the word itself is not found written in the law, the thing itself is nevertheless found.

units.la: Quartò ex Turrecremata Pontificio summ. de ecclesia lib. 4. part. 2. cap. 8. duobus modis dicitur aliquid contineri in sacra scriptura, aut in propria verborum forma, sicut ista est: Christus fuit homo, & aliquid implicitè quod scilicet bona & necessaria consequentia ex positis formaliter in litera sequitur, sicut ex illa, Christus fuit homo, sequitur quod habuit animam rationalem.
units.tr: Fourth, from the Papist Turrecremata, Summa on the Church, book 4, part 2, chapter 8: There are two ways in which something is said to be contained in Holy Scripture: either in the proper form of words, as this: "Christ was a man," or implicitly, namely by a good and necessary consequence which follows formally from what is set down in the letter, as from "Christ was a man" it follows that he had a rational soul.

units.la: Item cap. 9. Catholicarum veritatum primum genus est earum, quae in canone sacrae scriptura Veteris & N. Testam. continentur in propria verborum forma: secundum genus catholicarum veritatum est earum, quae ex solis contentis in sacra scriptura necessariâ & formali consequentiâ possunt inferri.
units.tr: Likewise, chapter 9: The first kind of Catholic truths is that which is contained in the canon of Holy Scripture of the Old and New Testaments in the proper form of words; the second kind of Catholic truths is that which can be inferred from what is contained in Holy Scripture alone, by a necessary and formal consequence.

units.la: Quintò, ex Melchiore Cano Pontificio, Loc. Theol. lib 12. cap. 16. Cùm veritas fidei bipartita sit, & hac ad fidem mediatè, illa immediatè pertineat, necesse est duos gradus propositionum fidei generales statim à principio collocare. Prior erit earum, quæ Theologiæ legitima principia sunt, hoc est, ea omnia quæ Deus in seipsis ecclesiæ revelavit. Posterior vero gradus harum erit, quæ ex prioribus illis necessario colliguntur. Hoc enim genus conclusionum, ut cum rebus fidei colligatum, ad fidem etiam spectat.
units.tr: Fifth, from the Papist Melchior Cano, Loci Theologici, book 12, chapter 16: Since the truth of faith is twofold, and the one pertains to faith mediately, the other immediately, it is necessary to set down at the outset two general grades of propositions of faith. The first will be those which are the legitimate principles of theology, that is, all those things which God has revealed in himself to the Church. The second grade will be those which are necessarily gathered from those first ones. For this kind of conclusion, being bound up with the things of faith, also belongs to faith.

units.la: Sextò, ex Bellarmino Pontificio lib. 4. de V. D. cap. 9. Id est de fide, quod Deus per Prophetas & Apostolos revelavit, aut quod evidenter inde deducitur. Et de Justif. lib. 3. cap. 8. Non potest aliquid certum esse certitudine fidei, nisi aut immediatè contineatur in verbo Dei, aut ex verbo Dei per evidentem consequentiam deducitur.
units.tr: Sixth, from the Papist Bellarmine, book 4 on the Word of God, chapter 9: That is of faith which God has revealed through the Prophets and Apostles, or which is evidently deduced from that. And on justification, book 3, chapter 8: Nothing can be certain with the certainty of faith unless it is either immediately contained in the Word of God, or is deduced from the Word of God by an evident consequence.

units.la: Maior ergo syllogismi Harscheriani universaliter vera non est, à nostris nunquam asserta, & sensu Jesuitico salsa. Minor quoquè iuxta distinctionem datam salsissima est. Licèt enim exempla superiùs allata omnia quoad verba formalia non reperiantur in scriptura sacra, continentur tamen in eadem quoad sensum, & solidâ consequentiâ ex ea deduci possunt, quemadmodum Harscherus à Doctoribus institutus fuit. Et sic adamantinus ille Pontificiorum syllogismus in momento factus est plumbeus.
units.tr: The major premise of Harscher's syllogism, therefore, is not universally true; our side has never asserted it, and in the Jesuit sense it is false. The minor premise too is most false, according to the distinction given. For although all the examples adduced above are not found in Holy Scripture in formal words, they are nevertheless contained in it as to the sense, and they can be deduced from it by a sound consequence, just as Harscher was taught by the Doctors. And so that adamantine syllogism of the Papists has in a moment been made leaden.

units.la: Eundem syllogismum quatenus à Theologis orthodoxis obiicitur Pontificiis Jesuita vocat plumbeum. Quàm benè videndum. Sic ratiocinamur: Quæcunque non sunt scripta in Dei verbo expresse, nec in eadem habentur quoad sensum, nec legitimâ consequentiâ ex ea deduci possunt, non sunt credenda. Atqui septendecim illa dogmata Pontificia à Dn. Molinæo Jesuitis proposita, in scriptura sacra expresse non leguntur, nec in ea habentur quoad sensum, nec legitimâ consequentiâ ex ea deduci possunt: Ergò non sunt credenda.
units.tr: When the Jesuit calls this same syllogism leaden, as the orthodox theologians urge it against the Papists, we must see how well he is right. We reason thus: Whatever is not written expressly in the Word of God, nor contained in it as to the sense, nor can be deduced from it by a legitimate consequence, is not to be believed. But those seventeen Papist dogmas proposed by the Jesuits, Mr. Molinaeus, are not read expressly in Holy Scripture, nor are they contained in it as to the sense, nor can they be deduced from it by a legitimate consequence. Therefore they are not to be believed.

units.la: Propositio maior probatur partim ex scriptura, partim ex antiquis Patribus. Deut. 4: 2. Ne addite ad verbum illud, quod ego praecipio vobis, neq; detrahite de eo, ut servetis praecepta Iehova Dei vestri, quae ego praecipio vobis. Deut. 12:32. Unamquamq; rem, quam ego praecipio vobis, eam observantes facite, neq; addito ei neq; detrahito ex ea. Hieronymus cap. 23. in Matth. Quod de scriptuKis authoritatem non habet, eadem facilitate contemnitur quâ probatur. Tertullianus adverf. Hermog. Non recipio, quod extra scripturam de tuo infers. Cyrillus Alexandrinus lib. 5. in Lev. In duobus testamentis licet omne verbum quod ad Deum pertinet, requiri & discuti atq; ex ipsis omnem veram scientiam capi. Si quid autem superfuerit, quod non divina scriptura decernat, nullam debere aliam tertiam scripturam ad authoritatem scientia suscipi.
units.tr: The major premise is proved partly from Scripture and partly from the ancient Fathers. Deut. 4:2: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you diminish from it, that you may keep the commandments of Jehovah your God which I command you. Deut. 12:32: Whatever thing I command you, observe to do it; you shall not add to it nor take away from it. Jerome, on Matthew, chapter 23: What does not have authority from the Scriptures is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. Tertullian, against Hermogenes: I do not accept what you bring in from your own resources beyond Scripture. Cyril of Alexandria, book 5 on Leviticus: In the two Testaments, every word that pertains to God may be required and examined, and all true knowledge taken from them. But if anything remains which the divine Scripture does not decide, no third Scripture ought to be received as an authority for knowledge.

units.la: Quâ fronte ergo audet Jesuita scribere, catholicos suos propositionem maiorem negare? Minorem quod concernit, veritas ipsa loquitur & Harscherus non negat, quod exempla & dogmata à Domino Molinæo Arnoldo Jesuitæ proposita, nec formaliter quoad verba, nec quoad sensum in scriptura sacra continentur, nec legitimâ consequentiâ ex eadem deducantur. Et hinc efficitur Pontificiorum syllogismus plumbeus. Concludam verbis Hieronymi, Com. Esai. cap. 8.
units.tr: With what brazenness, then, does the Jesuit dare to write that his Catholics deny the major premise? As for the minor, the truth itself speaks, and Harscher does not deny that the examples and dogmas proposed by Mr. Molinaeus, the Jesuit Arnold, are contained in Holy Scripture neither formally as to the words nor as to the sense, nor are they deduced from it by a legitimate consequence. And from this the Papists' syllogism is shown to be leaden. I will conclude with the words of Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 8:

units.la: Nobis Deus legem dedit, & testimonia scripturarum, quæ si sequi noluerius, non habebitis lucem, sed caligo vos opprimet quæ transfibit per terram vestram & doctrinam, ut cum decepti à vobis se in errore perspexerint & sustinere famem veritatis, vobis maledicant, quos quasi Deos suos & Reges putabant; & frustra ad cælum, terramque respiciant, cum semper in tenebris sint, & non possint de vestris avolare insidijs.
units.tr: God has given us the law and the testimonies of the Scriptures. If we are unwilling to follow them, you will not have light, but darkness will oppress you, which will pass through your land and your teaching; so that when those whom you have deceived perceive that they are in error and endure hunger for the truth, they will curse you, those whom they thought were their gods and kings; and they will look in vain to heaven and earth, since they are always in darkness and cannot fly out of your snares.

units.la: Aa
units.tr: Aa

units.la: PRÆDESTINATI.
units.tr: PREDESTINARIANS.

units.la: VIxerunt teste Sigeberto circa annum 414. Sic dicti, quod de prædestinatione & divina gratia disputantes, asserer-ent pie viventibus non prodesse bonorum operum laborem, si à Deo ad mortem ordinati fuissent, & impijs & peccatoribus non obesse quæcunq; scelera & flagitia ab illis commissa, si Deus illos ad vitam æternam prædestinasset, quæ assertio & bonos à bonis operibus faciendis avocabat, & malos ad mala provocabat.
units.tr: They lived, according to Sigebert, around the year 414. They were so called because, disputing about predestination and divine grace, they asserted that the labour of good works does not profit the godly if they have been ordained by God to death, and that no crimes or outrages committed by the impious and sinners do them harm if God has predestined them to eternal life. This assertion both kept good people from doing good works and provoked the wicked to evil.

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATION.

units.la: Jesuita Harscherus non est primus qui sub hæresi prædestinatiana beatissimum Augustinum insectatur. Id enim ante ipsum fecerunt Pelagiani & Semipelagiani. Quapropter de conficta hac hæresi aliquid præmittam.
units.tr: The Jesuit Harscher is not the first to attack the most blessed Augustine under the name of the predestinarian heresy. The Pelagians and Semipelagians did this before him. For that reason I shall first say something about this invented heresy.

units.la: Asseruit Augustinus in disputationibus contra Pelagium multis in locis electionem quorundam hominum sine prævisis meritis & sine prævisa fide, dicens etiam, Deum ex mera voluntate facere esse in Christi consortio, quem formavit in Diaboli domicilio (meretricis) & non velle esse in regno suo, quem formavit in templo suo, id est, sanctæ alicuius matronæ. Reperti in Gallia qui doctrinam Augustini improbabant, invehentes Pelagii quædam dogmata in ecclesiam. Hisce sese opposuerunt Prosper & Hilarius, qui etiam ea de re Augustinum adhuc viventem admonuerunt, qui idcirco suis censoribus sese oppofuit duobus libris, libro, inquam, de prædestinatione & de bono perseverantiæ, qui etiam ab ecclesia recepti fuerunt, tanquam orthodoxi, ut patet ex Fulgentii libro 1. ad Monimum.
units.tr: In his disputations against Pelagius, Augustine asserted in many places that certain men are chosen without foreseen merits and without foreseen faith, and he even said that God, by sheer will, makes some to be in the fellowship of Christ, whom he formed in the dwelling of the Devil (that of a harlot), and does not wish to be in his kingdom those whom he formed in his temple, that is, in the house of some holy matron. In Gaul there were men who disapproved of Augustine's teaching and brought some dogmas of Pelagius into the Church. Against these stood Prosper and Hilary, who also warned Augustine, while he was still alive, about this matter. He therefore opposed his censors in two books, namely the book on predestination and the book on the gift of perseverance, which were also received by the Church as orthodox, as is clear from Fulgentius, book 1, to Monimus.

units.la: Post Augustini mortem repullulaRunt in Gallia Semipelagiani, qui exprædictis duobus Augustini libris capitula quædam collegerunt, tanquam heterodoxa & fidei catholica contraria. His iterum respondit Prosper & dixit illos calumniatores Augustinum celeberrimi nominis virum, promptius culpare quàm nosse. Compellarunt etiam Prosper & Hilarius Cælestinum primum Pontificem Romanum, & rogarunt ut doctrinæ Augustinianæ patrocinium susciperet, quod Papa fecit in epistola ad quosdam Galliarum Episcopos, in qua Augustini sententiam & Prosperi ac Hilarii defensionem approbavit.
units.tr: After Augustine's death the Semipelagians sprang up again in Gaul. From the two books of Augustine just mentioned they gathered certain chapters, as heterodox and contrary to the Catholic faith. Prosper again replied to them, and said that these slanderers were quicker to blame Augustine, a man of most celebrated name, than to understand him. Prosper and Hilary also appealed to Celestine, the first Roman Pontiff, and asked him to take up the patronage of Augustinian doctrine. The Pope did so, in a letter to certain bishops of Gaul, in which he approved Augustine's opinion and the defence of Prosper and Hilary.

units.la: Haud multò post, Faustus Abbas Rhegiensis Semipelagianorum opinioni sese associans doctrinam ab Augustino propositam, & à Prospero, Hilario & Cælestino defensam, publico scripto damnavit & hærefin appellavit primus. Gennadius Massiliensis, qui vixit A. D. 490. Fausti doctrinam laudavit, & Augustinianam doctrinam (suppresso Augustini nomine) hærefin Prædestinatianorum appellavit. Sed postea anno 1494. hæc Fausti & Gennadii doctrina in concilio Romano à Gelasio Papa fuit reiecta, Augustini & Prosperi libri ut orthodoxi recepti, vide distinct. 15. can. Sancta Romana. Sed revixit contentio ista, quando Gottescalcus Rhemensis ecclesiæ monachus, Augustini, Prosperi & Fulgentii sententiam publicè prædicavit, cui statim sese oppositerunt Hincmarus ecclesiæ Rhemensis archiepiscopus, & Rabanus, qui iterum sub prætextu hæresecos prædestinatianæ sententiam Augustini reiecerunt, & reliquias Pelagianas in ecclesiam revocarunt. Quod animadvertens Remigius Episcopus Lugdunensis synodum Valentianam coëgit, in qua doctrina Hincmari damnata, Gottescalci orthodoxa pronuntiata. Quam etiam ut verbo Dei consentientem ecclesia Lugdunensis publico scripto comprobavit. Si quis autem Augustini, Prosperi & Hilarii,
units.tr: Not long afterwards, Faustus, abbot of Riez, joined the opinion of the Semipelagians. He condemned by public writing the doctrine proposed by Augustine and defended by Prosper, Hilary and Celestine, and was the first to call it heresy. Gennadius of Marseilles, who lived in the year 490, praised the teaching of Faustus and called Augustinian doctrine (with Augustine's name suppressed) the heresy of the Predestinarians. But later, in the year 494, this teaching of Faustus and Gennadius was rejected by Pope Gelasius in a Roman council, and the books of Augustine and Prosper were received as orthodox; see Distinction 15, canon Sancta Romana. Yet this contention revived when Gottschalk, a monk of the Church of Reims, publicly preached the opinion of Augustine, Prosper and Fulgentius. Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Reims, and Rabanus at once opposed him; under the pretext of the predestinarian heresy they again rejected Augustine's opinion and brought the Pelagian remnants back into the Church. Noticing this, Remigius, bishop of Lyons, called the Synod of Valence, in which Hincmar's doctrine was condemned and Gottschalk's pronounced orthodox. The Church of Lyons also approved this by public writing, as agreeing with the Word of God. If anyone compares the books of Augustine, Prosper and Hilary,

units.la: Hilarii, larii, & horum discipulorum libros cum Sigeberti & Hincmari libris conferat, animadvertet pientissimis illis viris magnam iniuriam fieri, ab hisce duobus scriptoribus, nec enim illi scripserunt pie viventibus non prodesse bonorum operum laborem si a Deo ad mortem ordinati fuissent, & impiis & peccatoribus non obesse quaecunque scelera & flagitia ab illis commissa, si Deus illos ad vitam aeternam praedestinasset, ut Harscherus ex Sigeberto allegavit.
units.tr: Hilary, and of their disciples, with the books of Sigebert and Hincmar, he will notice that a great injustice is done to those most devout men by these two writers. For they never wrote that the labour of good works does not profit the godly if they have been ordained by God to death, nor that the impious and sinners are not harmed by whatever crimes and outrages they commit, if God has predestined them to eternal life, as Harscher quoted from Sigebert.

units.la: Non potuit autem hactenus, ne quidem ad hunc usque diem Pelagii haeresis ex ecclesia eliminari. Nam in concilio Tridentino dissensio orta est inter Theologos. Alii enim doctrinam Augustini orthodoxam (quam & nos docemus) alii Semipelagianismum defenderunt. Haec contentio fuit continuata postea, inter Dominicanos & Jesuitas. Dominicanis Augustini sententiam, Jesuitis Semipelagianorum sententiam amplexantibus. Quamvis ne quidem inter Jesuitas omnimodus consensus, ut videre licet apud Bellarminum, lib. de Grat. & lib. Arbitrio cap. 15. Nam ibi Cardinalis asserit, homines non minus gratuito ad gloriam quàm ad gratiam eligi, quod multi ex Jesuitis negant. Sed accedo ad
units.tr: Nor, up to the present day, has the heresy of Pelagius been able to be removed from the Church. For at the Council of Trent a dissension arose among the theologians. Some defended the orthodox doctrine of Augustine (which we too teach), others Semipelagianism. This contention was afterwards continued between the Dominicans and the Jesuits: the Dominicans embraced Augustine's opinion, the Jesuits the opinion of the Semipelagians. Yet there is not even complete agreement among the Jesuits, as may be seen in Bellarmine, in the books On Grace and On Free Will, chapter 15. For there the Cardinal asserts that men are chosen no less freely for glory than for grace, which many Jesuits deny. But I pass on to

units.la: PARALLELUM CALVINIANUM.
units.tr: THE CALVINIST PARALLEL.

units.la: Calvinus l. 3. instit. cap. 21: §. 5. Prædestinationem vocamus Dei decretum, quò apud se constitutum habuit, quid de unoquoque homine fieri vellet. Non enim pari conditione creantur homines, sed aliis vita æterna, aliis damnatio æterna præordinatur. Itaque prout in alterutrum finem quisque conditus est, ita vel ad vitam, vel ad mortem prædestinatum dicimus.
units.tr: Calvin, book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 21, §5: We call predestination God's decree, by which he has determined with himself what he wishes to become of each man. For men are not created on equal terms, but eternal life is foreordained for some, eternal damnation for others. Therefore, as each is created for one or the other end, so we say he is predestined either to life or to death.

units.la: Parag. 7. quod ergò scriptura clarè ostendit, dicimus æterno & immutabili consilio Deum semel constituisse, quos olim assumere vellet in salutem, quos rursus exitio devovere. Hoc consilium quoad electos in gratuita eius misericordia fundatum esse asserimus: nullo humana dignitatis respectu. Quos verò damnationi addicit, his justo quidem & irreprehensibili, sed incomprehensibili eius judicio vitæ aditum præcludi. Et cap. 23. §. 3 ubicunq; verò hoc regnat Dei beneplacitum, nulla in considerationem veniunt opera. Et §. 11. si non possumus rationem assignare cur suos misericordia dignetur, nisi quoniam illi ita placet, nec etiam in aliis reprobandis aliud habebimus quàm eius voluntatem.
units.tr: Paragraph 7. Therefore, as Scripture plainly shows, we say that by an eternal and unchangeable counsel God once determined whom he would at one time take into salvation and whom again to devote to destruction. We assert that this counsel, as regards the elect, is founded on his free mercy, with no regard to human worth; but those whom he appoints to damnation are barred from access to life by his judgment, which is just and blameless, yet incomprehensible. And in chapter 23, §3: wherever the good pleasure of God reigns, works come into no consideration. And §11: if we cannot assign a reason why he deigns to show mercy to his own, except that it pleases him, then in reprobating others also we shall have nothing but his will.

units.la: Cap. 23: §. 1. minimè consentaneum est præparationem ad interitum alio transferre, quam ad arcanum consilium Dei. Lib. 11. instit. cap. 18 §. 1. absurdum videtur (catholicis) volente & jubente Deo excacari hominem, qui mox suæ cæcitatis pœnas daturus est. Tergiversando igitur effugi-
units.tr: Chapter 23, §1: It is by no means consistent to transfer the preparation for ruin to anything other than God's secret counsel. Book 2 of the Institutes, chapter 18, §1: It seems absurd (to Catholics) that a man should be blinded by God's will and command, when he is soon to pay the penalty of his blindness. So by shuffling they escape

units.la: uni Dei unt Dei tantum permissu, non etiam voluntate hoc fieri. Ipse vero palam se facere pronuntians effugium illud repudiat.
units.tr: only by God's permission, not by his will, that this is done. But he himself, openly declaring that he does it, rejects that evasion.

units.la: Non puduit Calvinum, nec nos pudet, cum Apostolo Paulo, beato Augustino, Prospero & Hilario decreti praedestinationis aeternitatem, certitudinem & immutabilitatem afferere, electionis etiam tam ad gratiam, quàm ad gloriam, item Non-electionis caussam moventem, nullam aliam quàm Dei voluntatem & beneplacitum statuere, quicquid Jesuitae hoc in loco faciant, qui Pelagianorum & Semipelagianorum placita de libero arbitrio & meritis humanis tàm studiosè retinent, & Augustini sententiam à conciliis & Pontificibus Romanis approbatam reiiciunt.
units.tr: Calvin was not ashamed, and we are not ashamed, to maintain with the Apostle Paul, blessed Augustine, Prosper and Hilary, the eternity, certainty and immutability of the decree of predestination; and also that the cause moving election, both to grace and to glory, and likewise non-election, is nothing other than God's will and good pleasure. Whatever the Jesuits do on this point, who so eagerly hold on to the opinions of the Pelagians and Semipelagians about free will and human merits, and reject the opinion of Augustine, which has been approved by councils and Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: AEternitatem decreti electionis scriptura in genere & in specie asserit. Illud, cum docet Deo ab aterno nota esse omnia opera ejus, Act. 15: 18. Nota, inquam, id est, non simpliciter cognita, sed approbata, constituta & decreta. Hoc cum dicit, nos esse in Christo Iesu & Deo Patre electos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, Eph. 1:4. & datam nobis esse gratiam in Christo Iesu ante tempora seculadria, 2. Tim. 1: 9. Id etiam docet nomenclatura vocis in utraque lingua, nam praedestinatio nihil aliud significat, quàm destinationem alicuius rei, antequam illa sit, & προορισμός à προορίζειν est constitutio seu determinatio alicuius rei antequam efficiatur. Idcirco Calvinus recte scripsit lib. 3. Instit. cap. 21. §. 5. Praedestinationem vocamus Dei decretum, quo apud se constitutum habuit, quid de unoquoque homine fieri vellet. Nam non possumus Deum spoliare istâ praefinitione, nisi simul ipsum vel omniscientiâ, vel omnisapientiâ, vel omnipotentiâ spoliemus.
units.tr: Scripture asserts the eternity of the decree of election in general and in particular. In general, when it teaches that all his works are known to God from eternity, Acts 15:18. "Known," I say, that is, not simply recognised, but approved, established and decreed. When it says that we were chosen in Christ Jesus and by God the Father before the foundations of the world were laid, Eph. 1:4, and that grace was given us in Christ Jesus before the eternal ages, 2 Tim. 1:9. The meaning of the word in both languages also teaches this, for predestination signifies nothing other than the destining of a thing before it exists, and proorismos [προορισμός] from proorizein [προορίζειν] is the establishing or determining of a thing before it is brought about. Hence Calvin rightly wrote in book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 21, §5: We call predestination God's decree, by which he has determined with himself what he wishes to become of each man.
