For we cannot deprive God of this predetermination without at the same time depriving him of either his omniscience, his omnisapience or his omnipotence.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem ista praedestinatio est actio Dei immanens & aeterna, & per consequens ipsa Dei voluntas & essentia, omnimodè independens: ita etiam independens quoquè est ab omni termino ante & post. Quæ causa est quod Theologi orthodoxi decretum hoc vocant absolutum.
units.tr: Just as this predestination is an immanent and eternal act of God, and consequently the very will and essence of God, completely independent of anything, so it is also independent of every term before and after. This is why orthodox theologians call this decree absolute.

units.la: AEternitas hæc decreti divini & ταυτότης cum essentia divina fundamentum est eiusdem immutabilitatis & certitudinis. Nam quàm verè Deus est, & sibi similis manet, tàm verè eius voluntas & decretum immutabile est. Hinc dicit apud Malachiam Prophetam cap. 3: 6. Ego Iehova non mutor. Et Jacobus cap. 1: 17. apud Deum non esse transmutationem aut conversionis obumbrationem. Nempe quia Deus fortis non est homo, qui mentiatur, aut filius hominis, quem pæniteat: an ipse dixerit & non faciet? an locutus fuerit & non præstabit illud? Num. 23: 23. Quo fundamento posito, quòd Deus sit æterna, sapientissima, potentissima, liberrima,
units.tr: This eternity of the divine decree, and its identity [ταυτότης] with the divine essence, is the foundation of its immutability and certainty. For just as truly as God is God and remains like himself, so truly is his will and decree unchangeable. Hence he says through the prophet Malachi, ch. 3:6, I, Jehovah, do not change. And James, ch. 1:17, says that with God there is no variation or shadow of turning. Indeed, God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent: has he said, and will he not do it? or has he spoken, and will he not make it good? Num. 23:19. Granted this foundation, that God is eternal, most wise, most powerful, most free,

units.la: immutabilis & independens caussa rerum futurarum, non potest etiam ipsa decreti divini executio non esse sapiens, immutabilis, & independens. Ita ut omnes illi ex Deo non Deum faciant, quicunque asserunt, evenire aliquid in tempore posse, contra id, quod Deus ab æterno statuit & decrevit, hoc est, semel electos à Deo, posse fieri reprobos, & vice versâ.
units.tr: and the immutable and independent cause of future things, the execution of the divine decree cannot fail to be wise, immutable and independent as well. So all those who make God not God, who assert that something can happen in time contrary to what God established and decreed from eternity, that is, that those once elected by God can become reprobate, and vice versa, are making God into something other than God.

units.la: Atquè hoc de primo. Circa alterum, quod de electionis ad gratiam & gloriam, item Non-electionis quorundam, caussa movente docuit Calvinus, magis tumultuantur Jesuitæ.
units.tr: So much for the first point. As for the second, which Calvin taught concerning the moving cause of election to grace and glory, and likewise of the non-election of some, the Jesuits make a greater uproar.

units.la: Ego breviter & quantum fieri potest perspicuè hîc tradam, quid Calvinus circa hanc quæstionem secundùm scripturam docuerit. Prædestinationis vocem Calvinus generalius accipit pro omni Dei decreto circa hominem in ordine ad ultimum eius finem, & sub eo complexus est etiam decreta reliqua omnia, quæ hominem concernunt. Unde lib. III. Instit. cap. 21. §. 5. scribit: Prædestinationem vocamus Dei decretum, quô apud se constitutum habuit, quid de unoquoque homine fieri vellet. Ubi ita generaliter voce prædestinationis utitur, ut sub ea complectatur præfinitionem & βουλήν, definitum consilium Dei de fine ultimo hominis, & mediis ad eundem, hoc est, circa hominem sive condendum, sive conditum & nondum lapsum, sive hominem lapsum, & in corruptionis massa constitutum, ex eaque vel eligendum vel in ea relinquendum.
units.tr: I shall set out here briefly, and as clearly as I can, what Calvin taught on this question according to Scripture. Calvin takes the word predestination more generally, for every decree of God concerning man in relation to his ultimate end, and under it he includes all the other decrees that concern man. Hence in Institutes book 3, ch. 21, §5, he writes: We call predestination God's decree, by which he has determined within himself what he wishes to become of each man. Here he uses the word predestination so generally that it embraces the foreordination and βουλή [counsel], the defined purpose of God concerning man's final end and the means to it; that is, concerning man either as to be created, or as created but not yet fallen, or as fallen and placed in the mass of corruption, and from that mass to be either chosen or left in it.

units.la: In explicatione autem huius decreti sic generaliter accepti Calvinus ita procedit, ut dicat, 1. Deum ante omnia (veluti sapientissimum artificem) statuisse, quid de homine creatura sua fieri vellet, sive quoad statum huius vitæ præsentis, sive futuræ. 2. Hunc finem à priori à nemine posse cognosci, quia nemo novit mentem Domini, nec ullus ei fuit à consilio, Rom. 11. 34. intelligi autem ex decreti eius executione in tempore. Nam quia Deus omnia agit ex consilio voluntatis suae, Eph. 1: 11. sequitur nihil evenire in tempore, & quoad res, & quoad modum rerum, quod non ante ab æterno, ut sic eveniret decreverit. Act. 4: 28. 3. Executionem in tempore nos docere, non omnes homines ad salutem æternam pervenire, sed pusillo gregi placuisse Deo tradere regnum, ut Mediator nolter loquitur, Luc. 12: 32. Unde sequi Deum ab æterno non voluisse aut decrevisse omnibus dare salutē, quia nemo potest voluntati ejus resistere, Rom 9: 11. sed quibusdam tantùm, multis praeteritis. 4. Decretum illud dationis vitæ æternæ, vocari electionem, decretum non dationis, reprobationem, seu, quod idem est, praeteritionem. 5. Electionem istam & reprobationem pro obiecto habuisse hominem lapsum & in corruptionis massa constitutum. Sic enim loquitur in libello peculiari de praedestinatione: illam sententiam, quòd ex damnata Adæ sobole, Deus quos visum est elegit, quos vult reprobat, sicuti ad fidem exercendam longè aptior est, ita majori fructu tractari.
units.tr: In explaining this decree, taken in this general sense, Calvin proceeds as follows. He says: (1) that God, before all things, as the most wise craftsman, determined what he wished to become of the man he created, whether as to the state of this present life or of the future. (2) That this purpose cannot be known a priori by anyone, because no one has known the mind of the Lord, nor has anyone been his counsellor, Rom. 11:34; it is to be understood from the execution of his decree in time. For since God works all things according to the counsel of his will, Eph. 1:11, it follows that nothing comes about in time, either as to the things themselves or as to the manner of things, which he did not decree from eternity that it should so come about, Acts 4:28. (3) The execution in time teaches us that not all men attain eternal salvation, but that it has pleased the Father to give the kingdom to the little flock, as our Mediator speaks, Luke 12:32. Hence it follows that God did not from eternity will or decree to give salvation to all, because no one can resist his will, Rom. 9:19, but only to some, while many were passed over. (4) That decree of granting eternal life is called election; the decree of not granting it is called reprobation, or, what is the same, preterition. (5) That this election and reprobation had as their object man fallen and placed in the mass of corruption. For he speaks thus in a separate little book on predestination: That opinion, that God, out of the damned offspring of Adam, elects whom he pleased and reprobates whom he wills, is, as it is far more suited to exercising faith, so to be handled with greater profit.

units.la: 6. Ex hac ipsa corruptionis massa Deum aliquos elegisse ad vitam æternam sine illorum merito, quia omnes deflexerunt & inutiles facti sunt, nec ullus justus fuit, ne unus quidem, Rom. 3: 10, 12.
units.tr: (6) That God chose some to eternal life out of this very mass of corruption, without any merit of theirs, because they have all turned aside and become worthless, and there is none who is righteous, no, not one, Rom. 3:10, 12.

units.la: 7. Elegisse autem eos ex mera voluntate & beneplacito, cùm per se omnes essent damnabiles. Sic enim scriptura docet & quoad decretum & quoad executionem decreti. Quod ad illud, Eph 1: 5. qui praedestinavit nos, quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum in se, pro benevolo effectu voluntatis suæ, ad laudem gloriosæ suæ gratiæ. Quoad icтam, Matth. 11: 25. 26. in illo tempore respondens Iesus dixit, gloriam tibi tribuo Pater, Domine cœli & terræ, quòd hæc occultaveris à sapientibus & intelligentibus, & ea retexeris infantibus, etiam Pater, quia placuit tibi. Phil. 2: 13. Deus enim is est, qui efficit in vobis, & ut velitis, & ut efficiatis, pro gratuita sua benevolentia. Et sicuti Thomas recte dixit, quae Deus decrevit per sapientiam, illa exsequitur per virtutem, ita haec executio nos docet, quomodo homo in electionis decreto fuerit a Deo consideratus, cum scriptura dicit Deum elegisse infantes, Matth. 11: 25. elegisse μωρα, ςὰ ςῦ ἀσθενῆ infirma, 1. Cor. 1: 27. cum nullis adhuc essent viribus, sed per lapsus mortui Eph. 2: 5. Talis ergo procul dubio in electionis decreto exstitit homo eligendus. Adeo ut tota scriptura Pelagii logicam & Semipelagianorum ex eadem desumptos διαλογισμὸς refutet.
units.tr: (7) That he chose them from his mere will and good pleasure, since all were in themselves deserving of damnation. For Scripture teaches this both as to the decree and as to its execution. As to the decree, Eph. 1:5: who predestined us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace. As to the execution, Matt. 11:25-26: At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants; yes, Father, for so it has pleased you. Phil. 2:13: For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his gracious goodwill. And just as Thomas rightly said, what God decreed through wisdom, he carries out through power, so this execution teaches us how man was regarded by God in the decree of election, since Scripture says that God chose infants, Matt. 11:25, and chose the foolish things [μωρά] and the weak things [ἀσθενῆ], 1 Cor. 1:27, when they had as yet no strength, but were dead through trespasses, Eph. 2:5. Such, therefore, beyond doubt, was the man to be elected in the decree of election. So much so that the whole of Scripture refutes the logic of Pelagius and the reasonings [διαλογισμός] of the Semipelagians drawn from it.

units.la: 8. Non-electionis autem sive praeteritionis multorum in eadem corruptionis massa in relatione ad electos, causam interne Deum movientem verbum Dei non aliam quam Dei beneplacitum assignare: si vero consideretur respectu prædamnationis, decreti reprobationis caussam esse peccatum in quod iam inciderunt. Cùm enim omnes essent ob peccatum reprobabiles, nec tamen omnes reprobati, ratio nulla dari potest quàm Dei εὐδοκία. Atque hæc est Theologia Paulina, ex qua hæc verba habemus: Annon habet potestatem figulus in lutum, ut ex eadem massa faciat, aliud vas ad decus, aliud ad dedecus? Rom. 9: 21. Item, cujus vult miseretur, quem autem vult indurat, v. 18.
units.tr: (8) As for the non-election, or preterition, of many in the same mass of corruption, in relation to the elect, the word of God assigns no internal cause moving God other than his good pleasure [εὐδοκία]. But if it is considered with respect to condemnation, the cause of the decree of reprobation is the sin into which they had already fallen. For since all were liable to reprobation because of sin, yet not all were reprobated, no reason can be given except God's good pleasure. This is the Pauline theology, from which we have these words: Has not the potter power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? Rom. 9:21. Likewise, he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills, v. 18.

units.la: Non-electionis decretum non minus suam habet executionem & executionis media, quàm decretum electionis. Qualia sunt 1. Denegatio vocationis, tum omnimodæ, respectu multarum gentium, quando Deus præteritis aliis gentibus solum populum Israëliticum vocavit, tùm internæ & efficacis respectu multorum, qui sunt in ecclesia, de quibus loquitur Christus, Luc. 8: 10. Vobis (apostolis & electis) datum est nosse mysteria regni Dei, reliquis autem per parabolas loquor, ut videntes non videant, & audientes non intelligant. 2. Denegatio iustificationis, ut Christus loquitur, Joh. 17:9. non pro mundo rogo, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. Nam hi duo actus officii sacerdotalis, intercedere apud Deum & sacrificare sunt inseperabiles, Rom. 8: 34. Christus est qui mortuus est, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Ego eorum (pro quibus rogo) causa sanctifico meipsum, ut sint & ipsi sanctificati in veritate, id est, vere iustificati. 3. Denegatio sanctificationis. Nam sanctificatio est glorificatio inchoata, & glorificatio sanctificatio perfecta. Quibus ergo glorificatio non competit, eis nec competit sanctificatio. Reprobis autem glorificatio non competit, Matth. 11: 41. Ergo.
units.tr: The decree of non-election has its execution and its means of execution no less than the decree of election. Such are: (1) the denial of calling, both absolute, with respect to many nations, when God, passing over the other nations, called only the people of Israel; and internal and effective, with respect to many who are in the Church, of whom Christ speaks, Luke 8:10: To you (the apostles and the elect) it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest I speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand. (2) The denial of justification, as Christ speaks, John 17:9: I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. For these two acts of the priestly office, to intercede with God and to sacrifice, are inseparable, Rom. 8:34: Christ is the one who died, and who also intercedes for us. And John 17:19: For their sake (for whom I pray) I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth, that is, truly justified. (3) The denial of sanctification. For sanctification is glorification begun, and glorification is sanctification perfected. Therefore, those to whom glorification does not belong, to them sanctification does not belong either. But glorification does not belong to the reprobate, Matt. 11:41. Therefore...

units.la: Hi actus negativi aliquando exprimuntur per actus affirmativos, locutione impropriâ, ut cùm Deus dicitur indurasse cor Pharaonis, Exod. 4: 21. tradidisse gentes cupiditatibus cordium ipsorum ad impuritatem, & fœdis affectibus Rom. 1: 24, 26. misisse efficaciam deceptionis, ut credant mendacio, 2. Thess. 2: 11. Atquè hæc omnia Deus facit ad illustrationem, gloriæ tùm potentiæ suæ, tum libertatis & iustitiæ.
units.tr: These negative acts are sometimes expressed by affirmative acts, in an improper manner of speaking, as when God is said to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh (Exod. 4:21), to have given up the nations to the lusts of their hearts, to uncleanness, and to vile affections (Rom. 1:24, 26), to have sent the working of deception, that they should believe a lie (2 Thess. 2:11). God does all these things to display the glory both of his power and of his freedom and justice.

units.la: Talis est doctrina Calvini, quam ex Dei verbo addidicit, & cum qua consentiunt quoquè veteres ecclesiæ Doctores. Augustin. serm. 67. in Cant. Dominus ait non tu me, sed ego elegi te, intervenit non tuum meritum, sed meum placitum. Est gratia prima, quâ prævenita est ecclesia, postea verò & subsequens gratia est. Illam refero ad decretum electionis, hanc ad executionem eiusquè media. Sunt duæ hominum societates, quarum una prædestinata est in æternum regnare cum Deo, altera verò æternum subire supplicium cum Diabolo. lib. 15.
units.tr: This is the teaching of Calvin, which he learned from the Word of God, and with which the early Doctors of the Church also agree. Augustine, sermon 67 on the Song of Songs: The Lord says, not you chose me, but I chose you; the cause is not your merit, but my pleasure. There is a first grace, by which the Church is anticipated, and afterwards also a subsequent grace. I refer the former to the decree of election, the latter to its execution and means. There are two societies of men, of which one is predestined to reign with God forever, the other to undergo eternal punishment with the Devil, book 15, On the City of God, chapter 1.

units.la: 15, de civitate Dei cap. 1. Non quia credimus, sed ut credamus elegit nos, ne priores eum elegisse dicamus. De prædest. sanct. lib. 1. cap. 1. Augustinum sequitur Thomas, qui multis in locis potissimum in cap. 9. epist. ad Rom. veram de prædestinatione doctrinam asseruit. Et in 1. part. summ. q. 23. art. 3. Ubi quærit, an Deus aliquem hominem reprobet? & respondet affirmando. Postea ad obiectiones ex Hose. cap. 13. Perditio tua ex te ô Israël, ex me vero tantummodò auxilium tuum est, respondet Thomas: aliter se habet reprobatio in causando, quàm prædestinatio, (accipit prædestinationis vocem strictè cum Apostolo ad Rom. 8. quatenus idem est quod electio) nam prædestinatio est causa & ejus quod expectatur in futura vita à prædestinatis, scilicet gloria, & ejus quod percipitur in præsenti (vita) scilicet gratia. Reprobatio verò non est causa ejus, quod est in præsenti, scilicet culpa, sed est causa derelictionis à Deo. Est autem caussa ejus, quod redditur in suturo scilicet pœna æterna.
units.tr: He chose us not because we believe, but that we may believe, lest we say that we first chose him (On the Predestination of the Saints, book 1, chapter 1). Thomas follows Augustine, who asserted the true doctrine of predestination in many places, especially on chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans. In the first part of the Summa, question 23, article 3, he asks whether God reprobates any man, and answers in the affirmative. Then, to the objection from Hosea 13, Destruction is yours, O Israel; your help is only in me, Thomas replies: Reprobation differs from predestination in its causing (he takes the word predestination strictly, with the Apostle in Romans 8, insofar as it is the same as election), for predestination is the cause both of what is expected in the future life by the predestined, namely glory, and of what is received in the present life, namely grace. But reprobation is not the cause of what is in the present, namely sin, but it is the cause of desertion by God. It is, however, the cause of what is rendered in the future, namely eternal punishment.

units.la: Hanc doctrinam Augustini, Thomæ, Calvini, quam in schola Apostoli Pauli addidicerunt, reiiciunt Jesuitæ, in schola Pelagii nutriti. Harscherus equidem Jesuita in præsenti disputatione contra Calvinum non disputat (nisi quod aliquot scripturæ dicta tanquam doctrinæ Calvinianæ, ut putat, contraria, adducit) sed 1. Calvinum sibiipsi obiicentem & respondentem producit. 2. consequentiam exstruit ex Calvini dictis. Hæc autem omnia tàm miserè ut nauseam faciant legenti. Ego primò scripturæ dicta examinabo, deinde ad reliqua quoquè respondebo.
units.tr: The Jesuits, brought up in the school of Pelagius, reject this doctrine of Augustine, Thomas and Calvin, which they learned in the school of the Apostle Paul. Harscherus, the Jesuit, in the present dispute against Calvin, does not really dispute at all (except that he adduces some passages of Scripture which he thinks contrary to Calvinist doctrine). Rather, first, he brings forward Calvin objecting to himself and answering himself; second, he builds an inference from Calvin's statements. All of this is so wretchedly done that it makes the reader sick. I will first examine the passages of Scripture, and then answer the rest.

units.la: Gen. 1. Creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam.
units.tr: Gen. 1. God created man in his own image and likeness.

units.la: Addit Jesuita; ubi sub imagine etiam Calvinus lib. 1. Instit. cap. 15. n. 4. comprahenprehendit quicquid ad spiritualem & æternam vitam spectat, atq; n. 7. ornamenta illa Adami, non uni homini data fuisse, sed universæ hominum naturæ: In margine scribit: Deus creavit hominem ad vitam æternam, teste Calvino.
units.tr: The Jesuit adds: where, under the image, Calvin also in Institutes book 1, chapter 15, section 4, comprehends whatever pertains to spiritual and eternal life; and at section 7 he says those ornaments of Adam were given not to one man only but to the whole nature of man. In the margin he writes: God created man for eternal life, according to Calvin.

units.la: Non male hæc duo in Calvino observavit Harscherus, quòd homo in prima creatione dona acceperit, quæ ad vitam præsentem & futuram facerent, & quòd illa universæ naturæ humanæ, quam tùm repræsentabat Adamus fuerint concessa. Nec male etiam ad marginem notavit, Deus creavit hominem ad vitam æternam, teste Calvino. Nam ita etiam docemus Catechumenos nostros, ex quæstione 6. Catechismi nostri, in qua docetur, Deum creasse hominem ad imaginem suam, hoc est, verâ justitiâ & sanctitate præditum, ut Deum creatorem suum rectè cognosceret ex animo diligeret, & cum eo beatus in æternum viveret, idq; ad eum celebrandum & laudandum. Dicet Jesuita; quomodo hæc simul stare possunt, homines esse ad vitam æternam creatos, & homines non pari conditione creari, sed aliis vitam æternam, aliis damnationem æternam præordinari, ut Calvinus docet lib. 3. Institut. cap. 21. §. 5. sicuti supra fuit demonstratum? Respondeo optimè posse. Quando enim orthdoxi dicunt, Deum creasse hominem ad vitam æternam, loquuntur de statu hominis, in quo fuit creatus, qui certè talis fuit, ut ad vitam æternam obtinendam fuisset sufficientissimus, si modò in eo homo perseveraret. Quando autem dicunt Deum ab æterno alios ad vitam, alios ad interitum præordinasse, loquuntur de decreto, quod iam respectum habet non ad statum integritatis, sed ad lapsum, quem Deus ab æterno prævidit. Quæ duo non sunt commiscenda. Nam si Dei intentio præcisè fuisset hominem ad vitam æternam perducere, non ipsum creasset labilem, nec lapsum permisis-set, set, imò non tantùm ipsi dedisset velle, ut posset sed etiam posse, ut vellet. Idcircò rectè Calvinus lib. 1. Instit. cap. 15. §. 8. cùm de creatione hominis disputasset. Hîc intempestivè, inquit, quaestio ingeritur de occulta praedestinatione Dei, quia non quaeritur, quid accidere potuerit nec ne, sed qualis fuerit hominis natura.
units.tr: Harscherus rightly observed two things in Calvin: that in the first creation man received gifts which would serve for both present and future life, and that these were granted to the whole of human nature, which Adam then represented. Nor is he wrong to note in the margin, God created man for eternal life, according to Calvin. For we teach our catechumens the same, from question 6 of our Catechism, where it is taught that God created man in his own image, that is, endowed with true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God his Creator, love him from the heart, and live blessedly with him forever, and this to celebrate and praise him. The Jesuit will say: how can these things stand together, that men were created for eternal life, and yet that men are not created on the same condition, but that some are predestined to eternal life and others to eternal damnation, as Calvin teaches in Institutes book 3, chapter 21, section 5, as was shown above? I answer that they stand together very well. For when the orthodox say that God created man for eternal life, they speak of the state of man in which he was created, which was certainly such that he would have been fully sufficient to obtain eternal life, if only he had persevered in it. But when they say that God from eternity foreordained some to life and others to destruction, they speak of the decree, which has regard not to the state of integrity but to the fall, which God foresaw from eternity. These two must not be confused. For if God's intention had been simply to lead man to eternal life, he would not have created him mutable, nor would he have permitted the fall; rather, he would have given him not only the power to will but also the ability to will. Therefore Calvin rightly says, in Institutes book 1, chapter 15, section 8, after discussing the creation of man: Here, he says, the question of the hidden predestination of God is untimely raised, because we are not asking what could or could not have happened, but what the nature of man was.

units.la: Secundum testimonium citat ex Ezech. 18. Num quid voluntatis meae est mors impij dicit Dominus Deus, & non ut convertatur à vitijs suis & vivat. Et: Cùm enim averterit se justus à justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem, morietur in eis, in justitia quam operatus est, morietur. Et cùm averterit se impius ab impietate sua, quam operatus est, & fecerit judicium & justitiam ipse animam suam vivificabit. Et: Quia nolo mortem morientis dicit Dominus Deus, revertimini & vivite.
units.tr: The second testimony he cites is from Ezekiel 18: Is it my will that the wicked should die? says the Lord God, and not that he should turn from his ways and live? And: When the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in them; in the righteousness which he has done he shall die. And: When the wicked turns away from his wickedness which he has done, and does judgment and righteousness, he shall save his soul alive. And: For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, says the Lord God; turn yourselves and live.

units.la: In his dictis Propheticis duo notanda, quae ad praesentem quaestionem faciunt, nam Bellarminus iis in alia controversia quoque utitur. Primum est, quòd Deus dicitur non velle mortem peccatoris, alterum, quòd velit, ut peccator convertatur ab iniquitate sua & vivat. Quod primum concernit verba hebraea אל לא verf. 23; & 32. vel verti possunt non delector; quemadmodum radix חפץ etiam delectatus, oblectatus est, significat, vide 1. Sam. 18: 25. Ubi in hebraeo legimus, אין חפץ למלך כמהר non est oblectatio Regi in dote. Secundùm hanc interpretationem non sequitur, si Deus non delectatur morte improbi, quòd idcirco illam nolit certo alio fine. Nam sicuti aegrotus non delectatur potu amaro, tamen vult, permittit & procurat ad bibendum, valetudinis causa: ita etiam Deus licèt non delectetur morte peccatoris, tamen eam vult, quia facit ad declarationem iustitiae suae, quae non minor gloriosa proprietas in Deo est, quàm misericordia: vel possunt verti non volens seu non volo, uti Sept. habent, & ubique Vulgatus: sic nos natura Dei & scriptura cogit distinguere mortem, quae consideratur, vel ut est destructio hominis & interitus creaturae Dei, eatenus Deus mortem hominis non vult, nec potest velle, quia hac ratione homo bonum quid est; vel ut est poena peccati, & iustitiae Dei declarandae medium. Quomodo consideratur in obiecto Non-electionis, quod est homo corruptus & in peccatum lapsus. Ita Deus mortem improbi vult, nec potest non velle, quia ipse Deus peccatori mortem minatus est, Gen. 2: 17. quo die comederis de eo, morte morieris. Unde Rex David Psal. 5: 17. perdes omnes loquentes mendacium. Matth. 25.41. execrati abite a me in ignem aeternum.
units.tr: In these prophetic words two things are to be noted which bear on the present question; Bellarmine also uses them in another controversy. The first is that God is said not to will the death of the sinner; the second, that he wills that the sinner turn from his iniquity and live. As to the first, the Hebrew אל לא (verses 23 and 32) may be rendered I do not delight, just as the root חפץ also means to be pleased or delighted; see 1 Sam. 18:25, where in the Hebrew we read אין חפץ למלך כמהר, the king has no delight in the dowry. On this interpretation it does not follow that, if God takes no delight in the death of the wicked, he therefore does not will it for some other end. For just as a sick man does not delight in a bitter drink, yet wills, permits and procures it for drinking, for the sake of his health, so also God, although he does not delight in the death of the sinner, yet wills it, because it serves to declare his justice, which is no less a glorious property in God than mercy. Or the words may be rendered not willing or I do not will, as the Septuagint has, and the Vulgate everywhere. Thus the nature of God and Scripture compel us to distinguish death as it is considered either as the destruction of man and the perishing of God's creature, and so far God does not will the death of man, nor can he will it, since in this respect man is a good thing; or as the punishment of sin, and a means of declaring God's justice. In this second sense it is considered in the object of non-election, which is man corrupted and fallen into sin. So God wills the death of the wicked, and cannot not will it, because God himself threatened death to man: Gen. 2:17, in the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die. Whence King David says: You shall destroy all who speak lies (Ps. 5:6), and Matt. 25:41: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire.

units.la: Alterum quod Deus velit omnium impiorum conversionem, dici non potest, licet ea delectetur. Quia Deus ipse apud Esaiam testatur cap. 46: 10. confilium meum stabit, & omnem delectationem (voluntatem) meam facturus sum. Atqui plurimos Deus non convertit, imò conversionis media ex professo denegat, ut videmus in exemplo Pharaonis, & in Gentibus, quas Deus praeteritis atatibus sivit suis ipsarum vijs incedere. Act. 14: 16. Aut ergò dicendum, Deum noluisse, ut converterentur, aut si voluit & decrevit consilium eius non fuisse stabile, nec potuisse omnem suam voluntatem facere. Quod absit.
units.tr: The second proposition, that God wills the conversion of all the wicked, cannot be said, although he takes delight in it. For God himself testifies through Isaiah, ch. 46:10, "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure (will)." Yet God does not convert very many; indeed he expressly withholds the means of conversion, as we see in the example of Pharaoh and in the Gentiles, whom God in past ages allowed to walk in their own ways. Acts 14:16. Therefore we must say either that God was unwilling that they should be converted, or, if he willed and decreed it, that his counsel was not stable and that he could not do all his will. Far be that thought.

units.la: Dicit Jesuita: damnatio non in Dei beneplacitum sed in opera mala & bonorum neglectum confertur: Matt. 25. discedite à me maledicti in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis eius. Esurivi enim & non dedistis mihi manducare, sitivi & non dedistis mihi potum, hospes eram & non collegistis me, nudus & non cooperuistis me, infirmus & in carcere & non visitastis me.
units.tr: The Jesuit says: damnation is not imposed by God's good pleasure, but by evil works and by the neglect of good works: Matt. 25, "Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food; I was thirsty and you gave me no drink; I was a stranger and you did not take me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me."

units.la: Valde molestum est in disputationibus theologicis, quando adversa pars statuit quæstionis, aut negligit, aut nö intelligit, quod hîc facit Jesuita Harfcher3. Nusquâ Calvinus aut quisquam alius ex nobis asseruit, damnationis hominum caussam esse Dei beneplacitum. Licèt enim caussam Non-electionis quorundam comparativè consideratæ, quatenus ex omnibus ob peccatum reprobabilibus, alios elegit Deus, alios non elegit, meram Dei ἐυδοκίαν statuamus: neminem tamen Deus damnat sine peccato. Idcirco inter præteritionem, quam scholastici indebitæ gratiæ denegationem vocant, & damnationem seu præparationem pœnæ, perpetuò distinguimus. Posterior enim hic actus semper est respectivus peccati. Sicuti enim Deus neminem in tempore punit, nisi ob peccatum, ita neminem ab æterno damnare decrevit, nisi ex hypothesi peccati. Interim & hîc beneplacitum Dei suo modo concurrit, licèt non ut caussa. Nam quia Deus justificatur, quando ipse judicat, ut Apostolus Paulus Rom.3:4. ex Psal.51:6. docet, non potest Deus non, in iustitiæ suæ gloria εὐδοξεῖ. Unde Christus Matth. 11:26. gloriam Deo Patri tribuit, quod ipsius εὐδοξία fuerit mysteria salutis sapientibus & intelligentibus hujus mundi occultare.
units.tr: It is very irksome in theological disputations when the opposing side either neglects or fails to understand the state of the question, as the Jesuit Harscher does here. Nowhere has Calvin or anyone else among us asserted that God's good pleasure is the cause of men's damnation. For although we hold that the cause of the non-election of some, considered comparatively (insofar as, from among all who are reprobable on account of sin, God chose some and did not choose others), is God's pure eudokia [εὐδοκία], yet God damns no one without sin. Therefore we always distinguish between preterition, which the scholastics call the denial of undeserved grace, and damnation or the preparation of punishment. For the latter act is always respective to sin. Just as God punishes no one in time except on account of sin, so he decreed from eternity to damn no one except on the hypothesis of sin. Meanwhile God's good pleasure also concurs here in its own way, though not as a cause. For since God is justified when he judges, as the Apostle Paul teaches, Rom. 3:4, from Ps. 51:6, God cannot but take pleasure in the glory of his justice [εὐδοξεῖ]. Hence Christ, Matt. 11:26, gives glory to God the Father, because it was his good pleasure [εὐδοκία] to hide the mysteries of salvation from the wise and understanding of this world.

units.la: Locus ergò ex Matthæo citatus nihil ad quæstionem facit, quia de prædestinatione non agit. Hoc ex Maldonato Jesuita addiscere potuisset Harscherus qui ita ad verf. 34. commentatur: Illud dico videri mihi Christum glorificationis potius de qua agebat, quàm prædestinationis caussam reddere voluisse, ut ex antitheto manifestum est, discedite in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & angelis &c. hic enim cum eodem loquatur modo, non reddit caussam, cur jam illis ab æternitate ignis paratus sit, sed cur in ignem mittantur.
units.tr: Therefore the passage cited from Matthew has nothing to do with the question, because it does not treat of predestination. Harscher could have learned this from the Jesuit Maldonatus, who comments on verse 34 as follows: I say that it seems to me that Christ wished to give the cause of the glorification of which he was speaking, rather than the cause of predestination, as is clear from the antithesis, "Depart into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels," etc. For here, speaking in the same manner, he does not give the reason why the fire has been prepared for them from eternity, but why they are sent into the fire.

units.la: 1. Tim. 2. Obsecro igitur omnium primò fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, hoc enim bonum & acceptum est coram Deo, qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri & ad agnitionem veritatis venire, unus enim Deus, unus & mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit semetipsum redemtionem pro omnibus.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 2: "I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all men; for this is good and acceptable before God, who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all."

units.la: An impotens est Deus qui vult omnes salvos fieri & non fit? An Diabolus potentior est Deo, aut homines validiores, qui facere possunt, ut Deus finem suum non assequatur? Absit hoc, nam Deus noster in coelis est & facit quodcunque ipsi placet, cuius voluntati nemo resistere potest, Rom. 9: 19. Videndum ergo quomodo verba ista apostolica secundum analogiam fidei dextrè explicanda. Et quia Harscherus toties ad antiquos patres provocat, potissimum etiam in parallelo postremo, audiamus illos circa praesentem locum. Augustinus enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 102. sub finem, & ab initio cap 103. locum Apostoli bifariam explicat. Voculam enim omnes vult accipi posse per reduplicationem, ac si diceretur, nullum hominem fieri salvum, nisi quem salvum ipse voluerit, non quod nullus sit hominum, nisi quem salvum fieri velit, sed quod nullus fiat, nisi quem velit, & ideo sit rogandus ut velit, quia necesse est fieri si velit. Deinde eandem voculam pro genere singulorum accipiendam esse docet, cum dicit: aut certe sic dictum est: qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri, non quod nullus hominum esset quem salvum fieri nollet, qui virtutes miraculorum facere noluit apud eos, quos dicit acturos fuisse poenitentiam si fecisset, sed ut omnes homines omne genus hominum intelligamus, per quascunque differentias distributum, reges, privatos, nobiles, ignobiles &c. Postea locutionis istius usum probat exemplo in eodem capite. Isto locutionis modo, inquit, & Dominus est usus in Evangelio, ubi ait Pharisaeis, decimatis mentam & & rutam & omne olus. Neq; enim Pharisæi & quacunq; aliena & omnium per omnes terras alienigenarum omnia olera decimabant. Sicut ergo hic omne olerum genus, ita & illi omnes homines omne hominum genus intelligere possumus. In lib. de correpт. & grat. cap. 14. ista legimus: hic unum dicam, ita dictum, omnes homines vult salvos fieri, ut intelligantur omnes prædestinati, quia omne genus hominum in eis est. Recte etiam Theophylactus, qui dicit, Apostolum hic de salute agere, quæ sit per fidem, non autem de salute quapiam universali credentium & non credentium. Certè Apostolus connectit salutem & veritatis agnitionem, quibus hæc denegatur, illa non conceditur. Thomas Aquinas sic in prædictum locum commentatur: In Deo salus omnium hominum habet rationem ut sit volibilis, & sic est voluntas ejus antecedens, de qua hic Apostolus, vult omnes salvos fieri: sed si consideretur bonum justitia, & quod peccata puniantur, sic non vult, & hæc est voluntas consequens. Hæ responsiones sufficere possunt, imò debent ex hypothesi Harscheriana, quamvis aliter istum locum explicare possemus.
units.tr: Is God powerless, since he wills all to be saved and it does not happen? Is the devil stronger than God, or men more powerful, so that they can prevent God from attaining his end? Far from it, for our God is in heaven and does whatever pleases him, and no one can resist his will, Rom. 9:19. We must therefore consider how these apostolic words are rightly to be explained according to the analogy of faith. And since Harscher so often appeals to the ancient Fathers, especially in the final parallel, let us hear what they say about the present passage. Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, ch. 102 near the end, and from the beginning of ch. 103, explains the Apostle's words in two ways. The little word omnes ("all") may be taken by reduplication, as if it were said that no man is saved except whom he himself has willed to save, not that there is no man whom he does not wish to be saved, but that no one is saved unless he wills it, and therefore he is to be asked that he may will it, because it necessarily comes about if he wills it. Then he teaches that the same little word is to be taken for the kind of each, when he says: or certainly it is said thus: who wills all men to be saved, not that there is no man whom he would not wish to be saved, since he was unwilling to work miracles among those whom he said would have repented had he done so, but that we understand "all men" as every kind of men, distributed through whatever differences: kings, private persons, nobles, commoners, etc. Afterwards, in the same chapter, he proves the use of this manner of speaking by an example. The Lord also used this manner of speaking in the Gospel, he says, where he says to the Pharisees, "you tithe mint and rue and every herb." For the Pharisees did not tithe every herb of foreign lands and of all foreigners throughout all lands. Just as, therefore, here every kind of herb is meant, so we can understand "all men" to mean every kind of men. In the book On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 14, we read these words: I will say one thing: it is said thus, God wills all men to be saved, so that all the predestined are understood, because every kind of men is among them. Theophylact also rightly says that the Apostle here is treating of the salvation which comes through faith, not of some universal salvation of believers and unbelievers. Certainly the Apostle connects salvation and knowledge of the truth: to the one the latter is denied, and the former is not granted. Thomas Aquinas comments on the said passage thus: In God, the salvation of all men has the character of something willed, and so it is his antecedent will, of which the Apostle speaks here: he wills all to be saved. But if the good of justice is considered, and that sins are punished, then he does not will it, and this is his consequent will. These answers can suffice, or rather ought to suffice on the Harscherian hypothesis, although we could explain this passage in another way.

units.la: 2. Pet. 3. Non tardat Dominus promissionem suam, sicuti quidam existimant, sed patienter agit propter vos, nolens aliquos perire, sed omnes ad pænitentiam reverti.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 3: "The Lord does not delay his promise, as some suppose, but acts patiently on your account, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

units.la: Explicatio huius loci ex scopo Apo- stoli est elicienda.
units.tr: The explanation of this passage must be drawn from the Apostle's purpose.

units.la: Scopus autem eius est confirmare animos electorum adversus irrisorum obiectionem, quasi nullus esset Christi futurus adventus ad iudicium. Quorum argumentum tale erat: si omnia permanent ab initio creationis, ex quo patres obdormierunt, ad hunc usque diem, sequitur pollicitationem adventûs Christi nullam esse. Prius est verum. Ergo & posterius. Apostolus Petrus consequentiam negat, quia Deo cur adventum tardet, sua constet ratio, nempe patiens exspectatio, donec omnes ad resipiscentiā veniant, quos non vult perire. Simili locutione, quâ animabus sub altari clamantibus responsum fuit, ut requiescerent adhuc paululum temporis usque quo compleantur conservi eorum & fratres eorum, qui trucidandi sunt sicut & ipsi, Apoc. 6: 11. De electis igitur & fidelibus hæc sunt intelligenda, quia reprobi & infideles adventum Christi deprecantur, utpote quibus nihil aliud exspectandum, quàm horribilis illa sententia: Execrati abite à me &c.
units.tr: His purpose is to strengthen the minds of the elect against the objection of scoffers, who argued as if there would be no future coming of Christ for judgment. Their argument ran like this: if all things continue as they have been since the beginning of creation, ever since the fathers fell asleep, up to this day, then it follows that the promise of Christ's coming is empty. The first premise is true; therefore the second is too. The Apostle Peter denies the consequence, because the reason why God delays his coming is sound: namely, his patient waiting until all come to repentance, whom he does not wish to perish. He answers in a similar way to the souls under the altar who cried out, that they should rest a little while longer, until their fellow servants and brothers, who are to be killed as they themselves were, should be complete, Rev. 6:11. These things, then, are to be understood of the elect and the faithful, because the reprobate and unbelievers pray against Christ's coming, since for them nothing is to be expected but that dreadful sentence: Depart from me, accursed, etc.

units.la: Postremò Calvini ἀνασκευὴν quorundam argumentorum adversus orthodoxam doctrinam prædestinationis obiectorum, quæ legitur lib. 3. Institit. cap. 23. hîc subiicit Jesuita. Sed ita subiicit ut fieri solet apud eos, qui caussæ suæ diffidunt, id est, mutilatè responsiones Calvini citando, potiora omittendo, nec accuratè quæ à Calvino dicta examinando, sic igitur porrò scribit:
units.tr: Finally, the Jesuit here appends a refutation [ἀνασκευήν] of certain arguments raised against the orthodox doctrine of predestination, which Calvin made, and which is found in book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 23. But he appends it in the way that is customary with those who distrust their cause: that is, by quoting Calvin's replies in a mutilated form, leaving out the stronger points, and not examining accurately what Calvin said. Thus he writes further as follows:

units.la: CONSEQUENTIA BONA Ex Calvini praedestinatione deducta.
units.tr: A GOOD CONSEQUENCE, Drawn from Calvin's Doctrine of Predestination.

units.la: Objectiones sunt: stante praedestinatione (à Calvino asserta) concidit omnis sollicitudo & benè agendi studium. Nam
units.tr: The objections are: if predestination is held as Calvin asserts it, all care and zeal for doing good fall away. For

units.la: I. Si immutabili Dei decreto uni-cuiquè fixa est aut vita,aut mors,nihil intereft quomodo fe gerat, quia suo opere nihil promoveri potest Dei prædestinatio. Et sic deploratum in morem, quocunquè libido tulerit, præcipites ibunt.
units.tr: 1. If by the unchangeable decree of God, either life or death is fixed for each person, it makes no difference how he conducts himself, since predestination cannot be advanced by any work of his. And so, as a matter of course, given over to despair, men will rush headlong wherever lust carries them.

units.la: 2. Scit Deus quid de nobis agere semel statuerit: fi salutem decrevit adducet nos ad eam suo tempore, fi mortem destinavit, frustra contra tenderemus.
units.tr: 2. God knows what he has once decided to do about us. If he has decreed salvation, he will bring us to it in his own time; if he has destined us to death, we would strive against it in vain.

units.la: 3. Securos fe in vitiis pergere dicunt, qui fi sint in numero electorum nihil obfutura sint vitia, quò minùs tandem ad vitam perducantur.
units.tr: 3. They say that those who persist in their vices are secure, since if they are among the number of the elect, their vices will in no way hinder them from finally being brought to life.

units.la: 4. Dicunt, qui sit à Deo reprobatus perditurum operam, si innocentiâ & probitate vitæ se illi approbare studeat.
units.tr: 4. They say that one who is reprobated by God will lose his labour if he strives to approve himself to God by innocence and uprightness of life.

units.la: Hæc argumenta Calvinus vocavit blasphemias & impudentissima mendacia, quibus porci quidam conspurcant prædestinationis doctrinam, & ad ea respondit ibidem. Harscher responsiones repetit & suam Ὑπόκειμον addit. Hoc ordine.
units.tr: Calvin called these arguments blasphemies and most shameless lies, with which certain swine defile the doctrine of predestination, and he answered them in the same place. Harscher repeats the replies and adds his own Hypokeimon [Ὑπόκειμον]. He does so in this order.

units.la: RESPONSIO CALVINI.
units.tr: CALVIN'S REPLY.

units.la: Prima est (ut à posteriori loco incipiam) negando quòd talis perditurus sit operam, causa, quia reprobus non desinet perpetuis flagitiis iram Dei in se provocare, hoc est, nunquam quicquam boni facere poterit, quia ad malum ad peccatum creatus est. Sic, ait, Calvinum respondere. Jesuita verò addit: Ergo hi recte inferunt, contra Calvinum, ergo neque debemus esse sollicîti, neque admittere objurgationes, neque bene vivendi studio invigilare, quia reprobi sumus, quia jam in nos latum est Dei judicium.
units.tr: The first reply (to begin with the last point) is by denying that such a man will lose his labour, the reason being that the reprobate will not cease, by constant wickedness, to provoke the wrath of God against himself; that is, he will never be able to do anything good, because he was created for evil and sin. So, he says, Calvin replies. But the Jesuit adds: Therefore these men rightly infer, against Calvin, that we ought neither to be anxious, nor to admit rebukes, nor to keep watch over the zeal of living well, because we are reprobate, because God's judgment has already been passed upon us.

units.la: Respondeo primo de Calvino: Harscherum in hac responsione omittere praecipuum, quod Calvinus respondit, & addere, quod Calvinus nunquam dixit. Illud est, quod Calvinus in responsione sua habet, studium innocentiæ & probitatis vitæ, oriri ex electione quod verum est. Nam quos Deus praedestinavit, illos etiam sanctificavit, tanquam conformandos imagini filii sui, Rom. 8:29, 30. Reprobi autem cum non sint electi, nec studium habeant innocentiæ vitæ & probitatis, quomodo argumentari possunt praedicto modo? Christus Joh. 15: 5. dicit, is qui manet in me & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructum multum, nam sine me nihil potestis facere. Atqui reprobi in Christo non sunt.
units.tr: I reply first concerning Calvin: in this answer Harscher omits the chief point that Calvin made, and adds what Calvin never said. The point Calvin makes in his answer is that zeal for innocence and uprightness of life arises from election, and this is true. For those whom God predestined, these he also sanctified, as being conformed to the image of his Son, Rom. 8:29, 30. But the reprobate, since they are not elect and have no zeal for innocence of life and uprightness, how can they argue in the aforesaid manner? Christ says, John 15:5, he who abides in me, and in whom I abide, he bears much fruit, for without me you can do nothing. But the reprobate are not in Christ.

units.la: Nam cùm Christus Matth. 25. mala execratorum opera allegasset, dixit postremò, nunquam novi vos. Sunt ergò ἀπόβλητα, reprobatum esse, & innocentiâ & probitate vitæ se Deo probare. Deinde addit Jesuita quæ non sunt Calvini, nunquam enim Calvinus docuit, reprobos idcirco nihil boni facere posse, quia ad malum & ad peccatum sint creati. Verba enim illa ad contumeliam formata, non ad decretum creationis sed reprobationis sunt referenda, quod ordine naturæ illo est posterius. Nec diffitetur Jesuita, qui paulò post ad marginem notavit: Deus creavit hominem ad vitam æternam, teste Calvino.
units.tr: For when Christ in Matt. 25 had recounted the evil works of the damned, he finally said, I never knew you. They are therefore ἀπόβλητα [apoblēta, cast-off ones]. To be reprobate and to approve oneself to God by innocence and uprightness of life are not compatible. Next, the Jesuit adds things that are not Calvin's, for Calvin never taught that the reprobate therefore can do nothing good, because they were created for evil and sin. For those words formed for dishonour are to be referred not to the decree of creation but to that of reprobation, which in the order of nature comes later. Nor does the Jesuit deny this, for he noted a little later in the margin: God created man for eternal life, as Calvin testifies.

units.la: Quod deinde Harscheri prosyllogismum attinet, quæro quis hominem ita iusserit argumentari? Jesuita ne aliquis audaculus? Quis novit mentem Domini, aut quis ei fuit à consilio ut possit dicere, ego sum reprobatus à Deo? Utinam hi sapere discerent sese intra patefactæ veritatis fines religiosè continere. Voluntas Dei est sanctificatio nostra, eam studiosè quæramus, neque ὑπὸ τῶν ἐσφραγισμένων profilientes, in adyta decretorum divinorum perrumpamus.
units.tr: As for Harscher's further syllogism, I ask: who taught anyone to argue in this way? A Jesuit, or some over-bold fellow? Who knows the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor, that he could say, "I am reprobated by God"? Would that these men had learned to hold themselves religiously within the bounds of the truth revealed. The will of God is our sanctification; let us seek it diligently, and not, leaping over the things sealed [ὑπὸ τῶν ἐσφραγισμένων], break into the sanctuaries of the divine decrees.

units.la: Secunda responsio Calvini pertinet ad argumentum, quod ex electorum ratiocinatione formant, qui dicere possent, se securos in vitijs pergere, quia si sint in numero electorum, nihil obfutura sint vitia, quò minus ad vitam perducantur. Calvinus respondebat, contrarium potiùs concludendum fuisse. Quia enim scopus electionis sit vitæ sanctimonia, magis ad eam alacriter meditandam nos stimulare debere.
units.tr: Calvin's second reply concerns the argument which they build from the reasoning of the elect, who might say that they remain secure in their vices, because if they are in the number of the elect, their vices will in no way hinder them from being brought to life. Calvin answered that the opposite ought rather to be concluded. For since the aim of election is holiness of life, we ought to be all the more stirred to meditate on it eagerly.

units.la: Ad hæc Harscherus. Sed in forma Calvine & ad rhombum sic argumentor: si sum praedestinatus cum praedestinationis decretum sit infallibile, omninò independens, ex meis operibus antecedentibus & consequentibus, consequar salutem quomodocunque me geram. Ergo nullum bene vivendi studium habendum est.
units.tr: To this Harscher replies: But in Calvin's form, and to the rhombus, I argue thus: if I am predestinated, since the decree of predestination is infallible and wholly independent, I shall obtain salvation however I conduct myself, whether from my preceding or my following works. Therefore no zeal for living well is to be had.

units.la: Sic de fine praedestinationis disputat, de mediis ita porro:
units.tr: In this way he disputes about the end of predestination, and then goes on about the means:

units.la: 1. Si sum electus, ut sanctam & inculpatam vitam agam, cum electionis decretum sit infallibile, sanctam & inculpatam agam quomodocunque me geram, etiamsi me non exstimulem & expergefaciam.
units.tr: 1. If I am elect in order to live a holy and blameless life, since the decree of election is infallible, I shall live a holy and blameless life however I conduct myself, even if I do not stir up and rouse myself.

units.la: 2. Licet electus admoneatur, ut sanctam & inculpatam vitam agat, aget illam etiamsi studium bene vivendi non habeat. Et si est praedestinatus ad se expergefaciendum, stimulandum faciet id sine nullo suo studio.
units.tr: 2. Although the elect person is admonished to live a holy and blameless life, he will live it even if he has no zeal for living well. And if he is predestined to rouse himself, he will make himself stirred up without any effort of his own.

units.la: Respondeo argumentum principale, quod putat esse ad rhombum, plane ad rhombum non esse. Nam cum aere, non nobiscum pugnat. Licet enim nos asseramus decretum praedestinationis esse independens respectu causae efficiefficientis impulsivæ: neutiquam tamen est independens respectu mediorum, quorum respectu dicimus, hominem esse ad salutem ordinatum intuitu bonorum operum, ita ut etiam bona opera in definitionem electionis veniant. Sicuti ergo electio est infallibilis quoad finem, ita etiam infallibilis est quoad media. Antecedens ergo est falsum. Hoc præsuppositio, cætera omnia, quæ subnectit, sunt ἀσυνήτως καρ-δίας Pelagii διαλογισμοί. Nam hisce figmentis Jesuitæ sublatam eunt omnem Dei providentiam & prædestinationem.
units.tr: I reply that the principal argument, which he thinks is to the rhombus, is plainly not to the rhombus. For it fights not with us but with the air. Although we assert that the decree of predestination is independent with respect to the efficient and impulsive cause, it is by no means independent with respect to the means. With respect to these we say that man is ordained to salvation with a view to good works, so that good works also enter into the definition of election. Just as therefore election is infallible as to the end, so it is also infallible as to the means. The antecedent is therefore false. This is a presupposition; all the rest that he adds are foolish-hearted reasonings of Pelagius [ἀσυνέτως καρδίας Pelagii διαλογισμοί]. For by these fictions the Jesuits remove all divine providence and predestination.

units.la: Primò enim, quod providentiam divinam attinet, Deus certò & infallibiliter, omnia ita præfinivit, ut ne passerculus in terram cadere possit absque Dei providentia, qui etiam capillos nostros numeravit, & dies, quos præterire non possumus. Hoc noverunt omnes pii & fideles. Nullus tamen inde argumentatur, ergo media quæ Deus ordinavit, negligam.
units.tr: For first, as far as divine providence is concerned, God has foreordained all things with certainty and infallibility, so that not even a sparrow can fall to the ground without God's providence, who has also numbered our hairs, and the days which we cannot pass over. All the godly and faithful know this. Yet no one argues from this, "Therefore I will neglect the means which God has ordained."

units.la: Christus noverat quando sibi moriendum esset, sæpe tamen declinavit mortis pericula. Ezechias scivit per Dei revelationem ad dies vitæ suæ adiectos esse quindecim annos, non tamen abstinuit à cibo & potu. Procul dubio Harscherus non est tam indoctus, ut nô sciat si ægrotet, ex Dei providentia id fieri, non tamē negliget aut medicamenta, aut medicos. Sic quoquè de prædestinatione loquendum. Quos Deus ad vitam æternam liberè ordinavit per fidem & bona opera perducendos, illis etiam media præordinavit, quæ electis neutiquam sunt negligenda. Ita ut si qui sit, qui sic ratiocinetur, ut Harscherus supra, planè ex electorum numero non sit. Imò electi sic non possunt ratiocinari, quia sciunt se electos esse ante iacta mundi fundamenta, ut sint sancti & inculpati coram eo cum charitate, Eph. 1: 4. Industriâ ergo suâ decreto Dei subserviunt.
units.tr: Christ knew when he had to die, yet he often avoided the dangers of death. Hezekiah knew through God's revelation that fifteen years had been added to the days of his life, yet he did not abstain from food and drink. Without doubt Harscher is not so unlearned as not to know that if he falls sick this happens by God's providence, yet he will not neglect either medicines or physicians. So too we must speak of predestination. Those whom God freely ordained to be led to eternal life through faith and good works, for them he also pre-ordained the means, which the elect must by no means neglect. So if anyone reasons as Harscher does above, he is plainly not of the number of the elect. Indeed the elect cannot reason thus, because they know that they were elected before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and blameless before him in love, Eph. 1:4. Therefore by their diligence they serve the decree of God.

units.la: In tertiæ responsionis Calvinianæ tractatione multas habet quisquilias nihil solidi. Dicit 1. cùm Calvinus negat antecedens negat consequens negare posset, utpote evidentia, suam doctrinam pro mysterio obtrudit, magnâ reverentiâ & religione cogitandum, jubetq; ad tale Dei judicium tremere, misericordiamq; Dei suspicere potiùs, quàm inaccessa Dei secreta, nefariâ temeritate tentare. 2. hunc esse novum respondendi modum, ait, cùm ego falsam doctrinam impugno, ex eo quod sit incentivum impietatis, negq; id negare possis, voces eam mysterium magnâ reverentiâ & religione cogitandum. 3. dicit nihil esse hic mysterij, si sum prædestinatus, vel damnatus sive reprobatus, tum nihil interest quomodo me geram: vel est verum, vel falsum, vel ita obscurum & recònditum, ut mysterium appelles cujus cognitio nobis non pateat. Ai hîc vel nega si verum est, non solvis argumentum, quod rectè urgent. Si falsum est, ergo aliquid interest quomodo me geram, veniuntq; in consideràtionem rationem opera mea, ubi hoc Dei regnat placitum, transferturq; præparatio ad interitum alìò quàm ad Dei arcanum consilium, quæ sunt contra doctrinam Calvini supra relatam. Si verò ita obscurum & reconditum est, cur tam aperte tam clarè asserere audet, quòd juxta obscuritatem, impietatem & falsitatem tantam conjunctam habet, ut ejus pallianda nullam rationem reddere possit? neq; monente S. Petro 1. Epist. cap. 3.
units.tr: In his treatment of Calvin's third reply he has many trifles and nothing solid. First, he says that when Calvin denies the antecedent, he could as well deny the consequent, since it is evident; Calvin imposes his doctrine as a mystery, to be pondered with great reverence and religion, and bids us tremble at such a judgment of God and look rather to the mercy of God than with impious rashness try the inaccessible secrets of God. Second, he says this is a new way of answering: when I attack a false doctrine because it is an incentive to impiety, and you cannot deny this, you call it a mystery to be pondered with great reverence and religion. Third, he says there is no mystery here: if I am predestinated, or condemned, or reprobate, then it makes no difference how I conduct myself. Either this is true, or false, or so obscure and hidden that you call it a mystery whose knowledge is not open to us. If it is true, then deny it; you do not solve the argument, which they rightly press. If it is false, then it does make a difference how I conduct myself, and my works come into consideration, where God's pleasure reigns, and preparation is directed to destruction rather than to God's secret counsel, which are contrary to the doctrine of Calvin related above. But if it is so obscure and hidden, why does he dare so openly and clearly to assert that, in accordance with this obscurity, it has such impiety and falsity conjoined with it that he cannot offer any reason to excuse it? Nor does the warning of St Peter, 1 Epistle, chap. 3, permit it.

units.la: Respondeo 1. Calvinus pro mysterio non habet, quod scriptura revelavit, itaque quòd electi non minùs prædestinati sint ad fidem & bona opera quàm ad vitam æternam ipse ex scriptura docuit, est enim voluntas Dei revelata, Eph. 1: 4. Rom 8: 29.
units.tr: Answer 1. Calvin does not treat as a mystery what Scripture has revealed. That the elect are predestined no less to faith and good works than to eternal life he himself teaches from Scripture, for this is the revealed will of God, Eph. 1:4; Rom. 8:29.

units.la: 2. Thess. 4: 3. nec pro mysterio & arcano habet, quod reprobis non datum est pervenire ad vitam æternam, nam & hoc revelatum est, Act. 13: 4. 5. Rom. 11: 7. electi assecuti sunt, reliqui occaecati occalluërunt. Pro mysterio autem habet 1. quòd solus Deus novit, qui sint sui 2. Tim. 2: 19. 2. quòd numerus electorum & reproborum penes ipsum solum est, qui eos descriptos habet in libro, in quem nemo hominum nec in cælo, nec in terra potest inspicere, Apoc. 5: 3. 3. quòd ex mero suo beneplacito, alios ex corruptionis massa ad vitam æternam elegit, alios in eadem reliquit. Hoc & Paulus agnovit, Rom. 11: 33. o profundas divitias tum sapientiæ tum cognitionis Dei! quàm inscrutabilia sunt ejus judicia & ejus viæ imperversigabiles.
units.tr: Nor does he regard it as a mystery or secret that the reprobate have not been granted to attain eternal life, for this too has been revealed: Act. 13: 4. 5; Rom. 11:7, "the elect obtained it, the rest were hardened." But he does regard as a mystery (1) that God alone knows who are his, 2 Tim. 2:19; (2) that the number of the elect and the reprobate rests with him alone, who has them written in the book which no one of men, neither in heaven nor on earth, can look into, Rev. 5:3; (3) that from his mere good pleasure he chose some out of the mass of corruption to eternal life and left others in the same mass. Paul acknowledged this too, Rom. 11:33: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

units.la: Quid igitur Calvinus respondeat, aut quid pro mysterio habeat, ex integris syllogismis patebit. Primus est: Reprobatus sua innocentia & probitate vitæ, quà se Deo approbare studet, operam omnem perdit. Ego sum reprobatus. Ergo.
units.tr: What Calvin answers, and what he holds as a mystery, will become clear from the complete syllogisms. The first is: The reprobate, by his innocence and uprightness of life, by which he strives to win God's approval, loses all his effort. I am reprobate. Therefore.

units.la: Alter est: Electus, ad vitam æternam certò & infallibiliter perveniens, non opus habet, ut bona opera faciat, sed placidè in utramvis aurem dormire potest, ratio, quia illuc perveniet quidcunq; agat propter infallibilitatem. Ego sum electus. Ergò.
units.tr: The other is: The elect, who certainly and infallibly attains eternal life, has no need to do good works, but can sleep soundly on either ear, the reason being that he will arrive there whatever he does, because of infallibility. I am elect. Therefore.

units.la: 1. Ad primum respondet Calvinus propositionem maiorem esse ineptam, quia in ea opposita de se invicem prædicantur affirmando. Bona enim opera non esse effecta reprobationis sed electionis, quod ex scriptura probavit: Minorem continere mysterium & arcanum, quia nemo hominum novit, an sit reprobatus. In altero syllogismo negavit propositionem maiorem, & dixit consequens illius per contrarium asserendum esse hoc modo: qui ad vitam æternam est electus, is necessariò bona opera præstare debet, ratio, quia non minùs ad hæc, quàm ad vitam æternam est prædestinatus, quod scriptura passim asserit.
units.tr: 1. To the first, Calvin replies that the major premise is absurd, because in it opposites are predicated of each other affirmatively. For good works are effects not of reprobation but of election, which he proved from Scripture. The minor contains the mystery and the secret, because no one knows whether he is reprobate. In the second syllogism he denied the major premise and said that its consequence must be asserted by the contrary, in this way: whoever is elect to eternal life must necessarily perform good works, the reason being that he is predestined to these no less than to eternal life, which Scripture asserts everywhere.

units.la: 2. Quæ ergò Harscherus de novo respondendi modo habet, Jesuititati eius tribuo, ad Calvinum enim nihil pertinent.
units.tr: 2. What Harscher says about a new way of answering I attribute to his Jesuitry, for it has nothing to do with Calvin.

units.la: 3. Si Harscherus hoc observasset, non opus fuisset crambem recoquere, cum dicit: si sum prædestinatus vel reprobatus, tum mihi nil interest, quomodo me geram, Hoc, inquit, verum est vel falsum, vel abscônditum. Ai hic vel nega. Imò Calvinus iam negavit consequentiam tanquam falsam. Quia prædestinato omninò interest, ut se gerat dignum vocatione, quâ vocatus est, Eph.4:1. & eandem firmam reddat per bona opera.
units.tr: 3. If Harscher had noticed this, there would have been no need to warm up old cabbage when he says: If I am predestined or reprobate, then it makes no difference to me how I conduct myself. This, he says, is either true or false, or hidden. Answer: either deny it, or... indeed Calvin has already denied the consequence as false. For it matters entirely to the predestined how he conducts himself, that he should live worthy of the calling with which he was called, Eph. 4:1, and make it firm by good works,

units.la: 2. Pet. 1: 10. quia ad hæc quoque prædestinatus est. Reprobato autem non est potestas, ut possit se indifferenter gerere ad bonum & ad malum, quia, qui non est prædestinatus ad finem, non est prædestinatus ad media. Ideo plane interest quomodo electus se gerat, veniuntquè in consideration bona operra, ubi hoc Dei regnat placitum. Tertium ergò hîc excluditur, quòd hæc tantùm ad arcanum Dei consilium sint referenda. Ideoquè hæc Calvinus clarè & apertè afferere audet, sinè obscuritate, sinè impietate, sinè falsitate, quia omnia secundùm scripturam tradita, ut ex superioribus intelligi potest.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 1:10, since he is predestined to these also. But the reprobate has no power to conduct himself indifferently toward good and evil, because he who is not predestined to the end is not predestined to the means. Therefore it plainly matters how the elect conducts himself, and good works come into consideration, where this purpose of God reigns. So the third option is excluded here, namely that these things are to be referred only to God's secret counsel. Hence Calvin dares to assert these things clearly and openly, without obscurity, without impiety, without falsehood, because all are delivered according to Scripture, as can be understood from what has gone before.

units.la: Post hæc omnia, sub finem huius paralleli adfert, ut ipse ait, ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦
units.tr: After all this, at the end of this parallel, he brings forward, as he himself says, ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦ ❧✿❦

units.la: CATHOLICAM SOLUTIONEM argumenti Calviniftici.
units.tr: THE CATHOLIC SOLUTION of the Calvinist argument.

units.la: Vel sum prædestinatus, vel sum reprobus: si primum, salvabor quicquid egero: si secundum, damnabor quicquid egero.
units.tr: Either I am predestined or I am reprobate: if the first, I shall be saved whatever I do; if the second, I shall be damned whatever I do.

units.la: Hunc disputandi modum 1. vocat ineptum, quod simili ostendit de currente & comedente. Id deinde applicat prædestinationi & reprobationi. 2. negat, quòd homo salvari possit quicquid egerit, quia qui hominem vidit salvandum, non exclusit viam salutis, &c.
units.tr: He calls this way of disputing 1. absurd, showing it by a similar example of the runner and the eater, and then applies that to predestination and reprobation. 2. He denies that a man can be saved whatever he does, because one who has seen a man destined for salvation has not shut off the way of salvation, etc.

units.la: Respondeo; me mirari istam subitaneam metamorphofin Jesuiticam: vix compos mentis fuit Harfcherus quando hæc scripsit, quia in momento factus est Calviniita. Nam primò argumentum hoc non est Calvini aut discipulorum eius, sed porcorum illorum de quibus supra. 2. est argumentum, quod Calvinus superius refutavit, & communiter orthodoxi vocant diabolicum, impium, detestandum. Non enim est hominis Christiani dicere aut electus sum, aut reprobus, sed iubetur potius fidem suam tanquam electionis medium explorare. 2. Cor. 13:5,6. 3. est argumentum, quod in hoc ipso parallelo calidè Harscher defendit contra Calvinum. 4. refponsio Harscheri (exceptis pauculis verbis, quæ Pelagianismum sapiunt) ex orthodoxa schola desumpta est, & continet id, quod nos ad idem argumentum respondere solemus, bona opera tanquam subordinata ab electione minime divellenda esse. Cum Harschero ergo dicimus modum argumentandi esse ineptum, & Jesuitam hunc nostrum sero sicut phryges sapuisse, quòd non citiùs istam ineptam argumentandi rationem observarit, quod si factum fuisset, non tantum laboris sumpsisset in defendenda impia sententia.
units.tr: I answer: I marvel at this sudden Jesuit metamorphosis. Harscher was hardly in his right mind when he wrote this, for in a moment he has become a Calvinist. For first, this argument is not Calvin's or his disciples', but that of those swine of whom I spoke above. Second, it is an argument which Calvin refuted above, and which orthodox writers commonly call diabolical, impious and detestable. For it is not the part of a Christian man to say "I am elect" or "I am reprobate," but he is rather bidden to test his faith as the means of his election, 2 Cor. 13:5, 6. Third, it is an argument which Harscher himself vigorously defends in this very parallel against Calvin. Fourth, Harscher's answer (apart from a few words which smack of Pelagianism) is drawn from the orthodox school and contains what we are accustomed to reply to the same argument: that good works, as subordinate to election, must by no means be torn away from it. So with Harscher we say that this mode of arguing is absurd, and that our Jesuit has grown wise too late, like the Phrygians, in not observing sooner this absurd way of arguing; for if he had, he would not have taken so much trouble in defending his impious opinion.

units.la: Phrases de prævisione perseverantiæ in bono, & quòd in eadem homini persistere liberum sit, tanquam Pelagianas non approbo in hac responsione, sed de illis hîc nulla controversia.
units.tr: Phrases about foreknowledge of perseverance in good, and that it is free for a man to persist in it, I do not approve in this answer as Pelagian, but there is no controversy about them here.

units.la: NESTORIANI.
units.tr: NESTORIANI.

units.la: Dicti sunt à Nestorio Episcopo celebri ob naturalem facundiam, de quo scribit Socrates in ecclesiastica historia, probè quidem eruditus esse putabatur, re autem ipsa indoctus fuit, & veterum interpretum libros versare noluit, siquidem expedita linguae volubilitate elatus, animum ad illorum scripta non accurate intendit, sed seipsum omnibus praestantiorem esse dixit. In Christo ponunt duas personas. Negant B. Virginem Theotocon, sed volunt esse Christotocon. Sub utraque specie sacramentum eucharistiae sumebant, quod non crederent sub una specie Christum aeque contineri &c.
units.tr: Named after Nestorius, the bishop, who was famous for his natural eloquence. Socrates writes of him in his ecclesiastical history that he was thought to be well learned, but in fact was unlearned, and he refused to study the books of the ancient interpreters, since, puffed up by his ready fluency of speech, he did not give close attention to their writings, but said that he was superior to all of them. They posit two persons in Christ. They deny that the Blessed Virgin is Theotokos, but hold that she is Christotokos [χριστοτόκος]. They received the sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds, because they did not believe that Christ is equally contained under one kind, etc.

units.la: CASTIGATIO.
units.tr: CASTIGATIO.

units.la: De Nestorio pauca habet Augustinus. Socrates lib. 7. hist. eccl. & Nicephorus lib. 14. prolixius vitam, actiones, haereses & damnationem eius in concilio Ephesino 3. describunt. Summa rei est (non enim hic placet historicum agere) Nestorium Episcopum Antiochenum, ob facunditatem & castitatis laudem a Constantinopolitana ecclesia ad Episcopatum vocatum, ab Anastasio quodam Presbytero a pietate & veritate abductum fuisse. Inter caetera eius dogmata hoc imprimis urgebat,
units.tr: Augustine has little to say about Nestorius. Socrates in book 7 of his ecclesiastical history, and Nicephorus in book 14, describe at greater length his life, actions, heresies and condemnation at the Third Council of Ephesus. The sum of the matter (for I do not wish to act the historian here) is this: Nestorius, bishop of Antioch, was called to the bishopric of the Constantinopolitan Church because of his eloquence and reputation for chastity, and was led away from piety and truth by a certain presbyter, Anastasius. Among his other doctrines, he especially insisted on this:

units.la: B. Mariam non Θεοτόκον, Dei genetrician esse, cùm illa fuerit homo, ab homine autem Deum gigni non posse, esse autem tantùm χριστοτόκον. De virtutibus eius non multa, plura de vitiis referunt. Scribunt enim fuisse Nestorium hominem arrogantem, levem, vanæ gloriæ cupidissimum, naturali facundia praeditum, reipsa indoctum, qui veterum libros neglexit, propterea quòd se omnibus praestantiorem putaret. Harschesrus ad hoc postremum, digitum intendit in hoc parallelo, & dicit Calvinum & cum eo omnes Orthodoxos, veteres Patres negligere, abiicere, contemnere, uti olim faciebat Nestorius. Qua in re nobis pro more suo maximam iniuriam facit, & cum hoc plerique alii Jesuitæ. Veneramur Patres, & debitum ipsis honoré & reverentiam referimus, ut passim ex scriptis nostrorum Theologorum, & inprimis ex Calvini institutionibus, clarum est. Si autem ipsorum scripta, scriptis Prophetarum &
units.tr: that the Blessed Mary is not Theotokos [Θεοτόκος], the bearer of God, since she was a human being, and a human being cannot give birth to God, but she is only Christotokos [χριστοτόκος]. They report little of his virtues, but more of his vices. For they write that Nestorius was an arrogant, frivolous man, greedy for empty glory, endowed with natural eloquence but in fact unlearned, who neglected the books of the ancients because he thought himself superior to all. Harscherus, on this last point, points his finger at this parallel, and says that Calvin, and with him all the Orthodox, neglect, cast off and despise the ancient Fathers, as Nestorius once did. In this he does us, as is his custom, the greatest injustice, and many other Jesuits with him. We venerate the Fathers, and render them due honour and reverence, as is clear everywhere from the writings of our theologians, and above all from Calvin's Institutes. But if we do not put their writings on a par with the writings of the Prophets and

units.la: Apostolorum, id est, Dei verbo non æquiparamus, eius rei iustissimas caussas habemus. Venerandi sunt Patres, honorandi antiqui autores, sed non nisi usq; ad aras. Hoc Patres ipsi nos docuerunt, hanc salubrem hortationem non semel tradiderunt. Augustin. lib. 2. cont. Donatist. cap. 1. magnum quidem meritum novimus Cypriani Episcopi & Martyris, sed numquid majus quàm Petri Apostoli & Martyris? Cyprianus lib. 2. epist. 3. ad Cæcilium: non debemus attendere, quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putarit, sed quid, qui ante omnes est, Christus prior fecerit. Nec enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed Dei veritatem. Cyrillus hierosolymitanus catech. 4. ne mihi ea tibi proferenti simpliciter fidem adhibeas, nisi de divinis scripturis eorum, quæ dicam demonstrationem accipias. Nam fidei nostræ salus non oratonis facundiâ nititur, sed scripturarum divinarum comprobatione. Aug. epist. 112. ad Paulinam: si ambobus (Ambrosio & Augustino) aquâ lance putas esse credendum, nunquid ullo modo nos Evangelio comparabis? aut scripta nostra scripturis canonicis coæquabis? profectò si rectè in judicando sapis, longè nos infra vides abilla authoritate distare, & ne quidem longius, sed utriq; nostrum quantumlibet credas, utrumq; illi excellentiæ nequaquam comparas.
units.tr: Apostles, that is, with the Word of God, we have most just reasons for this. The Fathers are to be venerated, and the ancient authors honoured, but only up to the altars. The Fathers themselves taught us this, and more than once handed down this wholesome exhortation. Augustine, book 2 against the Donatists, chapter 1: We know the great merit of Cyprian, bishop and martyr, but is it greater than that of Peter, apostle and martyr? Cyprian, book 2, letter 3, to Caecilius: We ought not to attend to what someone before us thought should be done, but to what Christ, who is before all, first did. For we must follow not human custom but the truth of God. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 4: Do not give simple faith to me when I tell you these things, unless you receive demonstration of what I say from the divine Scriptures. For the salvation of our faith rests not on the eloquence of the speaker, but on the proof from the divine Scriptures. Augustine, letter 112 to Paulina: If you think that both (Ambrose and Augustine) are to be believed on an equal footing, will you in any way compare us with the Gospel? Or will you equate our writings with the canonical Scriptures?
