Surely, if you have sound judgement, you see that we are far below that authority, and not even so far, but however much you believe in each of us, you by no means compare either of us to that excellence.

units.la: Neutiquam ergo sanctos Patres ex supercilio Nestoriano vilipendimus, aut negligimus, sed diligenter evolvimus, rara ipsorum dona admiramur, quæ scripserunt tanquã humana scripta ex Dei verbo examinamus, & errata eorum communi humanæ imbecillitati ascribimus. Hæc omnia cum reverentia sinè contemptu.
units.tr: By no means, then, do we despise or neglect the holy Fathers from a Nestorian haughtiness; rather we read them diligently, we admire the rare gifts they had, we examine their writings as human writings by the Word of God, and we ascribe their errors to the common weakness of humanity. All this we do with reverence and without contempt.

units.la: PARALLELUM.
units.tr: PARALLELUM.

units.la: Quia autem Harschero placuit circa istam materiam parallelum subiicere & benè multa testimonia ex Calvini institutioni-tutioni. tutionibus proferre, ego illa cum scriptis Pontificiis & Jesuiticis novo parallelo sub finem huius disputationis conferam, unde clare patebit, quàm iniquè & impudenter nobiscum agant Jesuitæ, dùm nos accusant in re, in qua illi non minùs accusandi forent, si quid hîc esset erratum.
units.tr: But since it pleased Harscherus to append a parallel on this subject, and to bring forward many testimonies from Calvin's Institutes, I will set these beside the writings of the Papists and Jesuits in a new parallel at the end of this disputation, whence it will be clear how unjustly and shamelessly the Jesuits deal with us, while they accuse us of a matter in which they would be no less deserving of accusation, if there were any error here.

units.la: Calvinus lib. 2. Instit. cap. 2. §. 4. certè quas retulimus Patrum sententias esse salsissimas paulò post constabit.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes, book 2, chapter 2, section 4: it will shortly become clear that the sayings of the Fathers which we have cited are most insipid.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 13. de verbo Dei cap. 10. Quis neget multos veterum Patrum habuisse excellenter donum interpretandi, & fuisse spirituales, & tamen constat quosdam ex præcipuis eorum non leviter lapsos esse.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 13, chapter 10: Who would deny that many of the ancient Fathers had an excellent gift of interpreting, and were spiritual men, and yet it is certain that some of their principal men fell not lightly?

units.la: Calvinus ibidem: tametsi Graci prae aliis in extollenda humana voluntatis facultate modum excesserunt, veteres tamen omnes, excepto Augustino in hac re vacillant.
units.tr: Calvin, ibid.: Although the Greeks, above others, have gone beyond measure in extolling the power of the human will, yet all the ancients, except Augustine, waver in this matter.

units.la: Canus loc. Theol. lib. 11. cap. 6. Sozomeni mendacia non excuso, Græcus namque fuit, & natio hæc fuit semper ad mentiendum promptula.
units.tr: Canus, Loci theologici, book 11, chapter 6: I do not excuse the lies of Sozomen; for he was a Greek, and that nation was always ready to lie.

units.la: Calvinus ibid. qui postea secuti sunt sensim aliy per alios in deterius continuò delapsi sunt.
units.tr: Calvin, ibid.: Those who afterwards followed them, by degrees, one after another, have continually slid into worse things.

units.la: Roffensis adverf. Lutherum : Patres aliquoties erraffe non diffitemur, homines enim erant, sicut & nos.
units.tr: Roffensis, against Luther: We do not deny that the Fathers sometimes erred, for they were men, as we are.

units.la: Calvinus cap.3. S.7. Non recte à Chrysoftomo scriptum est, nec gratiam sine voluntate, nec voluntatem sine gratia quicquam posse operari.
units.tr: Calvin, chapter 3, section 7: It was not rightly written by Chrysostom that neither grace without the will, nor the will without grace, can accomplish anything.

units.la: Suarez Jesuita in 3. tom. q.27. art.3, Chrysostomus exponens illud, Joh.2. vinum non habent (volebat Maria si clariorem facere per filium) respondendum est Chrysostomum & qui eum secuti sunt modum excessisse, & est eorum sententia erronea.
units.tr: Suarez, the Jesuit, in part 3, disputation 27, article 3: Chrysostom, explaining that passage of John 2, "They have no wine" (Mary wished to make it clearer through her son), must be answered: Chrysostom and those who followed him went beyond measure, and their opinion is erroneous.

units.la: Calvinus S.10. illud ergo toties à Chryfostomo repetitum repudiari necessum est. Quem trahit, volentem trahit.
units.tr: Calvin, section 10: That saying, so often repeated by Chrysostom, "He whom the Father draws, draws willingly," must therefore be rejected.

units.la: Pererius in Gen. disp. 6. Chrysostomus veritatis & pietatis terminos excessit; nempe super verba Psalmi, non est, qui faciat bonum, ne unus.
units.tr: Pererius, On Genesis, disputation 6: Chrysostom transgressed the bounds of truth and piety, namely in his comment on the words of the Psalm, "There is none who does good, no, not one."

units.la: Calvinus eodem lib. cap.14. §. 3. Atque hic excusari non potest veterum error, qui dum ad mediatoris personam non attendunt, totius fere doctrina, quæ in Evangelio Iohannis legitur, genuinum obscurant sensum, seq; implicant multis laqueis.
units.tr: Calvin, same book, chapter 14, section 3: And here the error of the ancients cannot be excused, who, while they did not attend to the person of the Mediator, have almost obscured the genuine sense of the whole doctrine that is read in the Gospel of John, and have entangled themselves in many snares.

units.la: Bellarminus lib.1. de Clericis cap.15. Michaël Medina lib.1. de sacrorum hominum origine & continentia cap. 5. affirmat, sanctum Hieronymum idem omnino cum Aerio sensisse, neque solum Hieronymum in ea hæresi fuisse, sed etiam Ambrosium, Augustinum, Sedulium, Primasium, Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Oecumenium & Theophylactum.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On Clerics, book 1, chapter 15. Michael Medina, On the Origin and Continence of Holy Men, book 1, chapter 5, affirms that Saint Jerome thought exactly the same as Aerius, and that not only Jerome was in that heresy, but also Ambrose, Augustine, Sedulius, Primasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius and Theophylact.

units.la: Ee Calvinus lib. 3. Instit. cap 11. §. 15. Nec Augustini sententia per omnia recipienda est. Tametsi enim egregiè hominem omni justitiæ laude spoliat, ac totam Dei gratiæ transcribit, gratiam tamen ad sanctificationem refert, quâ in vitæ novitatem per Spiritum regeneramur.
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes, book 3, chapter 11, section 15: Nor is the opinion of Augustine to be received in every respect. For although he admirably strips man of all praise for righteousness, and transfers the whole of it to the grace of God, yet he refers grace to sanctification, by which we are regenerated by the Spirit into newness of life.

units.la: Maldonatus Jesuita, in Evang. Joh. cap. 10. non possum hîc Augustini opinionem admittere.
units.tr: Maldonatus, the Jesuit, on John, chapter 10: I cannot admit the opinion of Augustine here.

units.la: Calvinus eodem lib. cap. 4. §. 38. Parum autem me movent, quæ in veterum scriptis de sanctificatione passim occurrunt. Video omnesferè, quorum libri extant, aut hac in parte lapsos esse, aut nimis asperè & durè locutos.
units.tr: Calvin, same book, chapter 4, section 38: The things that occur everywhere in the writings of the ancients about sanctification move me little. I see that almost all whose books survive have either slipped in this part, or spoken too harshly and roughly.

units.la: Salmero Jesuita in epist. Pauli lib. 1. durum in Hilario, Christum mortem non timuisse. Durum & indignū Chrysostomo, B. Virginem ambitiosam & cupidam gloriæ vanæ extitisse.
units.tr: Salmeron, the Jesuit, on the Epistles of Paul, book 1: harsh in Hilary, who said that Christ did not fear death. Harsh and unworthy of Chrysostom, who said that the Blessed Virgin was ambitious and greedy for empty glory.

units.la: Calvinus lib. 3. cap. 5. Instit. (ut omnia in summam contraham) 1. veteres ante mille annos precationes pro defunctis habebant, sine Dei verbo, sine revelatione, sine exemplo. 2. veteres qui preces fundebant pro demortuis, aliquid humani passi sunt 3. cap. 15. §. 2. quicunque meriti nomen operibus humanis ad Dei judicium comparatis aptavit, fidei sinceritati pessime consuluit. 4. veteres ecclesiae scriptores nomine meriti erroris materiam praebuerunt. 5. lib. 4. Instit. cap. 12. §. 8. veterum auctoritas mirum in modu est periculosa. 6. §. 20. mirum est, tam crassam hallucinationem (in observatione quadragesimae) hominibus acuti judicij obrepere potuisse. 7. quod in periculo mortis laici baptizarent, in ecclesiae exordio, non video, qua firma ratione defendi queat. 8. cap. 18. §. 21. excusari non posse arbitror veteres, quin aliquid in actionis modo peccaverint, imitati sunt enim Iudaicum sacrificandi modum.
units.tr: Calvin, book 3, chapter 5, Institutes (to sum up all in brief): (1) the ancients a thousand years ago had prayers for the dead, without the Word of God, without revelation, without example. (2) The ancients who poured out prayers for the dead were subject to something human. (3) Chapter 15, section 2: whoever attached the name of merit to human works, weighed against God's judgement, has most badly served the sincerity of faith. (4) The ancient ecclesiastical writers provided material for error under the name of merit. (5) Book 4, Institutes, chapter 12, section 8: the authority of the ancients is wonderfully dangerous. (6) Section 20: it is wonderful that so gross a hallucination (in the observance of Lent) could creep upon men of sharp judgement. (7) That in danger of death laymen baptized, at the beginning of the Church, I do not see how it can be defended by any firm reason. (8) Chapter 18, section 21: I think the ancients cannot be excused from having sinned somewhat in the manner of the action, for they imitated the Jewish manner of sacrificing.

units.la: Salmero Jesuita cum foenore reponit, loco supra citato. 1. Augustinus,
units.tr: Salmeron the Jesuit pays it back with interest, in the passage cited above. 1. Augustine,

units.la: Origines & Platonici Angelos dixerunt corporibus aereis constare. 2. Gregorius noster Angelum vocavit animal rationale. 3. Cypriani dogma de baptizatis ab haereticis, ab ecclesia refutatum fuit. 4. Eusebii Caesariensis opinio, quòd Filius Deo Patre sit inferior, ut salsissima est reiecta. 5. Arnobius dixit animas damnatorum poenis annihilari. 6. Hieronymus tradit Christum cruentum ex utero virginis prodiisse. 7. Mald. Iesuita in cap. 24. Luc. Cassianus autor catholicus putavit Christum verè esse mentitum, licereque nobis aliquando eius exemplo mentiri. Ab hac opinione non removendum esse Chrysostomum, Pererius Iesuita docet. 8. Melchior Canus lib. 7. Loc. Theol. cap. 3. Quisque sanctorum (exceptis illis qui libros Canonicos ediderunt) spiritu humano locutus est, & erravit in eo, quòd ad fidem spectare postea demonstratum est. Sic ergo Pontificii & ex his Iesuitae de Patribus loquuntur alibi illos supra scripturam extollunt. Semper pro libitu. Quia his Magistris in Theologia voluntas est pro ratione. Unde Lipsius ad Aegidium Schondonchū Jesuitam epist. 81. scribit: abysti sane à nobis, nec vel solenne illud vale dixisti aut scripsisti. Accusem? absit. Scio vestrorum imperia, quibus statim & ἐμμέτρως (simul, ut dictum) sit parendum.
units.tr: Origen and the Platonists said that angels consist of aerial bodies. 2. Our Gregory called the angel a rational animal. 3. Cyprian's doctrine about those baptized by heretics was refuted by the Church. 4. The opinion of Eusebius of Caesarea, that the Son is inferior to God the Father, was rejected as most absurd. 5. Arnobius said that the souls of the damned are annihilated by their punishments. 6. Jerome reports that Christ came forth bloody from the virgin's womb. 7. Maldonatus the Jesuit, on Luke chapter 24: Cassian, a Catholic author, thought that Christ had truly lied, and that we may sometimes lie after his example. Pererius the Jesuit teaches that Chrysostom is not to be excluded from this opinion. 8. Melchior Canus, Loci Theologici, book 7, chapter 3: "Every one of the saints (except those who wrote the canonical books) spoke with a human spirit, and erred in what was afterwards shown to pertain to faith." So the Papists, and the Jesuits among them, speak of the Fathers, and elsewhere they raise them above Scripture, always as they please, because for these masters in theology will takes the place of reason. Hence Lipsius, in letter 81 to Aegidius Schondonck the Jesuit, writes: "You have indeed vanished from us, not even saying or writing that customary farewell. Should I complain? Far from it. I know the commands of your people, to which one must at once submit in due measure [ἐμμέτρως] (at the same time, as I said)."

units.la: Scripturæ dicta parallelo huic annexa, aut de exemplis beneficiorum & poenarum divinarū loquuntur, quæ maiores iussu Dei suis posteris enarrare debebant, ut ex iis discerent sapere, Deum revereri, & in viis eius ambulare, quale est illud ex Psal. 77. aut de præceptis moralibus agunt (ut illud Eccl. 8.) quæ à senioribus plerumq; haberi possunt. Nam qui multa expertus est enarrat sermones intelligentes, inquit Syracides cap. 34: 9. Hic tamen observandum illud Jobi, quò stultitiam senum amicorum redarguit: in decrepitis erit sapientia? & in longitudine dierum intelligentia? penes Deum est sapientia & fortitudo, illius est consilium & intelligentia. Iob. 12. 12, 13. Verbum ergo Dei seniorum dictis praeferendum: aut denique de presbyterio ecclesiastico, eiusque potestate in censuris & iudiciis circa contentiones fratrũ, ut illud Matth. 18. Quae omnia prorsus nihil faciunt ad disputationem, in qua quaeritur de scriptorum ecclesiasticorum αὐτοπιστία & ἀξιοπιστία in articulis fidei probandis.
units.tr: The sayings of Scripture annexed to this parallel either speak of examples of God's blessings and punishments, which the elders were bound by God's command to recount to their posterity, so that from them they might learn to be wise, to revere God, and to walk in his ways, such as that passage in Psalm 77; or they treat of moral precepts (such as that in Ecclesiasticus 8), which may for the most part be held by the elders. For "he who has had much experience will tell sensible sayings," says Sirach in chapter 34: 9. Yet here we must observe what Job says, rebuking the folly of his elder friends: "Is wisdom among the aged? and understanding in length of days? With God are wisdom and strength; he has counsel and understanding" (Job 12:12, 13). Therefore the Word of God is to be preferred to the sayings of the elders. Or finally, these passages concern the ecclesiastical presbytery and its power in censures and judgements concerning the disputes of brothers, as in Matthew 18. All of which has nothing whatever to do with the dispute, in which the question is about the self-credibility [αὐτοπιστία] and trustworthiness [ἀξιοπιστία] of ecclesiastical writers in proving the articles of faith.

units.la: Multum refert, quales sint à quibus haeretici vocamur, & quorum collatione nos pro haereticis habeamur. Hieronymus in epistola ad Marc. Presbyterum Celedensem sic scribit: Si ab Arianis haereticus vocor, merito. Quare merito se ab Arianis haereticum vocari dicit, cum non ipse sed illi essent haeretici? quia illorum respectu erat haereticus. Sic enim ab haeresi illorum discrepabat, ut non posset ab illis aliter quàm haereticus censeri. Si fides Arianorum recta fuisset utiq; haeresis fuisset fides Hieronymi. Sic autem illi censebant, ideoq; merito se ab illis haereticum vocari dicit. Sane haereticum esse Arianis non est haereticum esse Christianis. Nemo verum Christianus non est haereticissimis quibusvis haereticus. Sed aliud est haereticus esse Christianis, & aliud haereticum haberi ab haereticis.
units.tr: It matters greatly what sort of people call us heretics, and by comparison with whom we are regarded as heretics. Jerome, in his letter to Marcus, presbyter of Celeda, writes thus: "If I am called a heretic by the Arians, I deserve it." Why does he say that he rightly is called a heretic by the Arians, when it was not he but they who were the heretics? Because with respect to them he was a heretic. For he differed from their heresy in such a way that they could regard him as nothing but a heretic. If the faith of the Arians had been right, the faith of Jerome would certainly have been a heresy. But they judged so, and therefore he says he is rightly called a heretic by them. Certainly to be a heretic to the Arians is not to be a heretic to Christians. No true Christian is a heretic to any heretics whatever. But it is one thing to be a heretic to Christians, and another to be regarded as a heretic by heretics.

units.la: Dicemus igitur & nos: Si à Papistis vocamur haeretici, merito. Nihil enim minus sumus, nec quicquam minus esse volumus quàm Papistae, quotquot Christo Servatori datam fidem illibatam servare studemus. At illis haereticus est quisquis Christianus Papista non est. Nam nulla nos alia ratione pro haereticis habent, quàm quòd non per omnia cum ipsis sentimus. Ego sanè malo ipsis haereticus esse, quàm catholicus, quibus ipsi Apostoli, si in vivis agerent, omnium essent haereticissimi, nisi placitis eorum subscriberent in omnibus. Fidem Apostolicam unà cum symbolo Athanasii firmiter tenemus, & sacras utriusq; Testamenti scripturas omnes pro canonicis & authenticis amplectimur, & tamen papistis non sumus catholici, quia ab illis in quocunq; ipsorum dogmate dissidemus, cujus veritas authoritate sacrarum scripturarum doceri ac confirmari non potest. Itaq; non modò patienter fero, sed & gaudeo, hoc mihi per gratiam Domini contigisse, ut in eorum sim numero, qui papistis hodie ob id sunt haeretici, quòd nolunt amplius esse papista. Et quod de papistis dico, de omnibus quarumcunq; sectarum haereticis pariformiter sentio.
units.tr: So we too shall say: If we are called heretics by the Papists, we deserve it. For we are nothing less, and we want to be nothing less, than Papists, all of us who strive to keep the faith given to Christ our Saviour unspotted. But to them whoever is not a Papist Christian is a heretic. For they regard us as heretics for no other reason than that we do not think in every respect as they do. I for my part would rather be a heretic to them than a Catholic, for to them the Apostles themselves, if they were alive, would be the greatest of heretics, unless they subscribed to their opinions in everything. We firmly hold the Apostolic faith together with the Athanasian Creed, and we embrace all the sacred Scriptures of both Testaments as canonical and authentic; and yet we are not Catholics in the eyes of the Papists, because we dissent from them in whatever dogma of theirs, the truth of which cannot be taught or confirmed by the authority of the sacred Scriptures. Therefore I not only bear it patiently, but I also rejoice that by the grace of the Lord it has fallen to me to be among those who today are heretics to the Papists for this reason, that they no longer wish to be Papists. And what I say of the Papists, I feel in the same way about the heretics of all sects whatever.
